en: The Seventh Chapter.

Having thus established both the single-stage system and the four-stage system along with their alternatives, [the author] now, for the sake of protecting them, shall proclaim the duties of the king, so that the monarch may conduct himself accordingly:
I shall now declare the duties of kings, so that a ruler may act in accordance with them.
And how his birth occurred, and how his supreme perfection was attained. || 7.1 ||

But the supreme success for a king who has brought the entire circle of kings under his control consists, immediately thereafter, in the attainment of the unsurpassed prosperity of the three aims—dharma, artha, and kāma—as sovereign lord of the whole earth, accompanied by the excellence of his ministers and other constituent elements of state. 7.1.

Having observed the attainment of success therein, this is said: "By a Kṣatriya who has received the Brāhmaṇical consecration according to rule, the protection of all this [world] must be performed in accordance with justice. (7.2)

The *brāhma* [duty] is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to a Brahmin or belonging to a Brahmin, beginning with the initiation (*upanayana*) and ending with the ceremonial bath (*snāna*). This must be undertaken by a Kṣatriya who has attained it, and not by one of another caste. "According to rule" means according to the scriptures. By the phrase "of all this," he indicates the castes and stages of life through this gesture. "In accordance with justice" and "according to instruction" mean that protection must be performed; this is either a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) excluding other occupations or a preclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*).

Some, however, consider the instruction to be for the sake of livelihood because its purpose is visible; and that being so, when ancestral wealth or the discovery of a treasure is otherwise obtained, a Kṣatriya need not necessarily occupy the kingship.

That is incorrect, because it has been stated: "The study of the Vedas is for the Brāhmaṇa, protection for the Kṣatriya, and the occupation of trade for the Vaiśya; these are the specific duties among their own tasks. Furthermore, their status as "specific" is appropriate due to their connection with both visible and invisible results. The connection with invisible results consists in the adherence to restrictive rules (*niyama*). Moreover, those who provide livelihoods, the helpless, and the wretched are protected by the king; therefore, protection is not solely for the sake of a visible purpose. (7.2)

Furthermore, even for a Kṣatriya who is not a king, the maintenance of fear is now described through the praise of the restrictive rule (niyama-śāstra) which has this purpose, even in the protection of villages and the like:
"For when this world was without a king and everything fled in every direction out of fear, the Lord created a king for the protection of all this. (7.3)

Let there not be the "law of the fish" (*mātsyanyāya*) where the Golden Embryo (*hiraṇyagarbha*) is the sole authority. By the words "of the subjects," the origin of the king for the sake of their protection is demonstrated by this; this is a praise of the preceding injunction. (7.3)
Having extracted the eternal particles from Indra, Anila, Yama, and Ārka; from Agni and Varuṇa; and indeed from Candra and Vitteśa—7.4.

These ten verses are to be understood as supplementary to the injunction that will be stated [later], namely, "Even a child is not to be despised" (MDh 7.8). Thus, it is said that he is fashioned from their constituent parts (mātrās) by means of that same activity by which Indra and the others act within their own respective domains. (7.4)
Since the king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods, he therefore surpasses all beings in his splendor. (7.5)

He demonstrates this meaning by means of the effect: because he overcomes all beings with his own splendor through sovereign power and lordship, he is praised as having been fashioned from the very essence of deities such as Indra. (7.5)
And because:
"It blazes like the sun, scorching both eyes and minds; and no one on earth is able even to look upon it. (7.6)

Endowed with the insignia of a great king—such as the fly-whisk, the parasol, and the water-pot—he torments the eyes like the sun because of his brilliance, and the minds by the infliction of punishment. Therefore, no one is able even to look upon him, much less to do him harm. As before, this verse is for the purpose of praise. (7.6)
And this being so, for the sake of accomplishing their respective tasks in those various states, he becomes fire and wind; he is the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma (Yama);
he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and Mahendra by virtue of his power. (7.7)
And thus these world-protectors are designated by those through whom this king is likewise designated. (7.7)
Since this is so, therefore:
"A king must not be despised even if he is a child, thinking 'he is merely a man';
for he is a great deity dwelling in human form. (7.8)
For even this boy is able to turn back ministers and others from performing improper deeds. (7.8)
Furthermore:
Fire burns only the man who approaches it too closely;
but the fire of a king consumes the entire family, along with its livestock and accumulated wealth. (7.9)

Since it consumes the families of those who commit an offense, their accomplices, and even those merely connected to that transgression, for this reason also, he must not be treated with contempt. (7.9)
And because:
"Having duly considered the task, his own power, and the place and time, he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma. (7.10)
Therefore, he should not be disregarded on account of his being a favorite, or out of friendship, or through the influence of kinship. 7.10.
And because, when he is properly served:
"In whose favor dwells the goddess Padmā Śrī, in whose valor dwells victory, and in whose anger dwells death—for he indeed consists of all splendor. (7.11)

Therefore, he is not to be propitiated merely out of fear for the sake of avoiding transgression; for from him, when properly served, even spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) arises in an especially distinguished manner. || 7.11 ||
And this being so:

he who, out of delusion, hates that [instruction] repeatedly, disregarding the teaching as it was spoken, will undoubtedly perish. For one should not hate that which is a transgression committed for another's sake, by which:
For the king sets his mind upon the swift destruction of such a person. || 7.12 ||

But one who is hated may, out of regard for dharma or due to incapacity, sometimes endure it; however, when a king endures it, there is a direct opposition to his own independent authority, since he is unable to exercise restraint. Therefore, he must always be followed by virtuous men free from guile. (7.12)
Therefore, O lord of men, one should not question that law which a king decrees for those he favors, nor that which he decrees as undesirable for those he disfavors. (7.13)

For the king is not the cause for the engagement in the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), since dharma and adharma are characterized by the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*). Moreover, there would be a lack of settled order (*avyavasthā*) in this case; and there must be a scripture that establishes such order. Furthermore, it has been stated many times that [the king] is for that purpose, and it would be improper to contradict that. Therefore, one should understand from the context that this is intended as praise of the king. With respect to worldly duties, this scripture is to be understood as the Veda. The section on the origin of the king is concluded. 7.13.
Now, the rod of punishment, which is its auxiliary, is explained:
For the sake of that [dharma], the Lord formerly created the rod, the protector of all beings, born of dharma, and composed of Brahmanic splendor. (7.14)

Starting from this point, twelve verses concern the origin of the rod of punishment (*daṇḍa*). Before the origin of kingship, he created Dharma, his own son, who is named the rod, consisting of splendor, and the protector of all beings. This is what is meant: "Without the rod, the nature of a king does not prevail; therefore, a king will certainly not protect his subjects by relinquishing the rod. (7.14)
And because: "All beings, both stationary and moving, out of fear of him perform their duties and do not deviate from their own nature. (7.15)

And he, having been born, is intent on assisting the King—out of fear of whom even immobile things provide enjoyment through fruits, shade, and so forth, let alone others. For if an immobile tree does not provide enjoyment, one certainly begins its pruning and other treatments; and since it is not purified [by such means], it is abandoned and turned into charcoal. And for that which behaves in opposition, punishment is indeed inflicted by means of cutting, uprooting, and so forth, just as in the case of a clump of *vīraṇa* grass or the like grown along a royal highway. (7.15)
Having truly considered the place, the time, the power, and the learning [of the offender],
he should impose appropriate punishment upon men who act unjustly.

Place refers to villages, forests, the interior or exterior of a city, streets, and so forth; time refers to day or night, and [the state of] being a child, youth, or old man; and capacity refers to that pertaining to the body and to wealth. Knowledge consists of the three Vedas along with their auxiliary and secondary branches (*śāṅga-upāṅga*). Punishment should be administered in consideration of these factors. If administered otherwise, it produces harm and does not achieve its purpose; thus, this restatement is for the sake of praising punishment. As for the rule for inflicting punishment, he will explain it later after defining the offense. (7.16)
That king is the personification of punishment; he is the leader and the ruler, and he is recorded as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.

The rod alone is the king, for kingship exists because of it. It alone is the man, by which even powerful men are humbled like women and brought under control. It is the leader, since it is out of fear of it that affairs of state are properly guided. It alone is the ruler, for it is with reference to it that the latent impression (vāsanā) becomes the instrument of governance. It alone is the guarantor, acting as a surety in the event of transgression against the castes and stages of life. (7.17)
And since this is so, therefore:
Punishment governs all subjects; punishment alone protects them.
Punishment keeps watch while others sleep; the wise know punishment to be dharma. (7.18)

Neither the scripture nor the king commands; yet even when both scripture and king exist, the members of the social classes and stages of life (varṇāśramins) comply with the command solely out of fear of punishment. Thus, he alone protects others from those who perform improper acts. Even while the king’s officers are asleep, the world does not act according to its own whims, whether out of fear of this world or fear of the next world. (7.18)
When properly supported after due deliberation, he delights all his subjects;
but when applied without deliberation, he destroys them on every side. (7.19)

We are not released by this much alone, on the grounds that "one who is not properly supported does not perform his duty. Just as one who is properly supported pleases the subjects, so too one who is not properly supported destroys everything. (7.19)
If the king did not tirelessly inflict punishment upon those deserving of it, the stronger would roast the weaker on spits like fish. (7.20)
Not only is there the attainment of merit through the infliction of punishment; if it is not inflicted, the "law of the fish" prevails. (7.20)

A crow might eat excrement, and a dog might lick the sacrificial offering; there would be no sense of ownership in anything, and the social order would be overturned, with the low rising above the high. (7.21)

All creatures—crows, dogs, and the like—even by the most supreme gods endowed with supernatural powers, cannot be turned back except by means of punishment; how much less so by anyone else? This is because of the words of friends, companions, and kinsmen. (7.21)
And this being so:
"The world is entirely governed by the rod; for a pure man is hard to find.
Indeed, out of fear of the rod, the entire world is fit for enjoyment. (7.22)

In this world, everyone is indeed conquered by punishment; for that which is naturally pure and compliant with the teaching is difficult to find. Although this infliction of punishment produces suffering, it is nevertheless ordained by the scripture because there exists no other means for the maintenance of Dharma. (7.22)
Even the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds, and serpents are made to serve for the enjoyment [of others] when they are oppressed by the rod alone. (7.23)

In this way, even though gods and others possess lordship (*īśvara*), they favor those worthy of favor and strike down those worthy of punishment solely out of fear of punishment. For if they did not fear punishment, they would act according to their own whims by virtue of their sovereignty; yet they do not so act. Therefore, we consider that even gods and others, despite possessing sovereignty, proceed toward favoring or striking down according to karma only out of fear of punishment, and not according to their own whims. This is a praise of punishment expressed through hyperbole (*atiśaya*). (7.23)
And so it is said:
"All social classes would become corrupted and all boundaries would be shattered;
moreover, there would be universal upheaval in the world through the misuse of punishment. (7.24)

If the rod of punishment were not upheld according to justice, the duties based on the social classes would fall into corruption; and those very barriers that sustain virtue, wealth, and pleasure would be destroyed. What more need be said? Who is able to praise the Blessed Rod, which is named Dharma, the establisher of order, because of its manifold virtues? (7.24)
Where the dark, red-eyed Punisher stalks, destroying evil, there the subjects do not go astray, provided that he perceives correctly. (7.25)

This form is praised and desired by men; therefore, having fashioned it from that which is insentient, he extols it. Alternatively, the staff is of two forms: one that causes suffering and one that causes fear. For it is praised by means of these two forms: its being the cause of fear through its dark color, and its being the cause of suffering through its red-eyed appearance. Thus, this divine form of the Veda is restated here exactly as it is perceived through the scriptures. The praise of the staff is concluded. (7.25)
They say that the king who is a speaker of truth,
who acts after due deliberation, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, is the one who properly administers it.

The administrator of that rod [of punishment] is by birth a Kṣatriya, endowed with the qualities of sovereignty and majesty resulting from his consecration; he is truthful and, being impartial, inflicts the rod neither out of favoritism nor out of hatred. Acting with circumspection in determining the rod, he is wise in considering the specific circumstances of the region and so forth, perceiving the exceptions and general rules regarding the land and other factors. He is learned in matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, knowing their particular states and remaining even-minded. Such a person they call the administrator of the rod. (7.26)
And such a king, leading [his subjects] properly, prospers through the three aims of life; but one who is self-indulgent, unjust, and base is destroyed by his very rod of punishment. (7.27)

Setting aside what is unseen, he brings this [kingdom] to excellence by means of what is seen; thus, when properly guided, he causes the ruler to prosper through the three aims of life, while those who desire pleasure and the like are struck down by punishment alone. (7.27)
For it is said:
"Punishment is indeed a very great power, difficult to be wielded by those of undisciplined soul;
for it destroys the king himself along with his kinsmen if he has strayed from righteousness. (7.28)

Those whose discipline is both innate and acquired through learning are masters of themselves; by them this Śakra can be sustained. But for one who has turned away from that and wavered, punishment alone destroys him along with his kin.
Then he would afflict the fortresses, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
as well as the sages and gods dwelling in the intermediate space.

If the punishment were to remain after killing the king along with his kinsmen, what would not have been gained? But for that [punishment] by which it does not stop at this much, what would not have been gained? For that [punishment] does not stop at this much, but destroys even the fortresses and so forth; it destroys even the gods and others who dwell in the atmosphere and the heavenly world. Because the gods and sages live upon offerings from here, when there is a disruption of the country and so forth due to the improper administration [of punishment], the gods and others are indeed destroyed by the cessation of those sacrifices to whom nothing is offered. And thus say the authors of the Purāṇas:
"Indeed, that sacrifice which proceeds in this world from among the castes and stages of life is traditionally held to be the cause of the stability of all divine beings. Thus [it was said].
Yet he [acted] with no assistance, being deluded, greedy, and of unrefined intellect.
Nor can one who is attached to sense-objects be led [to the truth] by means of right reasoning.

Since punishment, when wrongly administered, destroys both the seen and the unseen, it cannot be properly executed by one who is without assistants, or who is foolish, greedy, of unrefined intellect, or excessively devoted to sensual pleasures—one possessed of these five defects. || 7.30 ||
And he can be led by one endowed with these five qualities which are the opposite [of those mentioned]. To demonstrate this, it is said:
"By one who is pure, true to his word, acting in accordance with the scriptures, possessing good assistants, and being wise, the rod of punishment can be rightly applied. (7.31)

By one who is pure, has conquered the senses, is true to his word—implying, from the context, that he is not greedy—and who follows the instructions of the treatises, is undeluded, possesses good companions rather than being without companions or having foolish companions, and is wise through the insight gained from the scriptures or through a retentive memory. || 7.31 ||
And being such as this, the king should conduct himself with justice within his own realm, be severe in punishment toward his enemies,
straightforward with his friends, and full of forbearance toward affectionate Brahmins. (7.32)

Severity of punishment is prescribed regarding foreign kingdoms for the purpose of demonstrating one's valor. A friend is one who shares both prosperity and adversity; he whose friendship is independent of self-interest is a "loving" friend (*snigdha*). One should not employ deceitful conduct toward such a person, though toward others one may act deceitfully depending on the requirements of the task. Regarding Brahmins, one should be endowed with forgiveness: even when restraining Brahmins who commit wrongful acts through punishment, one should restrain them with forgiveness rather than with anger or impulsiveness. (7.32)
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he subsists by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon the water.

For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even without a treasury, his royal fame expands through the mere application of correct punishment; by means of this, he is able to bring even foreign kingdoms under his own control and protect them. 7.33.
But for a king who is the opposite of this— whose self is unconquered—
his fame in the world diminishes like a drop of clarified butter upon water.

Consequently, for one who acts contrary to this, even his kingdom shrinks due to his lack of virtue; how then could anything else remain? This concludes the praise of the administration of punishment. 7.34.

But why is it so? Because he possesses such qualities: "The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, each established in their respective duties, in due order. (7.35)
This has been stated for the purpose of introduction and for the purpose of intending to speak further; thus it is said: "ap. 7.35.
Therefore, whatever must be done by one who protects his subjects along with his retinue,
all that I shall declare to you correctly and in due order.
This verse is intended to secure the attention of the listeners. 7.36.
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon the brahmins;
he should stand before those who are learned and advanced in the three Vedas, and abide by their instruction. (7.37)

That which has three parts (*avayava*) is called the *trayī* (the triple Veda). Those who are elders in both the text and the meaning of that [Veda] are the "elders of the triple knowledge" (*traividyavṛddha*); [the king should approach] them. Alternatively, those who study the triple knowledge and are elders among the knowers of the triple knowledge—being advanced both in age and in wisdom—and who are well-trained in *ānvīkṣikī* (logic) and *daṇḍanīti* (statecraft), are the "learned ones" (*vidvas*); rising early in the morning, he should attend upon those learned men with an undistracted mind. And whatever they may say, he should do it without hesitation; for, because of their supreme righteousness, they will not say anything harmful to the king. (7.37)
One should always serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who constantly serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas. (7.38)

One should attend upon these other Brahmins who are advanced in learning solely for the sake of dharma. By serving the elderly, one is not only joined with dharma, but also becomes most trustworthy in the world; for this reason, it is said that one is honored even by the *rakṣas* (demons). (7.38)
From them he should constantly learn discipline, even though his own self is already disciplined;
for a king whose self is disciplined never perishes. (7.39)

For discipline (*vinaya*) is twofold: innate and acquired. Knowledge disciplines one who is endowed with qualities such as a desire to learn (*śuśrūṣā*). Therefore, even if one’s self were disciplined by nature, one should nevertheless produce proficiency through practice. Why? Because such great effort is exerted toward the instilling of discipline. (7.39)
For by means of discipline: many kings, though possessing great wealth, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those dwelling in the forest have attained kingdoms through discipline. (7.40)
For the instruction on both sides is for the purpose of instilling discipline and respect. || 7.40 ||
He now points them out:
Vena was ruined through lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa, Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi. (7.41)
Pṛthu indeed obtained his kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera attained mastery over wealth, and the son of Gādhi attained the status of a Brahmin.
With three verses, he demonstrates the perceptible fruit of discipline through the examples of Vena and others, in order to inspire enthusiasm for the adoption of discipline. 7.42.

And this being so, the king, whose discipline was firmly established, learned from those versed in the three Vedas the triple knowledge, the eternal science of government, and the science of inquiry (logic); and he learned the science of the self and the various undertakings of trade from the people. (7.43)

The word "should attain" (*adhigacchet*) carries over from the previous context. Since the acquisition of the Vedas has already been mentioned for those learned in the three Vedas (*traividyas*), this renewed undertaking must be understood by implication to mean the acquisition of their meaning while still in the state of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). Alternatively, it may be intended for one who has not yet acquired that knowledge, or for the sake of instructing the *vratasnātaka* (one who has completed his vows) in the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*). Or, this instruction may serve as an illustration or an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Thus, one should learn the science of government from those who know it. The term "eternal" (*śāśvatīm*) is purely for the sake of praise; for the science of government, unlike the Vedas, does not possess such [infinite] eternity. And although everything based on the science of government can be learned from the world, since its means are achieved through visible methods, people might nevertheless fail to practice it if they do not understand it, or they might act with unrestrained severity once they do understand it. Therefore, a restriction is required: "Abandoning greed, [the punishment] for this [offense] is branding, and for that, exile; and this is the extent of his punishment. This restriction is desired because the recollection of the rule serves a visible purpose. For this reason, the king must certainly study the science of government. And he should study the science of inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*) from those who know the self (*ātmavid*) and from experts in that field. This being so, having attained through that science a knowledge of reality, and having reached the internal contemplation (*adhyātma-prasaṃkhyāna*) whose purpose is the calming of the fluctuations of joy and sorrow during times of prosperity or calamity, he will not neglect the administration of the kingdom. Furthermore, proficiency in wisdom, speech, and action arises from the mastery of *ānvīkṣikī*; and that proficiency becomes useful to him in matters derived from scripture, such as conversing with neighboring kings and envoys. And he should learn from the world the undertakings of trade (*vārtā*) which are the causes for the accumulation of the treasury. (7.43)
Moreover, this king, having acquired knowledge and discipline through diligent effort, should apply himself day and night to the conquest of the senses;
for one who has conquered his senses is able to keep his subjects under control. (7.44)

The mastery of the senses is the engagement of the ears and other faculties with their respective objects—sound and so forth—in accordance with the scriptures. And that has been described among the duties of the social classes as "primary discipline" (mukhya-vinaya); it is therefore taught here once again. (7.44)
How indeed can this man be said to have conquered his senses?
For one must strive to avoid these ten calamities born of desire, as well as those eight born of anger, which lead to such miserable ends. (7.45)

The mention of the two sufferings arising from desire and anger is for the purpose of their abandonment—namely, through the renunciation of desire and anger. And it has been stated that their renunciation occurs through the conquest of the senses. Now, the relative strength and weakness of the group of vices is being described for the sake of emphasis, so that he might indeed abandon this most grievous group of vices with due care. (7.45)
But a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; however, one addicted to those born of anger is deprived of his very self.

However, one who is addicted to these two groups [of faults] arising from desire—such as drinking, gambling, singing, dancing, and instrumental music—is deprived of both wealth and virtue, since such activity cannot possibly occur without being in conflict with wealth and virtue. But one who persists in those arising from anger, such as slander and violence, having fallen into a state of hatred, is inevitably destroyed. (7.46)
Hunting, gambling, sleeping by day, slander, women, intoxication, the triple symphony [of song, dance, and music], and idle wandering—this is the tenfold group born of desire. (7.47)

"Born of desire" (*kāmaja*) means born from desire or from longing, or for the sake of a specific object of desire. And that [desire] arises either for the purpose of enjoying pleasure, or it arises for those devoted to sensual pleasures from the pleasure of reflecting upon objects previously experienced; therefore, this group of ten is called "born of desire. The description of the nature of the category of vices born of desire begins with hunting and so forth: *yāna* (here) refers to hunting; *divāsvapna* is the failure to engage in duties at the time when duties ought to be performed; *parivāda* (slander), however, when directed against ministers and others, results in independent opposition—for when one is constantly consuming the flesh on the back [of others], one does not properly attend to royal affairs due to a state of laxity; furthermore, there is a well-known contradiction of dharma in slandering those who should not be slandered. "Women" and "intoxication"—these two are well known. *Tauryatrika* consists of dancing, singing, and instrumental music. *Vṛthāṭyā* is wandering about without purpose, or wandering for a trivial purpose devoid of dharma, artha, or pleasure. This being the case, all of this exists in contradiction to the king's interests; therefore, the instruction that this category of vices born of desire must be avoided is most appropriate. (7.47)
Slander, violence, malice, envy, finding fault with others' merits, and the harshness of speech and punishment—this is the eightfold group born of anger. (7.48)

Slander is the state of being malicious, and that is committed out of anger; the same applies to violence. This [violence] consists of the employment of a virtuous person in a base task, or the obstruction of their work without cause. Malice is secret killing or the obstruction of someone's livelihood while they are still alive. Envy is the desire to exclude another from sharing in common objects. Jealousy is the engagement of speech or physical gestures for the purpose of harming another’s prosperity, such as by contorting the tongue and lower lip or making expressive movements with the hands. Spite regarding wealth is the failure to give, or its seizure. Harshness of speech and punishment have well-known meanings. Thus, the group born of anger is also eightfold. (7.48)
One should strive to worship that greed which all poets know to be the root of both these; for both these groups are born from it.

One who is greedy for women and such things indulges in the group of vices born of desire (*kāmajagaṇa*). And when he is thwarted therein, anger arises. Thus, this greed is said to be the root of the two groups of vices, desire and anger. The purpose of this instruction is to demonstrate that by abandoning it, the absence of both groups of vices follows, due to the lack of their cause. Alternatively, the unjust seizure of another’s property is committed out of greed; and one engaged in hunting, through the exhaustion of his own independence, inevitably seizes the property of others unjustly. Furthermore, one who practices the abandonment of hunting will necessarily strive to increase the treasury for the sake of achieving self-reliance, and being occupied with that, he does not engage in hunting. This should be explained in the same way regarding daytime sleep and other such habits. In the case of gambling, however, engagement is well known to proceed from greed. Likewise, even among those vices born of anger, such as slander and the like, it is only the greedy person who goes to the extreme. But one who acts out of mere anger stops at a small transgression or reaches a state of appeasement. Because of the similarity of their effects on one who indulges in both groups of vices, greed is called the root of both these groups of vices. Since the literal meaning [of greed as a root] is impossible in the other case, it is here established by implication. This is an expression of extreme censure, intended to encourage its abandonment for the sake of achieving success in the administration of the kingdom. (7.49)
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting—one should know this tetrad to be the most grievous among the group of vices born of desire, in their respective order. (7.50)
It is well known that this quartet is more difficult [to overcome] than daytime sleep and so forth; thus this [verse] is to be explained. 7.50
One should always know that this triad—the infliction of punishment, verbal abuse, and the violation of property—is most grievous even within the group born of anger. (7.51)
It is well known that this group of three is even more wicked than slander and the like. 7.51.
A self-possessed person should know that, among this group of seven vices which are everywhere interconnected, each preceding one is more grievous than the next. (7.52)

Between drinking and gambling, drinking is the more serious vice. For in that case, there is a loss of consciousness; one who is sober becomes intoxicated, the living become like the dead, and their loincloth is exposed. There is the abandonment of learning and wisdom, the loss of friends, separation from the virtuous, and association with the wicked. Furthermore, there is an addiction to singing and other such things that destroy wealth, and the disclosure of secret counsel through the force of intoxication—these are the faults of drinking. In gambling, however, even for one skilled at dice, victory is uncertain, whereas for one ignorant of the game, defeat is inevitable. Between the vices of gambling and women, gambling is more serious. For in gambling, even the wealth won belongs to the opponent, and it leads to a continuous chain of enmity. Victory is common to both, but defeat alone results in the total ruin of one's possessions. Moreover, by suppressing the urges of urine and feces, there is a weakening of the body’s constitution and the onset of disease through habitual practice, along with excessive suffering caused by hunger and other ailments. A gambler continues to play even when his mother has died, and when questioned during times of distress, he even becomes angry with his own friends—these are the faults of gambling. In the vice of women, however, there is the procreation of offspring, the frequent performance of personal adornment and the consumption of food, and the constant acquisition of religious merit and wealth. Furthermore, a woman can be employed for the king’s benefit or used to lure away an enemy. Between the vices of women and hunting, the vice of women is more serious. It leads to the neglect of duties, a sense of indifference toward royal affairs due to attachment to women, the wasting of time, the neglect of dharma, and a connection to the faults of drinking. There is also an addiction to dancing and other such things that destroy wealth. In hunting, on the other hand, there is physical exercise, the destruction of bile, phlegm, fat, sweat, and so forth, familiarity with targets at both moving and stationary distances, the development of skill in weapons, and the acquaintance with rustic people. Thus, among these four vices born of desire, each preceding one is worse than the next within its own category; therefore, one should avoid each preceding one with greater effort. Among the three vices born of anger, between the infliction of physical punishment and verbal abuse, the infliction of physical punishment is more serious. For once the body is destroyed by physical punishment, it cannot be restored; but in the case of verbal abuse, the fire of anger born of resentment can be extinguished by the waters of gifts and honors. Between verbal abuse and the disparagement of property, verbal abuse is more serious. For those possessed of spirit find no remedy for the agitation of the mind caused by harsh words. And thus says the proverb:
Having firmly and deeply pierced one's own position and entered into the opponent's,
words do not cut through the limbs nor even the heart, once the barb has been extracted.
A forest pierced by arrows or struck down by an axe grows back;
but a wound inflicted by harsh, loathsome speech does not heal.

Because wealth depends upon fortune, those possessed of splendor do not take account of the impairment of that wealth. In this very same way, it has been explained that among this triad born of anger, each preceding one is more serious than the next.
Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous;
for one who suffers a calamity goes downward, whereas one who dies without calamity goes to heaven.

This censure of *vyasanas* (vices) is general, intended for their avoidance. Although death is a *vyasana* that destroys everything, nevertheless, there is this distinction between the two: death destroys everything in this world alone, whereas a *vyasana* [destroys everything] in both worlds. Alternatively, the meaning of this verse should be stated exactly as it is heard [in the text]. By speaking thus, a prohibition is expressed regarding those human qualities born of desire and anger when they have become *vyasanas*, but not regarding their slight indulgence. For when these are practiced excessively, having become *vyasanas*, they destroy virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and life, and cause the relaxation of the administration of the kingdom. Furthermore, excessive indulgence is also mentioned [elsewhere], stating that it is possible for a king; therefore, there is a prohibition of these things called *vyasanas*. Thus, for the sake of a king free from *vyasanas* possessing a collection of virtuous assistants, the characteristics of a minister are now stated. (7.53)
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the treatises, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested. (7.54)

[Mūla: *Anvaya* (the lineage), and the hereditary subjects who have descended through that lineage. By the mention of "one learned in the *śāstras*," all the qualities of a minister (*amātya*) are included by implication. These are as follows: wise, self-controlled, retentive, dexterous, eloquent, bold, resourceful, endowed with energy and majesty, enduring of hardship, pure, friendly, possessed of the power of virtue (*śīla*), noble application (*ārya-yoga*), and spiritual strength (*sattva*), free from arrogance and fickleness, beloved, and one who does not create enmities—this is the excellence of a minister. By the word "hero" (*śūra*), one who is indifferent even toward his own body, wife, children, and wealth in matters of state business is understood; or else, its meaning depends on common usage. By the mention of "one who has attained the mark" (*labdhalakṣa*), one who has observed and practiced those specific duties is meant. For those born of noble family generally do not engage in improper acts. The word "counselor" (*saciva*) is a synonym for "companion. The mention of "seven or eight" is for the sake of restriction; for if there are too few, there is the defect of a lack of unanimity, and if there are too many, there is the risk of secret counsel being leaked or factions forming. "Well-tested" means tested by the trials of virtue, wealth, desire, and fear. This testing is described as follows: The domestic priest (*purohita*), having been dismissed by the king under some pretext for a minor matter and feeling resentful, should secretly instigate each minister individually with an oath, saying: "This king is unrighteous. It would be well if we were to install a righteous person—one of noble birth, already in favor, uniquely favored, a neighboring vassal, or a forest-dweller—in his place. This is pleasing to the other ministers; what do you think? If he rejects it, he is pure in the trial of virtue (*dharmopadhā*). A general (*senāpati*), dismissed by the king for accepting improper gifts, should openly, in the presence of all, instigate each minister through trusted men by offering vast sums of wealth for the purpose of destroying the king, saying: "All the ministers agree to this; how about you? If he rejects it, he is pure in the trial of wealth (*arthopadhā*). A female ascetic (*parivrājikā*) who has gained confidence within the harem should instigate each minister, saying: "The queen desires you, and she has devised a means for a meeting with you. [If he rejects it, he is pure in the trial of desire (*kāmopadhā*). Certain men employed by the king should spread a rumor: "The king is to be killed by the ministers who have made a pact. Once the rumor is known, a trusted man should leak the secret counsel among the ministers, saying: "Having overheard this rumor, the king has determined to punish you. Then, one of those very men, having made an agreement, should incite them one by one against the royal ministers. Among them, those who refuse are pure in the trial of fear (*bhayopadhā*).

Alternatively, he should first appoint hereditary collectors of revenue, treasurers, and administrators of state affairs; he should appoint those learned in the *śāstras* as counselors for wisdom; and he should appoint brave men as executors of severe punishments. All of these must be "men of proven mark," meaning they have been tested for integrity, loyalty, and capability. The phrase "of noble birth" applies as a prior qualification to all of them. He should appoint seven or eight counselors according to the requirements of royal business, having carefully examined them. The term "well-tested" is a qualification for all ministers. How so? It means they have been cleared by all the secret tests (*upadhā*) through spies. This testing is different from that used in other contexts; it is not like the previous [method]. Otherwise, this very [test] would be the sole cause for determining their purity. Once the ministers are trained, they are employed by the king for various tasks and purposes. (7.54)
For even that action which is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone;
how much more so a kingdom of great consequence, especially when undertaken without assistance? (7.55)

This being the case, since there is no separate prescription for ministers, these very [officers] shall serve as the king’s ministers according to their respective capacities; and it has been stated accordingly. (7.55) In that regard, with those who are his ministers and counselors (*mantrisaciva*), he should constantly deliberate upon matters common to all, such as peace and war.
The station, the origin, the protection, and the methods for calming what has been acquired. || 7.56 ||

Together with them, he should deliberate upon the six measures of statecraft (*ṣāḍguṇya*), such as making peace or declaring war, examining common virtues and defects, strengths and weaknesses. However, that which is not overly secret—namely, the determination of what must be done—he should decide within his own mind alone; thus this king will not fall under the influence of others. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he should deliberate on the [four] bases (*sthāna*) together with them," these are fourfold: the army (*daṇḍa*), the treasury (*kośa*), the city (*pura*), and the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*). Among these, the army consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. One must deliberate upon their training, maintenance, protection, and so forth. Likewise, for the treasury, one must deliberate upon the abundance of gold and silver, as well as income, expenditure, and security. Similarly, for the kingdom—which is the country and its inhabitants—one must deliberate on whether it provides a livelihood for oneself and sustenance for others, whether it is self-defensive in times of calamity, suitable for cattle, free from enemies, rich in arable land (*sītā*), secure for grazing, abundant in livestock, not dependent solely on rain (*adevamātṛka*), and capable of supporting the army and taxes in times of distress, and so on. Regarding the city, the author will say later: "It should be well-supplied with weapons," and so forth.

Alternatively, *sthāna* (stability) is non-deprivation from one’s own territory. In this manner, the sources of revenue (*samudaya*) are to be considered; these include agriculture, cattle-rearing, forest settlements, trade routes, customs duties, fines, and so forth. He will later describe the protection (*gupti*) pertaining to one’s own kingdom. The pacification of what has been acquired consists of the application of gifts, honors, and renunciation toward deities, hermitages, learned men, the righteous, and heroes; the granting of permission to those who are accustomed to such practices; the release of all prisoners; favor shown to the poor, the helpless, and the sick; the inauguration of new festivals and the continuation of those already established. Furthermore, having removed any conduct that harms the treasury and the army or is unrighteous, he should establish a system of administration based on Dharma. As it is said: “One should cause righteous conduct not yet practiced to be performed, and likewise cause it to be maintained by others; one should not cause unrighteous conduct to be practiced, nor should one allow that which was practiced by others to continue. In this way, stability and the other factors are to be considered. (7.56)
Having ascertained each of their individual intentions separately, he should act for his own benefit in matters concerning those who are assembled. (7.57)

Desiring to acquire wisdom from others, he should question those ministers both individually and collectively. For there may be some person who is lacking in presence of mind in an assembly, yet is bold in private; or one whose intellect falters when confronted in a public gathering. Therefore, disregarding such biases, he should question them in both ways. He should determine what they have said, whether it was taught by any one of them, provided it is consistent, faultless, and beyond contradiction. (7.57)
But with a distinguished, wise Brahmin among all his counselors,
the king should deliberate on the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy.
For a brahmin, possessing superior wisdom and being righteous, is trustworthy due to his faultlessness. || 7.58 ||
This being the case, one should always place all affairs in his hands with full confidence;
having deliberated together with him, one should then carry out the work. (7.59)
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue.

He should appoint these men, endowed with the qualities of ministers, after they have been thoroughly tested by means of all the secret trials (*upadhā*). Whether there be seven or eight collectors of revenue and treasurers—this exception to the fixed number is stated regarding the king's assistants. (7.60)
He should appoint as many vigilant, skillful, and discerning men as are required for his duties. (7.61)

The assembly of these ministers of the king should be according to the scale of his affairs; for because of the pressure of business, someone might fall into despondency due to some other demand, or even one who is capable may become negligent. (7.61)
For their sake, he should employ those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth at the mines and in industrial works;
and those who are pure and timid within the inner apartments.

For their sake, pure individuals should be appointed over income and expenditure. Those who have proven themselves in action and are not despondent should be made commanders of the army; however, those who are timid should be employed for matters such as food and provisions. All of these should be made capable, for they, disregarding the onset of adversities, do not let the time for their master’s business pass by due to their habit of industriousness. (7.62)
And he should appoint as his envoy one who is learned in all the scriptures,
who understands gestures, facial expressions, and conduct, and who is pure, capable, and of noble birth.

An envoy should be endowed with the full array of ministerial qualities, according to the instruction that he must be proficient in all treatises (*śāstra*). Furthermore, these gestures, facial expressions, and physical movements must necessarily be understood by the envoy regarding the king in a foreign territory. In that context, when the king desires peace, these are the gestures of one who intends to make peace: respectful reception of the envoy, placing trust in him, honoring him repeatedly, and welcoming his words without malice or envy. These same traits, when reversed, belong to one who desires to seize the enemy. As for facial expression (*ākāra*), it pertains to the body: a withered face, a change in complexion, silence, long and hot sighs, and other such bodily distortions indicate dejection. Conversely, a bright face, eloquence in speech, and grooming of the body and so forth indicate joy. Regarding physical actions (*ceṣṭā*), failing to rise to meet someone reveals dejection accompanied by despair over the failure of an undertaking; rising to greet them, on the contrary, indicates joy in the opposite case. Purity in this envoy must concern both women and wealth; this is specifically taught because, in connection with women, there is the risk of leaking secrets and being treated with contempt, while in the acquisition of wealth, there is the loss of the mission. Thus, the purpose of one born of noble lineage has been stated. (7.63)
For what reason, then, is this definition of an envoy stated with such care?
Because: "One who is devoted, pure, skillful, mindful, and knowledgeable of place and time; one who is handsome, fearless, and eloquent—such an envoy is praised by kings. (7.64)

Being devoted, he is incorruptible; being pure, he is unbreakable in his purpose and among women. Being skillful, he does not transgress the proper time and place. Being mindful, he communicates the master’s message without any lapse in memory. Knowing the proper time and place, he accomplishes every task. Being handsome, he is invincible, and because he is pleasant to behold, his words are persuasive. Being free from fear, he delivers the master’s message exactly as it is, even if it is harsh. He does so repeatedly. Being eloquent, he is capable of providing replies and counter-arguments to the message. Why is this instruction on the characteristics of an envoy given in such detail? (7.64)

The power of punishment rests with the minister; the administration of discipline depends on punishment; the treasury and the kingdom depend on the king; and peace and its opposite depend on the envoy.

Just as the military force consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth depends upon the one in charge of the army, and the kingdom prospers through the king’s exertion and intention, yet declines through neglect—so too, peace and war depend upon the envoy. This is a praise of the envoy based on this factual connection; for this indeed is the established view. (7.65)
For it is the messenger indeed who unites those who are divided and divides those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are alienated. (7.66)
For it is said that by means of both the differentiation and the concealment of the mantra, this [mantra] performs these two functions. || 7.66 ||

He should discern, through secret hints and gestures, the king's facial expression, his internal disposition, and his conduct regarding his undertakings, as well as among his servants and royal enemies. (7.67)

And having understood in truth everything intended by the enemy king— whether it be good or bad— he should exert effort regarding his circle of servants in such a way that he does not bring suffering upon himself. (7.68)

A messenger should carry out matters such as peace or war without causing distress to his master. Likewise, he should enter the capital only when permitted. He should establish alliances with forest-dwellers and frontier guards. He should observe the terrain suitable for obstructing battle. He should ascertain the dimensions of forts and kingdoms, as well as their essential strength. Even at the risk to his own life, he should deliver the message exactly as instructed. He should not be arrogant due to honors received. He should endure unpleasant speech. He should avoid intoxicants. He should instigate those who are susceptible to intrigue. He should know the degree of loyalty and disloyalty among the subjects of the enemy. He should not disclose the size of his own army, using some pretext such as ignorance or distraction. Furthermore, he should accomplish whatever else is necessary to assist the enemy's undertaking, including the seizure of relatives and jewels, and the gathering of secret intelligence. (7.68)

One should dwell in a region that is arid yet rich in crops, predominantly inhabited by noble people, free from turmoil, delightful, with submissive vassals, and providing a means of livelihood. (7.69)

One should dwell in a country that is *jāṅgala*—abounding in various kinds of grain, roots, fruits, flowers, grass, and fuel; rich in crops and free from famine; inhabited mostly by noble people and preponderantly by Brahmins for the sake of protecting the Dharma and other virtues; unperturbed and not troubled by wild beasts, reptiles, thieves, gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like; delightful with groves and trees flourishing with blossoms in all seasons; where neighboring vassals are submissive and bowed down; providing a good livelihood with clear-watered reservoirs and lined with rows of spacious houses and palaces. One should settle in such a land, endowed with these qualities of a *jāṅgala* region and other regional virtues. (7.69)
Having taken refuge in a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort, or even a forest fort, or a human fort, or a mountain fort, he should dwell there as his city.

A *mahīdurga* (earth-fort) is one surrounded by a rampart made of brick or stone, twelve cubits high or more, with a foundation as wide as it is twice its height, topped with battlements and parapets, and provided with a solid breastwork. An *abdurga* (water-fort) is one encircled by deep water that cannot be drained. A *vārkṣadurga* (tree-fort) is one covered on all sides for half a *yojana* by dense, massive trees. A *nṛdurga* (human-fort) is one occupied by a fourfold army and consisting mostly of men skilled in excellent weapons. A *giridurga* (mountain-fort) is a mountain ridge difficult to ascend, accessible by a single path, and protected by rivers, springs, and waterfalls within. (7.70)
But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress;
for by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fortress is distinguished above all others.
Among these types of fortresses, the mountain fortress is the best because it is the most unassailable. (7.71)
Of these, the first three are inhabited by beasts, those dwelling in holes, and those moving in water; the latter three are inhabited, respectively, by monkeys, humans, and gods. (7.72)
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a fortress, so too do foes not injure a king who has taken shelter in a stronghold. (7.73)
The two verses concerning the examples are for the purpose of ensuring respectful practice. 7.72–73.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is constructed. (7.74)
This demonstrates that a mountain fortress yields perceptible results; and thus, one should understand that specific advantages exist in each respective type of fortress. (7.74)
That [city] shall be well-provided with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles;
with Brahmins, artisans, machines, fodder, and water. (7.75)

This verse is intended to demonstrate those who possess the necessary purpose and timing for besieging a fortress. This being the case, whatever other purposes and timings exist—such as those concerning the physicians of surgery, poisons, and astrology—those too are to be included. 7.75.
In the center of that [site], he should have his own house constructed—spacious, well-protected from all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees. (7.76)
He should have a house constructed according to his own means, spacious, with rooms suited to the seasons, and provided with underground passages and other such features. (7.76)
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks, born of a noble family, pleasing, and endowed with beauty and virtue. (7.77)

This is a restatement of those previously mentioned—such as those of the same caste and so forth—in connection with the requirement that [a king] take a wife from a great family for the sake of assistance in the administration of the kingdom. (7.77)
He shall appoint a domestic priest and choose officiating priests; they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires. (7.78)

The domestic priest (purohita) should be endowed with the qualities of a minister as well as the qualities of a Brahmin; the officiating priests (ṛtvij), however, need only possess the qualities of a Brahmin. (7.78)
The king should sacrifice with various rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the brahmins. (7.79)

These two—sacrifice and giving—are prescribed as superior duties for a king; indeed, even in the case of these two, there is sin incurred by their non-performance, just as with the obligatory rites. (7.79)
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trustworthy men;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward his subjects like a father. (7.80)

From the sources of revenue as previously described, he should collect the tribute—such as the sixth or eighth part of the produce—in accordance with the authority of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). He should behave toward other tax-payers as he does toward his own father. He should appoint various learned supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the people as they carry out their duties. (7.81)

He should appoint various learned officials, such as superintendents over the gold treasury, raw materials, forest produce, weapons, weights and measures, tolls, ships, elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; all of these should be understood as being endowed with the qualities of a minister. (7.81)
He should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the teacher's house;
for this inexhaustible treasure of the Brahman is ordained for kings. (7.82)

This gift of a restriction is also ordained for a king to give to those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātaka). For there is sin for one who does not give even to these; as it has been said: "One who is unwilling to give deserves to be abandoned" (MDh 10.113). || 7.82 ||
Neither thieves nor enemies can carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this inexhaustible treasure with the Brahmins. 7.83

Just as there is no destruction of a treasure from any quarter through the giving of gold and other goods to Brāhmaṇas and others, unlike [the loss suffered] by thieves, forest-dwellers, enemies, or those who steal the king's property—this is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended to praise the necessity of making such gifts. (7.84)
And this is another [point]:
it overflows not, it suffers no harm, and it never perishes;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brahmin is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices. (7.84)

Just as a sacrificial oblation that has spilled leads to a fault, or one that is disturbed by the breaking of the vessel, or one for which the deity is unknown perishes; so too says the Brāhmaṇa: "That oblation which is offered without knowing the deity is indeed only half an oblation. This being the case, the censure regarding the three defects of the oblation is intended as praise for the gift mentioned in the present Brāhmaṇa passage. Thus it is said: "It is superior to the Agnihotra offerings. The meaning is "superior to the Agnihotra and other such rites. This should be understood in this way for the purpose of including all obligatory duties (*nityakarman*). Some say that because of the mention of the "mouth," this refers specifically to the giving of food; however, that is incorrect. Because of the scriptural statement, "For the twice-born is remembered as having his hands for a mouth" (MDh 4.117), this should be understood as referring to the subject of receiving all kinds of gifts. (7.84)

And this is another [point]: A gift given to a non-Brahmin is equal [in merit]; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it is twofold; to a teacher, it is a thousandfold; but to one who has mastered the Vedas, it is infinite. (7.85)

Furthermore, gifts should be given to these [categories of persons]. Since this section concerns the praise of giving under specific constraints to virtuous *snātaka* Brahmins, it should be understood that the mention of non-Brahmins and others here is for the purpose of praising the gift given to the learned. How so? It is not appropriate [to give] to a non-Brahmin or one who merely calls himself a Brahmin. And it has been said: "One should honor with offerings to gods and ancestors those *śrotriyas* who have completed their Vedic study and vows; however, one should avoid those who are the opposite. (MDh 8.63)

Nor is this an injunction regarding the fruit [of the action], for if it were an injunction regarding the fruit, it would apply to optional giving (*kāmyadāna*). Thus, by the force of the meaning as stated, this verse is not an injunction regarding the fruit, but is intended to provide an instruction on the ritual procedure (*kalpa*); otherwise, the context would be interrupted. Alternatively, this may be a specific duty of kings intended to demonstrate the distinction in fruits resulting from giving to non-Brāhmaṇas and others when the aforementioned cause—the distress of the needy—is present; for praise is never bestowed without a reason. (7.85)
And so says the following verse:
"Indeed, depending especially on the worthiness of the recipient and the very nature of one's faith, whether small or great, the fruit of a gift is obtained after death. (7.86)

This being the case, just as there is a distinction in the fruit according to the distinction of the recipient (*pātra*), so too, even when giving to Brāhmaṇas who are equal [in other respects], this [statement] should be understood as an exception to the rule regarding the distinction of the recipient. Now, the explanation of the second half of the preceding verse is being provided. It is neither logical that the gift-object (*deyadravya*) should be equal to the fruit [of the gift] in terms of its genus (*jāti*), nor in terms of its quantity (*parimāṇa*), because that would contradict both the scriptures (*śāstra*) and reason (*nyāya*). How, then, should this [verse] be explained as "equal"? According to worldly convention (*lokaprasiddhi*), it is neither superior nor inferior; taking that which is "equal" and is thus well-known in the world as the limit, the doubling and so forth of the fruit should be stated. Others, however, think that an equal fruit for the gift-object is not possible; therefore, the equality must be understood as residing in the giver. Having given even alms and such to a non-Brāhmaṇa, one obtains the enjoyment of the fruit of that gift with a human body alone, and not through the gift to a superior recipient (*pātra*). This point requires investigation. Furthermore, the non-Brāhmaṇas are the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. Thus it is stated in Gautama’s section on the giving of alms: "The two immediately following the Brāhmaṇa caste [are the recipients]" (GDh 5.20). And the usage is: "Acquisition of knowledge from a non-Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 7.1). There is no acquisition of knowledge from a Śūdra who is a non-Brāhmaṇa, due to greed for wealth and because of scriptural prohibitions. [The term applies] to those excluded from the Brāhmaṇa caste. However, in the case of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are religious students (*brahmacārin*), the acceptance of alms and so forth is indeed permitted by the force of the instruction itself; thus, it should be understood that they too are more appropriately designated by the word "non-Brāhmaṇa. (7.86)
When challenged by those who are equal, superior, or inferior, a king protecting his subjects must not retreat from battle, mindful of the duty of a Kshatriya. (7.87)
When summoned by anyone, there should be no retreating from battle; for this is indeed the distinguished duty of kings. || 7.87 ||
Not retreating from battles, the protection of subjects, and service toward the brahmins— this is the supreme means for the welfare of kings. (7.88)
Just as protecting the subjects and serving the Brahmins are the preeminent duties of kings, so too is not retreating from battle; this is a praise of non-retreat. (7.88)
And so it has been said: "In battles, kings who desire to slay one another, fighting with their utmost strength and not turning their backs, go to heaven. (7.89)
And therefore, not retreating from battle is the specific duty of kings; and for one who fights, a rule of conduct is prescribed. (7.89)

While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with deceptive weapons, nor with those that are barbed, nor with those that are burnt, nor with those whose tips are ablaze with fire. (7.90)
One should not strike one who has ascended to dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with palms joined in reverence;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours. (7.91)

One must not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unprepared for battle, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who is engaged with another. (7.92)

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, he did not strike one who was suffering from a weapon-wound, nor one who was distressed, nor one who had not been thoroughly tested, nor one who was terrified, nor one who had turned his back in flight. (7.93)
This is the rule for the regulations of battle, intended to prevent the sin of killing them. 7.90–93.
But he who, being afraid, turns back in battle and is slain by his enemies, takes upon himself whatever evil deed his master has committed. (7.94)
Furthermore, whatever merit he may have acquired for the sake of the next world, his master takes all of that from one who has turned back and been killed. (7.95)

The censure of the king and of any other royal officer who has turned back [from his duty] is expressed in two verses; and that censure is indeed appropriate, for by failing to do that for which he is carried off, he incurs sin. (7.94–95)
Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, wealth, grain, livestock, women,
all kinds of goods, and base metals— whatever one conquers belongs to him.
The restriction is intended to exclude the inclusion of the king on the grounds of his sovereignty. || 7.96 ||
"But the king shall receive an extra share; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which was not won individually. (7.97)

The king shall take for himself the *uddhāra*—the surplus wealth—from all the warriors. The Vedic revelation (*śruti*) states: "Having slain Vṛtra, he took Mahendra as his *uddhāra*," and so forth. That which was won not individually but by the group as a whole must be distributed among all the warriors in proportion to the hardship and exertion they endured in battle. (7.97)
This eternal law of warriors has been declared as it truly is; a Kṣatriya, slaying his enemies in battle, must not deviate from this dharma. (7.98)

"Unadorned" (*anupaskṛta*) means uncreated, in the sense that its qualities are established by its very nature (*svabhāva*). That which lacks qualities is "adorned" for the purpose of bestowing qualities upon it. This is a verse of summary. || 7.98 ||
One should seek what has not yet been obtained, guard with effort what has been obtained, increase what has been guarded, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (7.99)

Desiring yet not obtaining what he seeks, or being content with little, a king may be destroyed by his great rivals and powerful kinsmen due to his weak administration; or, failing to protect what he has acquired, he is diminished by the mere toil of acquisition which yields no fruit; or, failing to properly increase what he has protected, it perishes. If he consumes it himself because there is no one else to receive it, he is deprived of that which was acquired, protected, and increased through three great efforts, as well as of the next world for failing to bestow it upon worthy recipients. Through this lack of desire, he incurs the threefold affliction resulting from those very three efforts. (7.99)
One should know that this fourfold [dharma] is the means for achieving the goals of human life;
one should perform its practice constantly and correctly, without sloth. (7.100)

One should seek what is not yet obtained by means of force; one should protect what has been obtained without wastefulness; one should increase what has been protected through growth; and one should bestow what has increased upon worthy recipients. (7.101)

In this context, the means for the sake of increase is expressed by the word "increase" (*vṛddhi*), due to the force of the subject matter. [The fourfold] instruction: one should bestow [wealth] upon worthy recipients through giving. [The fourfold] instruction: for the accomplishment of the king’s human goals. 7.100–01.
Since this is so, therefore:
He should always have his rod of punishment raised, always display his manly prowess, always keep his movements concealed, and always track the vulnerabilities of his enemy. (7.102)

He should constantly train his forces of elephants and the like through exercises and other means, and he should maintain his weapons and armor in good condition. By doing so continually, his state of being one who wields the rod of punishment becomes manifest throughout the circle of kings. At border posts, forest settlements, and other such locations, he must remain perpetually vigilant with trusted men who are armored and equipped for battle; thus, his display of personal prowess is revealed. Furthermore, by protecting and winning over those on the side of potential traitors, he remains one whose movements are concealed; and by exposing the treacherous designs of others, he becomes one who tracks down their vulnerabilities. (7.102)
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds his rod of punishment uplifted;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod alone. (7.103)
For one who has raised the rod of punishment, the submission of enemies occurs without even effort. || 7.103 ||
One should conduct oneself with complete sincerity and never with deceit;
yet, being always well-guarded, one should recognize the deception employed by the enemy.

One should not first attempt to instigate a rebellion among the subjects of another king who are angry, greedy, fearful, or proud. Because one whose conduct is righteous (*dhārmika*)—whether established in his own territory or that of an enemy—is easily loved by all. In this regard, the group of the "angry" (*kruddha*) consists of those who have been deceived, those treated with contempt despite performing equal service in craft or assistance, those excluded from the favor of a favorite, those whose kinsmen have been exiled, those forbidden from practicing their traditional rites, those separated from their relatives by their own kin, and those whose entire property has been confiscated. The group of the "fearful" (*bhīta*) consists of those who commit evil deeds, those distressed by punishments for similar offenses, those from a neighboring territory, those who have submitted after being attacked, those stationed in all administrative offices, and those who have suddenly accumulated great wealth. The group of the "greedy" (*lubdha*) consists of those who are impoverished, miserly, addicted to vices, and so forth. The group of the "proud" (*mānin*) consists of those who are self-important, those incensed by the honors given to enemies, those humiliated by base persons, the fierce, the reckless, and those dissatisfied with their enjoyments. Having identified these individuals both in the enemy's realm and one's own, one should protect them and win them over through subversion. (7.104)
An enemy should not know one's own vulnerability, but one should know the vulnerability of the enemy;
like a tortoise, one should hide one's limbs and guard one's own weak points. (7.105)

Through excessive application, it is possible to conceal one's own vulnerabilities and observe the vulnerabilities of others; and this one should ascertain through the dispatch of secret agents (*gūḍhapuruṣa*), such as fraudulent spies (*kāpaṭika*) and others, both within one's own territory and in the territory of the enemy. (7.105)
Like a crane, one should contemplate matters; like a hare, one should spring away;
like a wolf, one should snatch; and like a lion, one should display prowess. (7.106)

Just as a crane, by resorting to a fortress of water, observes the strength of the fish by its very nature and, through the application of meditation (*dhyāna-yoga*), discovers the means to capture them; so too, one should not fall into despondency, thinking that even goals most difficult to attain are reached through an extraordinary application of effort in deliberating upon one’s objectives. Just as a hare, because of its small body, is able to escape even from the attack of an enemy elephant; so too, even a single person, though without allies and unable to remain when provoked by enemies on all sides, should take refuge in a fortress and escape from there, seeking the protection of those possessed of virtues. And just as a wolf, intent on seizing livestock, seizes its prey upon finding the negligence of the herdsman; so too, one should not abandon the effort to seize [the enemy] by making oneself intent on self-protection, thinking, "That time will come when I shall plunder like a wolf. And just as a lion, through the application of the power of valor, kills even large-bodied animals such as elephants by exerting his prowess; so too, one should not be deterred by the thought that the enemy force is great. For even that which is great may have little strength and can be slain by a small being of great strength. (7.106)
Thus, while he is conquering, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control by means of the expedients beginning with conciliation.
Thus, for a king established in victory, those who do not submit to his majesty he should subsequently bring under control through conciliation and the other [stratagems]. || 7.107 ||
If, however, they do not abide by these through the first three expedients, one should gradually bring them under control by force with the rod. (7.108)
When the three means beginning with conciliation have been exhausted, there is the rule for the employment of punishment. 7.108.
Regarding the four expedients beginning with conciliation, the wise always praise both conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom. (7.109)

In the employment of conciliation, there is no loss, expense, or exertion; whereas in the case of force, every success arises from its very majesty. Therefore, these two are praised in this context. (7.110)
An illustration of this is as follows: "Just as a wood-cutter cuts down the brushwood yet protects the grain, so should a king protect his realm and slay those who stand in his way. (7.110)
That king who, out of delusion, oppresses his kingdom without regard for its welfare, shall soon fall from both his kingdom and his life, along with his kinsmen. (7.111)
Just as the vital breaths of living beings are diminished by the emaciation of the body,
so too are the vital breaths of kings diminished by the emaciation of the kingdom.
"For the kingdom is indeed his body. Since this is so, therefore, for the purpose of avoiding those defects: 7.11012.
One should always observe this regulation for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness. (7.113)
He should establish a *gulma* (military outpost) within two, three, or five [villages], and likewise for hundreds of villages, for the protection of the kingdom. (7.114)
For the purpose of collecting what is due to the king and for the sake of protection. 7.113–14.
One should appoint a lord of a village, as well as a lord of ten villages,
a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and likewise a lord of a thousand.
The village headman himself should gradually report the faults that have arisen in the village to the leader of ten villages;
the leader of ten should report them to the leader of twenty.
The lord of twenty should report all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, however, should himself announce it to the master of a thousand.
The appointment of overseers in villages and other locations by means of three verses [7.115–17] is for the purpose of making known that a task is imminent.
Whatever daily offerings are to be given to the king by the village dwellers—such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth—the village headman shall receive those. (7.118)
The collector of ten should enjoy one family, while the collector of twenty should enjoy five families;
the superintendent of a hundred villages [should enjoy] a village, and the lord of a thousand [should enjoy] a city.
This conceptualization of the activity of the dominant factors is [set forth] by means of two verses (7.118–19).
Another minister of the king, who is affectionate and vigilant, should oversee their village affairs as well as their individual matters. (7.120)
One should observe what has been done and what has not been done by the sovereigns, according to their actions. || 7.120 ||
In every city, he should appoint one overseer of all affairs, stationed in a prominent place, formidable in appearance like a planet among the stars. (7.121)
He should appoint a city magistrate for each city, endowed with a force consisting of elephants, horses, and other troops. || 7.121 ||
He himself should always personally inspect them all;
he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct in the realms through his spies. (7.122)

He should always cause these superintendents to patrol for the sake of protection, and he should obtain information regarding their conduct from royal spies, fraudulent agents, and others. || 7.122 ||
For this reason: "The king's officials charged with protection generally become deceitful servants who seize the property of others; from them he must protect these subjects. (7.123)
Even those who are pure consume wealth, for that is the purpose of human beings; therefore, they should not be disregarded on the grounds of an inference regarding their purity. 7.123.
Those of evil intent who would seize wealth solely from those performing services for them, the king shall confiscate their entire property and carry out their banishment. (7.124)
