For those officials of the king who are known to have transgressed their duties, he should order the confiscation of all their property and their banishment; the meaning is that this is for the sake of protecting the realm. (7.124)
He shall provide daily maintenance for women and servants engaged in royal service, according to their rank and the nature of their work. (7.125)
The meaning is that it is characterized by such things as the preparation of clothing, anointing, and eating. 7.125 ||
One paṇa should be given as wages for a low-ranking servant, and six for a high-ranking one;
likewise, clothing every six months and one droṇa of grain every month. (7.126)
The preparation of the meal is described in two verses; [the author] will state the measurements for the *paṇa* and the *droṇa*. 7.126.

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of their acquisitions and preservation, the king should cause the merchants to pay taxes.
This is its general definition: || 7.127 ||
Just as the king and the doer of actions are joined with their fruit,
so should the king, having duly considered this, always apportion taxes within his realm.
An illustration of this is as follows:
Just as the calf, the fish, and the bee consume their food only in very small amounts, so too should the king take from his kingdom an annual tax that is ever so slight. (7.129)
This verse of illustration is for the purpose of praising the method of collecting taxes. || 7.129 ||
The king shall take a fiftieth part of cattle and gold;
an eighth part of grain, or a sixth, or even a twelfth. (7.130)
A fiftieth part shall be taken from cattle and gold that exceed their market value; for grains, a specific portion shall be determined according to the ease of harvesting.
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, honey, clarified butter,
fragrant substances, medicinal herbs, juices, and flowers, roots, and fruits.
Of leaf-vegetables, grasses, hides, and bamboo; of earthenware vessels and of everything made of stone. || 7.132 ||
The taking of a sixth part [of produce] occurs due to the receipt of trees and other such things as previously mentioned. 7.131–32.
Even when dying, a king shall not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya dwelling within his realm perish from hunger.
This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda). 7.133.
In whose kingdom a learned man of sacred knowledge perishes from hunger, his kingdom likewise shall perish from hunger before long. (7.134)
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, the king should provide him with a righteous livelihood;
he should protect him in every way, just as a father protects his own biological son. (7.135)
Whatever dharma he performs day by day while being protected by the king, by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase. (7.136)
Three verses (7.134–36) concerning the purpose of attaining greater security for one learned in the Vedas.
Whatever little tax, designated as *kara*, the king may cause to be paid upon the common people living by trade within his realm for the sake of the year's revenue. (7.137)
A commoner other than a Brahmin, living by even a small amount of trade, must be made to pay taxes. (7.137)
The lord of the earth should cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day each month. (7.138)
Those who subsist solely by their craft, as well as those who subsist for themselves, he shall compel to perform labor for one day each month. (7.138)
One should not, out of excessive greed, cut off one's own root nor that of others;
for by cutting off one's own root, one would bring suffering upon both oneself and them. (7.139)
Therefore, because of that very prohibition, one should not destroy the system (tantra) of oneself or of others. 7.139.
The lord of the earth should be both severe and mild, having regard for what must be done;
indeed, a king who is both severe and mild becomes esteemed by all.
O King, you must constantly practice this conduct of kings. || 7.140 ||
When weary from overseeing affairs, the king should appoint to that seat his chief minister—one who knows the Dharma, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth. (7.141)
When weary from overseeing affairs, he should appoint the most eminent minister to the position of supervising the court. || 7.141 ||
Having thus performed all these duties pertaining to himself, he should protect these subjects with vigilance, as has been prescribed. (7.142)
He from whose kingdom the subjects are carried off by bandits while they cry out for help—even as he looks on, along with his servants—he is dead; he does not truly live. (7.143)
The supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of his subjects;
for a king who enjoys the fruits prescribed by law is truly united with righteousness.

And for him who is disciplined, vigilant, and possessed of unerring intellect—there are three verses concerning the purpose, the injunction, and the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the protection of the subjects. (7.142–44)
Having risen during the final watch of the night, having performed his purifications and composed his mind,
and having offered oblations into the fires and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects with joy;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.
Together with his ministers, the king’s daily conduct is described in two verses (7.145–46).
Having ascended a mountain ridge or a palace, or having gone to a secluded place, or in a forest free from undergrowth, one should deliberate in secret, unobserved. (7.147)

He should deliberate upon the five limbs of counsel. They are as follows: the means for initiating undertakings, the excellence of personnel and materials, the distinction between place and time, the remedy for setbacks, and the successful accomplishment of the task. He should question them individually and collectively. Through logical reasoning, he should discern the distinct opinions of all. Having determined the objective, he should not let the proper time pass, nor should his counsel be protracted. He should not deliberate on matters with those who belong to the faction of his enemies—those whom he might harm—and he should keep his counsel secret. (7.147)
That king by whose counsel ordinary people, having come together, do not know, enjoys the entire earth even if he is destitute of treasure. (7.148)
And this being so, for the sake of protection:
"One should exclude from the mantra those who are dull-witted, blind, mute, or deaf; those born of animal wombs; those advanced in age; women; barbarians; the diseased; and the deformed. (7.149)
For those who are despised, as well as animals, and especially women, betray a secret; therefore, one should be cautious in that regard. (7.150)
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue, he should contemplate virtue, pleasure, and wealth, either together with those [objects] or alone. (7.151)
One should contemplate the increase of virtue, wealth, and pleasure; for when any one of these mutually conflicting factors increases excessively among kings, their destruction ensues. (7.150–51)
The acquisition of those things that are mutually contradictory, the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of sons. || 7.152 ||

When there is a conflict between the interests of dharma, artha, and kāma among ministers, one must consider their relative strength and weakness. The giving away of daughters should be considered in view of the accomplishment of one’s own objectives. The protection of princes must be ensured by spies who say, "We are yours," so that they may be made to accept both dharma and artha. For a new substance absorbs whatever kind of liquid it is smeared with; likewise, this prince of fresh intellect accepts whatever is said to him. By means of appropriate stratagems, they should turn him away from vices, and through constant instruction, the king should at the proper time establish him as heir-apparent when he is endowed with virtues, while relegating those lacking virtue to the border regions. Thus, with such exceptional diligence, the king should reflect daily upon the protection of his sons. (7.152)
The dispatching of envoys, as well as the remaining tasks,
the movements within the inner apartments, and the activities of the secret agents.

One should deliberate upon the dispatch of envoys to that person with whom one intends to enter into either an alliance or a conflict. One should also consider the completion of undertakings already begun, for the sake of stabilization. Guarded by the troops of the inner apartments (*antaḥvaṃśika*), he should enter the harem. There, he may see the queen only when she has been purified by elderly women, and never when she is unpurified. For it was a brother, hiding in the queen’s chamber, who slew Bhadrasena; a son, hidden within his mother’s bed, who slew the King of Kārūṣa; the queen herself who slew the King of Vairantya with an anklet smeared with poison; the King of Sauvīra with a jewel from her girdle; and Vidūratha with a weapon concealed in her braid. Therefore, he should carefully inspect these potential points of danger. He should prohibit the association of the women of the harem with shaven-headed ascetics, those with matted hair, sorcerers, or mendicants, as well as with outside female slaves. And he should deliberate upon the conduct of spies, such as fraudulent scholars and others, through a succession of secret reports. (7.153)
The entire eightfold ritual action and the fivefold excellence in their true nature, as well as attachment and non-attachment, and the practice of the mandala.

Undertaking what has not yet been begun, the performance of what has been begun, the specific refinement of what has been performed, and the collection of the fruits of action; likewise, conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force—this is the eightfold action. Alternatively, it consists of agriculture, trade routes, waterworks and the building of embankments, the construction of fortresses, the improvement of what has already been built, the capture of elephants, mining, the settlement of uninhabited lands, and the clearing of timber forests. Others, however, say: "In taking and in giving, as well as in commanding and forbidding, in the fifth matter of speaking for a purpose, and in the oversight of legal proceedings."
Constantly engaged in both punishment and purification, the king who possesses these eightfold paths and performs the eight duties goes to heaven, honored by Śakra.

These are the two verses of Auśanas. Their commentary follows: *Ādāna* (seizure) is the taking [of wealth] by one who is powerful. *Dhanavisarga* (distribution of wealth) is the granting of funds to servants. *Praiṣa* (command) is the dismissal of the wicked. *Niṣedha* (prohibition) is the restraint of excessive activity by those authorized over wealth. *Arthavacana* (instruction on matters) is the speaking of what is necessary for those who have not yet begun their work. *Vyavahārekṣaṇa* (supervision of legal proceedings) is the oversight of judicial matters when members of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramins*) rely upon their own duties. *Daṇḍanipātana* (infliction of punishment) is the application of penalties against those defeated in mutual litigation. *Śuddhi* (purification) refers to the self; however, *prāyaścitta* (expiation) applies to lapses through negligence. These constitute the eightfold duty (*aṣṭavidhaṃ karma*). The *pañcavarga* (five-fold group) consists of: the spy appearing as a fraudulent student (*kāpaṭika*), a renunciant (*udāsthita*), a householder (*gṛhapati*), a merchant (*vaidehaka*), and an ascetic (*tāpasa*). A *kāpaṭika* is a student who knows the secrets of others and is bold. The minister, having won him over with wealth and honor, should say: "Taking both the King and me as your authority, whatever you perceive to be harmful must be reported by you immediately, without hesitation. An *udāsthita* is one who has returned from the life of a wandering mendicant (*pravrajyā*) and is endowed with wisdom and purity. On land capable of providing all kinds of food, he should employ many disciples with abundant gold. From the fruits of agricultural labor, he should provide food, clothing, and shelter for all wandering mendicants. Those among them who desire a livelihood, he should recruit, saying: "By this very means, the king’s business must be carried out, and you must present yourselves at the time of receiving food and wages. All these wandering mendicants should, in turn, recruit their respective groups. A *gṛhapati-vyañjana* (spy appearing as a householder) is a cultivator whose livelihood is failing, who is endowed with wisdom and purity. He should perform agricultural work on the aforementioned land. A *vaidehaka-vyañjana* (spy appearing as a merchant) is a trader whose livelihood is failing, who is endowed with wisdom and purity. He should perform the work of trade on the designated land; the rest is the same as before. A *tāpasa-vyañjana* (spy appearing as an ascetic) is one who is shaven-headed or has matted hair and desires a livelihood. Near the city, with many disciples who are shaven-headed or have matted hair, he should publicly eat vegetables or a handful of grass once every month or two months under the pretext of religious practice, while secretly consuming food as he pleases. His disciples, appearing as ascetics, should honor him with perfected spells (*siddhayoga*). His students should inform him of gains, fires, threats from thieves, the execution or imprisonment of the wicked, and news from foreign lands, saying: "This will happen today or tomorrow," or "The King will do this. Secret agents (*sattrins*) employed by him should then bring about these things. Those who must necessarily be supported by the king should become secret agents while studying the science of marks (*lakṣaṇavidyā*), the science of limbs (*aṅgavidyā*), the science of sorcery (*jambhakavidyā*), the art of illusion (*māyāgata*), the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*), and the knowledge of omens (*nimittajñāna*). In this regard, the King should station these five types of spies, together with these ministers, in his own territory and in the territories of others. He should dispatch secret agents under the guise of commoners among the ministers, the domestic priest, the commander-in-chief, the crown prince, the door-keeper, the chamberlain, and others—provided they know how to assume credible localities, dress, crafts, and languages. Likewise, those disguised as hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, the mute, the dull-witted, the deaf, or the blind, as well as actors, dancers, singers, and women, should carry out internal surveillance.
In the forest, forest-dwellers such as ascetics and foresters should be employed;
they must be swift and form a continuous chain of spies for the purpose of knowing the activities of others.
These must be understood by the enemy as being of such a kind;
they are the spies moving about, both those stationed openly and those known as secret agents.

Having thus conceived of the fivefold group for both the enemy and oneself, one should likewise know the attachment and aversion toward this group of ministers, priests, and others. Likewise, one should know the movements within the royal circle: which regional ruler is engaged in what course of action regarding peace, war, and so forth. (7.154)
One should diligently observe the conduct of the middle king, the activities of the one seeking conquest, the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy. (7.155)

In this circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*), these four royal elements (*rājaprakṛti*) are primary: the seeker of conquest (*vijigīṣu*), the enemy (*ari*), the middle king (*madhyama*), and the neutral king (*udāsīna*). Among them, he who is endowed with the qualities of a king and is emboldened by the thought, "I alone shall conquer this earth," is the seeker of conquest, owing to his possession of the power of energy (*utsāhaśakti*). The enemy is of three kinds: the natural (*sahaja*), the ordinary (*prākṛta*), and the artificial (*kṛtrima*), as well as the one whose territory is immediately adjacent (*bhūmyanantara*). The middle king is one capable of suppressing both the enemy and the seeker of conquest when they are not united. The neutral king is one who remains indifferent toward the enemy, the seeker of conquest, and the middle king when they are not united. (7.155)
In brief, these constituent elements are the root of the circle;
eight others are also enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve. (7.156)

These constituent elements of the circle have been explained. Furthermore, for each of these constituent elements, two others are mentioned—namely, the friend and the friend-of-the-friend. Thus, one plus another eight are enumerated; in this way, there are twelve on both sides. (7.156)
The five others are known as the minister, the city, the realm, the treasury, and the army;
each of these has been described in brief, making seventy-two in total. (7.157)

These other five—namely, the ministers, the city, the realm, the treasury, and the army—are each established upon twelve [factors]. Thus, there are twelve constituent elements of the king and sixty constituent elements of the ministers and so forth; in brief, there are seventy-two. (7.157)
Immediately after [the enemy], one should know the ally of the enemy; immediately after the enemy, the friend; and beyond those two, the neutral party. (7.158)

One who desires victory should recognize the enemy as being immediately adjacent to his territory, as well as the enemy’s friend and the friend of that friend. In this manner, one separated by another territory becomes the friend of the conqueror. Beyond these two is the neutral king (*udāsīna*). This definition of enemy and friend should be understood to apply to both natural and acquired relations. (7.158)
He should win over all of them by means of conciliation and the other expedients, whether employed individually or collectively, through personal effort and statesmanship.

By means of the four methods beginning with conciliation, either collectively or individually, or by human policy alone, or by force alone—this is called the sequence of the six measures of royal policy according to the Samāsika school. (7.159)
He should always consider the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge. (7.160)

In this context, peace (*saṃdhi*) is that which is based on gold and other such means for the mutual benefit of both parties; its opposite is war (*vigraha*). Marching (*yāna*) is the superior advancement of one side. Remaining quiet (*āsana*) is indifference. Double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*) is the simultaneous adoption of both peace and war. Seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*) is surrendering oneself to another. One should always deliberate upon these six measures of policy (*ṣaḍguṇāḥ*). Among these six, whichever measure one considers capable of enabling him to build fortresses, capture elephants, dig mines, establish trade routes, found settlements in uninhabited lands, promote agriculture, clear timber forests, and secure fields not dependent on rain, and by which he can thwart the enemy and obstruct their growth—that particular measure he should adopt. (7.160)
And this being so:
having considered the matter at hand, he should employ sitting in wait, marching forth, making peace, waging war, dividing his forces, or seeking refuge. (7.161)

One should employ a sitting posture after making peace (*saṃdhāyāsana*), or a sitting posture after declaring war (*vigṛhyāsana*); likewise, one should employ marching after making peace (*saṃdhāya yāna*) or marching after declaring war (*vigṛhya yāna*), having considered the task at hand; and the same applies to dual policy (*dvaidha*) and seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*). When two kings—one an enemy and the other a conqueror—desire to overreach each other but are unable to strike a blow, they may either sit after making peace or sit after declaring war. In that regard, when he perceives: "I am capable of weakening the enemy by my own strength; my constituent elements (*prakṛtis*) are energetic, united, prosperous, and will act unimpeded in their respective duties; or the enemy's elements are greedy and depleted, such that they can be won over through instigation," and so forth—then he should remain seated after declaring war (*vigṛhyāsīta*). In the absence of a reason for sitting after declaring war, he should remain seated after making peace. Having gained superiority over the enemy, provided he has made defensive preparations within his own kingdom and is exempt from mobilizing the entire army, he should march after declaring war, or when the enemy is in calamity, when his elements are diminished, or when his elements are provoked to rebellion, or when he possesses a powerful ally (*ākranda*) and a solid force. However, in the absence of a reason for marching after declaring war, he should march after making peace with the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), or having marched in concert with others and agreed upon a share of the fruits of the expedition, and so forth. Or, being capable, he may march after simultaneously declaring war against both the enemy and the rear-enemy; or, being incapable and attacked by a powerful foe, he should remain divided (*dvaidhībhūta*) by taking refuge in a fortress, or seek shelter with a middle king or a neutral king (*udāsīna*), or resort to whichever course was practiced by his ancestors, or seek refuge with those who have close ties, or with friends who are numerous and capable. (7.161)
A king should know that alliance and war are each of two kinds, as well as marching and sitting encamped, the dual policy, and seeking refuge. (7.162)
These six qualities, in brief, are divided into two kinds; for this presentation is made for the purpose of what is to be said hereafter. (7.162)
When the undertaking of the journey is common and likewise the opposite, then that alliance, joined with future prospects, should be known as having two characteristics. (7.163)

A peace (*saṃdhi*) in which the undertaking of a journey is shared is one where the action of traveling is common to both parties; for example, "You go from here, and I shall go. A peace in which the undertaking of a journey is not shared is the opposite; for example, "I shall go [alone]. Likewise, through the acquisition of treasure and other resources, one party is provided with immediate benefit while the other is provided with future benefit. Thus, this peace comes to possess these two characteristics. (7.163)
War is declared to be of two kinds: that waged by oneself for the sake of one's own body, whether at the improper time or the proper time, and that waged because a friend has been wronged. (7.164)

When one strives by one's own power to conquer an enemy, that is a war undertaken by oneself; it may occur even out of season, depending on the accumulation of resources. When an enemy of another king is a friend of the one seeking victory (*vijigīṣu*), and that enemy of the other inflicts harm upon him, then—since the enemy has been harmed by the *vijigīṣu*'s friend—the war is "contrary" (*viparīta*) when the enemy falls into calamity. Among the existing causes for war, whether there is staying put (*āsana*) or marching (*yāna*), war is always of two kinds. (7.164)
When an urgent matter has arisen by chance, marching alone or in conjunction with an ally—these two types of marching are prescribed. (7.165)

Marching alone when the enemy is in distress, or when a sudden emergency has arisen—provided that he is able to defeat him while alone; or marching with a united friend: thus is twofold the march. 7.165.
When one's power has gradually diminished due to fate or past actions, or out of consideration for a friend, neutrality is declared to be of two kinds. (7.166)

Even one who acts rightly may come to ruin through fate; another [comes to ruin] through the negligence previously mentioned. When he is thus ruined in either way, his course of action is to remain in a state of neutrality (*āsana*). Furthermore, he who is an enemy to another becomes a friend to one who desires victory; when that [enemy] is ruined, one should remain even if capable, out of consideration for him. Thus, neutrality is of two kinds. An alternative reading of the cause is: "through delusion or by what was done previously. (7.166)

The maintenance of both the army and the sovereign for the sake of accomplishing the task is declared to be of two kinds as "dual policy" by those who know the qualities of the six measures of statecraft. (7.167)

One who has been overcome by a powerful foe and has taken refuge in a fortress should accomplish his own purpose by employing a twofold strategy. Or, if he is capable of favoring others, he should assist another king with a portion of his force, looking toward results such as the acquisition of iron and other minerals. || 7.167 ||

Seeking refuge is considered to be of two kinds: that which is for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose while being oppressed by enemies, and that which consists in not being falsely accused among the virtuous. (7.168)

One who is being oppressed by a great enemy should seek refuge; and once having sought refuge, he should accomplish his own purpose with all possible efforts, even if he is a sinner, so as not to bring reproach upon the virtuous. He should seek refuge because of the calamity that necessitates it. For one who has sought such refuge becomes invincible to his equals. (7.168)
When one perceives that in the future there will certainly be a great advantage for oneself, while at present there is only slight suffering, then one should resort to peace. (7.169)
Considering the future, one should resort to peace by inflicting only slight injury upon oneself. (7.169)
When he considers all his subjects to be exceedingly well-pleased, then he should consider himself to have gained the upper hand for war. (7.170)
One who has risen through the excellence of his army and other resources for the sake of war, and whose subjects are contented and well-supported, may engage in peace or war. || 7.170 ||
When he perceives his own force to be joyful and robust in spirit, and that of the enemy to be the opposite, then he should march against the foe. (7.171)

When his own forces are joyful and well-nourished due to their exclusive causes, and those of the enemy are the opposite, he should march forth, either after declaring war or after making peace. (7.171)
But when he is depleted of both mounts and troops, then he should sit with diligence, gradually wearing down the enemy. (7.172)
When his gold and other resources are exhausted, he should remain focused on his own advancement, conciliating the enemy through both peaceful negotiation and the offering of gifts. 7.172.
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect, then, having divided his army into two parts, he should accomplish his own purpose. (7.173)
When overcome by a powerful foe and unable to hold his ground, he should take refuge in a stronghold, divide his forces in two, and remain there. || 7.173 ||
But when he becomes most vulnerable to attack by the forces of the enemy, then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king. (7.174)

Even if one resorts to a state of double-dealing, if one considers self-preservation impossible, then before being overcome, one should quickly seek refuge with a powerful and righteous king; in his absence, with any other person of virtue. (7.174)
One should always serve with every effort that person who effects the suppression of both the subjects and the enemy's forces, just as one serves a teacher. 7.175.

When one has become most vulnerable due to the fault of certain constituent elements (prakṛtis), he should, with all his efforts, serve him who is capable of suppressing those elements as well as the enemy's forces; at that time, he should serve him like a teacher, relying on the highest sincerity with a mind free from obstruction. || 7.175 ||
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from taking refuge, he should engage in fair combat itself, free from hesitation. (7.176)

For reliance upon kinsmen is a great blemish for kings; thus, if he should bring about his ruin through such a course of seeking refuge, then he should engage in fair combat there as well, free from hesitation. For it is seen that even one of small strength may conquer one of great strength. Moreover, even defeat for one who fights is superior by virtue of the attainment of heaven, whereas one who relies [on others] finds no success in the hereafter. (7.176)
In short,
a king who understands policy should employ every means such that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him. (7.177)

Through [the pursuit of] wealth and other such things, even a friend turns into an enemy; what then need be said of a neutral person or an enemy? Therefore, by employing the aforementioned means to incite them [to action], one should make oneself appear more distinguished to friends and others than they are; one should not place reliance on the thought that "he is a friend" or "he is neutral. (7.177)
One should examine the future of all undertakings as well as their present state, and the merits and defects of all past ones in accordance with reality.

(7.178) Because undertakings have many facets and because they are momentary, a particular task arises in each respective state; thus, [the verse] demonstrates the general determination of all undertakings. (7.178)

Therefore, this is indeed so, because: "One who knows the virtues and faults of the future, who makes swift decisions in the present, and who understands the consequences of past actions, is not overcome by enemies. (7.179)

In all undertakings, one must first understand the merits and defects pertaining to the future; the determination of the remainder and its execution are for the sake of favoring the royal administration by avoiding faults. Thus, the destruction of that enemy—which follows all undertakings like armor—must be constantly contemplated by the seeker of victory. (7.179)
He should arrange everything in such a way that his allies, neutrals, and enemies do not deceive him; this is the summary of political strategy.
This verse serves as a summary. 7.180.
But when the lord sets out upon his vehicle toward the enemy kingdom, he should then proceed slowly toward the enemy city according to this following rule. (7.181)
The presentation of the journey is for the purpose of directing the mind toward the vow. || 7.181 ||
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his journey;
or else, according to his strength, toward the months of Phālguna or Caitra.

For by marching here, one destroys another's autumn and spring crops, while the roads for those marching become abundant in fodder and water. Therefore, one should set out on a long-duration expedition in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa against a country where the autumn harvest predominates; and in the months of Phālguna and Caitra, one should set out on a long-duration expedition against a country where the spring harvest predominates. Likewise, one with a fourfold army should march in Mārgaśīrṣa, but one whose strength consists primarily of cavalry should march in Phālguna and Caitra. (7.182)
Moreover, at other times as well, when he perceives certain victory, he should march forth having declared war, or when a calamity has arisen for the enemy. (7.183)

One should march against an enemy whose strength consists primarily of elephants during the rainy season, or one whose strength consists primarily of horses during the autumn; for when marching at such a time of one's own strength, victory for the king is inevitable. Furthermore, one may march when the enemy is in distress, or when one is capable of doing so, or when the enemy has no place of refuge. (7.183)

Having performed the ritual arrangements at the base according to the rule, as well as those pertaining to the journey, and having secured a place of refuge and properly established a system of scouts; || 7.184 ||

The consolidation of one's subjects through wealth and honor; the special protection of those who are greedy or angry; the making of peace with the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*); the settlement of the countryside; and the provision of provisions at the base, as well as the transport of elephants, horses, and so forth. Furthermore, those who are seditious (*dūṣya*) in the enemy's territory become the traveler’s footholds; having won them over and properly established spies for the sake of knowing the activities in the enemy's territory—just as this is so—[one should proceed]. (7.184)
Having cleared the threefold path and his own sixfold strength,
he should proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to the rules for a future campaign.

Having cleared the three types of roads and paths—namely, those through arid lands (*jāṅgala*), those in the open (*ātapa*), and those through thickets (*āṭavika*)—by ensuring the supply of fodder, fuel, and water, and by clearing away creepers and obstructions; and having cleared the sixfold army—consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, laborers (*viṣṭi*), and the treasury—he should march according to the rules for future contingencies and the rules for one desiring to fight. (7.185)
One should be especially vigilant regarding a friend who serves one's enemies and remains hidden, as well as one who goes and returns; for such a person is indeed a most dangerous enemy.
Having become even more cautious toward a friend who has experienced suffering and returned, one should not trust him at all. 7.186.
He should march along that path in the staff-array, or the wagon-array, or the boar, the eagle, the needle, or the crocodile array. (7.187)

The leader is in front, the commander and the lord are in the rear, the elephants are on the flanks, and the horses are behind them; this is the method for the battle array. A long, even deployment is the *daṇḍavyūha* (staff array), which should be employed when there is danger from all sides. The *śakaṭavyūha* (cart array) is narrow at the front and broad at the rear; it should be deployed when there is danger from the rear. The *varāhavyūha* (boar array) has a smooth front and rear half and a broad middle; it is praised when there is danger from the flanks. By this, the *garuḍavyūha* (eagle array) is explained. The *sūcīvyūha* (needle array) consists of troops capable of rapid mobilization, being long with brave men at its head; it is most effective when there is danger from the front. The *makaravyūha* (crocodile array) is broad at the head and tail; it is praised when there is danger from both sides.
And from whichever side the danger arises, thence he should extend his force;
he himself should always take up his position in the lotus array.
This is the instruction in every respect: wherever one perceives danger, there one should extend the force; one should always encamp with the lotus-array (padmavyūha) deployed on all sides. 7.188.
The commander-in-chief and the general should station their forces in all directions;
and from whichever quarter he suspects danger, he should designate that as the eastern direction.

The generals, commanders, and men should station themselves everywhere. Furthermore, other various types of formations have been devised which will conquer the enemy; therefore, they are appropriately called "men" (*puruṣa*). Having placed a mountain or a forest behind them, and facing the danger and the enemy in front, they should either fight there or take up their positions. (7.189)
And he should station trusted troops as outposts on all sides—men skilled in both their positions and in battle, who are fearless and steadfast. (7.190)
Especially among the Guhyakas, those with such qualities should be appointed; for from them arises fear that leads to great misfortune through one's own power. (7.190)
One should make a small number of troops fight in a compact formation, while one may extend a large number as desired;
having arrayed them in either the needle or the thunderbolt formation, one should cause them to fight.

A few [troops], when closely arrayed and fighting with mutual regard for one another, do not fear. The *vajra* array is established in three parts. The *sūcī* (needle) array has been explained. However, all arrays should be arranged according to one's capability. 7.191.
One should fight with chariots and horses on level ground; likewise, with boats and elephants in marshy terrain;
and with bows, swords, shields, and other weapons against forces in places covered by trees and shrubs. (7.192)
This instruction is for the purpose of demonstrating capability. 7.192.
He should cause the men of Kaurukṣetra, the Matsyas, the Pāñcālas, and those born in Śūrasena—both tall and short—to fight in the vanguard ranks. (7.193)
For these men, with broad chests, arms reaching to their knees, capable of touching both [ears], and of great stature, cause a slight mental blow to the enemies at the head of the armies. || 7.193 ||
He should encourage his army, properly inspect the battle formation, and also observe the gestures of the enemies as they fight. (7.194)

He should gladden [the soldiers] by demonstrating the true meaning of the treatises through such statements as, "Victory brings dharma and wealth; defeat brings dismissal," and so forth. He should personally observe the actions of those engaged in battle, for men with wavering minds may cause harm even to one who is helping them. (7.194)
Having besieged the enemy, he should remain there and afflict his kingdom;
he should also constantly corrupt his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel. (7.195)
He should break down tanks as well as walls and moats; he should launch a sudden assault upon him at night and terrify him. 7.196.
He should instigate those who can be instigated and remain ever aware of their actions; intent on his purpose, he should fight with divine resolve, free from fear and desiring victory. (7.197)
The method of besieging one who has taken refuge in a stronghold and is not fighting back is described in three verses (7.195–97).
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, and sowing dissension—either all together or individually—and never engage in battle. (7.198)

In that regard, conciliation (*sāma*) is of two kinds: the employment of speech and the employment of physical action. The employment of speech consists of speaking of virtues, speaking of what is beneficial, speaking of past favors, self-deprecation, and so forth. The employment of physical action consists of joining the palms in salutation, taking the hand, showing one's face, showing one's own wife, conversing with one another, and so forth. Generosity (*dāna*) is the production and bestowing of pleasure through various kinds of material goods. Sowing dissension (*bheda*) is the winning over of one person while repudiating another, as well as intimidation. One should strive to conquer by means of these three methods. (7.198)
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two who fight, and defeat likewise in battle, one should therefore avoid war. (7.199)

Since victory and defeat are uncertain, one should avoid battle through diligent effort. Therefore, even a small man who is free from doubt is better than a great man whose purpose is uncertain. (7.199)
If even the three previously mentioned expedients are not possible, he should nevertheless fight with full resolve in such a way that he may conquer his enemies. (7.200)

For one desiring victory, the employment of conciliation and the other means [of policy] becomes effective only when these have been exhausted. Likewise, when victory is uncertain, one may certainly fight, because in victory there is worldly gain (*artha*), and in defeat there is heaven (*svarga*). Therefore, in such a case, war alone is superior. However, when defeat is certain while the matter is still open to doubt, then fleeing is better; for one who has escaped may again achieve his purpose. (7.200)
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties of safety. (7.201)
But having understood the intended purpose of all these people in brief, he should install a member of their lineage there and establish a formal covenant. (7.202)
He should establish authoritative standards for them and their appropriate duties;
he should honor these [elders] with precious gems along with the principal men. (7.203)
The next three verses (7.201–03) are for the purpose of pacifying [the afflictions] once they have been acquired.
Non-giving is disagreeable, while giving brings what is agreeable;
the timely bestowal of desired objects is highly praised. (7.204)
Giving or withholding at the proper time brings happiness; when performed by a king according to the right occasion, it brings about the welfare of the entire world. (7.204)
All this action is dependent upon the two ordinances, the divine and the human;
of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, whereas in the human there exists the possibility of action.

Whatever human fruit there is, such as agriculture and the like, that depends entirely upon human effort. Furthermore, even fruits such as the birth of a son are obtained through destiny (*daiva*); yet even that occurs only by means of visible factors. Therefore, one should strive in all undertakings by relying solely on visible means. One should not remain inactive, making destiny the supreme authority. (7.205)
Or else, having diligently made a treaty, he may march together with [the enemy], perceiving the threefold fruit consisting of allies, gold, or land. (7.206)

This act of conciliation, however, is the fruit of the expedition against the enemy; having conquered him, one should establish him [in his own position]. Thinking, "Having been assisted and protected, he will become a friend and perform the duties of a friend at the proper time," one should either conclude a treaty with him by means of land and gold and then withdraw, or [act otherwise as deemed necessary]. (7.206)

Having carefully observed the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*) as well as the ally-in-distress (*ākranda*) within the circle of states, one should obtain the fruit of the expedition from either a friend or even an enemy. (7.207)
Without considering the rear-attackers, the cries for help, or the consequences, he would collect gold and other wealth where it yields no fruit. (7.207)
A king does not prosper so much by acquiring a land of gold as he does by gaining a firm friend, even if that friend is weak, provided he is capable of enduring for the future. (7.208)
A light friend who knows the dharma, is grateful, has a cheerful disposition, is devoted, and is steadfast in his undertakings is highly praised. (7.209)
With these two verses beginning "Better than land and gold is a friend," his praise is intended for the purpose of winning over Mitra. 7.208–09.
The wise say it is a painful thing to have an enemy who is intelligent, of noble birth, brave, skillful, generous, grateful, and resolute. (7.210)

The purpose of this instruction: One who desires victory should form an alliance with such an enemy by all possible means, so that one who possesses such qualities can be destroyed, weakened, or oppressed. Therefore, one should diligently seek to make such an enemy a friend. (7.210)
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, and a compassionate nature; constant magnanimity and the arising of the qualities of one who remains impartial—these are his traits. (7.211)

The word *udaya* denotes a collective whole, yet it is not appropriate to take it in the sense of "fruit," because of the context. The purpose of this instruction is as follows: having sought refuge with a neutral king (*udāsīna*) endowed with these qualities, one may even oppose an enemy possessing the characteristics already described for the sake of achieving the results of a military expedition (*yātrā*). It is only when a neutral king possesses such qualities that he becomes capable of performing the duties of a protector; however, a neutral king lacking these qualities will become an adversary due to the enemy's instigation and his own lack of firm resolve. (7.211)
A king should, without hesitation, abandon even land that is secure, always productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle, for his own sake. (7.212)

But when a king desiring victory, having fallen into such a state of siege by an enemy, seeks refuge with a neutral king, he should then abandon even a territory that is secure, productive of crops, and constantly conducive to the increase of cattle—even though it be so; for it is thus recorded in the duties of kings: 7.212. Wealth should be protected for the sake of times of distress; a wife should be protected even with wealth;
but one's own self must always be protected, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. (7.213)

"One must always protect oneself even by the renunciation of everything. For it was by this [means] that he, though capable [of other ways], abandoned his wife—even though it was contrary to *dharma*—and having regained his kingship, was able once more to perform great religious duties (*dharmānuṣṭhāna*). However, for no king other than him is it proper to protect himself by abandoning his wife through the act of taking another wife. For having abandoned his wife, what other virtuous deed (*satkarma*) could he perform whereby he would not bring sin upon himself or incur the reproach of the world? And so it has been said: "And precisely that which is censured by the world... This [protection of self] was achieved by him through practices such as worship, because he possessed realized knowledge even while his wealth was destroyed; it was not merely by the instruction on royal duties (*rājadharmopadeśa*). (7.213)
Having thoroughly observed that all calamities arise together, the wise man should employ every means, both those that bring about union and those that bring about separation. (7.214)

Having closely observed all calamities that have arisen—whether they are combined in their entirety, or whether two or three are joined together, or even if they are separate—the wise man should employ and then relinquish all means, beginning with concentration (*samādhi*). The meaning is that he should not suddenly become despondent. He concludes this by summarizing the fears arising from one's own nature (*svaprakṛti*) through the mention of "throwing down" (*upakṣepataḥ*). 7.214.
Relying upon these three—the practitioner, the goal to be attained, and all the means in their entirety—one should strive for the accomplishment of the purpose. (7.215)
Because states are infinite, this is a concise demonstration of all methods for the purpose of self-protection. (7.215)
Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king, after exercising and bathing at midday, should proceed to the inner apartments to eat. (7.216)
This verse serves as a summary. 7.216.

There, he should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who are like his own self, who know the proper time, who cannot be led astray, and who have neutralized poison with mantras. (7.217)
One should mix all his substances with water that neutralizes poison, and, being self-restrained, he should always wear gems that counteract poison. (7.218)
And women who have been examined with ointments, water, and incense, being well-composed and adorned with their dress and ornaments, should touch him. 7.219.
In this manner, one should exert effort regarding vehicles, beds, food, and seats, as well as in bathing, grooming, and the application of ornaments. (7.220)
Having eaten, he should likewise enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments; and having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again attend to his duties. (7.221)
And having adorned himself, he should inspect the armed forces once more,
as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should remain armed within his inner apartments and listen to the reports of those who reveal secrets and to the activities of his secret agents.
Having gone to another inner chamber and dismissed those people, he should enter the inner apartments again, surrounded by women, for the purpose of eating. (7.224)
Having eaten there a little more, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments, he should go to sleep at the proper time and rise with his fatigue dispelled. (7.225)
A healthy lord of the earth should carry out this entire course of conduct;
but when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants.

From the verse beginning with "Having exercised and bathed" (*vyāyamyāplutya*) onwards, these eleven verses concerning the protection of the self during recreation are not commented upon here, as they are well known. Thus, having established the system of government and secured his own safety, the king shall preside over legal proceedings for the accomplishment of the affairs of his subjects. (7.217–26)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Manuśāstravivaraṇa* composed by Ṛjuvimala.
The Eighth Chapter.
Thus, having properly established the administration of the kingdom according to the principles of royal science taught in the Seventh Chapter, the king,
desiring to examine legal cases for the sake of protecting his subjects, [should sit] together with Brahmins.
Disciplined by ministers who are experts in counsel, he should enter the assembly hall.

For the sake of maintaining the stability of the world by turning back the lawlessness of the fish (mātsyanyāya), this king—being habitually intent on investigating legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*)—should enter the court together with Brāhmaṇas, whom he will describe later: "In whatever place three Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas sit... It is for this reason that they are qualified as "knowers of the *mantras*. Thus, even if they are knowers of the Vedas, if they are not knowers of the *mantras*, this qualification is intended to ensure the attainment of the additional characteristic. Those who know the worldly conventions are the "knowers of the *mantras*. And in the phrase "with ministers who are knowers of the *mantras*," the preceding qualification is common [to both]. However, there is this much distinction: ministers who are knowers of the royal administration are required by necessity, whereas in the other case (the court), there is no prohibition. Therefore, he qualifies them in this way as well. "Disciplined, he should enter the court. "Disciplined" means one whose dress and ornaments are not ostentatious. "The court" refers to that which will be described: "They know that to be the court of Brahman. And although a Brāhmaṇa possesses the status of a teacher of Dharma and a spiritual preceptor (*guru*), he is not made the primary authority in the investigation of legal proceedings. For he is incapable of subduing wrongdoers because of his small circle of dependents. But for a Kṣatriya, since the protection of subjects is taught through the collection of taxes, tolls, tributes, enjoyments, and fines, his possession of a great retinue is understood from his livelihood and wealth; thus, he has the capacity to restrain wrongdoers for the sake of protecting the subjects. This being so, the Kṣatriya is taught as the primary authority in the investigation of legal proceedings. Alternatively, the instruction for the Kṣatriya to investigate legal proceedings serves a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭa*). Legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is the act of transacting (*vyavaharaṇa*). Here, one person transacts for his own sake, while another does so otherwise; thus, there is a manifold dealing, or a conflicting dealing with one another, which is legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*). 8.1.
Seated there or even standing, raising his right hand and wearing modest dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal cases of the litigants.

Seated, he should look after the affairs of other people, with the exception of ascetics, learned Brahmins, and gurus; or standing, he should do so for those of the highest castes, beginning with ascetics. The mention of "taking the hand" (pāṇigrahaṇa) is for the purpose of indicating the right arm. For this is a court of Brahman (brahmasabhā). Thus it has been said regarding the fire-sanctuary and other such places: "The raising of the right arm. Indeed, suitors will approach the king comfortably when his dress and ornaments are modest. Alternatively, this [rule] may have an invisible (transcendental) purpose (*adṛṣṭaprayojana*) alone, for the sake of making the scripture meaningful. Since he should thus look into the cases of litigants and petitioners, and not himself create cases in which the efficacy of scriptural instruction is not observed—since it is understood that this instruction on the inspection of legal proceedings concerns only petitioners—it follows that its non-prescriptive nature (*avidhitva*) is established. Otherwise, there would be no exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of instruction regarding others who possess property. Furthermore, a single instruction cannot have efficacy in both respects simultaneously, because a sentence has but a single meaning. And thus, the inspection of legal proceedings by Brahmins and others in their own households remains unprohibited. Now, one might object: since he will later state, "He should not himself create a case," the phrase "the cases of litigants" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) and lacks independent meaning here. To this we reply: let it be an independent instruction here, while in the subsequent passage it serves as a restatement for the sake of specification, namely, "nor shall any man act for him. (8.2)
As it was stated, "He shall oversee the affairs of those who have business," the reason for this must be explained; therefore, this [section] is commenced for the purpose of establishing that reason:
"Day by day, by means of reasons observed in the country and observed in the scriptures, [the king] shall examine separately the matters settled within the eighteen titles of law. (8.3)

In the eighteen paths, which are the bases of legal procedure beginning with the non-payment of debt and others to be described hereafter, the king—having established them separately for each case according to local custom among farmers, merchants, herdsmen, and so forth, and according to scriptural rule through the reasons stated in the scriptures such as witnesses and oaths—should daily examine the cases of the litigants without weariness. Although worldly signs are also mentioned in the scriptures, such as: “One should discern [the truth] by external signs,” and “Thus the king should reach a conclusion regarding dharma through inference,” nevertheless, this present verse reiterates worldly means of proof (*pramāṇa*). However, the scriptural means of proof consists of witnesses, oaths, and the like. Even though there is a reiteration of worldly means of proof in this scripture for some reason, the scripture nonetheless authorizes the world itself as a means of proof in certain matters. And so he will say later: “Those skilled in sea-voyages, who have seen the lands, regions, and goods,” and so forth. Therefore, the separate mention of “local custom” (*deśa*) is appropriate. (8.3)
And these subjects of legal procedure are now set forth:
among them, the first is the non-payment of debt, followed by deposits, sale without ownership, partnership, and the non-delivery of what has been given. (8.4)
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract, rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between owners and herdsmen; 8.5.
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault, theft, violence, and the abduction of women. (8.6)
The duties of husband and wife, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—these eighteen topics constitute the basis of legal procedure here. (8.7)
The subject of dispute is here indicated by four verses. The first is primary; for this legal proceeding concerning debt touches even forest-dwellers, and thus its primacy is asserted. (8.4–7)
In these matters, for men who are mostly engaged in disputes,
one should determine the outcome of the case by resorting to the eternal dharma.

These are the primary subjects of legal procedure (*vyavahāra-vastu*). Because their subdivisions are infinite, it is impossible to provide a complete enumeration of them all. From the use of the term "most" (*bhūyiṣṭha*), one understands that these subjects of legal procedure are numerous. Even regarding matters not explicitly mentioned, one should determine the case by relying on the eternal Dharma through wisdom that follows the scriptures. One should set aside even that which has been practiced by one's father, grandfather, and others, if it is unjust; for the world generally follows what has been done, and kings especially so. Therefore, this effort is undertaken; and while this instruction is general, its specific details will be stated in relation to its particular scope. (8.8)
When the king himself does not personally oversee legal cases, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee those cases. (8.9)

When, due to some other circumstance, the king himself does not perceive the legal matter, then he should appoint a Brāhmaṇa to oversee the case, and not one of another caste—even if that person knows the Dharma and is knowledgeable in legal procedure—nor even a learned Brāhmaṇa [if he is not proficient] in those scriptures which must be known by a Brāhmaṇa. This is stated for the purpose of ensuring that the duties incumbent upon him are not transgressed: "But his learning for the purpose of overseeing legal proceedings is not subject to instruction, because it is acquired through wealth. (8.9)
Surrounded by three members of the court, he should examine his legal cases,
having entered the foremost assembly hall, either seated or standing.

If the king is unwell in body or distracted by other duties, he should enter the assembly hall itself and sit at the head, not elsewhere; nor even in the assembly hall should he ascend the royal throne, but rather remain in the assembly hall seated on another seat. Regarding the phrase "seated or standing," there is an option between standing and sitting. The purpose has been stated. Those who are virtuous (*sādhu*) in the assembly are the *sabhyas* (members of the court); they, possessing the aforementioned qualifications, should indeed be assistants to the Brāhmaṇa who occupies the king’s position. 8.10.
Regarding the statement that "the assembly is the best," it is for this purpose that the following is said:
"In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together with a learned minister of the king, they know that assembly to be a *brahma-sabhā*. (8.11)

Because of the mention of three [qualities], they would not be those who do not know the Veda; by the logic of the "stick and cake" (the inclusion of the whole when a part is mentioned), even four qualities are not contradictory. And the statement that the king has a "learned assistant" (*vidvān*) is a restatement for the sake of what follows. They know that assembly to be the *brahman*. Some, however, read "brāhmaṇa"; that is incorrect, because this [term] has already been mentioned as a caste in the previous passage: "Then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to the investigation of the case. The mention of the *brahman* is appropriate for the purpose of praising the assembly, as in the term "Brahma-assembly" (*brahmasabhā*). Alternatively, this is stated to indicate that which was previously said: "He should enter the assembly modestly"; it serves to exclude the worldly assemblies, such as those described by the phrase "in whatever place they sit," and so forth. 8.11.
When Dharma, pierced by Adharma, stands before the assembly, and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced. (8.12)

"Dharma" refers to its piercing, which is the perception of it otherwise. The result of that is stated for the appointed Brahmin, because it is the cause for the collapse of the established order of Dharma: "And the members of the assembly do not extract his thorn," meaning they do not cut out this thorn—which is so called because it is the cause for the establishment of the thorn (the pain)—if these members of the assembly, having been pierced themselves, do not do so even earlier. Since this is the case, a king who acts improperly, or the appointed Brahmin, must not be tolerated by the members of the assembly, for fear of transgressing the law and the resulting piercing of Dharma. (8.12)
Therefore:

"Either the court must not be entered, or what is just must be spoken; or else the authority to adjudicate legal cases must not be accepted from the king by the members of the court, or if that authority has been accepted, truth that is just must be spoken therein. By this—
Whether one speaks or does not speak, a person becomes guilty of sin. || 8.13 ||

One does not become a sinner merely by speaking falsely; rather, one becomes so even by remaining silent. Therefore, you should not remain indifferent here, thinking, "This man is being overlooked by the court members; he is acting thus because he is a servant of the king, and we are not like that. 8.13.

And so they have said: "Where indeed dharma is [subverted] by adharma, and established order by disorder— characterized by the contradiction of preceding and succeeding [statements], by the denial [of truth], and so forth— "
Where truth is slain by falsehood, by means of perjured witnesses, while the members look on— there the members of the assembly are themselves slain. (8.14)
Therefore, the members of the court must not remain indifferent; they are not exempt from responsibility simply because they do not act as witnesses. (8.14)
And this being so:
"Dharma alone, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, preserves.
Therefore, Dharma must not be violated, lest violated Dharma slay us. (8.15)

With this intention, the king himself is being addressed: "This sovereignty has been obtained by you through faith in Dharma," and not from the favor of the king; therefore, he ought not to destroy Dharma. Furthermore, because of the singular number in the indicative mark (liṅga) in the subsequent verse, "Therefore, one should not violate Dharma," it refers to the king, and not to the members of the court, because of their plurality. (8.15)
And because this is its etymological derivation:
"The Blessed One is indeed Dharma; he who causes the destruction of that [Dharma], the gods know him as a *vṛṣala* (outcaste); therefore, one should not violate the Dharma. (8.16)

One is not a *vṛṣala* (outcaste) merely by birth; rather, it is through one's improper conduct (*vikarman*) that one becomes a *vṛṣala*. This being the case, what will your Brahmin birth avail you when you are being swallowed up by unrighteousness due to such transgression? For this reason, this is merely a reproach directed at the Brahmin appointed by the king. (8.16)
This further enumeration is stated for the purpose of establishing the order of the aforementioned Brahmins:
"Dharma alone is the true friend that follows one even unto death;
for everything else goes to destruction along with the body. (8.17)

For this reason, dharma must not be abandoned even out of regard for friends, relatives, and the like. Otherwise, by neglecting it, not only does the wrongdoer incur sin through such a failure to perceive the truth, but furthermore: "A quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, a quarter reaches the witness, a quarter reaches all the members of the court, and a quarter reaches the king. (8.18)

Therefore, one must not remain indifferent with the thought: "The doer or the witness is connected with the fault; what will happen to us who are neutral? For in every case, sin is distributed when one observes an improper legal proceeding. Although there is no distribution of the sin committed by another, this principle is demonstrated through an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the connection with fault for the purpose of preventing such improper observation. (8.18)
The king becomes [tainted with] sin by this, yet the members of the court are released; the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured. (8.19)
Thus, when right conduct is observed, all this becomes successful; although this point is already implied by the sense, it is restated here due to the inherent nature of the sentence. 8.19.
One who lives merely by his birth may indeed be called a "pseudo-Brahmin" (brāhmaṇabruva), but a Śūdra can never be a teacher of dharma to the king. (8.20)

In the absence of learned Brāhmaṇas appointed by the king, this [next] undertaking is for the purpose of authorizing Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are conversant with the scriptures, and not those who subsist merely on the basis of their caste. How so? For it has been stated: "Then one should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee the affairs. Here, it was said that the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of excluding the other three castes. This being the case, since the exclusion of the Śūdra is already established by that very prohibition, the fact that a further prohibition of the Śūdra is made here is understood to be for the purpose of permitting Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. For a scripture that does not act when its purpose is unfulfilled would thus have an improper commencement rather than a proper one; otherwise, due to the fault of redundancy, it would constitute an improper commencement. Furthermore, in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa learned in the scriptures, the scripture cannot authorize a Brāhmaṇa who subsists merely on the basis of his caste and is ignorant and incapable of overseeing legal proceedings, because such a person lacks the necessary capacity. Indeed, no one in the world who is blind is authorized to perceive forms. This being the case, this Brāhmaṇa is not an optional substitute in the event of absence; rather, this statement is solely for the purpose of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) regarding those who subsist merely on the basis of their caste. And thus, in such sentences, a double negation is observed in common usage: "One may eat even poison, but do not eat in his house. Since there is thus a double negation, the authorization of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas follows. (8.20)
And this being the case—
[if a Śūdra performs] the judicial discernment of dharma for a king in a position reserved for Brāhmaṇas—
His kingdom sinks away while he looks on, like a cow in the mud. (8.21)
This prohibition against the Śūdra is for the purpose of praising the appointment of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; it was with reference to that very subject that this was also stated:
"That kingdom which is mostly composed of Śūdras, overrun by atheists, and devoid of the twice-born, quickly perishes entirely, afflicted by famine and disease. (8.22)

"Abounding in Śūdras" means that the instructors of dharma are mostly Śūdras. By implication, such a kingdom becomes overrun by nihilists (*nāstika*). He states the reason for this: because it "consists mostly of non-twice-borns," meaning it is devoid of Brāhmaṇas who instruct in dharma. And this is logical: such a kingdom perishes. It has already been stated that this verse, like the preceding one, is intended as praise for the appointment of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas [to judicial office], and not as praise for the appointment of those belonging merely to the [Śūdra] caste. When the king, being free from distraction, desires to personally oversee legal proceedings, then—
Having occupied the Dharma-seat, with his body properly covered and his mind composed,
he should bow to the world-protectors and begin the examination of legal cases.

A seat for the sake of dharma is a *dharmāsana*. Having sat upon it, with his limbs properly covered—this being a restatement (anuvāda) because the quality of modest dress and ornamentation has already been established—he should remain composed while presiding over legal proceedings. Having paid homage to the guardians of the world (*lokapālas*) depicted in the court paintings or stationed in their respective places, he should begin the examination of cases through both speech and mind. This rule regarding the king’s desire to see legal proceedings is intended for visible results (*dṛṣṭārtha*), or else for invisible results (*adṛṣṭārtha*) so that the treatise may not be rendered purposeless. (8.23)
Having discerned both profit and loss, as well as merit and demerit in their entirety, he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes. (8.24)

He should perceive that the favor and anger of the kingdom result in profit and loss, being respectively favorable or unfavorable to the administration of the state; and he should regard merit and demerit in the afterlife as independent of visible results, conducting himself with an observation of what ought to be done. Or rather, having understood that profit and loss have their causes in either the persistence of enmity or its opposite. And when lawsuits are brought together, he should attend to them according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*). It has been stated that "he shall look into the cases of the litigants"; furthermore, that investigation of legal proceedings is especially based on inference, for which reason it is now explained:
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs: through their voice, complexion, gestures, appearance, gaze, and movements. (8.25)

"Voice" (*svara*), "complexion" (*varṇa*), and "gestures" (*iṅgita*) constitute "voice, complexion, and gestures. "Appearance" (*ākāra*) is a transformation of the body or the senses. These—voice, complexion, gestures, and appearance—are referred to by this designation through the principle of general and specific characteristics (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-dharma*). Among these, "variety" consists of: a change in voice such as stammering; a change in complexion which is a distortion of the form of the limbs; and gestures such as perspiration, trembling, and horripilation. By means of the eyes—that is, by a change in the eyes—and by movement, such as the twitching of hands or eyebrows, one should recognize that the false speech of the plaintiff, the defendant, or the witnesses is perceptible even through the alteration of their voices and other traits. This is an instruction regarding the general [indications]. However, some say: "Since inference (*anumāna*) is subject to error, the settlement of legal disputes (*vyavahāra-sthiti*) must be based on witnesses; but when witnesses are unavailable, inference must also be resorted to. This is improper. If inference is seen to be fallible, then surely the acquisition of testimony from witnesses is likewise seen to be so. If you argue that a decision is reached here [in the case of witnesses] through an effort at discernment, then the same will apply to inference and the like. Furthermore, if inference is fallible, explain why it should be employed for the sake of a decision when witnesses are unavailable! Therefore, inference is a logically sound instruction. And having established it thus, worldly people employ it in matters other than legal disputes as well. (8.25)
By means of facial expressions, gestures, gait, physical movements, and speech, as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived. (8.26)

*Ākāra* is the manifestation [of internal states], namely the transformation of the body and the senses. This is the specific detail of that general statement. Through those *ākāras*—those transformations such as gestures (*iṅgita*) and so forth—a person's underlying intention is perceived in the world even apart from verbal communication. Thus, at the time of legal proceedings, it should be grasped by those in charge who are neither hostile nor biased, and who have applied their skillful attention. And so, this should be understood as a supplement to the preceding verse. (8.26)
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor until he has returned from his studies or until he has passed his childhood. (8.27)

"Riktha" means permanent wealth; this is the meaning of the compound. This being so, it follows by implication that he is "without protector" (anātha) because he has no mother or father. Therefore, that wealth should remain protected by the king until he has returned from his teacher's house (*samāvṛtta*). His "return," however, is intended as an indicator of his fitness for worldly transactions. This being the case, even if he is a child who has returned, the king should not hand over [the property] if he is incapable of managing his own affairs. Or rather, even if he has not yet returned, [the king] should hand it over once he has passed childhood, since it was stated that the handing over depends on his capacity. Because this is a section concerning the instruction for protecting the wealth of those without protectors, this other point of a similar nature is now stated. (8.27)
The same protection should be afforded to women who have no sons, to those whose families are extinct, to women devoted to their husbands, and to widows who are afflicted. (8.28)

A barren woman (*vaśā*) is one who should be honored; a woman whose offspring are daughters or whose offspring have died—both of these, by implication, are to be understood as widows (*vidhavā*). A woman without a family (*niṣkulā*) is like a maiden who has neither father nor mother. A devoted wife (*pativratā*) is one who does not stray even in the absence of her husband. A widow (*vidhavā*) is one deprived of her husband; here, by implication, a widow who is a devoted wife or one whose son is away is intended. Whatever property belongs to these women—whether it be their own *strīdhana* or the wealth of their husbands—that too must be protected by the king for their own relatives. Just as with the property of children, the king must generally provide protection for the wealth of those who are without protectors (*anātha*); this is the instruction. However, a specific teaching regarding those without protectors is appropriate here for the sake of showing special regard. (8.28)
But those kinsmen who should seize the property of those women while they are still alive, the righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves. 8.29.

This indicates that, because they are alive, the kinsmen of those [women] who have died may claim their property according to their degree of proximity. Furthermore, he will later describe the acquisition of the property of one who dies without offspring by the *sapiṇḍas* and others. For this very reason, when there is suspicion of theft, they deserve punishment like a thief. And another similar point is stated here incidentally:
"Property whose owner has disappeared, the king shall cause to be kept for three years.
Within three years, the owner may take it; after that, the king may take it. (8.30)

After three years, the king is authorized to enjoy property whose owner has disappeared; this does not constitute its seizure. It is not proper for him to seize it even after three years once the owner has arrived, for it is impossible—both because it contradicts justice and because it contradicts the scriptures—to authorize the appropriation of another's property through such a legal construction. Nor does the statement "the owner may take it back before three years" imply that the owner loses his ownership after three years. Rather, the phrase "after [three years] the king shall take it" merely restates the connection between the king’s enjoyment or the act of relinquishment (atisarga) based on the nature of the sentence. And this being the case, even if the owner arrives after three years—
He who says, "This is mine," shall be questioned according to the rule; after verifying the form, number, and other details, the owner deserves that property. 8.31.
When the cause of ownership has been declared,
he who does not truly state the place and time of the loss, nor its color, form, and size, deserves a fine equal to the value of that property. (8.32)

In this context, color consists of white and so forth; shape is form; number, weight, and dimension constitute measurement. And here, punishment is invariably applied for the purpose of purifying these. 8.32.
Then, remembering the Dharma, the king should take a sixth part of lost property that has been recovered, or even a tenth or a twelfth part.

After three years have passed, one may take possession of [the property], but one should not hand over everything; rather, one should hand it back after deducting a sixth part or other such portion. Furthermore, the regulation regarding the taking of a sixth part or other portions is determined by consideration of the [owner's] qualities and the effort required for protection. (8.33)
Property that has been lost and then found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
whatever thieves the king may catch therein, he should have them executed by means of an elephant.

Because this [elephant] is ownerless, the following is stated for the purpose of protecting it with effort; furthermore, the killing of an elephant by guards who are on duty serves a visible purpose. (8.34)
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king may take a sixth part of it, or even a twelfth. (8.35)

If a person should claim as his own, on the basis of some reason, a treasure-trove whether it has been discovered or not yet discovered, a distribution of shares must be determined for him in consideration of his Vedic learning and other qualifications; and if there is a discrepancy regarding the grounds of his discovery—then he who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own wealth, or a smaller fraction of the number of that very treasure. (8.36)

One should cause a person to pay a certain amount of wealth such that, being punished by it, they do not fall into despair and yet accept the discipline; furthermore, the variation of the punishment must be applied with regard to the specific status of the individual. (8.36)
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited, may take it entirely, for he is the master of all. (8.37)
This being the case, under this preceding rule—"this is mine"—the taking of a share by option applies either to the case of a non-Brāhmaṇa or to the case of an ignorant Brāhmaṇa. (8.37)
But whatever treasure a king may discover buried in the earth from ancient times, he should give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in his treasury. (8.38)
This rule regarding the distribution of wealth upon the discovery of a treasure trove applies to the king, but not to anyone else, because of the force of the statement. 8.38.
For the king is the lord of the earth, and as such he receives a half-share for protecting the ancient treasures and the mineral ores within the ground. (8.39)
