"One who receives half" (*ardhabhāk*) means one who possesses a share; for the word *ardha* is seen to denote a share as well, as in the expression "the heir and the family friend" (*ardhikaḥ kulamitraś ca*). This being so, the allotment of shares must be determined either by considering the qualities of the recipients or according to the king's intention. Thus, the word *ardha* also signifies an equal division. (8.39)
The king must restore to all classes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.40)

In this reading, the king should support one who has brought his own property [to him], provided that it is impossible for thieves to recover what was stolen from them. However, in the reading *corāhṛtam* ("stolen by thieves"), the meaning is this: having recovered it from the thieves, the king should not take any share of it for himself, but rather restore it to its original place; and in this way, both his righteousness (*dharma*) and his fame (*yaśas*) remain undiminished. (8.40)
One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of regions and castes, the laws of guilds, and the laws of families, should establish one's own duty. (8.41)

The law of caste (*jātidharma*) is well known. [Caste refers to the Brahmins and so forth, and that is said to be eternal because it is characterized by the scriptures. Local custom (*jānapada*) is conventional; it is not based on the authority of the scriptures, such as the grazing of cattle or the protection of water sources. The law of guilds (*śreṇīdharma*) is established for the sake of accomplishing the specific tasks of merchants, artisans, and performers. The king should also uphold that law. One should not treat it with disregard, thinking, "This is merely conventional. For if the king were to show disrespect toward conventional practices, then, due to the collapse of established order, the "law of the fish" (*mātsyanyāya*) would prevail. (8.41)
Even when they are far away, men who perform their own duties and remain steadfast in their respective tasks become dear to the world. 8.42
This is a praise for the observance of the conventional rules (sāmayika-dharma), intended to inspire enthusiasm. 8.42.
Neither the king himself nor his official should initiate a legal case;
nor should he ever seize a matter that has not been brought before him by another. (8.43)

The king himself should not initiate a lawsuit against anyone out of malice toward the citizens or the rural folk, nor out of hatred for a wealthy person, nor out of greed. Nor should the royal Brahmin who presides over legal proceedings consume a matter that has not been brought before him through a lawsuit by any other means whatsoever. Alternatively, another reading is explained as follows: "Nor should he consume a matter that has been brought [before him] by any means other than through a lawsuit. Or yet another reading is explained: "Nor should he consume a matter that has been brought [before him] by any means other than through a lawsuit. For otherwise, there would be harm to the king in the next world due to greed, and a visible fault consisting of the ruin of the administration of the kingdom. But another says: "The king himself should not initiate a case, even if he personally perceives someone committing an improper act; nor should a royal official appointed for that purpose [initiate it]. By this, the rule is stated that the king's role is restricted to the observation of legal proceedings according to his own desire. Therefore, there is no fault for him if, having seen someone committing a transgression, he lets him go. For if a king were to establish a lawsuit on his own authority without a plaintiff, the violation of the principles of the administration of the kingdom would follow upon the perception of greed, passion, or hatred. And thus, even one equal to Bṛhaspati should not seize a matter that is not brought before him through a lawsuit. For in this way, through pleasing all the people, his fame as a King of Dharma and his administrative glory spread abroad. And thus, even by rejecting witnesses, he should remain primarily focused on legal proceedings by relying on the purity of the means of inference (*anumāna*), being well-trained in *ānvīkṣikī* (logic). He states an illustration for this in the second half of the preceding verse. (8.43)
Just as a hunter tracks the path of a deer by drops of blood, so should a king track the path of dharma by means of inference. 8.44

And thus, this is a praise of inference, intended to show that one should proceed in worldly transactions by prioritizing inference while setting aside perception and scripture. For it is not the case that every object perceptible to the world is fit for such rational praise as would require the rejection of perception and scripture. Furthermore, the preceding and following verses are not redundant, as they stand in a relationship of subordinate and principal. Now, for the sake of determining the ultimate reality within worldly transactions, this contemplation of the Seer is being stated. (8.44)
Established in the procedure of legal proceedings, one should examine the truth, the matter, oneself as the witness, as well as the place, the time, and the form. (8.45)

One should perceive the relative worthiness and worthlessness of truth and material gain, making oneself the witness. Likewise, one should consider the abiding of the self in a great station such as heaven through dharma, and the great duration of that stay. Or else, one should consider the duration of life here on earth to be short due to being overcome by old age, and the transformation of the self’s form resulting from the onset of many diseases. Alternatively, having fully considered the form of those dwelling in heaven—which brings satisfaction to body and mind, is irreproachable, free from adversaries, and provides unsurpassed enjoyment of pleasure—one should, by renouncing material gain, embrace truth as the means for attaining heaven. Or else, there is another reading: "one should perceive truth regarding matters," meaning in legal disputes. This effort is undertaken for the purpose of prohibiting deception (*chala*). The rest is as previously stated. (8.45)
Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous, most excellent twice-born men, that one should establish as not contradictory to the customs of one's country, family, and caste. (8.46)

By the virtuous (*sadbhiḥ*) who avoid what is forbidden, and by the righteous (*dhārmikaiḥ*) who perform what is enjoined; or rather, by the righteous who are virtuous—the word *sat* here has the sense of "existence" (or "being") and is not redundant due to its inherent capacity. By Brāhmaṇas characterized by both these qualifications. Or else, by the virtuous who possess learning and wisdom, and by the righteous who are established in the meaning of the scriptures—whatever they may practice, that one should establish for the regions, families, and castes, provided it is not in conflict with the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the Śāstras. Thus, another Smṛti states: "The conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), when not opposed to the Śāstras, is authoritative. But not that which contradicts them, such as the eating [of food] by parrots and starlings. And thus, whatever has been practiced by the learned at any time or in any way, being accepted as a valid matter, that should be maintained by the King. Alternatively, this undertaking is for the purpose of instructing on the duties of castes, localities, and so forth; for even though those duties have visible purposes, they must be performed by the King only if they are not opposed to the Śāstras, and not those that contradict them. For the phrase "the duty of castes and localities" is the remainder of this very verse. In this way, its lack of redundancy (*apaunaruktya*) is to be understood.

As for what he says regarding "that which is practiced by the virtuous"—this is the meaning of the verse. Whatever is practiced in another region by righteous and virtuous people, provided it is not in conflict with the *Śruti* or another *Smṛti*, the king should establish that even in his own region and cause those residing there to follow it. Likewise, whatever is practiced as restricted to a particular family, locality, or time—such as the piercing of the ear and so forth—he should establish that for the entire family. Similarly, whatever custom has been introduced at the time of marriage for a specific caste, such as the suspension of Vedic study (*adhyāya*) and so on, he should establish that for the whole caste. It is for this purpose—the expansion and stabilization of these customs through the support of the king—that the duties of the king are stated here. Now begins the exposition of the judicial procedure (*vyavahāra-darśana*), for which the preliminary definitions have already been established. (8.46)
When urged by the creditor for the sake of recovering the debt, the king shall cause the debtor, once his liability has been proven, to pay the amount due to the creditor. (8.47)

The debtor is the *adharmarṇa*. Who is he? The borrower. For what reason? Because he receives that debt along with its increase (*sopacaya*) as something to be returned; it is difficult to clear and involves much trouble. The creditor, however, is the *uttamarṇa*, because he gives that which is to be received back along with its increase. And for this reason, he is called "superior" (*uttama*) when the debt is being paid. This being so, whether the debt has doubled in time or not, when the debtor, upon being requested, does not pay that debt, then—urged by the creditor for the sake of establishing the claim—the king shall cause the debtor to pay the money to the creditor, or [recover] the debtor from the debtor. This is the general rule for legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). (8.47)
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own wealth, by those very means he should win over and compel the debtor. 8.48.

When urged by the creditor, the king should cause the debtor who has acknowledged the debt to pay by means of conciliation and other such methods; he should not, however, carry out the seizure of his property (tantrotsādana). This is the purpose of the instruction regarding these means. Righteousness (*dharma*) is primary. Thus, because there is no conflict between the two, the king fulfills his duty of showing favor to both parties. These means of compelling payment have been stated in general; they are now specified in detail. (8.48)
One should recover a debt through legal process, through trickery, through customary conduct, and by the application of force as the fifth means. (8.49)

He should cause [the debtor] to pay gradually by means of righteous persuasion (*dharma*) and conciliation (*sāman*), without causing alarm, or by means of an oath (*śapatha*) once there is agreement. If there is still no compliance, he will deal with it through legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), or by gaining his confidence through various kinds of trickery (*chala*), or through customary practice (*ācarita*) such as sitting at the door of his house during meals and other local customs, or even by force (*bala*) such as confining him in his own home—provided that there be no loss of wealth for him due to appearing before the king. And this being so, there is no transgression of *dharma* here, because of this: "If a creditor should recover his property from a debtor by himself..."
He should not be prosecuted by the king; rather, let him recover his wealth himself.

The king shall not prosecute one who, while being confined in his own house or similar circumstances, is performing improper acts; rather, a debtor who has acknowledged the debt should be made to pay it by such means as may be possible. But as for the other—the one who denies the debt when it has been proven by evidence—he shall be made to pay the creditor’s due and a small fine according to his capacity: "But when one denies a debt that has been established by evidence, the king shall compel him to pay the amount to the creditor and a small fine according to his ability. (NSM 8.51)
He will state the fine of one-tenth for one who denies what has been proven by evidence:
"When a debt is admitted as due, he deserves a fine of five percent;
if he denies it, that fine is doubled—such is the ordinance of Manu" (MDh 8.139).

This [penalty], however, is prescribed for the sake of establishing a rule for a virtuous person who is penniless and unable to pay even a tenth part; it is intended merely as a fine. It does not mean that one who is destitute should be abandoned. Furthermore, a *karaṇa* (means of proof) is that which serves as the instrument for reaching a decision regarding a disputed matter, and that is of three kinds. Thus Uśanas recites: "Where there is no written document, no witness (*karaṇa*) exists, and no prior accusation has been stated, there the divine ordeal (*daivī kriyā*) shall take place. Now, since the principles of victory and defeat for the plaintiff and defendant engaged in a lawsuit must be explained, this section is commenced for the purpose of specifying them. 8.51.
When the debtor denies the debt in court upon being told "Pay it," the plaintiff must point out the place [of the transaction] or produce the evidence. (8.52)

Now, the general grounds for victory and defeat for the plaintiff and the defendant engaged in a lawsuit are taught. When the debtor denies having received the object [of a loan]—having been told by the creditor or the judge in the assembly at the place of legal proceedings, and not in casual conversation—"When did you give it?"—the accuser (the creditor) shall point out the place of the transaction. Here, the mention of "place" (*deśa*) is by implication intended to indicate witnesses; thus, the meaning is that he should name those who were present at the time of receiving the object. And this follows from the fact that [the text] says: "Or he may point out the instrument," namely, the document known as a *patra*, at the very place of legal proceedings. From this, it is understood that the mention of "place" is intended to indicate the "instrument. Regarding the phrase "one who establishes the object received," this is the same meaning as the alternative reading. Alternatively, when the debtor denies the debt and the creditor says in the assembly, "I gave it to you," and the debtor replies, "It was given by me," then the accused shall now point out the place. Since the mention of "place" is illustrative, it should also be understood as referring to time: "In what place and at what time was the money returned to me by you? Or, "He may point out the instrument" means he should state the instrument used in establishing the repayment of your money. Or, the term "accused" (*abhiyukta*) should be understood as "the one to be pointed out" (*deśya*); that is, he should describe the manner in which it was received. Everything else is the same in both cases. (8.52)
He who points out that which is not to be pointed out, he who denies after having taught,
and he who does not understand the meanings of what is below and above as they are contested— (8.53)

"He who points out an improper place to the claimant, or an improper object to the defendant; he who, having pointed something out, subsequently denies it; and he who does not comprehend the lower and higher points of the case—whether regarding place or the object itself, or other matters such as time, substance, form, number, and so forth—which are contradictory and inconsistent with what preceded or followed: him one should designate as 'defeated,'" as the author will state concerning either the plaintiff or the other party. (8.53)
He who, having stated and restated his case, then evades it;
or who, when questioned, does not accept a matter that has been correctly established. (8.54)

Having cited an excuse, or that which is to be excused, he then evades; or he speaks otherwise—having cited, "Gold was taken from me by this man," he instead points to his son or servant in another instance. When questioned by the king or the judge regarding such matters as, "At what time or place was a transaction conducted by you?", he does not welcome being properly questioned. Through the investigation [of the case], let there be no concealment of the ultimate truth. (8.54)
He who speaks privately with witnesses in a place where it is not permitted, he who does not wish to answer when questioned, and he who runs away—[these are grounds for defeat]. (8.55)

If he converses privately with witnesses in a secluded spot outside the assembly hall, even he is defeated due to the suspicion that the witnesses may have been suborned. Furthermore, if he does not wish for the witnesses to be questioned—under some pretext related to the lawsuit itself, or by showing favor from the royal administration, or by claiming at the time of questioning that he is occupied with other business, or by departing from the place of legal proceedings, or by showing service to the king—it is said that "therefore he loses the case," as the author will state later. (8.55)

If, when told "Speak!", he does not speak, or if he fails to clarify what has been said, or if he cannot discern the consistency between what precedes and what follows, he is defeated on that point. (8.56)

When told "Speak," he does not speak; at the time of presenting his case, he gives no answer out of fear of defeat. And he does not have it established by witnesses—either because they are unavailable, or because of their lack of desire to testify, or because of their failure to see the matter correctly. Nor does he know what came before or after; that which was stated regarding the witnesses elsewhere in the legal proceeding is precisely what is meant here. Therefore, he loses on account of the facts of the case. (8.56)

"If there are witnesses," having said this, if one who is established in the Dharma, when asked "Point them out," does not point them out, then by these reasons he should be declared to be devoid of truth. (8.57)

When a matter cannot be established by means other than witnesses—such as proofs that demonstrate the claimed fact—in every respect, the witnesses are the refuge. However, if one is found lacking due to the aforementioned grounds for defeat, such as giving false testimony, the judge should declare him defeated, whether he be the plaintiff or the defendant, since the causes of defeat may apply to either side. By these grounds, the judge should recognize him as "defeated"; here, the particle *iti* carries the sense of the word *eva*. This has been explained accordingly. Now, this [verse] is commenced for the purpose of regulating the time for the statements of the plaintiff and the defendant. (8.57)

If the plaintiff does not speak within three fortnights, he shall be punished with a fine according to the law; if he does not state his case within that time, he is defeated in accordance with justice.

If the plaintiff does not speak, he shall not have the lawsuit recorded by the king immediately after reporting his own case; in that case, he would be liable for imprisonment and liable for punishment. Depending on the nature of the meritorious subject matter of the lawsuit, these two [punishments] may be applied individually, optionally, or cumulatively. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), the punishments of corporal punishment and verbal reprimand are also included according to their stated capacity. Here, a reconciliation should be understood as occurring when one has been defeated according to the law (*dharmataḥ*) due to a transgression of merits, because of being "with a pretext" (*sopadhātva*) due to some other cause, since the claimant must indeed be one whose purpose is well-established. Now, if by some other means of proof this person is known to be straightforward and without a pretext, then this matter of corporal punishment and so forth should not apply. Thus it has been said: "For one who is defeated regarding the law, there is no other way for the defendant. Now, a time for response other than the time for the claimant is specified: "If he does not speak within three fortnights"—the meaning is "he should respond. Therefore, he is to be bound and punished according to the law, having been defeated regarding the law, and not otherwise; this was what was stated. Now, this verse is commenced for the purpose of regulating the punishment of the claimant or the defendant who has been victorious. (8.58)

Whether as a plaintiff or a defendant, whoever conceals a matter or speaks falsely regarding its extent, those two, being ignorant of dharma, shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount. (8.59)

Therefore, from a denial following a false accusation, the king shall cause the one who brings a false charge and the one who denies the claim—provided they acknowledge something with a supporting instruction—to pay double that amount. This section is now stated for the purpose of defining witnesses. 8.59.

But one who, having been questioned by a seeker of wealth while remaining steadfast, denies [the debt], must be proven [guilty] by three witnesses of the previous generation in the presence of the king and Brahmins. (8.60)
Since the status of a witness for a single person is prohibited, the status of two as witnesses will follow by implication from the exclusion of three; it does not apply solely to three. (8.60)
I shall now fully describe what kind of witnesses should be appointed by wealthy men in legal proceedings, and how the truth must be spoken by them. (8.61)

And while the characteristics of witnesses are being stated in relation to financial transactions, they should be understood as being of this same nature in other legal proceedings as well, due to the similarity of the matter and the absence of contradiction. (8.61)

Householders who have sons, who are native-born, belonging to the kṣatriya, vaiśya, or śūdra castes, and who are possessed of wealth—such persons, provided they are not in distress, are worthy of giving testimony; not just anyone at all. (8.62)

Since the testimony of a *śrotriya* is prohibited, it is understood that a Brāhmaṇa who is not a *śrotriya* may serve as a witness. Since those of the lowest castes are prohibited, it follows that Śūdras of both low and high standing are included [among those disqualified]. (8.62)
Trustworthy persons from all castes should be made witnesses in legal matters;
they must be knowledgeable in all affairs and free from greed, while those who are the opposite should be avoided. (8.63)

"But one should avoid those who are perverted"—this is a restatement of what is already established by the sense of the matter, made for the sake of emphasis due to the nature of the statement. And because all castes are mentioned here, the status of even a Brāhmaṇa as a witness is understood; however, because of the prohibition regarding one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), this applies to others. (8.63)
In another legal proceeding, those who have a financial interest in the case, friends, companions, enemies,
or those whose faults are known should not be appointed as false witnesses.
Neither those afflicted by disease nor those who are defiled [should be initiated]. || 8.64 ||

For according to their own tradition, they would not exist in either case by the authority of their Smṛti; moreover, because of the prohibition based on a specific cause, one who is not afflicted would be considered afflicted, and even one defiled by accusations of mortal or minor sins would not be so. (8.64)
A king shall not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor a Vedic scholar, nor one dwelling in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments. (8.65)

The prohibition against a king acting as a witness—even for the purpose of establishing the truth—is due to the suspicion that he might favor one side, and because his silence would lead to the ruin of the common people. Alternatively, the prohibition is because a king residing in the same territory is not independent. Or else, it is improper for a king who oversees legal proceedings to act as a witness. Artisans are constantly occupied with their work, and actors are frequently away from home; furthermore, because they have connections with all parts of the countryside, there is a suspicion that they might speak falsely, which would result in sin for them. For a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), the prohibition is due to the fear that his religious duties might be obstructed and the fear of the hardship involved in being summoned. By this, the case of one living in a religious order (*liṅgastha*) is explained. Moreover, if he is fraudulent (*sopadha*), his exclusion is even more strictly justified. Because he is beloved by the people, he might be swayed by other improper motives. (8.65)
Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
neither an old man, nor a child, nor one who is alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties. (8.66)

One who is *adhyadhīna* is a slave from birth (*garbhadāsa*), because he is entirely dependent on another. It should also be stated that those who are subject to discipline include those with physical deformities (*aṅgavyasana*) and those afflicted by leprosy and similar diseases; for even in another birth, there is a suspicion of such defects. Thus, the author will later state that this applies to one whose karma remains unexhausted. A *dasyu* is a slave (*dāsa*); he is so called because he brings others near to his own tasks or because he exhausts their labor. Furthermore, a *dasyu* is a thief. He is not merely one who performs forbidden acts (*vikarmakṛt*), because the latter is simply unrighteous. The prohibition regarding the elderly and the infant is due to their having passed beyond or not yet reached the capacity for legal transaction (*vyavahāra*). The prohibition of a single person as a witness is established by the rule "by three or more" (*tryaparaiḥ*); since this verse provides a specific exception even for a single person, the previous verse is considered optional. This present verse, however, serves as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to what was prohibited. The author will later state, "But a single person may be a witness if he is free from greed," thereby permitting the testimony of a single individual. An *antya* is a Śūdra; since he is subject to both injunctions and prohibitions, his status as a witness is optional depending on his qualities. Alternatively, the *antya* is a Caṇḍāla; for the author will later say, "Women shall give evidence for women," and after mentioning Śūdras, "for the lowest castes, those of the lowest birth. Or it may refer to any outcaste from the four castes (*varṇāpasada*). One with impaired senses is prohibited because of his lack of full consciousness. (8.66)
Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane; neither one oppressed by hunger or thirst, nor afflicted by fatigue, nor tormented by passion, nor angry, nor even a thief. (8.67)

"Afflicted" means one who is distressed by the death of a kinsman or similar causes; thus, he is distinct from those afflicted by the aforementioned diseases. "Intoxicated" and "insane" are well known; so too is one "tormented by hunger and thirst. "Angry" refers to one whose conduct is unreliable due to a disposition toward wrath. A "thief" should be understood, according to the maxim of the cow and the bull, as one who performs forbidden acts (*vikarmakṛt*), as indicated by the instruction [in the preceding verse]. (8.67)
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men; virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of low birth for those of low birth. (8.68)

In legal transactions concerning property, those of sound character who are similar to the parties in terms of caste and other attributes may serve as witnesses; these include the original borrowers, others related to the matter, or even ascetics, renunciants, merchants, actors, cowherds, and so forth, by virtue of their similarity [to the parties]. Thus, since this [text] is intended for illustration, one should understand the general designation "those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes" to be inclusive. However, in matters other than legal transactions concerning property—anyone who has personal knowledge may give testimony for the litigants.
Whether within the house or in the forest, or even when the body itself is in peril. (8.69)
In a matter that is urgent, even one who is otherwise disqualified may give testimony within the house and similar locations. And so it is said:
"In the absence [of other witnesses], even women, children, the elderly, a pupil, a relative, a slave, or a hired servant may perform the legal business. (8.70)

The purpose [of this verse] is precisely to set aside the [general] similarity [rule]. This being so, just as women and others may sometimes be witnesses even in the absence of similarity—being indeed dissimilar—so too should the witnesshood of children and others, though otherwise prohibited, be understood to apply in certain disputes. Furthermore, regarding those not mentioned here in this verse but who are among the prohibited, such as children, their re-admission as witnesses should be understood from the fact that this instruction is intended to provide a specific exception for them. [Objection: But surely, it is not logical to again prescribe the witnesshood of children and others who have been prohibited on account of specific causes, since the reasons for the prohibition remain in force. (8.70)
To clarify this inference, he said:
"One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, and the sick, when testifying falsely, as well as that of those with agitated minds, is unstable. (8.71)

By what means? By inference for the purpose of distinguishing between truth and falsehood; and it has been stated: "One should discern [the truth] by external signs," and so forth, as well as "Just as one leads [by] drops of blood," and so on. Thus, the instruction regarding inference has this meaning: if, in the absence of the aforementioned witnesses, even those witnesses who are prohibited in cases of *sāhasa* (heinous crimes) and the like become available, they are purified by inference, and sometimes even those who are not prohibited. And this being the case—in all cases of *sāhasa*, theft (*steya*), and *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual offenses).
And in cases of verbal or physical assault, one should not examine witnesses.

In cases such as the tearing of clothes, the lighting of torches, or the cutting of hair—acts arising from anger or impulsiveness—a man who provides no testimony regarding them [is not a witness]. Theft and similar acts are well known. In such matters, one should not examine a witness by means of the defining characteristics such as "householders who have sons. However, they must indeed be examined by inference through their capacity, such as their connection to the matter at hand. Even those who are prohibited [from being witnesses] must be examined as witnesses by means of inference. Thus, the instruction on inference here becomes meaningful, as has been stated. But where there is a conflict among witnesses of equal qualities, in that case—

In a conflict between witnesses, O King, the ruler should accept the majority; but if they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and if their virtues are equal, he should accept the best among the twice-born.

This same principle applies when there is a failure to follow the prescribed rule. Regarding inference as previously described, he will also mention in some cases even oaths and the like: "But in matters where there are no witnesses... one may also cause [the truth] to be obtained by means of an oath. Furthermore, "the blessed Dharma is ever awake"; it reveals itself for some reason even when there is equality [of the parties]. The phrase "the best of the twice-born" is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding the witnesshood of Brāhmaṇas; thus it has been said: "Trustworthy persons among all castes. Nor is the use of the word "all" intended merely to restate the castes already mentioned; rather, it is for the purpose of indicating the Brāhmaṇa caste. And having established such indicative marks in this way, there follows the prohibition of the *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas). 8.73.
Testimony is established by seeing or hearing in person;
by speaking the truth therein, a witness does not fall away from dharma or worldly prosperity. (8.74)

The status of being a witness is established through seeing and hearing, not by virtue of a formal obligation. Therefore, one may indeed be a witness even without such an obligation; however, this is the rule for witnesses: even when questioned under obligation, one must speak the truth. For: "If a witness, in an assembly of noble men, speaks otherwise than what was seen or heard, he goes headfirst to hell after death and is excluded from heaven. (8.75)

It has been stated that one is not merely deprived of heaven through the non-arising of merit; this is indeed an explanatory supplement (arthavāda) to the preceding verse, and thus this meaning has already been demonstrated by the context. Furthermore, the establishment of witness-status results from seeing and hearing, not from a formal record. 8.75
Even where one might see or hear something without being appointed [as a witness], if questioned thereon, one should speak exactly as it was seen and exactly as it was heard. (8.76)
This verse is for the purpose of conclusion. 8.76.

Only a single witness who is free from greed may be accepted, even if he is capable and pure; but women are not [eligible], because of the instability of the female intellect, nor indeed those others who are tainted by faults. (8.77)

Even though one person has been excluded, this [statement] is for the purpose of permitting those who are free from greed on account of their superior qualities. Furthermore, the word "api" (even/also) should be understood in both instances—as in "even if they are pure" and "even if he is not greedy. Or rather, this very [rule] implies that even a single person who is not greedy may not be a witness. And this commencement is for the sake of a subsequent distinction: just as a single person, even if not greedy, may not be [a witness], so too many women, even if pure, may not be [witnesses]; for their intellect has an unstable connection with dharma and artha. The explanation that this is for the purpose of permitting these two—namely, one who is not greedy or one who is excluded due to greed—is not very clever, because it contradicts the treatise (*śāstra*), since the prohibition applies equally to men and women elsewhere as well. This being the case, many women, even if pure and not greedy, would not be [witnesses] according to the context, as it has been stated that the intellect of women is unstable. As for men who are overwhelmed by faults and vices, they are prohibited even if they are not greedy; how much more so, then, in other cases? And the purpose for which this repetition was made has already been explained here. (8.77)
Whatever they may say by their very nature should be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak for the sake of Dharma is useless. || 8.78 ||

Regarding the phrase "by their very nature": in an assembly, because of the timidity of villagers and others, trembling, loss of eloquence, and so forth arise. When these people speak in legal proceedings, their true nature must be discerned through inference or by observing their character—whether these tremblings and other symptoms are caused by falsehood, or rather by timidity, or by the presence of a great multitude to whom they are unaccustomed. For there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be reached through inference. In this same way, the true nature of those who are bold and confident must also be ascertained. (8.78)
Within the assembly, the presiding judge, consoling them, shall examine all witnesses in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant according to this rule: [8.79]

Now, hereafter will follow the rules for the examination of witnesses so that they may speak the truth. The *prāḍvivāka*—whether a Brāhmaṇa or a king’s appointed official—is one who knows the law; he is not necessarily the king himself, though the term applies to him by virtue of his authority. As the author will state later: "Whatever the minister or the *prāḍvivāka* should do in a legal matter otherwise... [referring to Pāṇini 3.2.178: *kvibvacipracchyāyatastukaṭaprujuśrīṇāṃ dīrgho 'prasāraṇaṃ ca*, by which the suffix *kvip* is applied]. He is called *prāṭ* because he asks (*pṛcchati*), and *vivākaḥ* because, having asked, he specifically declares [the truth] regarding difficult points of law (*dharma-saṃkaṭeṣu*). Thus, a *prāḍvivāka* is both an inquirer and a declarer. This *prāḍvivāka*, being a Brāhmaṇa learned in the law, should examine the witnesses according to the following procedure, conciliating them without harshness. For what reason? So that the witness, remaining in his natural state, may speak the truth. (8.79)
"Whatever wealth belongs to these two, and whatever was done between them in this matter, declare all that with truth; for you are the witnesses here. (8.80)
This being so, this statement regarding truthful speech is now explained as a figurative eulogy (arthavāda). || 8.80 ||
A witness who speaks the truth in testimony attains abundant worlds;
he also gains unsurpassed fame in this world, for such speech is honored by Brahman.

This praise for truthful speech is based on its connection to both visible and invisible results. It is not merely that by failing to speak the truth this aforementioned [benefit] does not occur; rather, there is also another consequence, namely demerit (pratyavāya). He demonstrates this as follows: || 8.81 ||
A man who speaks falsely when giving testimony is bound by the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred lifetimes, rendered helpless; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony. 8.82.
Because—the witness is honored by truth; dharma increases through truth.
Therefore, truth indeed must be spoken by witnesses among all social classes. 8.83
By which—
for the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self;
for this reason—
Do not despise yourself, the supreme witness of men. (8.84)

"Indeed, the evildoers think: 'No one sees us'"; by the context here, those who speak untruth are called "evildoers. However, by implication, this refers to everyone who commits a transgression—"the gods see them, as does the inner person within oneself. (8.85)
They are called "gods" (devas) thus: heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, sun, fire, night, the two twilights, and Dharma—these know the conduct of all embodied beings. (8.86)

The inner person, the knower of his own field, the inner controller, is the Supreme Self. And thus, no one at all would commit even a secret sin. Since this is so, therefore the rule for them is stated:
"O twice-born ones, in the presence of gods and Brahmins, let the pure [judge] question the pure [witnesses] regarding the truth in the forenoon, facing either north or east. (8.87)
And just as they are to be questioned, so too is this scripture—which establishes the restrictive rules concerning the basis of birth, such as the Brahmin caste and so forth—being spoken. 8.87.
One should ask the Brāhmaṇa, "Speak"; the king, "Speak the truth";
the Vaiśya, with [threats of] cattle, grain, and gold; and the Śūdra, with these [same] sins.

Inquiries concerning a sin are designated by the term "sin" (*pātaka*), meaning they are for the purpose of prohibiting false testimony. This is another illustration of the Brahmin’s role as a witness. (8.88)
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and those for the killer of women and children,
and for the betrayer of friends and the ungrateful— those shall be the fate of one who speaks falsely.
"Whatever merit you have performed, O gentle one, from the time of your birth—should you speak otherwise, all of that would go to a dog. (8.90)
"O virtuous one, as for this self that you consider to be 'I am alone,' this sage who observes merit and demerit is ever-present within your heart. (8.91)
The god Yama Vaivasvata, who dwells here within your heart—
if you have no dispute with him, then go neither to the Gaṅgā nor to the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, and tormented by hunger and thirst, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy as a beggar. (8.93)
Headlong into blind darkness shall the sinner go to hell, who, when questioned during a legal determination, speaks falsely in response to a query. (8.94)
That man who, having entered the assembly, speaks of a matter that is not witnessed and which is deficient in its meaning, eats fish along with thorns like a blind man. 8.95.
For the gods know no other person in this world to be more excellent than that learned man whose speech the Knower of the Field does not distrust. 8.96

There are eight verses concerning the application of oaths for Śūdras. Thus, through these various modes of explaining the meaning of the statements, the purpose of speaking the truth is accomplished, just as it is for the applications of oaths for the Brāhmaṇa and other castes. (8.89–96)
Hear now, gentle one, in due order and according to their number, how many kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely in testimony concerning each of them.

Now this section is commenced for the purpose of defining the duration of time regarding false witnesses; it is intended for all classes of witnesses by implication, not for Śūdras alone on account of the context. Therefore, this verse is begun for the sake of focusing the minds of everyone. How so? So that witnesses, having heard this [concerning] the extremely great sin resulting from speaking falsely, might refrain from lying, being firmly resolved in their minds. (8.97)
One kills five by lying regarding cattle, ten by lying regarding horses, a hundred by lying regarding elephants, and a thousand by lying regarding humans. (9.98)
Regarding those that come before and after: as for what he says—"One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold kills both the born and the unborn;
one kills everything by lying regarding land; therefore, do not speak falsely regarding land"—(8.99).

"But surely this Vedic text is contradicted: 'No mortal whatsoever is able to give me [the earth]. Therefore, there is an absence of ownership; from that absence, there is an absence of legal transactions; and consequently, in the absence of such disputes, there is no fault of falsehood for the witnesses. That is not so, because of a misunderstanding of the meaning. For the meaning here is not that "no one is capable of giving the whole [earth] due to the impossibility of victory"; rather, it is because of the force of the scriptural undertaking which demonstrates the merits and defects regarding the giving, seizing, and false testimony [concerning land]. Thus Vyāsa and others say: "The giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years; the seizer and the one who consents to the seizure shall dwell in hell for exactly those many years. Some hold that giving, seizing, and so forth refer only to the *bhūmicchala* (fraudulent claims regarding land). But that must be examined. According to the Mīmāṃsā system, however, it is stated: "Land cannot [be given], because it is common to all, being undifferentiated with respect to all the injunctions of subsidiary qualities (*guṇavidhi*) intended for sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). For a quality is prescribed regarding the substances of the sacrificial fee: "They lead the sacrificial fee between the *sadas* and the *patnīśālā*. And this injunction of a quality is absolutely impossible in the case of the entire earth. Therefore, by this very fact, the fault of seizure would apply elsewhere as well. And thus, in a dispute over it, the fault of falsehood for the witnesses is established. Furthermore, since the earth is the cause of every action, it is said that "in falsehood regarding it, one destroys everything. Thus, through the personification of the Earth, the Smṛti respectfully forbids one: "Do not speak falsely regarding land. (9.99)
Regarding women's enjoyment and sexual intercourse, as well as aquatic gems and all those made of stone, they say: "It is like [throwing] earth into water. (8.100)
As with cattle, so it is with honey and ghee; as with horses, so it is with vehicles;
as with cows, so it is indeed with silver, garments, grain, and even with Brahmins. (8.101)
Having thus considered all the faults in speaking untruth, speak the truth directly, exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen. (8.102)

These five verses are common to all witnesses; they are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) intended to prohibit false testimony and to instill a sense of aversion toward it, not injunctions regarding rewards. For [if they were injunctions], there would result the fallacies of "acquiring what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*). Furthermore, in that case, the authority of the scripture (*śāstra*) with respect to each individual person would be undermined, and it would become purposeless. Since the purposefulness of the scripture consists in the fact that one experiences the fruits of one's own performed actions, these verses must be understood as merely explanatory statements for the sake of prohibition, due to their contradiction with both the scripture and logic. (8.100–102)
One should treat Brahmins who are cattle-herders, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers just as one would Śūdras. (8.103)

This is an exception to the rule regarding the administration of oaths to Brahmins, based on the context. Because of the statement, "But for a Śūdra, by these [oaths] involving sins," the administration of oaths to those such as cowherds and others occurs only when they are actually Brahmins. Thus, they should not behave like Śūdras in other circumstances; otherwise, the context would be contradicted. (8.103)
When a man speaks thus regarding matters of dharma, even though he knows otherwise, he does not fall from the heavenly world; they call that the speech of the gods. (8.104)

The judge, when addressing the interrogation of Śūdras in legal matters concerning property, is not joined with unrighteousness by interrogating them according to their respective castes—even though he knows that among Brāhmaṇas who are cattle-herders and the like, this would be otherwise. For Manu and others, recollecting that divine speech which is consistent with the scriptures, have declared: "One should treat Brāhmaṇas like Śūdras. This is an explanatory praise (arthavāda) for the rule immediately following. (8.104)

In cases where the death of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa would result from speaking the truth, one should speak an untruth; for in such a case, that [falsehood] is considered superior. (8.105)

This exception regarding truthful speech is for a specific reason and for the sake of showing respect for the Veda. The inclusion of Śūdras and others by way of inverse order (prātilomya) is for the purpose of permitting untruth; however, this reliance on the rule is justified because it serves to prevent the utterance of untruth in general. If that is so, then only a prohibition of truth should be stated here, rather than a permission for untruth. But even so, the permission for untruth is indeed established for this purpose. It is not that its utterance is ever permitted as a matter of course. Now, one might object: since the scripture functions for the benefit of man, an instruction intended to cause sin (pratyavāya) is not logical. On the contrary, precisely because it functions for the benefit of man, this instruction is appropriate, both in view of the occasional necessity of speaking untruth and in consideration of the duty of favoring a person. Furthermore, it is understood from the force of the instruction that this permission for untruth applies specifically to righteous persons. Thus, another Smṛti states: "There is no fault in speaking untruth if life depends upon it, but not if it is for the livelihood of a wicked person. Therefore, this transgression of speaking untruth is resorted to for the sake of avoiding a great sin. This [present verse] is commenced for the purpose of providing an expiation (prāyaścitta) for that act. (8.105)
They should worship Sarasvatī with oblations of cooked rice (caru) dedicated to Speech as the deity, thereby effecting the supreme expiation for that sin of falsehood. (8.106)

They should worship Sarasvatī with this hymn of eight verses beginning, "I move with the Rudras and the Vasus. There is a triple repetition of the sacrificial oblation (*caru*), because the injunction does not specify a particular plurality, just as in the case of the rule: "One sacrifices *kapiñjala* birds to Spring. (8.106)
Or he should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud," which is addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses whose deity is the Waters.

The mention of "taking fire" (*agnigrahaṇa*) should be understood as intended to specify a particular type of fire, even though it is already established by the term "offers" (*juhoti*). And this [penance] is optional in relation to the previously mentioned expiation. Furthermore, regarding the subsequent [case]: "If a man who is not ill fails to give testimony concerning debts and other matters within three fortnights, he shall incur that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth in accordance with the truth. (8.108)

One should cause the witness to pay a tenth part of the value of the property involved in the lawsuit, by means of which the witness—remaining healthy—does not state one side even after three fortnights. Even after having fined that witness, the judge should continue the hearing of the case, because it remains unfinished; however, in cases other than those concerning debt, the witness should be fined in proportion to the value of the matter at issue. (8.108)
If, within seven days, disease, fire, or the death of a relative should befall a witness who has given his testimony, he shall be made to pay the fine and the debt. (8.109)

If, within seven days, a witness is proven to have given false testimony by the observation of illness or other misfortunes occurring among his family members, he shall be punished immediately; he shall be made to pay whatever sum he caused [the debtor] to be compelled to pay through that falsehood, and he shall also be fined. However, in the case of a debt dispute, this applies elsewhere according to the requirements of the legal treatises. Thus, both [penalties] are to be applied when witnesses give false testimony. In lawsuits where there are no witnesses, the decision is thus based on the evidence of divine or inferential signs. (8.109)
But in matters where there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another,
if he cannot discover the truth in its actual state, he should cause it to be established even by means of an oath.
In order to praise truth, a narrative from a former age (purākalpa) is cited as an explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the purpose of encouraging the performance of prescribed duties. 8.110.
Oaths have been taken by great seers and gods for the sake of accomplishing their purposes;
even Vasiṣṭha swore an oath before the king, the son of Pijavana.

Other great sages have likewise spoken; for instance, Vyāsa related the narrative of the oath beginning with the words, "He who steals your lotus. And thus, with regard to the avoidance of falsehood and unrighteousness:
"A wise man should not take a false oath even for a small matter;
for by taking a false oath, one perishes both in this world and after death. (8.112)

And although this censure of false oaths, by demonstrating the resulting transgression, aims at the avoidance of what is prohibited, it also serves the purpose of praising truthful oaths; thus there is no contradiction. Since it follows by implication that this false oath is a cause of transgression in all cases, this [verse] is commenced as an exception (*apavāda*) for those instances where its status as a cause of transgression is not desired. (8.112)
In matters concerning women, at weddings, regarding cattle, food, or fuel, as well as in assisting a Brāhmaṇa and in taking an oath, there is no sin. 8.113.

The meaning is that when a false oath is taken by a woman in love during a pursuit according to the arts of love (*kāmatantra*), for the purpose of fulfilling a promised object, there is no sin therein. Likewise, in the case of a marriage where there is doubt as to whether it has been performed or not, or during a legal proceeding, [there is no sin], because the capacity for the settlement of the matter depends solely on the cows, even when the accusation involves the theft of fodder belonging to those cows who are part of the ritual act. And similarly, in an accusation involving the false oath regarding the theft of firewood for the sacred fires according to the scriptures, there is no unrighteousness (*adharma*), since righteousness and unrighteousness are defined solely by the scriptures. However, if the theft of the cow's fodder or the firewood is proven through other means, then punishment shall be meted out according to the scriptures. And in that case, for a Brāhmaṇa, the same would apply if he accepts the physical ordeal; it is not that everyone must accept the ordeal, but rather it should be administered to one who acts with justice. From this, it is understood that for anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa, [the ordeal] applies even to one who acts with justice, due to the capacity for undertaking it. Having thus established the practice of taking a true oath, the specific oaths are now described according to their essential nature in connection with the particular castes. (8.113)
One should curse a Brahmin by means of truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicles and weapons, a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all sins.

In a case where there are no witnesses, for the purpose of ascertaining the truth, he shall cause the accused members of the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, to swear by these following oaths according to their respective instructions. || 8.114 ||
One should cause fire to be brought for him, or have him submerged in water; or else, one should have his sons and wife touch his head individually. 8.115.

In the case of a Śūdra, even the fire and other requirements may be provided according to his means. The same applies to oaths. In that regard, concerning the carrying of fire, the rule regarding the number of steps and the number of *aśvattha* leaves used as an interval would apply based on the expectation of another *Smṛti*; here, there is no specific statement because it is a supplementary injunction and because the tradition of the *Smṛtis* remains uninterrupted. Likewise, the time for immersion in water is determined by the same principle. (8.115)
He whom the kindled fire does not burn, nor do the waters cause to float, and who quickly meets no misfortune—he should be known as pure in his oath. 8.116.

Suffering (*ārti*)—characterized by illness, fire, the death of a relative, and so forth—is distinct [from the aforementioned results] due to the force of the separate instruction. This was stated previously: "If, within seven days, disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman should be seen for the witness who has uttered the statement. Now, one might object: that [statement] was intended to demonstrate the falsehood of the witness; however, because the causes are the same, it should also serve here to demonstrate the falsity of the oath. Since no other suffering is specified here, it is understood to be that very [suffering]. On this point, someone says: "The fire called *iddha* will not burn, nor will the waters cause submersion"—this contradicts what is observed. For a change in the nature of a great element (*mahābhūta*) is never perceived without a cause, since they lack consciousness. Such a change occurs through mantras or medicinal herbs, but those are not present here. Indeed, in this case, this change in the nature of the fire and water, brought about by the employment of a truthful oath, would occur due to a specific cause. Because they possess divine essence (*devatattva*), this change at this particular time would be specifically caused, since their lack of consciousness renders them without agency. Victory follows from the opposite of that [falsehood], and defeat otherwise; this is what is to be established. Do these two [results] occur due to the smallness or greatness of the intervening period, or are they produced by fate (*daiva*)? This is inconsistent, because even when the intervening periods are equal, these two results are observed. Therefore, these two should not be understood as being caused by such disparity. Furthermore, since both [results] are observed through the touching of a heated iron ball with the tongue, the purpose of these two acts of speech is not merely to intimidate. How indeed might this person proceed without fear? Moreover, as for what is said: if this were merely a figurative statement for the sake of intimidation, then the statement "the fire did not burn even a hair" would be meaningless. Otherwise, if the rule for carrying the fire were being established, the mention of the non-burning of a hair would be useless, since there is an absence of hair on the palms of the hands. Furthermore, when the fire-carrying is actually witnessed, some connection with fire must occur in some way; thus, in this context, the word "hair" (*roma*) does not denote its literal meaning, but is used figuratively to conform to common worldly usage, due to the force of what was stated. Therefore, just like false testimony by a witness or a false oath, the carrying of fire and submersion in water should be understood in the same manner. (8.116)
For in the past, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother, the fire—the spy of the world—did not burn even a single hair of his because of his truthfulness. (8.117)

This composition is intended for the purpose of the injunctions and explanatory passages (arthavādas) that have been authorized. Some maintain that, because of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the phrase "for when a calf has been accused," this oath belongs to one who is accused; and thus, they argue, this would not be an oath for a Śūdra. Rather, on account of this indicative mark, this [oath] would belong to a Brāhmaṇa alone; yet this is not desired. Therefore, by the force of the scripture, just as it is heard to apply to a Brāhmaṇa, so too does it apply to a Śūdra. Thus, the scriptural mention regarding accusation applies elsewhere as well. The meaning of "the spy of the world goes forth" is based on the scriptural passage: "May your honor move about here as our spy. (8.117)
In whatever legal dispute a false witness has been employed, that very matter shall be reversed; even if it has been finalized, it shall be as if unperformed. (8.118)

If one desists when half the testimony has been completed, it shall be as if ungiven, even if the punishment has already been imposed. This being so, that testimony must be examined again because of the rule regarding desisting. And furthermore:
"Testimony is declared to be false due to greed, delusion, fear, friendship, lust, anger, as well as ignorance and childishness. (8.119)
This specification of the cause for speaking untruth is intended to determine a particular punishment. (8.119)
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for one who gives false testimony in any of these cases. (8.120)

For taking [property] out of greed, one should be fined a thousand; for out of delusion, the first amercement; for out of fear, two middle amercements; and for out of friendship, four times the first amercement. (8.121)
From desire, the former [retribution] is tenfold; from anger, the latter is threefold.
From ignorance, there are two full hundreds; from childishness, however, it is exactly one hundred.
The wise have declared these punishments for false testimony, intended to ensure that justice does not fail and to restrain unrighteousness. (8.123)

The three verses [8.120–123] concern the determination of punishment. Regarding what was stated concerning false testimony by witnesses—namely, "one thousand" and "one hundred"—it is said here with reference to that, or rather, as a modification thereof. Thus, he will specifically explain everything regarding the application of the first, middle, and highest fines. 8.120–123.
A righteous king, having punished them with a fine, shall banish members of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony; however, he shall exile a Brāhmaṇa. 8.124.

[The punishments for those who speak falsehood once have been stated previously]; however, for those who habitually give false testimony, this is the punishment for the three castes according to the scriptures: banishment and execution, as these are defined in other treatises; and here, because of that habitual practice, only expulsion is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa alone, according to the rule: "One should cause the Brāhmaṇa to be exiled. The meaning is that one should deprive him of his house. And in the former sense, the word *pravāsana* (banishment) refers specifically to the expulsion of the Brāhmaṇa. 9.124.
Manu, the son of the Self-Existent, has declared ten places for punishment; these may be applied to the three social orders, but a Brahmin shall depart unhurt. (8.125)
There are ten constituent parts of the staff; they are as follows: || 8.125 ||
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body. (8.126)

For the offense of sexual misconduct, one should inflict punishment upon the genitals alone; one should not administer flogging or other forms of corporal punishment upon any other limb besides that. For an offense regarding food, the punishment of the stomach is the prohibition of food. For the offense of verbal abuse, it concerns the tongue; for assault, the hands; for an offense involving the feet, the feet; and for an offense involving the eyes, the eyes. Likewise for the nose and the ears. For the theft of wealth, the punishment concerns the wealth; and for offenses against the body, one should apply a disciplinary measure such as cutting, directed at the offender's own body. Regarding this, however, the author will state elsewhere: "by whichever limb [the crime was committed] and in whatever manner. Furthermore, the "seizure of wealth" mentioned here should be understood as referring to cases such as the misappropriation of deposits, so as not to be redundant with the punishments prescribed for thieves. Moreover, even when punishing those deserving of punishment, one should not seize the root of their livelihood; rather— || 8.126 ||

Having fully understood the consequences, as well as the place and time in their true nature, and having considered both the strength of the offender and the gravity of the offense, he should inflict punishment upon those deserving of it. (8.127)

"Having fully understood the *anubandha* (consequence). Some here say that this refers to the repetition of the commission of a transgression, characterized by the habitual practice of performing such acts. We, however, declare that *anubandha* means the cause of the offense. How is it "bound by" (*anubadhyate*)? That by which one is bound is the *anubandha*, namely the factors such as greed and so forth. What is that? It is the offense, such as theft and the like. Having fully understood that—whether this offense of theft and so forth was committed by him out of desire, or out of anger, or out of greed, or out of delusion; or whether it was for the sake of maintaining his own family, or for the sake of favoring the system of Dharma—in this way. The purpose of knowing this *anubandha*, which is the cause of the offense, is so that there may be a specific punishment according to its distinctions. And the phrase "having fully understood the place and time in their true nature" carries over from the previous verse. In that regard, the specification of the house, the street, the threshing floor, the field, one's own territory, another's territory, and so forth, must be taken into account regarding the offense. Likewise, the time: whether it was a time of plenty or famine, whether the country was disturbed or peaceful, the age and condition [of the offender], and so on. The "substance" (*sāra*) of the offense consists of the object, the lineage, and so forth; and its opposite is the "insubstantial" (*asāra*). The mention of "substance" is for the sake of illustration. And having considered the offense in terms of its gravity or lightness, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally, or involving cloth, gold, and so forth, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of it, taking into account the place and other factors; for otherwise, there would be a failure of justice for him—(8.127).
Unjust punishment destroys fame and ruins reputation; it also prevents one from attaining heaven in the next world. Therefore, one should avoid it. 8.128.
One should diligently impose punishment in consideration of the place and other such factors; this being the case, the following rule for the sequence of its application is taught: || 8.128 ||
One should first impose the punishment of verbal censure, and immediately after that, the punishment of "fie" (reproach).
Third is the punishment of fines, and beyond that, the punishment of corporal death. (8.129)

This determination of punishment shall proceed according to the sequence of offenses. And here, "killing" (vadha) refers to striking, not to execution, as is evident from the context. Thus he demonstrates: || 8.129 ||
But when he is unable to restrain them even by execution because they are incorrigible, then he should employ all these four measures against them. (8.130)

Even when corporal punishment has been inflicted, if the offender does not desist from his transgression, then the full fourfold set of punishments beginning with verbal reprimand (*vāgdaṇḍa*) is to be applied; he must not be released on the grounds that he has already been punished for his offense, so as to maintain order in the world. Otherwise, the law of the fishes (*mātsyanyāya*) would prevail. Furthermore, this renewed undertaking is for the purpose of imposing a monetary fine (*dhanadaṇḍa*), since who would voluntarily inflict the mild punishments of verbal or light corporal reprimands? Accordingly, in another section, he will state this very sequence: "In the first seizure of a pickpocket, one should have his fingers amputated; in the second, his hand and foot; in the third, he deserves death. (8.130)
I shall explain in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold that are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.
The instruction regarding a substance of a specific genus and measure is for the purpose of designation and for the sake of specifying a particular staff. 8.131.
Eight *trasareṇu*s should be known as one *likṣā* in measure;
three of those are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*. (8.132)
Six mustard seeds make one medium barleycorn; three barleycorns make one kṛṣṇala;
five kṛṣṇalas make one māṣa; and sixteen of those make one suvarṇa. (8.133)
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*; ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together are to be known as one silver *māṣaka*. (8.134)
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* make one *purāṇa*;
furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*, or a *paṇa*. 8.135.
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one *śatamāna* of silver; a *niṣka* of gold should be understood by its measure to consist of four [such *śatamānas*]. (8.136)
Two hundred and fifty *paṇas* is declared to be the first *sāhasa* fine; five hundred is to be known as the middle, and one thousand is indeed the highest. (8.137)

These verses concern the meaning of all conventional designations (*saṃjñā*). In that regard, those particles of dust seen by the rays of the sun within these enclosed huts and monasteries—three of those constitute one *trasareṇu*. (8.132–127)
When a debt is admitted as due, the debtor deserves a fine of five percent;
if he denies it, that fine shall be double—such is the ordinance of Manu. (8.138)

In a dispute concerning debt, one who confesses it himself shall pay a twentieth part; one who is made to admit it by means of witnesses and other evidence shall pay a tenth part; and one who is unable to pay shall pay a small fraction of the fine, or whatever little [he can]. This has been stated previously: "And a small fraction of the fine according to his ability. These three are the fines for the debtor (adhamarṇa). As for those who cause the creditor (uttamarṇa) to receive a tenth part and the debtor to pay another fine based on other Smṛti texts, they cause these to be paid. However, this is the view of Manu. (8.138)
A moneylender may stipulate the interest ordained by Vasiṣṭha, which increases wealth;
he may take one-eightieth part of a hundred per month. (8.139)
The first part, consisting of eighty [verses], is the section on the increase of wealth for one who has applied himself to his purpose. 8.139.
Remembering the duty of the virtuous, one may take two per cent;
for by taking two per cent, one does not become a sinner regarding wealth. (8.140)
The fiftieth part is the secondary rule (anukalpa). || 8.140 ||
One may take interest of two, three, four, five, or a hundred percent per month, according to the order of the social classes. (8.141)

And this is the third *kalpa* according to the sequence of castes (*varṇa*). Among these, each preceding one is superior. However, others read "equal" (*samām*) instead; because of the inclusion of the word "equal," this interest (*vṛddhi*) applies here [only] up to a year and not beyond it. It would apply from the beginning of the period. Even beyond that, it may apply because the interest is small. Furthermore, the practice is twofold: having taken a pledge (*ādhi*), and otherwise. Regarding the case of taking a pledge, this is stated for the sake of specification: || 8.141 ||
But one shall not receive interest on a secured loan if it is used for the benefit [of the debtor];
nor, due to the lapse of time, can there be a transfer or sale of the pledge. 8.142.

For if the user enjoys the pledge, such as a field or other property, no interest shall accrue to the lender. By implication, interest shall accrue even on a pledge that does not provide utility, and likewise on one that does provide utility, provided it is not used [by the creditor] according to agreement. Furthermore, when the value of an unenjoyable pledge has doubled through the lapse of time, the creditor does not acquire ownership of it at that time; nor can he transfer it elsewhere by way of re-pledge (*adhamana*) without the consent of the borrower. Rather, it is understood by implication that he must continue to enjoy the pledge until the debt has doubled and the principal is repaid, for the purpose of securing the loaned amount. Because of its similarity to a sale, this transfer is understood to be a re-pledge. The same should be understood regarding a sale. Thus, while the loan is being utilized, the lender is prohibited from— || 8.142 ||
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
This [point] was already stated in the preceding verse for the sake of what follows. And this is what is said:
"Or he should satisfy him with its value."

One who lends property at an interest exceeding the daily rate of enjoyment, having recognized the deterioration of items such as copper cauldrons and the like, should [deal with them] according to those who know their value. However, one who employs secret spells incurs guilt even through visible harm; as it is said:
"Otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge. (8.143)

And those who [knowingly] consume [the pledge]: the king shall impose a fine. This treatise is effective only regarding the loss of enjoyment when the pledge is used, and not otherwise. However, another says: when the debt has doubled, one who uses the pledge with the owner's permission should use it only for the sake of the principal gold; or, having calculated the principal gold, he should satisfy [the owner] by paying the value [of the use], even if the price is not yet repaid. And thus, this prohibition against using the pledge applies when the gold has doubled, whereas in the former case (regarding the loss of enjoyment), it applies from the very beginning. 8.143.
Both a pledge and a deposit do not suffer from the lapse of time; yet, if they remain for an excessively long duration, both may be forfeited. 8.144

Because a pledge (*upanidhi*) is subject to the same rules as a mortgage (*ādhi*) due to their similarity, it is taught here [in this context]. Furthermore, since there is no possibility of relinquishing or selling a mortgage even when its time limit has expired, the mortgagor must strive to redeem it; for by the lapse of time, those two [pledges] might be destroyed by water, fire, thieves, and so forth, or else by ten years of possession. And thus he will say: "If anything [is used] for ten years... Now, what is the distinction between a mortgage and a pledge? A mortgage is a gold object intended for enjoyment; a pledge is intended for enjoyment through friendship. And thus he will say: "In the same way as with deposited wealth, so too with that which is pledged out of friendship. (8.144)
Things enjoyed with mutual affection never perish;
this applies to a milch cow, a camel carrying loads, a horse, and even a draft animal being employed for work. (8.145)

The terms *ādhi* (pledge) and *upanidhi* (deposit) are included here because of the context; for it has been stated: "Both a pledge and a deposit do not suffer by the lapse of time. Alternatively, this refers to a deposit (*upanidhi*) because of the mention of enjoyment through affection, and not a pledge (*ādhi*). And so he will describe such a deposit later with the words, "and of that which is deposited out of affection. Cows, camels, horses, and the like being enjoyed through affection yield their respective value. And even a draft animal that is employed, though not carrying a load, does not perish through excessive use. Or rather, houses and the like being enjoyed through affection are what are meant; however, other things besides these, such as cows and the rest, when enjoyed through affection, do perish [if misused]. (8.145)
Whatever property a wealthy man is seen to have been enjoyed by others for ten years while he remained silent and did not object, he is not entitled to recover it. 8.146.
Whatever is devoid of joy [is suffering]. 8.146

If the owner is not an idiot and has not lost his legal capacity, and the property is enjoyed by another in his presence, that possession is nullified by the legal proceeding; the enjoyer is entitled to that wealth. (8.147)

If he is not an idiot (*ajaḍa*) or a minor (*apogaṇḍa*), these two are capable of seeking out their own property, but one who is an idiot or a minor is not, because of his lack of capacity. Furthermore, in the case of an object, it is perceived by another's eye, for that which is not illuminated [by consciousness] cannot be seen. Or rather, [it is perceived] in its own domain, not in the domain of another, nor by one who is absent. This being so, when a capable person who is looking on neglects his own property while it is being enjoyed [by another], its seizure after ten years of enjoyment is justified. By the mention of "not an idiot or a minor," other causes for preoccupation with seeking one's own wealth—such as incapacity—are also included. It should be understood that causes such as preoccupation with sacrificial sessions (*sattra*) or initiations (*dīkṣā*) have already been stated. This [verse] is commenced for the purpose of providing an exception to the rule of ownership through possession for ten years. (8.147)
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of one learned in the Vedas do not perish through adverse possession. (8.148)

Women who are attendants are not to be married, because it contradicts the scriptures. Others, however, say: even those who have been married may be taken back through penance (*prāyaścitta*), since it is not proper to abandon them when they have been abducted in times of distress. Furthermore, the property of a king and of a *śrotriya* is not lost by mere enjoyment, even if it was obtained through seizure or purchase; for in the case of the *śrotriya*, his status as such is connected to his conduct (*ācāra*), and in the case of the king, his sovereignty is connected to his independent exercise of authority. But in the case of the property of others, which has been seized or purchased, there would indeed be a loss [of ownership] to another. (8.148)
The foolish man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of its owner must forfeit half the interest as compensation for that enjoyment. (8.149)

The master transacts business in the house, and the subordinate (adhyadhīna) is employed by him; as such, the author will say: "The *adhyadhīna* is for the sake of the family. Thus, the unwise person who enjoys a pledge (*ādhi*) without being authorized by the master does not realize that his wealth will be exhausted by half the interest. For this reason, he must relinquish that half-interest to compensate for the enjoyment. In this way, the authority regarding both the taking and the pledging belongs to the *adhyadhīna*, because he is a distinct entity; however, this does not apply to the authorization for enjoyment or to the act of giving. He who understands this is wise. Therefore, this reading alone is correct: "not unwise," because the *adhyadhīna* is subordinate to the master. But another says: the previous rule was stated for when the debt has doubled—"A pledge must not be enjoyed by force; one who enjoys it shall forfeit the interest"; this rule, however, is stated at the very beginning. (8.149)
Interest on a loan, once stipulated, shall not exceed double the principal;
for grain, meat, wool, and beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount.

Interest does not exceed double [the principal], even though the period of time is great. Interest that has been paid once and has not been transferred to another person [does not increase further]; however, when the debt has been transferred, it increases again from the point of transfer, because of the fault of the debtor in failing to repay the creditor's original capital. This applies first to gold. In the case of grain, however, at the time of harvest—that is, at the time of payment—it increases annually by its share; thus, the grain lent does not exceed fivefold.
