When the doubling [of gold] would otherwise occur, this rule of fivefold is introduced to prohibit that. Likewise, in the case of grain, it does not exceed fivefold as it turns over. Similarly, in the case of wool—that is, of sheep and goats—the interest lent increases by its share at each shearing. But in the case of draft animals, such as oxen, this same principle applies. (8.150)
An interest exceeding the legal rate is not valid;
they call that the path of usury, for it deserves a fine of five per hundred. 8.151.

For if a lender, knowing the course of business, should cause the borrower to pay interest exceeding five percent on a hundred, he shall not attain the fulfillment of his purpose; this is because it deviates from the sacred law (*śāstra*). For the borrower ought to pay only five percent on a hundred. Alternatively, interest that has been agreed upon may be specified at the time of borrowing, or it may be unspecified. However, for one who previously possessed nothing, whether by means of financial dealings, by having attained power otherwise, or through personal exertion characterized by prosperity, interest exceeding that amount—such as when it is reduced due to the greed of the lender but subsequently becomes excessive relative to the borrower's wealth—is not valid, because it deviates from the sacred law. For in that regard, the maximum interest is five percent on a hundred. That too applies specifically to the case of a Śūdra. While such interest might be permitted even for one who is not a Śūdra, it must not exceed that limit. Accordingly, it is censured: "They call that the path of usury. (8.151)

One should not take interest exceeding one year; that is, if because of the magnitude of the interest the principal becomes double within a single year, one should stop. Otherwise, however, one may take it even beyond the year until it reaches the state of being double. Thus says Gautama: “In a long-standing loan, there is doubling of the principal. Others, however, maintain that even the *labdhi* (accrued gain), characterized as the eightieth or fiftieth part, does not exceed a year, because of its conflict with *dharma*.
Nor should one take what is unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
One should recover from the debtor an interest other than that which has been stipulated by the legal treatises (*śāstra*) themselves, such as interest at double the principal or more;

or rather, one should recover that which is not seen [in the scriptures], meaning that which is not accumulated. One should not take it month by month; however, one may take that which accrues month by month until the debt reaches double the principal.
[Interest consisting of] increase of capital, increase of time, stipulated interest, and bodily interest. || 8.152 ||

Interest that is agreed upon by oneself out of regard for mutual assistance is permitted; interest joined with a vehicle like a wheel is "wheel-interest" (*cakravṛddhi*). Alternatively, it revolves like a wheel: that which increases month by month is "time-interest" (*kālavṛddhi*), meaning this wealth of his increases over time, not immediately. And this is arranged out of affection, because the other person is to be favored by oneself. Alternatively, for one who does not pay at this time, it increases exactly as determined by the lender himself, depending on the place, time, purpose, and circumstances of the borrower. This is greater than the interest resulting from what was expressly stipulated. "Bodily" (*kāyikā*) means to be cleared through bodily labor. (8.152)
He who, being unable to pay a debt, wishes to enter into a new transaction, shall, after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the bond. (8.153)

But there is no renewal of the principal for interest. How so? For if one who has taken a loan is unable to pay both the principal and the interest, and wishes to renew the contract by means of witnesses and other formalities, he shall pay the interest already accrued and renew the contract for the principal alone. He must not add further interest thereon. And whatever he may pay, that shall be deducted from the interest, but not from the principal. This is the instruction of the king; the king himself should cause a debtor who is oppressed by the interest to have it remitted. (8.153)
Without showing the gold back there, he may exchange it;
he ought to give back as much interest as has accrued. (8.154)
If one is unable to pay even a single kārṣāpaṇa together with interest, there shall be a renewal of the transaction.
One who has ascended to the increase of the wheel, being established according to place and time, will not obtain that fruit if he transgresses the requirements of place and time. (8.155)

When the creditor, due to his own fault, fails to collect from the debtor by transgressing the proper time and place, then this other matter concerning the interest already stipulated is now stated. (8.155)
Those skilled in sea-voyages, who perceive the proper place, time, and purpose, establish whatever profit there may be; that constitutes the attainment in that case. (8.156)

In that case, whatever interest those merchants might establish shall be accepted, for they are the ones who know the loss, expenditure, profit on the road, and the quality of the goods. This other rule regarding sureties is now taught in connection with debts. (8.156)
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance, he shall pay that person's debt from his own property if he fails to produce him. (8.157)

This verse has already been explained by its very wording. Now, regarding the surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*): when the debtor fails to appear before the creditor, and the obligation to pay the debt from his own property arises, the death of such a surety would—by virtue of the scriptural rule, "The heirs shall discharge the debt," and by logical implication—result in the payment of the debt falling upon his sons; this possibility is here prohibited. (8.157)
A son is not liable to pay for a guarantee, a frivolous loan, what is due from gambling or liquor, nor the remainder of a fine or a tax. (8.158)

In these cases, the son’s lack of connection [to the debt] is to be understood from the force of the legal treatise (*śāstra*). Because of the statement "the remainder of the nuptial fee" (*śulkāvaśeṣa*), the son has a connection to the debt when it is the entirety of the nuptial fee. Some authorities maintain that this same rule applies even to the remainder of a fine (*daṇḍāvaśeṣa*). Furthermore, because they share the same legal status regarding the connection of being a surety (*prātibhāvya*), sons are not connected to paternal debts such as "useless gifts" (*vṛthādāna*) and the like. Now, since it might be concluded that the son ought not to pay for either of the two types of sureties, this [verse] is commenced: 8.158. A son is not liable for a debt contracted by his father on account of a suretyship, nor for a debt contracted for spirituous liquor, gambling, or a futile gift; nor for one contracted for a woman. || 8.158 || A son is not liable for a debt contracted by his father on account of being a surety, nor for a debt contracted for spirituous liquor, gambling, or a useless gift; nor for a debt contracted for the sake of a woman. The term "suretyship" (*prātibhāvya*) refers to the state of being a surety (*prātibhāvuka*). There are three kinds of sureties: for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*), for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*), and for trust (*viśvāsa-pratibhū*). Among these, the son is not liable for a debt contracted by his father on account of a suretyship for appearance or for trust. However, he is liable for a debt contracted by his father on account of a suretyship for payment. Regarding the phrase "nor for a debt contracted for spirituous liquor, gambling, or a futile gift": "spirituous liquor" refers to the sale of intoxicants; "gambling" refers to playing with dice and the like; "futile gift" refers to a gift made out of mere affection or friendship, which is not for the purpose of religious duty (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), or pleasure (*kāma*). The son is not liable for a debt contracted by his father on account of these. "Nor for one contracted for a woman" means that he is not liable for a debt contracted by his father for the sake of a woman—whether for the purchase of a wife, for her maintenance, or for her gratification. The word "nor" (*ca*) is used in the sense of "and. || 8.158 ||
But regarding a surety for appearance, the previously mentioned rule shall apply;
however, if a surety for payment dies, the court shall compel even his heirs to pay. (8.159)
And this being so, there exists a connection for the son who acts as a guarantor for the gift. 8.159.
But when the debtor has not paid, and the guarantor—who was known for his reliable character—has subsequently died, by what means may the creditor seek to recover the debt? (8.160)

Words with identical case endings are to be explained as having a single referent. When a surety for payment (*adātṛ-pratibhū*) has died, one whose "nature" (*prakṛti*)—meaning the reason for his being a surety—is known is called "one whose nature is known. But what is that reason? It is his connection to the delivery of the debt. And thus, by virtue of his support of the wealth, he belongs to this debtor; for what is he like? Therefore, when such a surety has died, the creditor, desiring to recover the loan advanced, asks out of doubt for what reason. And how does he doubt? Because the reason for that is stated: first, it was said that the son of a surety for payment has a connection [to the debt], but not the son of a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*). Therefore, even though there is a connection to the father’s inheritance, he should not be made to pay on the strength of the legal text; and since [the son] should be made to pay when the surety who received the money has died—even if he is merely the son of a surety for appearance—it is because both cases are observed that a doubt arises, and regarding this, the author says: [Verse 8.160]

But if the surety has been provided with funds and is possessed of sufficient wealth, he shall pay that [debt] from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one for whom funds have been assigned. (8.161)

A surety (*pratibhū*) who has been "assigned the debt" (*nirādiṣṭadhana*) is one to whom the debt has been transferred; it does not mean by mere word alone. And he should be "one with sufficient wealth" (*alaṃdhana*), meaning one whose wealth is adequate for the purpose for which he is bound as a guarantor. Alternatively, even if he was initially "one assigned the debt" by word alone, if he subsequently becomes "one with sufficient wealth," having had the debt transferred to him and possessing adequate funds, then for this reason he ought to pay that from his own property, just like the son of a debtor-guarantor (*adhamarṇalagnaka*) to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). And this rule regarding giving and receiving is established on the grounds of legal efficacy (*siddhi*). (8.161)
And furthermore:

A legal proceeding conducted by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, dependent on another, a child, or an elderly person, as well as one entered into by someone unrelated, is not valid. (8.162)

Legal transactions entered into by those who are intoxicated and so forth are not valid. It is not only in the case of debt-transactions that this applies; rather, all legal transactions, when undertaken by those who are intoxicated and so forth, are invalid. (8.162)
A speech does not become true even if it is well-established, if it speaks of phenomena that are external to the fixed conventional [truth]. (8.163)

Furthermore, a legal transaction contrary to the Dharma—such as the sale of children or a wife—is not valid; for by such an act, one obstructs the Dharma. Interest that has doubled at the time of the loan continues to increase even further month by month; in this same way, other forms of interest, such as those involving the seizure of villages or heaps of grain, should be understood as prohibited. Because it is related to debt, this next point concerning that very subject is now stated. (8.163)
Whatever has been mortgaged, sold, given, or received through fraud, and whatever is seen to involve deceit—that the king shall annul in every case. (8.164)

What is called a *yogādhamana* (fraudulent mortgage) is that which is not explicitly stated in worldly dealings, such as: "You perform this task for now, while I shall perform this other task. Sale is also characterized in this same way. *Yogadāna* (fraudulent gift) is that which is given under a pretext of a procession or festival by debtors and others to creditors and the like. Furthermore, one who is about to die and has no offspring, fearing his kinsmen, gives out of despair; such is [dealing] through fraud (*yoga*). This is the distinction between giving and receiving: giving is done with friendliness, and receiving is done according to the law. Wherever the king, while examining legal proceedings, perceives fraud pertaining to giving or receiving, or pertaining to anything else, he should annul all of it. Because of its connection with debt, this and other matters related to it are discussed here. (8.164)

If that which was received has been lost, or if expenditure was made for the sake of the family, it must be paid by the relatives from their own property, even if they have already divided their inheritance. 8.165
The meaning of this verse is indeed self-evident. || 8.165 ||

Whatever legal transaction a dependent person may carry out for the sake of the family's maintenance— whether in his own country or abroad— in the absence of the master, that shall be upheld by the superior.
The owner of one who is under another's authority shall not exercise judicial inquiry. || 8.166 ||

One should not reflect: "Why has this act been performed by you, who are dependent, even in my absence? Without such reflection, one should settle that debt. Alternatively, the meaning of the remainder of the preceding verse should be explained as follows. How so? Even if he is dependent, whatever transaction a person performs for the sake of the family becomes authoritative for his superior; how much more so, then, for his kinsmen? This being the case, it has been stated that a transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, or dependent is not valid. However, from the statement "a transaction entered into by one who is unrelated is not valid," it might somehow be possible to assume that a dependent has independence regarding household matters in the absence of his superior. Therefore, this verse is indeed meaningful according to the capacity we have described. Furthermore, wealth may be employed by a dependent for the sake of the family— || 8.166 ||
"Whatever is given by force, whatever is enjoyed by force, and whatever is even recorded by force—Manu has declared all such matters effected by force to be as if not done at all. (8.167)

Money lent through force by one desiring interest, as well as land or a pledge taken for the purpose of enjoyment, shall be revoked by the king. Furthermore, a pledge that has been enjoyed by force while being prohibited [from use] shall be recovered by seeking restitution for the enjoyment of that pledge. Or else, even a house or other property that has been enjoyed by force with the intent, "I shall seize this after ten years of possession," shall be returned. Moreover, whatever has been recorded in a document by force—Manu declares that all such matters, as well as others of this kind, including witnesses, sureties, family seizure, time limits, and the doubling of the debt, shall be nullified. (8.167)
Those three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, sureties, and family members;
whereas four prosper: a Brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king. (8.168)

Since families of witnesses and sureties are seen to act for the sake of another, one should therefore not compel them to serve as witnesses and so forth against their will. However, four types of persons—the Brāhmaṇa and the others—are engaged solely for the sake of another: first, a Brāhmaṇa should not be made to cause a donor to pay whom he does not wish to give; nor should a wealthy man be made to accept interest from one who does not wish to take it; nor should a merchant be made to trade by one who does not desire to do so, even if he seeks profit. Likewise, a king should not institute a legal proceeding against one who does not wish to engage in it. This being the case, this verse should also be understood as demonstrating the cessation of a matter that has been undertaken through force. And since this is so, therefore, even though he is powerful, a king [should not act] in a legal proceeding except in cases other than those [involving force]. (8.168)
Even when impoverished, a king should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor, even when prosperous, should he relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be. (8.169)
By taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken, the weakness of the king is made manifest; he perishes both in this world and after death. (8.170)
And here, the rule regarding the avoidance of what is not to be accepted follows from the force of the treatise; therefore, [it applies] to one who avoids what is to be avoided. (8.170)
From taking what is his own, from not mixing with the castes, and from protecting the weak, the king’s power is born; he prospers both in this world and after death. (8.171)

Furthermore, for one who conducts himself according to the scriptures, there arises among the subjects a non-confusion of the social classes (*varṇa*)—that is, their mutual non-mixture—through the collection of wealth from the citizens and country-folk by means other than legal proceedings, and through the protection of the weak against the strong. Consequently, the king prospers both in this world and after death. This [verse] is merely a commendation of the rule concerning the king’s office. (8.171)

Since this is so, therefore, like Yama himself, a master should personally abandon both the pleasant and the unpleasant, and conduct himself with the impartiality of Yama, having conquered anger and mastered his senses. (8.172)

"He should be impartial toward his subjects"—this is the illustrative meaning for this king; and thus he states the explanation of the cause of impartiality: "having conquered anger and having conquered the senses. (8.172)
Furthermore, O King, that ruler of men who, having not conquered desire and anger,
performs his duties through unrighteousness out of delusion—
his enemies will soon bring that evil-souled man under their control. (8.173)

The king—whose subjects were disaffected, who had many affairs to attend to, and whose end was old age and so forth—having once again established a definitive understanding, [acted as follows]. || 8.173 ||
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives matters according to righteousness—toward him the subjects turn, as rivers flow toward the ocean. (8.174)

For just as rivers, having reached the ocean which is their destination, do not return but rather become one with it, so too the subjects—the ministers and others—do not offend a king who has become such [as described], but rather become one with him; this is the meaning of the simile. 8.174.

He who, having been summoned at will, informs the king against a debtor while that debtor is attempting to settle the debt, shall be made by the king to pay one-fourth of that amount as a fine, and the debt itself to the creditor. 8.175.

If a royal official, fearing [reprisals] due to his being a favorite of the king, reports the creditor to him, the king shall impose such instruction, punishment, and the payment of money upon that official. Another verse states: "But the man who, considering [the debt] irrecoverable, reports the creditor, shall be made to pay one-fourth of the king's share of the debt, as well as that money to the creditor. Here too, the meaning is the same, though slightly different in phrasing. This refers to the case of one who is unable to pay the money; this alternative method for the payment of money is stated as an option in the event of a lack of funds. (8.175)
A debtor of lower caste who is equal [to his creditor] in occupation may pay the debt to the creditor at the same time as he; however, one of superior caste should pay it gradually. (8.176)

Because one who is superior is worthy of honor, his [labor] must indeed be endured even if it is not assigned to him; however, due to a lack of patience, he must never be made to perform work alongside those who are equal or inferior. This verse is for the purpose of excluding such a person. (8.176)
By this procedure, the king should bring to a state of impartiality the legal cases of men disputing with one another, which have been established through the evidence of witnesses. (8.177)

The meaning is that they are established by evidence and established by witnesses. This verse serves to conclude the discussion on the legal procedure concerning debts. Now, this is stated for the purpose of the rules regarding deposits (nikṣepa). 8.177.
A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a great following, wealthy, and honorable. (8.178)

This verse has the purpose of defining the rules for depositing [property]. "Born of a noble family" means one of distinguished lineage. "[Endowed with good conduct]" means one who possesses proper behavior. By virtue of the context, this refers to dealings with property, or otherwise. And thus, in the case of property dealings, one becomes pure if one is a speaker of truth through knowledge of the Dharma. This being so, this qualification of conduct is to be understood. If one is of such conduct, then one becomes fit for receiving deposits. Furthermore, one who has a large following is unassailable by forest-dwellers and others, and because of the fear of defeat by his own side, he does not undergo corruption. In this way, the instruction regarding wealthiness is to be explained. Moreover, one of such conduct should be known as "noble" even if he is a Śūdra, because of his incorruptible nature. Others, however, declare him to be a twice-born (Dvija), and they say that his inclusion is for the sake of spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). (8.178)
Whatever object a person deposits in another's hand in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same way; as was the delivery, so shall be the recovery. (8.179)

Since a deposit is seen to be of two kinds—sealed and unsealed, witnessed and unwitnessed, numbered and unnumbered—it is therefore said: "As the delivery, so the recovery. And because of the mention of the *mānava* (the man of the [first] three classes), it is understood here that the mention of the *ārya* (noble person) in the preceding verse is for the sake of all castes (*varṇas*), and not restricted to the twice-born (*dvijāti*) alone. This being the case, when the acts of delivering and reclaiming are equal, no legal action can be brought against the holder of the deposit. (8.179)
He who, when asked for a deposit, does not return it to the depositor, shall be summoned by the presiding judge in the absence of that depositor. 8.180.

"He shall do so in the absence of witnesses," as he will state later. By implication, its connection [to the present verse] should be understood. When, in the absence of witnesses, one who is being asked for a deposit does not return it, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), having been informed by the depositor, should act as follows: under certain pretexts, he should have some gold or other property deposited with that same person who holds the original deposit, using objects similar in quantity, age, and appearance to the previously deposited items. Then, after some time has passed and the original depositor is absent, the judge should cause the second depositor to ask for his second deposit. (8.180)
If he should act according to what was entrusted and as it was done, there would be nothing therein by which he could be accused by others. (8.181)
If he should recover that second deposit exactly as it was placed, then there is nothing for which he can be accused by others. 8.181.
If, however, he does not pay that gold to them according to the rule, he shall be seized by both parties and compelled to pay; such is the established principle of the law. (8.182)

Now, if one who has been recognized by the judge and subsequently appointed [as a witness] fails to give [evidence], then, having arrested both, he shall be made to pay for both the first [claim] and the second. || 8.182 ||
In the absence of witnesses, having deposited gold with that person—who is endowed with suitable age and appearance—under various pretexts, [one should act] according to the truth. (8.183)
This is connected with what precedes. Thus it has been said: "He who, when asked for his deposit," and so forth. (8.183)
A sealed deposit and an open deposit must never be delivered to another person;
they would be lost in the event of his death, but they are not lost if he does not die. (8.184)

While the depositor is alive, the deposits—whether open (*nikṣepa*) or sealed (*upanidhi*)—must not be given to his immediate successor, such as a son or a brother who is entitled to that wealth, even if he requests them; for there is no legal recourse [for the claimant] so long as the immediate successor has not perished. However, upon the death of the immediate successor, what answer will the holder of the deposit give when questioned by the depositor? For it is not proper for him to give those items to the successor. (8.184)
But he who should himself give [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased must not be prosecuted by the king, nor by the relatives of the depositor. (8.185)

There is no legal action against one who personally delivers a deposit without it being recorded; however, if someone should point out some deficiency or excess regarding this matter, then— || 8.185 ||
One should seek that object with sincerity and with affection;
having investigated his livelihood, one should settle the matter through conciliation alone. (8.186)

If, while one is giving away something unknown [to others] himself, some doubt regarding that object should arise from a whisperer, then, having investigated his conduct through non-deceitful means, his acquisition of it should be ascertained by the deposit-holder through discernment. 8.186.
In all these types of deposits, the rule for recovery shall be as follows:
if [the depositary] does not withdraw anything from it, he shall receive nothing from the ocean. (8.187)

The deposit of that person’s property, both in terms of its nature and its quantity, must be placed in the ocean itself. Yet, the holder of the deposit is not released from liability merely because the ocean—the deposit—has not been returned, provided he does not take anything for himself from it by means of counter-sealing, siphoning off, or any other such method. Others also explain that if the holder of the deposit is on board a sea-going vessel and the vessel meets with disaster, he is not to be accused by the depositor if he does not appropriate any of his own property. This is what is meant: having abandoned one's own interests, one must exert effort in protecting the deposit. (8.187)
If [the property] has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or even burnt by fire, one need not give it back; for he does not take away anything from that [original owner]. (8.188)
Even in the event of destruction by thieves and the like, this very same rule for sea-voyages is explained; for the meaning of the preceding verse alone is superior. 8.188.
One should investigate the one who misappropriates a deposit and the one who did not actually entrust it by all possible means and even by Vedic oaths. (8.189)

But if one who has been asked for an object deposited without a witness does not return it to the depositor, this is called a "deposition without witnesses. Whether the depositor, having taken [the object back], should demand it again, or whether he should not have returned it initially, that person should be investigated by the King or the presiding judge through all means, beginning with conciliation (*sāman*) and so forth; and in the absence of such means, by means of oaths prescribed in the Veda, such as those involving the carrying of fire, and so on. By the word "and" (*ca*), even worldly methods such as the drinking of poison (*kośapāna*) are included here. And because the nature of the matter is similar, these methods are not prohibited in other cases as well than the rules regarding deposits. (8.189)
He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands it without having made a deposit—both of these should be punished like thieves, or be made to pay a fine equal to its value. (8.190)
This undertaking is for the purpose of punishment for one who has committed a prior transgression; it is presented as an alternative. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: || 8.190 ||
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value;
this is a specific statement regarding the Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of avoiding the punishment prescribed for a thief—namely, the confiscation of his property.
Likewise, the king [shall punish] the misappropriator of a sealed deposit without distinction. (8.191)

The commencement of the latter half of the verse is for the purpose of providing an illustration. Like [the punishment for] a thief, the forfeiture [of property] would apply even to a deposit, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa, as established by the context. (8.191)
But whatever man should steal the property of another by means of fraudulent tests, he, along with his accomplices, shall be put to death publicly by various modes of execution. (8.192)

One who steals the property of another, along with his accomplices, should be publicly punished by various means—such as by offering him a sacred seat, by granting him wealth, by arranging for him to enjoy his own wife, or by demonstrating future benefits—and through such tests (*upadhā*), he should be restrained by the most severe penalty, namely the confiscation of all his property. (8.192)
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses, it must be understood to be exactly that much; he who declares otherwise deserves punishment. 8.193.
When a deposit is made in the presence of witnesses, the authority regarding the value and quantity of the object shall rest with those witnesses, such as the villagers and others. 8.193.
If a gift was made privately by someone, or received privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so too must be the taking. (8.194)

This renewed undertaking has the purpose of *upanidhi* (a sealed deposit). Its meaning is precisely that which was stated in the previous verse regarding deposits (*nikṣepa*) in the section on deposits: "Whoever [should deposit in another's hand... and so forth. This [present verse], however, because it concerns *upanidhi*, might otherwise be considered redundant; it should be understood as such, or rather, the non-redundancy of these two verses should be described by way of the distinction between the general and the particular. || 8.194 ||
In this manner, the king shall reach a decision regarding deposited wealth as well as that which was entrusted out of friendship, without causing injury to the holder of the deposit. (8.195)

A deposit may be either sealed or unsealed; however, an open deposit (*upanidhi*) is one that is unsealed and intended for enjoyment with pleasure. This method for the investigation of these two should be understood. Now, the sale by one who is not the owner (*asvāmivikraya*) is being discussed. 8.195.
One who sells another's property as his own, being neither the owner nor authorized by the owner, should not be admitted as a witness; he is a thief who considers himself no thief. (8.196)
Since the statement "one should not lead him to give testimony" is intended as a general illustration, it excludes him from all forms of legal authority. (8.196)
He shall be liable to forfeiture of his property along with his family, and a fine of six hundred;
if he has no family property and no means of escape, he shall incur the guilt of a thief.

"One who is liable to have his property confiscated shall be fined six hundred panas, along with his family and his means of egress; one who has no family and no means of egress shall incur the guilt of a thief. By this [verse], he shows that the severity of the punishment is greater than the previous one due to the gravity of the offense. However, another says: "Egress" (apasaraḥ) refers to any acquisition of wealth other than by purchase. This being the case— || 8.197 ||
But whatever gift or sale is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings. (8.198)

Purchases and sales made by one who is not the owner must indeed be nullified; thus, the owner alone shall be the recipient of the wealth, and neither the buyer nor the seller, being owners of the property, need be satisfied. Now, lest ownership arise through ten years of possession from one who is not the owner after having purchased it, he says this— [8.198]
Where enjoyment is perceived but no scripture is seen anywhere, there scripture is the cause and not enjoyment; such is the established rule. (8.199)
Thus, according to scripture, ownership does not arise for an impure object even through ten years of possession. Since this is so, therefore— || 8.199 ||
If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of a family assembly, that wealth is purified by purchase; thus he acquires the property according to justice. (8.200)

But according to justice, a purchase should be made from a trustworthy person in the presence of the family for a suitable price; and this is proper for one who does not press the seller and who gains wealth through such a transaction. Thus it is for one who acts with forethought and deals justly. (8.200)

Now, if the price is not recoverable and the purchase is cleared by being made openly, the seller is released by the king without punishment, and the owner who lost the property recovers his wealth. (8.201)

Furthermore, at the time of the accusation, if it should be impossible to recover the price because the seller is absent, then it is proper that he be cleared of punishment through a public purchase (*prakāśakraya*). Moreover, wicked men arriving from other countries sell goods openly and without hesitation even in the presence of the king; if, in such a case, the buyer were liable for a fault despite the sale being purified by a public purchase due to the impossibility of recovering the price, then the king’s trade with all directions would be cut off, even for honest men. And this is not desired. Therefore, there is no fault here for the buyer. As for the original owner (*nāṣṭika*), since he makes his own property known through the proper cause, why should he not receive his own wealth? Thus, his recovery of the wealth is proper. And since the other party is without fault, his immunity from punishment is proper. Because of its similarity to the legal procedure regarding sale by one who is not the owner, this is stated in that very context. (8.201)
An object that is not mixed with anything else is fit for sale;
it must not be defective, nor deficient, nor distant, nor concealed. (8.202)

One substance, such as saffron (*kuṅkuma*) and the like, when mixed with another substance, such as safflower (*kusumbha*), is not fit for sale. Since this is prohibited, it is inferred that such an act is improper. Likewise, there is the "defective" (*sāvadya*) commodity which, though unmixed, is putrid, long-kept, or worn-out clothing and the like. Nor is there the "inferior" (*nyūna*), which is placed later with a similar [substance] so that it is deficient by a certain weight (*palasaṃkhyā*). It is not "far away" because it is not perceptible. By this, the "concealed" (*tirohita*) is explained: that which is made to appear as a substance when it is not a substance, through an action such as dyeing the goods, is "concealed. This being the case, since selling such a thing is a fault, the seller deserves punishment. It is not only the impurity of the seller; rather, even after ten days, this must be returned to the seller by the buyer. For otherwise, this scriptural prohibition regarding the sale of what is unfit would be set aside by the rule: "But after ten days, one need neither give it back nor cause it to be given back. Connected with the subject of sale, this other legal proceeding concerning customs duties (*śulka*) is now introduced: Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.202.
If, after showing one girl, another is given to the bridegroom,
Manu has declared that he may marry both for a single bride-price.
If, after showing a blameless girl, one gives a blameworthy one instead, both of them must be carried off with a single bride-price. 8.203.

A giver who has previously declared the defects of a girl—provided she is not intoxicated, not afflicted with leprosy, and has not already experienced sexual intercourse—is worthy of punishment. (8.204)

This being the case, if the faults of a woman who possesses defects are not mentioned, the giver is liable to punishment for his deception; furthermore, if she was previously announced [as faultless], there is no abandonment of her even if she later proves to have defects once married. Now, *saṃbhūyasamutthāna* (joint enterprise), which follows in the sequence, is discussed; for this purpose, he shows a Vedic illustration. 8.204.
If an officiating priest chosen for a sacrifice should abandon his own duty, a share proportionate to his work must be given to him by the performers together. 8.205

If the chief officiating priest (pradhānartvik), having commenced the ritual, should abandon his own duty due to reasons such as traveling to another region or physical incapacity, he shall receive a portion of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) proportionate to the work performed. How so? When one-fourth of the rite has been completed, one-fourth of the fee is due; likewise, this should be applied to three-fourths and other portions. The phrase "together with the performers" refers to the assistant priests (pratiprasthātṛ) and others who are subordinate to him. The exception to this rule is as follows: || 8.205 ||
But when the sacrificial fees have been given, if one causes his own work to be neglected, he shall receive his entire share and have it performed by another. (8.206)

After the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been given, the fee must not be recovered from those [officiants] who, for some other reason, fail to perform their respective duties. For those who do not perform the duties that ought to be performed near the altar, the sacrificer should have them performed by someone else—either by one of the priests' assistants or by another person—after giving whatever is appropriate in accordance with the remaining rites. Otherwise, that rite would not be fully accomplished through the sacrificial fee for the sake of the sacrificer. This very scripture is to be understood as applying to the giving of fees by one who performs the remaining rites. And in this context, another related point is stated: 8.206. If, however, he abandons it before the fee has been paid, he shall receive no fee at all, and the king shall impose a fine of one hundred *paṇas* upon him. In whatever rite specific fees for individual components have been prescribed, he alone shall receive them, or alternatively, all [the officiants] may share them together. (8.207)

The sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for each individual priest are always subject to doubt: Is there a restriction on receiving gifts for these officiating priests similar to that for the *pādika* Brahmins appointed by those learned in the four Vedas, or is it due to the inherent nature of the ritual act itself? This logical alternative is restated here; and having adopted the position that they are for the sake of that [ritual], this is now being explained. (8.207)
The Adhvaryu priest shall take the chariot at the establishment of the sacred fires, and the Brahman priest the horse;
the Hotṛ priest may also take the horse, and the Udgātṛ priest the cart at the purchase [of the Soma]. (8.208)

This verse is intended to demonstrate the many subsidiary fees (*aṅgadākṣiṇā*) established in various Vedic branches for the sacrificial rites (*kratu*). Thus, first, these are the principal priestly fees for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), and they apply likewise to the Soma sacrifices. (8.208)
Of all these, the principal ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that;
those entitled to a third receive a third part, while those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth part. (8.209)

Because of the statement, "They divide them by hundreds," there are forty-eight [shares]. In this way, the numerical indication as if from half of that becomes appropriate for what follows. Therefore, the Adhvaryu, Brahman, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ are the principal officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who receive half [of the cattle]. And by half of that—by twenty-four—the other "half-owners" (*ardhin*) are mentioned: the Pratiprasthātṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Prastotṛ, who occupy the second position. And thus Kātyāyana says: "Six each for the second ones. Those whose third position they hold are the "third-partakers" (*tṛtīyina*); they are the recipients of a third share. In total, sixteen are the sharers of the cattle. Kātyāyana also says exactly this: "Four each for the third ones. Those whose fourth part each is, they are the "fourth-partakers" (*pādina*); collectively, they are the sharers of twelve cattle. Kātyāyana also says: "Three each for the others. They are called "fourth-positioned" because they possess a quarter (*pāda*) relative to the initial number; this is a designation of the occupants (*sthānin*) by means of their positions (*sthāna*). However, the term "fourth-part" (*caturthāṃśa*) is a compound word used to designate the portion itself. And so it has been said: "Or rather, this should be explained in the reverse order. Furthermore, the mention of both [terms] here should be understood as being for the purpose of completing the meter. Even though the comprehension of both meanings may arise from either one alone, this entire rule is established by logic and scripture, and is cited here as an illustration. Just as among those performing a single task together, an unequal distribution of shares is ordained by the force of the scriptural injunction, regardless of whether they observe or do not observe the relative weight or lightness of their labor—so it is here. (8.209)
When men here come together to perform their respective duties,
the apportionment of their individual shares must be determined by this application of the rule.

In a single undertaking such as house construction, there is an allocation of the respective shares of the task for the thread-layer, the butcher, the architect, and so forth, whether considering their relative importance or not, according to tradition. For indeed, among men engaged in non-artistic activities or worldly transactions, equality cannot be assumed. He says this [verse 8.210] in order to preclude the taking of what has not been given.
If one has given wealth to someone who asks for it for the sake of the Dharma, but that wealth subsequently does not turn out to be so, then that gift should not have been given to him. (8.211)
The verse described in his own city [is as follows]: 8.211.
If, however, he should cause it to perish out of pride or greed, he should be made to pay one suvarṇa by the king as atonement for that theft. (8.212)

If someone has promised something for the sake of a religious duty (*dharma*) but has not yet given it, and if that person, failing to perform that duty, should nevertheless compel the non-giver on the grounds that it was "promised," then the king shall make him pay a fine of gold. Those who solicit with fraudulent intent (*sopadha*) are not considered thieves; rather, they are those whose punishment has been removed because their actions were unjust. (8.212)
Thus has been declared the lawful manner of non-repayment for what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-payment of wages. 8.213
This verse is for the purpose of stating the summary and the presentation. 8.214.
If a hired servant, though not ill, should out of pride fail to perform the work as prescribed, he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid. (8.214)

If wages have been paid, even one who has performed only a portion of the work may be fined and shall not receive the wages, because out of arrogance he did not complete the work that had begun. (8.214)
But one who was distressed and, having recovered his health, performs the work as originally described, shall indeed receive that wage even after a very long period of time. (8.215)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 8.215 ||
As it has been said: "Whether he be afflicted or healthy, if one does not cause that work to be done, his wages must not be paid, even for work that is only slightly incomplete. (8.216)
Whether in distress or in good health, one who does not perform the work as prescribed, nor causes it to be performed, shall not receive even a small portion of wages. (8.216)
This law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate agreements.
This verse is for the purpose of presenting a summary. 8.217.
A man who, having made a formal agreement with a village, a district, or a community by means of truth, should break that agreement out of greed—him the king shall banish from the realm. (8.218)

In matters consistent with dharma and artha, not conflicting with royal duties—such as the grazing of cattle, the protection of water sources, and the restoration of temples—whatever agreement (*saṃvit*) arises among the villagers and others, the king shall banish from that region anyone who violates it. (8.218)
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the agreement to pay four gold *suvarṇas*, six *niṣkas*, and one silver *śatamāna*. (8.219)

He shall be made to pay a fine of four gold pieces and so forth, and then he is to be banished. Alternatively, there is another reading of the legal option: "Having seized him, he should make him pay. This being the case, the punishment consists either of banishment or a fine. (8.219)
A righteous lord of the earth should apply this rule of punishment to those who violate their agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies. (8.220)
This verse is for the purpose of conclusion. 8.220.
If, after having bought or sold anything, one should have regret regarding it in this world, he may return that object or take it back within ten days. (8.221)

The reading *sāmnā* (by peaceful means) in the phrase *antardaśāham ādānapratyarpaṇe sāmnā* is an incorrect one. For who would be capable of forbidding the giving or taking [of goods] by peaceful means even after ten days have passed? Even in the case of goods acquired by chance (*labdhi*), it is impossible to forbid them by peaceful means, much less in the case of artificial goods where there is no recourse to legal principles. However, in the case of lawful acquisitions (*dharmya-pratigraha*), because the merit (*dharma*) is produced immediately thereafter, it is impossible—even by peaceful means—to make what has been done undone. In that regard, regarding the return [of the gift], either the gift must be made again or there must be a renunciation [of the claim]. Since this is so, the second half of the subsequent verse should be read as follows: "Therefore, after ten days, he should give back that property and likewise take it back. Regarding this very point, there is another reading for the second half of the subsequent verse: "But the giving and taking may indeed occur within ten days, even in the case of perishable goods. Alternatively, the mention of "peaceful means" (*sāman*) is intended to exclude punishment during the ten-day period; thus, when those two dispute over a rescission within ten days, there should be an exclusion of punishment from the king upon his adjudication. And accordingly, a punishment for such a dispute is heard of after the ten-day period. (8.221)
But after ten days have passed, one should neither give nor cause [the gift] to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be made to pay six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (8.222)

This verse is not commenced for the purpose of prohibiting conciliation (*sāman*) after ten days—meaning that after ten days one should neither give nor cause [the debt] to be given through conciliation. For it has already been stated that conciliation cannot be prohibited. However, where there is no repayment even through conciliation, it does indeed impose a restriction, as in the rule: "The share falls once. Even here, regarding the falling of the share, it could have been prohibited by means of conciliation alone, because there is no restrictive rule and because it serves the purpose of establishing an order. But in the case of giving a daughter in marriage, conciliation is not applicable due to the specific restriction: "by the departure and the dismissal. (8.222)
In connection with the discussion of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), this other matter is now stated here:
"If a man gives away a defective maiden without having disclosed her faults, the king himself shall impose upon him a fine of ninety-six *paṇas*. (8.223)

A woman afflicted by a disease that obstructs conception or who has had sexual intercourse is considered defective. For one who gives her away without disclosing that she is defective, there is a punishment. The phrase "not for one who is insane," etc., is already covered by the previously cited verse; therefore, we do not study it here. Alternatively, the position of a mere restatement (anuvāda) can be shown for this and the preceding [verse] due to some specific reason, since a formal study is appropriate even in this case. [8.223]
But if a man, out of malice, should declare of a maiden that she is not a virgin without demonstrating her fault, he shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (8.224)
This verse is explained by its own words. For what reason, then, is this great punishment ordained, such that— || 8.224 ||
The mantras for taking the hand are established only for maidens; they are never for non-maidens among men, for such women have lost their eligibility for religious rites. (8.225)

Likewise, regarding the marriage mantra beginning with, "The maidens have worshipped the god Aryaman and Agni; may that god Aryaman release us from the husband, Svāhā," the meaning here is that [the status of wife] is established in those very women through marriage and other rites. This being the case, even if she has been accepted prior to the grasping of the hand, if she has experienced sexual intercourse, she is to be abandoned. (8.225)
And those mantras recited at the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of wifehood;
their completion, however, should be understood by the wise to occur at the seventh step. (8.226)

The *pāṇigrāhaṇikā* mantras are those employed for the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) characterized by the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*). These are the mantras that serve as the means for performing that act. The characteristic of a wife consists in the formal acceptance of a wife, which, according to the *Gṛhya-śāstras*, applies only to maidens and not to non-maidens. Thus it is shown: "At the wedding, during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious day, one should take the hand of a maiden—during any three of the asterisms beginning with Uttarā, or under Svāti, Mṛgaśiras, or Rohiṇī. Furthermore, it demonstrates this same point: "The bride's brother pours fried grain mixed with *śamī* and *palāśa* leaves into her joined palms; she offers them while standing with her right foot placed forward. Since this is the case, therefore their completion (*niṣṭhā*) should be understood by the wise to occur at the seventh step. The completion—the final conclusion—of those mantras used for the purpose of taking the hand occurs at the seventh step. This is because the world to be attained after death through his actions, consisting of the seven worlds, is of such a limited extent. For there are seven worlds, from the Earth (*bhūr*) up to Satya; he desires to go to those, corresponding in number to the steps, together with her by means of Vedic and Smārta rites. And thus the mantra is merely a restatement of this fact: "Become my companion at the seventh step. This being so, up to the seventh step, she is to be abandoned if she is known to have had sexual intercourse. But beyond the seventh step, even if she has had sexual intercourse, she is not to be cast off. Therefore, this follows from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word "completion. And this being so, the scriptural instruction regarding the *sahoḍha* (born of a pregnant bride) and the *kānīna* (maiden-born) sons becomes meaningful. As for a woman who, though diseased, is capable of fulfilling either religious duty (*dharma*) or procreation (*prajana*), having accepted her, one should not abandon her. For when there is no conflict with religious duty or procreation, there is no other duty to be performed by a man toward her. Even if her union were for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), even then he would marry another before the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). However, she who is capable of both religious duty and procreation is equal to one who already exists [as a wife] and must indeed be abandoned. And this legal proceeding regarding a maiden is spoken of at this limit because of its similarity to the rescission of a purchase or sale. (8.226)
In whatever matter one may feel remorse after it has been performed, one should establish that person on the path of dharma by means of this procedure. 8.227
In cases of subsequent disputes arising from the time of the advance dowry and so forth, the final settlement shall take place within ten days. 8.227.
I shall now duly declare, according to the true principles of dharma, the legal dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen regarding livestock.
This is the verse stating the purpose of the introduction. 8.228.
During the day, the responsibility for what is said rests with the keeper; at night, it rests with the owner in his own home.
If, however, the security of the property is otherwise compromised, the keeper shall incur the responsibility for what is said.
The meaning of the verse is clear. || 8.229 ||

A cowherd who is maintained with milk may milk the best of ten cows; this shall be the wages for a herdsman if he is not otherwise paid, provided he has the consent of the owner of the cattle. (8.230)

A cowherd is of two kinds: one supported by milk and one supported by food and clothing. Therefore, this is specified: that cowherd who is supported by milk shall milk "from ten," meaning from ten cows he may take one excellent or superior cow; and even that, only with the consent of the owner of the cattle, not by his own will. That shall be his wages, provided he is otherwise not supported by another wage. This being so, when there are five stages of the cows or many stages, the owners of the cattle and the cowherds have agreed upon a third part of the milk, to be enjoyed or not enjoyed according to the form determined by this very scripture. And because of this very observation, supporting oneself on milk in the protection of cattle is not a fault, since it is not prohibited. This being so— || 8.230 ||
If an animal is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by a dog, or dies in a dangerous place due to a lack of human effort, the keeper alone shall be held liable. (8.231)
Through the negligence of the cowherd. || 8.231 ||
The exception to this rule is:
"But if cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay, provided he reports it to his own master at the proper place and time. (8.232)

If, after having made a public proclamation at the place and time of the theft, the owner has been informed, the herdsman shall not have to pay; nor shall he be liable if the animals die by their own nature, provided the herdsman was acting with due diligence. (8.232)
He shall give the ears, the hide, the tail-hairs, the bladder, the tendons, and the bile to the owners of the animals; and when they have died, he shall show them the branded marks. (8.233)
And this rule is without exception. 8.233.
He said this for the sake of goats and sheep:
"But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come, if a wolf should kill one by force, the guilt for that shall lie with the herdsman. (8.234)

If a wolf should kill [the cattle] while the herdsman is present, or in his absence, he alone shall make restitution; for he is not present to guard those that have been penned up. The mention of the "wolf" is intended to illustrate other predators as well. (8.234)
If, among those cows kept within the fold grazing together in the forest, a wolf should spring upon and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter. (8.235)

Because it is impossible to protect [the cattle] in a forest filled with many trees, shrubs, and pits while they are roaming about together, there is no fault on the part of the herdsman. By this, the case of cows, buffaloes, and so forth is explained. The rule for the protection of cattle has been stated; now this is said for the purpose of addressing injury to cattle and the destruction of cattle. (8.235)
The boundary of a village should extend one hundred bows on all sides, or else three throws of a wooden pin; for a city, however, it should be triple that amount. 8.236.
That region which, all around the villages and cities, is a place where cattle may roam and rest at ease, and where no crops are sown. || 8.236 ||
If cattle should damage grain that is not enclosed there, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of those animals. (8.237)
But if it has been sown there by the owner of the land and is not enclosed by anyone, then there would be no fault for cows eating it, nor for those who tend cattle. (8.237)
One should construct a fence there such that even a camel cannot look over it, and one should block every opening through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass. 8.238.
But when a fence capable of restraining cattle has been constructed, the fault for damage to the crops shall lie with the herdsman. (8.238)

On a path, in an unfenced field, or again at the edge of a village, the keeper is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas] for failing to restrain the animal; however, he need not restrain an animal that is unattended. (8.239)

If a herdsman allows [the cattle] to eat by letting them fall upon [the crop] with a staff, he deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; furthermore, he should drive away the cattle that are without a keeper. And the herdsman shall be exempt from punishment if the cattle were not under his immediate supervision. However, there is another meaning here: "with a keeper" (*sapāla*) refers to the field-owner (*kṣetrika*) together with the keeper; it does not refer to the cattle here. As stated previously, he (the field-owner) would deserve a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. Because of the fault of both parties—namely, that the field-owner did not protect his own field—it is a punishment for both due to the fault of both. It is also stated in the *Gautamīya*: "On a path or in an unenclosed field, [the responsibility falls] on the keeper and the field-owner. (8.239)
In other fields, however, the animal deserves a fine of one paṇa and a quarter; in all cases, it is the settled rule that a portion of the crop must be given to the owner of the field. 8.240.

"Other fields" refers to those outside the previously mentioned boundary. Because of the instruction regarding a cow and a *paṇa* and a quarter, the king’s share of the fine for buffaloes and other animals shall be proportionate to the damage. And because of the word "everywhere," the field-owner’s compensation (*śada*) must be paid even when there is no herdsman. (8.240)

Manu has declared that one should not punish a cow that has recently calved and is within ten days of birth, nor bulls, nor animals dedicated to the gods, whether they have a keeper or are without a keeper. (8.241)

This is an exception to what was stated previously. Bulls that are "sprinklers" (vṛṣāḥ) are those intended for breeding; and animals dedicated to the gods (*devapaśavaḥ*), such as those released according to the rule of the bull-consecration (*vṛṣotsarga*), as well as other wild animals—even goats and the like—that serve as ornaments in temples, are exempt from punishment. Now, one might object: since the property of the gods is held to be ownerless (*niṣparigraha*), this [exemption] is inappropriate regarding divine animals. However, because these [animals] are followed by those who possess them, they acquire the same status [as private property], and thus this exception is established. Alternatively, animals are mentioned here merely for the sake of illustration: just as divine animals are exempt from punishment, so too are a cow that has calved within ten days, bulls that are "sprinklers," or those belonging to a possessor. In the case of temples, it is not fitting to impose this punishment. And if this were the case, whatever rule applies to others who possess property would also apply to them; but this is not desired. (8.241)
In the event of a transgression by the landowner, the fine shall be ten times his share;
for the servants, however, the fine shall be half of that, provided the landowner was unaware. 8.242.

Since a cultivator might steal from a crop, a fine ten times the value of that share should be prescribed according to the calculation of the portion. The servants should receive half of that fine. However, if the theft occurs through the negligence of the cultivator himself, this same fine shall apply to the servants. This transgression of the cultivator is mentioned here because of the context concerning crops, and because it is considered a form of theft. (8.242)
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule in cases of transgression involving owners of cattle, the animals themselves, and their keepers. (8.243)
This verse has the purpose of providing a summary. 8.243.
When a dispute has arisen concerning a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the landmarks are clearly visible.
The presentation is for the purpose of directing the mind; in the month of Jyeṣṭha, the embankments—the causes for the demarcation of boundaries—become clearly discernible. 8.244.
One should establish boundary trees such as the *nyagrodha*, the *aśvattha*, the *kiṃśuka*, the *śālmali*, the *śāla*, the *tāla*, and other milky-sap trees. (8.245)
By means of thickets, various bamboos, *chamī* creepers, grassy plots, reeds, and *kubjaka* shrubs, the boundary is not lost. 8.246.
Reservoirs, wells, ponds, and springs, as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries. (8.247)
And one should cause other boundary markers to be concealed, having observed that in this world there is constant confusion among people regarding the knowledge of boundaries. (8.248)
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand— (8.249)
And whatever items of this kind the earth might consume over time, those he should cause to be deposited secretly at junctions [or within the boundaries]. (8.250)
These six verses are intended to show the methods for establishing boundary markers. (8.245–250)
By these marks, as well as by constant prior possession and by the flow of water, the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties. (8.251)

Where boundary marks have been established and have perished, yet the absence of either party is not remembered, there prior possession (*pūrvabhukti*) is the authority. However, when there is the absence of one party, prior possession is not relied upon, according to the principle that "possession is not lost by mere enjoyment. For the status of enjoyment as a cause exists, since a demarcation is made only when [the other side] is not absent. What is the use of establishing boundary marks here? For the stream itself, being eternally flowing, will serve to establish the boundary. Indeed, while prior possession exists, it is not reasonable to assume that the arrival of water is without cause or that it can be sublated by mere doubt. Therefore, the arrival of water is postulated only in cases where the subject is absent, for the sake of easy understanding regarding the future interests of both parties. Alternatively, the great stream should be understood as having a non-vacuous subject. For great streams sometimes flow even by an improper path; in such a case, even transcending prior possession, the stream itself shall serve to determine the boundary. (8.251)
If there were doubt even when the boundary marks are visible, the decision in a dispute over boundaries would depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses. (8.252)
When a sign arises from nothing whatsoever, and when there is recollection of a sign in both ways, there is direct perception by a witness. 8.252
But the witnesses to the boundary must be questioned in the presence of the villagers' families and of those two litigants concerning the boundary marks. (8.253)
The procedure for questioning. 8.253.
But when they have been questioned, he should fix the boundary exactly as they all unanimously declare it, and he should record all of them by name. (8.254)
One should also write down a formal document as a record for the purpose of memory. 8.254.
Bearing the earth upon their heads, wearing garlands and red garments,
and sworn by their own meritorious deeds, they shall lead him in accordance with justice.
The procedure for eye-opening. 8.255.
Those witnesses of truth who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified;
those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.

The praise is for the purpose of encouragement, and the punishment is as previously stated; however, the subversion [of the rules] by another must be understood through other legal proceedings. 8.256.
But in the absence of witnesses, four neighboring villagers shall,
being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
Those were the ones who had experienced it previously; these neighbors, however, have heard of it through oral tradition.
But in the absence of neighboring witnesses on the boundary of the original landowners, he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests: ||| 8.258 ||
But in their absence, those whose domain is the forest shall be the authority. || 8.258 ||
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers, snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest. (8.259)
Whatever those witnesses may declare as the boundary markers at the junctions of the borders, the king shall establish that accordingly between the two villages in accordance with the law. (8.260)
This verse serves as a summary. 8.260.
The determination of boundaries and landmarks for fields, wells, tanks, groves, and houses is to be known as dependent upon the testimony of the neighbors. (8.261)

Because the value of the object within its boundaries is great, they might occasionally fail to bring a legal action for ten years; therefore, in that case, it is said: "It is not lost by adverse possession. However, in the case of fields and the like, because the value of the object is very small, this very position—that "any [period] of ten years"—is adopted. Therefore, for these, a decision based on the testimony of neighbors is prescribed. Just as for other objects a decision is based on the testimony of witnesses, so too it is for these. (8.261)
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary, they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement. (8.262)
This is the specific punishment for witnesses regarding boundary marks. 8.262.
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred panas; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred. (8.263)
This is the punishment for the concealment of knowledge or ignorance. || 8.263 ||
When the boundary cannot be determined, the king himself, knowing the law, shall assign land to them for their benefit; such is the established rule. (8.264)

If the land is impossible to enjoy due to its distance, the king may grant it in one place through a connection with a visible benefit; and there is no fault in the king's taking it back. This instruction is for this specific purpose; therefore, even if he does not give it, there is no fault. (8.264)
Thus has the law regarding the determination of boundaries been declared in its entirety.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the legal decision concerning verbal abuse.

This verse is intended as a summary and introduction. Now, one might object that there is a discrepancy in the sequence [of topics], since in the enumeration of the grounds for legal dispute (*vyavahārāspanda*), it was stated: "In cases of verbal assault (*daṇḍavācika-pāruṣye*)," and according to that verbal order (*śabdakrama*), physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) should have been mentioned first. However, here the verbal assault is presented first by relying on the logical order (*arthakrama*). And the logical order is more authoritative than the verbal order; therefore, there is no discrepancy in the sequence, because in this *dvandva* compound, [the term with fewer syllables comes first]. (8.265)
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred;
a Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment. (8.266)

Except for the case of unspeakable abuse, these rules of punishment apply to other forms of verbal assault as appropriate. Regarding the abuse of a Brāhmaṇa: the punishment prescribed for a Vaiśya who abuses a Brāhmaṇa—half of that is incurred by a Vaiśya for abusing a Kṣatriya according to the rule. However, for a Śūdra, there is the punishment for a single birth (ekajāti), because that [punishment] is ordained for the mere abuse of any twice-born person (dvijāti) in the verse: "A once-born man [should pay a fine] for abusing a twice-born man" (MDh 8.266).
A Brahmin shall be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
in the case of a Vaiśya, the fine shall be twenty-five, and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve. (8.267)

The verse has been explained in the *Gadā*. Here too, according to the established principle, a Kṣatriya, having reviled a Vaiśya, should be fined double the penalty for reviling a Brāhmaṇa; whereas a Vaiśya, having reviled a Śūdra, should pay triple the penalty for reviling a Brāhmaṇa. (8.267)
In the case of an offense among twice-born men of equal caste, the fine shall be exactly twelve;
in disputes that are not fit for verbal discussion, that same fine shall be doubled.

[In the case of] a Brāhmaṇa, [the same applies]; likewise for the other two [castes]. Even in the case of a Śūdra, because the nature of the offense is the same, this very same [penalty] would apply. And thus, since the mention of the "twice-born" (dvijāti) is not intended to be restrictive, this [rule] would apply here even for the purpose of illustrating a single caste. However, in the cases of unspeakable disputes, such as "having reviled a Brāhmaṇa with a hundred [insults]," whatever has been stated therein shall be doubled in those instances. || 8.268 ||
One of low birth who insults a twice-born man with harsh words shall have his tongue cut out, for he is born from a base origin. (8.269)

For a Śūdra, corporal punishment is prescribed for insulting a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, this rule of punishment for insulting a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should be understood to apply to him as well. For, by implication, it is understood that his tongue shall be cut off in a manner that does not deprive him of life. (8.269)
And for one who utters their names or castes with malicious intent, an iron spike ten fingers long, glowing with heat, shall be thrust into his mouth. (8.270)
In this manner, the death penalty is prescribed for a Śūdra who, out of malice, reviles those who are beyond reproach. 8.270.
If he should out of pride give instruction in the Dharma to Brahmins, the king shall cause heated oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears. (8.271)

And this capacity for instructing in the Dharma is to be understood as pertaining to a Śūdra by implication; this being the case, this [capacity] does not constitute a sign of a Śūdra's entitlement to the scriptures. 8.271.
One who, out of arrogance, speaks falsely regarding another's learning, country, caste, or even their physical body, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas. (8.272)
Even though this occurs in the section concerning Śūdras, this rule should be understood to apply to all [classes], beginning with Brāhmaṇas, by virtue of its inherent applicability. (8.272)
Whether one says of another that they are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly deformed—even if it be the truth—one shall be made to pay a fine of at least one *kārṣāpaṇa*. (8.273)

And having fully ascertained the offense, such as its being less than one *kārṣāpaṇa*, [the punishment] should be fixed; likewise, the exception to the prescribed penalty mentioned in the scripture, "having fully ascertained the consequences," and so forth. (8.273)
One who defames his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; likewise, one who does not yield the path to his teacher. (8.274)

In this verse, the mention of "wife" (*jāyā*) and "son" (*tanaya*) is for the sake of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). How so? First of all, even in the case of slandering one's wife or son, this punishment would be appropriate; how much more so in the case of [slandering] one's mother and others, since the wife and son are inferior to the mother and others. From this implication, it should be explained in this way: if the brother is younger, then this same explanation applies here. But since the elder brother is mentioned, because of his superior status, it is logical that this [rule] is intended as a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). This being the case, the mention of "guru" is for the purpose of including those such as teachers of knowledge (*vidyā-guru*). Since the inclusion of the mother and others is already established by the mention of "guru," their separate instruction should be understood as being for the sake of showing special respect (*ādara*). Furthermore, this other sentence, which concerns a different matter, is stated within this very context because the punishment is the same: "And not yielding the path to a guru"—even if one does not slander him in any way, this same single punishment shall be imposed. And precisely because of this mention of "guru," it is understood all the more clearly that the previous mention of "wife and son" is for the sake of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), since two other forms of transgression involving similar punishments are heard elsewhere. Slander (*ākṣāraṇa*) is a specific form of verbal abuse (*vāk-pāruṣya*), such as reviling and the like. However, another says: "Slander is the causing of division by means of falsehood. Yet another says: "It is the making of a false accusation. Both of these, however, must be examined—whether they are appropriate or inappropriate—in light of the contradiction with the present context. (8.274)
A wise king should impose two different fines upon a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement. (8.275)

In the case of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, it is likewise determined that, with respect to their own respective castes, the application of punishment shall be exactly as prescribed, with the exception of corporal mutilation. 8.276.

This is another injunction stated for the purpose of providing an alternative option by virtue of the power of the instruction: when a Brāhmaṇa reviles a Kṣatriya, then the punishment for him is the first amercement; and when a Kṣatriya [reviles] a Brāhmaṇa, then in that case it is the middle amercement. In the same way [this applies] between a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, as well as between a Vaiśya and a Śūdra. This being so, it follows that for a Śūdra, the infliction of punishment is declared with the exception of cutting off the tongue. (8.275–76)
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault. 8.277.
If an outcaste should injure a superior person with any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu. 8.278.

This is a general statement regarding the detailed exposition that has been declared. Because of the illustration [using the phrase] "the best of the twice-born," it should be understood that this applies to the injury of even a member of a higher caste, not only in the case of a Śūdra’s prior offense. These four verses to be mentioned hereafter are the detailed expansions (*prapañca*) of this general verse. (8.277–78)
Raising his hand or his staff, he deserves the cutting off of a hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of a foot. (8.279)
One born of low status who seeks the same seat as one of superior status should be branded on the hip and banished, or his buttock should be gashed. (8.280)

The king shall cause both lips to be cut off of one who, out of arrogance, spits upon him; he shall cause the penis to be cut off of one who urinates upon him, and the anus of one who passes wind against him. (8.281)
If he seizes him by the hair, the king shall cut off both his hands without hesitation; the same applies if he seizes him by the feet, the nose, the neck, or the testicles. (8.282)

This being the case, violence (*hiṃsā*) is not merely killing; rather, it is the production of suffering in another by means of various methods. For the twice-born (*dvijāti*), when they transgress against one another, a monetary fine is prescribed as an alternative to the previously mentioned punishment, depending on their lack of faith and the nature of the offense. (8.282)
One who causes a wound in the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished.
He who causes a change in the skin that is not bloody is to be known as a "lacerator of the skin. The rest is straightforward. However, its specific application is to both humans and animals. (8.283)
