"Whatever the manner of use for all forest trees, in that same manner must punishment be inflicted for injury; such is the settled rule. (8.284)

In this context, the term *vanaspati* includes trees as well. Some say that this verse has already been explained by the phrase "having fully understood the consequences"; however, that is incorrect, for this verse is appropriate as a rule regarding punishment for one who commits such injury. (8.284)
When it is a matter of causing suffering to humans or animals, one should inflict punishment in proportion to how great that suffering may be. (8.285)

This being the case, this [verse] should be understood as providing a specific rule for the previously mentioned punishment for injury. How so? For the rule of punishment stated regarding the "one who pierces the skin"—namely, that it must be determined by the presiding judge according to the nature of the offense—this verse is intended to convey that meaning. (8.285)
In the case of crushing a limb, as well as in the case of [injuring] life or blood, he shall be made to pay the expenses of recovery, or else the full penalty. (8.286)

Furthermore, the person who causes injury shall be made by the king to pay the costs of restoration and the expenses incurred therein to the injured party. However, if the injured person does not accept these expenses from the wrongdoer, then the king himself shall collect both amounts and consolidate them into a single sum. (8.286)
If one should damage the property of another, whether intentionally or unintentionally, he must provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king. 8.287.

Whether acting intentionally or unintentionally, one who causes harm or destruction is subject to punishment; however, one should not be released on the grounds that it was done unknowingly. Furthermore, satisfaction [of the victim] arises either through the restoration of the object or, in the case of its total destruction without trace, by providing another item of a similar kind. (8.287)
For leather goods, articles made of leather, and those made of wood or clay, as well as for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value. (8.288)

In the case of destroying these [articles], the fine shall be fivefold, not equal to their value. And thus, in cases other than these, the rule from the preceding verse is to be understood as prescribing a fine equal to the value; however, the production of satisfaction remains firmly established. 8.288.
They say there are ten exemptions for the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle; in all other cases, a fine is prescribed. (8.289)

Regarding the ten grounds that will be mentioned hereafter, this "transgression" refers to the absence of punishment when there is destruction of property or the killing of a living being. Others, however, say that its status as one of the ten is not intended. (8.289)
When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the vehicle turns sideways or comes face-to-face with another, or likewise when there is a breakage of the axle or the wheel; 8.290.
In the case of breaking machines, as well as yokes and reins, and when one cries out "Get away!", Manu declared that these persons are not to be punished. (8.291)

In the case of a draft ox whose nose-string is severed, or when its yoke is broken; likewise, when the vehicle moves sideways or comes toward one's face; and when there is a breakage of the axle or the wheels; similarly, in the case of the thong or the reins; and when it cries out "Move aside!"—in these ten circumstances, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the owner of the vehicle or others. However, in cases other than these, the cause of their offense is stated for the purpose of the punishment to be declared later regarding injury to humans and other beings. (8.290–91)
But where a vehicle turns off course due to the driver's negligence, the owner shall be liable for the damage and must pay a fine of two hundred panas. (8.292)

When the driver is at fault, the offense belongs to the owner, because the driver is under his direction. Furthermore, the mention of the "two-hundred-paṇa fine" here is not intended to be definitive, since this section concerns the offense as a basis for punishment. For the punishment for injuring humans and so forth will be stated later, as it depends on the specific nature of the living being injured; he will say: "In the case of killing a human, the guilt is immediately equal to that of a thief. Likewise, regarding small animals, he will state a specific fine in that very same context: "For injuring small animals, however, the fine is two hundred. Therefore, the mention of the "two-hundred-paṇa fine" was stated without intending it to be a fixed rule. (8.292)
If the driver is trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the fine;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred. (8.293)

If the driver is skilled, only the driver is to be punished. However, those standing on the vehicle—whether they be the owner of the vehicle or others who are not the owners—if they are unskilled, each of them shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]. This applies only when the driver was employed by the owners of the vehicle to travel to another region, and not otherwise. Furthermore, the specific mention of "one hundred" as the fine is not intended to be restrictive; this is how the explanation is to be understood. (8.293)
But if, while obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot, he should cause the death of a living being, the punishment for that has been deliberated upon. (8.294)

If [an injury occurs] due to the driver's lack of skill, ignorance, or defects such as being obstructed; or by cattle yoked to one's own chariot that have turned toward the opponent; or by the chariot itself moving backward and obstructing the yoke-animals; or by the animals being crowded from this side or that by causes such as falling into a pit—then the punishment resulting from such an offense is called "punishment for an accident. This has already been examined in terms of its specific qualities immediately following the statement regarding the owner of the vehicle and others: "In cases where the yoke-animals turn away," and so forth. In the verses to be cited below, regarding the offenses of the owner of the vehicle and others mentioned just prior, if a human or other living being is killed by causes such as the turning away of the yoke-animals, the punishment to be declared is "in the case of killing a human, quickly," and so forth. However, this does not refer to punishment for the killing of humans or other living beings in general. Rather, what has been examined and taught in various ways is the punishment specifically for the particular types of injury to humans and others. Alternatively, the mention of "cattle and chariot" is not intended as a qualification for the obstruction of one's own vehicle as we have explained; rather, it refers to cattle known as oxen yoked to one's own chariot, or to one's own chariot itself, in some crowded place, falling from this or that path because of the congestion; if, in such a situation, one should cause the death of living beings, the punishment for that has been examined—this is the meaning of what was said. Now, the alternative punishments for the driver and others in the aforementioned offenses are stated. (8.294)
In the case of killing a human being, one quickly incurs guilt equal to that of a thief; for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, and horses, the guilt is half [of that]. (8.295)

Even though the offense is described without distinction [from that of a thief], there is no corporal punishment; rather, there is a fine of the highest amercement (*uttama-sāhasa*). And so, regarding large living beings—such as cows and the like by virtue of their power, and elephants and the like by virtue of their size—he prescribes half the fine, measured against the penalty for the offense of a thief. And that half-penalty, being a monetary fine, is appropriate only for the previously mentioned highest amercement, not for corporal punishment. Furthermore, since the fine of two hundred [paṇas] is prescribed in the subsequent verse for the injury of small animals in the third category, this indicates that in the first category, the monetary fine of the highest amercement is intended here. This being the case, when the offense is equal to that of a thief, the monetary fine of the highest amercement alone is appropriate, not corporal punishment. If this is so, then in the rule "the king should be approached by the thief," both options—"by punishment or by release"—are applicable to the thief upon approaching the king. And that release is appropriate only through a monetary fine. Thus, the subsequent rules regarding punishment become meaningful. Moreover, the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "horses etc. should be understood as referring to buffaloes and similar animals. (8.295)
For the killing of small animals that provide wool, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.

Because goats and sheep are mentioned separately, the mention of "small animals" here is for another purpose. Thus, in this context, cattle and other such animals are included because of their limited utility. Alternatively, the mention of goats, sheep, and so forth in the subsequent verse may be for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, "auspicious wild animals and birds"—such as the ruru deer, the peacock, and others—serve as ornaments for the abodes of the deities, or they are those not already claimed by others. (8.296)
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣas;
however, for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣa. (8.297)

And here, by the mention of a "māṣika" (one-māṣa coin), the inclusion of the material substance is to be understood through the capacity of the person, the nature of the offense, and the circumstances; furthermore, this penalty being prescribed specifically for the injury of living beings that possess property is to be understood as applying elsewhere as well, such as in the case of damaging a vehicle, due to the similarity of the act. (8.297)
A wife, a son, slaves, a pupil, and a uterine brother—when they have committed an offense, they may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane. (8.298)
This undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting punishment, and for the purpose of establishing the rules regarding beating and wounding. 8.298.
But never on the back of the body, nor on the head by any means. This half-verse is intended to define the specific parts of the body that may be struck.
However, striking otherwise than this, one would incur the guilt of a thief. (8.299)

Thus, this [rule] is to be understood as prescribing a beating in the event of a transgression of the rule. However, there is no absolute necessity for the beating of these offenders, such as sons and others, because the instruction is intended to establish a rule. The statement "he would incur the guilt of a thief" is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) meant to effect desistance from such a transgression of the rule. This being the case, if one beats them otherwise than this, there is merely a violation of the rule, but he is not to be punished like a thief; rather, there may be only a punishment of reproach (*dhig-daṇḍa*) or a punishment of words (*vāk-daṇḍa*), because of the similarity in that regard. (8.299)
Thus has the determination of punishment for assault been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment for a thief.

This verse is intended to provide a summary and introduction. Furthermore, lest there be an equality between this [offense] and previous ones, he says this because of its gravity, in order to show due respect for its suppression. (8.300)
A king should exert the utmost effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase. (8.301)

How so? For among the activities of the people—both those for the sake of livelihood and those with unseen purposes—the suppression of those who obstruct well-performed deeds [is necessary]. This being the case, thus [it is said]: 8.301.
For that king who is a giver of fearlessness is always worthy of honor;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) is ever-prosperous, having the gift of fearlessness as its fee.

The meaning is that for whatever [being] the sacrificial session (*sattra*) increases, there is never any form of restraint toward them for as long as one lives; it is not, however, as in the *vaitāna* [rites] where there is a fixed time. Thus, this [session] has "fearlessness" as its sacrificial fee (*abhayadakṣiṇa*); because of the absence of a fee in a [standard] *sattra*, this sacrificial session is distinguished from it. (8.302)
A king who provides protection receives a sixth part of all merit from the Dharma.

The word "from all" (*sarvataḥ*) means from those who possess property and even from those who receive a livelihood, let alone from others, since [in their case] there is not even a trace of a livelihood. Alternatively, because this instruction belongs to the *Smṛti* tradition, this inclusion of "all"—which would otherwise apply only to the six-fold share [of taxes] regarding the objects of *Smṛti*—is made for the sake of [including] the objects of *Śruti*; and thus he will state in the immediately following verse: "Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices," and so forth. If the king protects [his subjects], he receives a sixth part of their merit (*dharma*). Having established that the reason [for the tax] is reversed in this case, the following is said:
For one who does not protect [them], even a sixth part of their demerit falls upon him. (8.303)

Alternatively, this statement regarding the king’s share of one-sixth of the demerit for non-performance applies to a learned man (*śiṣṭa*) who, having been appointed by the Self-Existent One (*Svayambhū*) to the task of protection, fails to perform it according to the treatises on his fitness; or else, it refers to the failure at the time of consecration to protect the subjects, just as there is a loss of the promise made for another purpose. (8.304)
Now he explains this section of the Sūtra, "The king receives a sixth part of everything":
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one gives, and whatever one worships—the king becomes a sharer in a sixth part of that, provided he protects [his subjects] properly. (8.304)

Furthermore, because these [verses] serve to illustrate all ritual actions (*kriyā*), other [actions] should not be excluded from those already specified; moreover, let there be no contradiction with the Vedas, the Smṛtis, the Śāstras, or logic. Therefore, abandoning this construction according to the literal text, the mention of "taking a sixth part of the merit" (*dharma-ṣaḍbhāga-grahaṇa*) is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) that functions indirectly (*pranāḍikayā*) with reference to either the duty of restraint (*niyamadharma*) or the protection of virtuous persons. Thus, this mention of taking a sixth part of the merit is for the purpose of an indirect explanatory praise. It cannot, however, be merely for the sake of persuasion (*prarocanārtha*) based on the king having been hired for his livelihood, as there would otherwise be no connection to *dharma*. For this reason also, the king’s taking of a sixth part of the merit depends upon the protection of his subjects. (8.304)
As it is said:
"A king who protects all beings according to dharma and executes those deserving of death, performs sacrifices every day with sacrificial fees of hundreds and thousands. (8.305)

For praise does not proceed without cause; therefore, by this [praise], it follows that the king’s duty (*dharma*) must consist of the protection of his subjects according to the principles of the scripture as stated. And the restraint of those deserving of death is for the sake of protection by way of an indirect means. Thus, he shows protection as distinct from that [restraint] in the phrase "protecting according to *dharma*. He establishes those belonging to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*) in their own duties according to the scripture, by demonstrating the meaning of the scripture. How so? The meaning is: "You yourselves should be thus; perform what is instructed by the scripture"; and the meaning is: "You, however, should not be thus; avoid what is forbidden. He protects them either by punishing them according to the scripture for the transgression of these instructions, or by other means. This being the case, protection is understood to be something other than the act of executing those deserving of death. He protects them by punishing them according to the scripture for the transgression of these instructions. And this being the case, another form of protection is recognized as distinct from the execution of the condemned. And this being so, he will say: "From the protection of those of noble conduct and from the clearing away of thorns," as well as: "By the restraint of the wicked and by the gathering together of the virtuous," and so forth. (8.305)
Since this is so, therefore:
That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, tolls, the fee for pleasure-entertainments, and fines, shall immediately go to hell. (8.306)
Likewise, there is the tradition of the recollection of the learned. || 8.306 ||
They say that a king who fails to protect his subjects, yet takes a sixth part as tax, is the remover of all the impurities of the entire world. (8.307)
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, who causes destruction, who fails to protect, and who devours his subjects, is destined for a downward path.

And in the section concerning thieves, having praised the execution of the suppression of thieves for the sake of protection, [the author] now states this regarding the nature of that suppression: 8.308.
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by binding, and by various forms of corporal punishment. (8.309)

By means of beating and so forth, according to the offense: whoever commits an offense, him he should join with a punishment corresponding to that offense, relying upon the balance of Dharma and free from passion or hatred. For what reason? Because— || 8.309 ||
By the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous,
kings are constantly honored, just as the twice-born are by sacrifices.

And since there is no possibility of praising [the king] as being without seeds (i.e., without basis), the benefit as it is heard from scripture is understood to be the characteristic duty (*dharma*) of the king through his restraint [of wrongdoers], as well as that of the thief who is to be restrained. And thus he will say: "Those who have been punished by kings... (MDh 9.246). Furthermore, the connection with *dharma* is established through the protection of the subjects. Because of this abundance of favor toward himself and others, the king must not be negligent in his protection for the sake of restraining the wicked and protecting the virtuous. Now, however, if someone, out of delusion, should cast blame upon him while he conducts himself impartially toward his subjects, then by him... (MDh 8.310).
A lord who seeks his own welfare should always forgive men who bring business before him, as well as children, the elderly, and the sick. (8.311)
He states an explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the purpose of encouraging the performance of the matters already taught. 8.311.
He who, when insulted by those in distress, endures it with patience, is exalted in heaven because of that;
but he who, out of pride in his power, does not endure it, goes to hell because of that. (8.312)

Thus, this is a praise of the practice of forbearance (*kṣamā*). Even when causes for mental agitation arise, the king should diligently cultivate forbearance as the means for attaining both worlds. Due to the inherent nature of the composition, this praise of the practice of forbearance is presented here in both ways [in this verse]. Furthermore, because of its connection with the king, this [topic] regarding the expiation for theft is stated in this very section. (8.312)
The wise thief should go before the king with disheveled hair, confessing that theft: "I am a man of such deeds; punish me. (8.313)

The sin (*pātaka*) belongs to that which is connected with gold and the like, by virtue of which this man is called a thief, and not for the theft of mere property, because of the instruction regarding the magnitude of the penance. And thus, in the section on penances, he will specify [the offender] as "one who has committed the theft of gold," and so forth. Others, however, consider a thief to be one who steals any mere object. In this context, the wise man—recognizing through faith that approaching the king himself, accompanied by various forms of corporal punishment, is the cause of purification according to the authority of the legal treatises on penance—should approach the king. Others, however, read "running" (*dhāvatā*) for the sake of emphasis. Nor is approaching the king the only duty of a thief; what then? This and another [duty follow]. (8.313)
Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood, or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron mace; (8.314)

The conceptualization regarding a single object [of punishment] involves the mace and other implements, with the exception of the Brahmin. Others, however, maintain that these implements, such as the mace and so forth, are taught according to the sequence of the social classes (*varṇa*). And thus, a Kṣatriya or others who have approached him of their own accord, out of faith, [should act] in accordance with the scripture. (8.314)
Whether through instruction or through liberation, the thief is freed from theft.

Or, by royal command—either through release from the characteristic punishment of execution in consideration of the gravity of the offense due to his being destitute, or by being fined instead—he is released from the theft. Even when the offense is grave, a Brāhmaṇa thief is exempted from execution. For this very reason, there is this alternative in the application of punishment. Thus Gautama says in this very context: "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, even if a Brāhmaṇa thief who has not surrendered himself is brought by the king’s officers after his crime is known, he is still not to be executed. What then? "Exile, branding, confiscation of property, and disqualification from religious rites. Nevertheless, this rule of punishment is taught for every thief of gold and other valuables; for otherwise, such punishment would apply only to Brāhmaṇas and non-Brāhmaṇas who have voluntarily confessed. And that being the case:
But by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.315)

This being the case, this expiation (prāyaścitta) should be understood as the cause of purification for these two; thus, approaching the king personally becomes meaningful for them. For it will be stated: "But those who have been punished by kings... However, for one who is punished or executed by the king through force, there is no atonement through that punishment alone. Since even one who has been punished with such a penalty must still perform an expiation, and for one who undertakes the expiation on his own, there is no intervention by the king. And so it will be stated: "...while performing the expiation. Furthermore, the satisfaction of the owner of the property must be secured even by this punished individual. And if the king does not carry out the suppression of the thief, he would bring about his own ruin. (8.315)

For it has been said: "The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife to her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer to their teacher; and a thief to the king. (8.316)

One who eats food is an "eater of food" (*annāda*). Upon that eater of food, the killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahā*) wipes away his guilt. The same should be applied to the others as well. Therefore, a king whose wisdom is steady, acting without hesitation and avoiding for himself the fault of failing to restrain [the wicked], should proceed according to the scriptures in the restraint of thieves for the sake of benefiting himself and others. For, because he has approached [the task] personally, he might at some time—having a divided vision and his resolve impaired—not apply himself to that restraint. (8.316)
This effort is undertaken with regard to the relationship of benefit [as follows]:
"But men who have committed sins, having been punished by kings,
go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds" (8.317).

From the context, this statement regarding being "stainless" refers specifically to the removal of the sin of theft, by which this penance is prescribed solely on account of that theft. Therefore, this is appropriate: that they may go to heaven stainless, by means of the meritorious karma previously acquired for ascending to heaven. This being the case, since both [the thief and the king] have a connection to the benefit at that time through this act performed by the learned, this is a statement of praise regarding the option of approaching the king, and it is not without foundation. (8.317)
Now, he says this next regarding the subject of theft:
"But he who takes a rope or a jar from a well, or who breaks a water-shed, shall receive a fine of one māṣa and shall restore that [item] to its place. (8.318)
Since the *māṣa* is the primary unit and no specific substance is mentioned, it should refer to gold. (8.318)
For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he shall be made to pay eleven times the value, and that property shall be returned to its owner. (8.319)

Even in the case of beating, "killing" (vadha) is prescribed as the penalty. But here, if this applies to the theft of grain among Brāhmaṇas and others, and the thief happens to be of a lower caste, then because of the gravity of the offense, the rule regarding killing should not be understood as applying to him due to his lack of merit. In other cases, however, the calculation must be inferred by oneself. For ten [measures], the fine is elevenfold, but not death. (8.319)
Likewise, for goods measured by weight— such as gold, silver, and the like— and for the finest garments, there shall be execution if the amount exceeds one hundred.

Those things which are measured by weight on a scale are "measurable by weight" (*dharimameya*), such as gold and the like. The mention of "gold and the like" is for the purpose of excluding ghee and similar substances; for immediately thereafter, he will prescribe a fine double that value for ghee and other such items. Furthermore, the inclusion of the phrase "of gold, silver, and so forth" is intended to include all metals. On the other hand, for those who claim that grains and the like are "measurable apart from weights," this would result in redundancy with the rule "grain [stolen] from ten *kumbhas*. Moreover, if ghee and the like were considered "measurable by weight," there would be a repetition with the ghee and other items to be mentioned later. Therefore, the analysis of the compound *dharimameyānām* is exactly as stated above. And [this applies to] the finest garments, such as new cloth and the like. (8.320)
But for a theft exceeding fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remainder as well, one should determine a fine eleven times the value of the stolen property. (8.321)
If the amount exceeds fifty [paṇas], there shall be the amputation of a hand; even if it is less than that, the fine shall be eleven times the value. (8.321)
One deserves death for the theft of men of noble birth, and especially of women, as well as for the theft of the most precious jewels. (8.322)
In this case, a detailed injunction must be formulated in consideration of the caste and qualities of both the one being carried away and the one who carries them away. 8.322.
Upon seizing large animals, weapons, or medicinal herbs, the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the purpose of the act. (8.323)

Large animals (*mahāpaśu*) are elephants, horses, camels, and so forth, because their utility is great as observed in practice. Furthermore, in terms of quantity, these large animals belong to the king and his ministers; this is to be understood specifically from the context of their association with the taking up of weapons. Such weapons are generally large in quality only when they are intended for the king’s benefit. Thus, the word "great" (*mahaḥ*) here should be understood in the sense of "principal" or "primary. The same explanation applies to medicinal herbs (*auṣadha*). Regarding the seizure of these items, the king, having determined the time—whether it be characterized by war or its opposite, or the state of regional upheaval known as famine or plenty—and having ascertained the purpose of seizing the large animals—whether the seizure is for gambling and similar purposes, or due to a persistent enmity, or for the sake of maintaining a family distressed by hunger and lacking independence, and whether it is for a righteous purpose rather than for improper use—the king shall impose a punishment. This follows immediately from the verse on grain, where it was stated that the punishment may be death, non-death, or a fine eleven times the value, depending on the knowledge of place, time, the state of affairs, and the caste or quality of the thief. And this has been stated in the verse on the rules of punishment: "Having fully ascertained the motive," and so forth (MDh 8.126). [8.323]
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, for breaking a stall,
and likewise for the theft of livestock, one must immediately have half a foot amputated.

In the preceding verse, however, because the term *mahāpaśu* (large animal) was used, there was no mention of the cow; therefore, this present verse is commenced for the sake of providing a specific rule for her. Alternatively, since she has already been included [in the previous category], this verse serves to introduce a new matter (*apūrvārtha*). Furthermore, by the force of the word "commencement" (*ārambha-sāmarthyāt*), it is understood that the cows referred to here are those belonging to a Brāhmaṇa and remaining from sacrificial rites. This being the case, for one who steals a cow from a Brāhmaṇa who is habitually engaged in sacrifice, the thief shall suffer the punishment of half a *pāda* immediately, without regard for the previously mentioned causes for varying the punishment, such as time, the nature of the act, and so forth. Otherwise, since this would already be established by the rule "for the theft of large animals," the phrase "cows belonging to a Brāhmaṇa" would result in being redundant. Since this must be commenced when there is no consideration of time and other factors, its commencement is thus for the sake of a specific distinction, and not due to the fault of tautology. Alternatively, if the previous verse is disregarded as explained, this applies specifically to the domain of royal administration (*rājatantra*). Therefore, there is no fault in conceiving this as a new rule (*apūrvakalpanā*). Moreover, this same punishment should apply to the breaking of a *sthūrikā* (barren cow), even if it is one's own, due to the force of the commencement [of the topic]. A *sthūrikā* is defined in another region as a barren cow. And those who yoke her to ploughs and the like necessarily break her with a goad. This being so, the "breaking" of her should be understood as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for making her work. However, for one who reads it otherwise as "and for the driving of a *sthūrikā*," there is no need for inference because it is explicitly stated. But another says: the portion of the hoof four fingers above the heel is the *sthūrikā*; for breaking or cutting that, this same punishment should apply, since the mention of "breaking" is illustrative (*nidarśanārthatvāt*). And for the theft of animals, the punishment is as previously stated. This commencement is for the sake of goats and small animals. It refers to the theft of many sacrificial animals belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, such as goats and the like. Yet another says: it refers to many cows belonging to a Brāhmaṇa who does not perform rituals, and by implication, to the cows of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are habitually engaged in work. This repetition of the word "animal" (*paśu*) is for the purpose of including cows that remain after sacrificial rites. As for those who explain that this is the punishment for stealing curd or milk belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, that is inconsistent due to the absence of such a context. [8.324]
Of cotton thread, silk, and wool; of cow dung and molasses; of curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass. || 8.325 ||
In the case of stealing bamboo or split-bamboo vessels, as well as salts, earthenware, earth, or even ashes; (8.326)
Of fish, of birds, of oil, of clarified butter, of meat, of honey, and whatever else originates from animals. (8.327)
For other such items, as well as for uncooked rice and all kinds of cooked food, the fine shall be double their value. (8.328)

Now, the fine of double the value for the aforementioned articles is stated in four verses. In this group of verses beginning with "thread" (*sūtra*), the mention of ashes and earth is to be understood as illustrative of all such materials. Thus he concludes: "and of others of this kind. (8.325–28)
For flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
and small quantities of unwinnowed produce, the fine shall be five kṛṣṇalas.
"Green" refers to unripe grain with respect to a heap. 8.329.
When grain, vegetables, roots, or fruits have been cleaned, the fine shall be one hundred panas for a first offense, and fifty panas for a subsequent offense. 8.330.

In the case of one who has no connection [to the victim] and is neither protected nor authorized, seizure is most improper; therefore, a fine of one hundred is prescribed. However, in the case of one who has a connection, because of the fault in both cases or because it constitutes an act of violence (*sāhasa*), half [of that fine] is prescribed. But another says: in the case of one who has no connection—that is, no following—if he does not offer conciliation, then his taking [the property] makes him liable to a fine of one hundred; but if he does offer conciliation, then [the fine is] fifty. (8.330)
But others say:
"Sāhasa (violence) would be that act which is committed by force when there is a connection [to the owner];
it would be steya (theft) when it is done without such connection and when one denies having done it after committing it. (8.331)

That which is done by one who is not apprehensive despite the presence of a guard is *sāhasa* (an act of violence). However, that which is done without a trace and without a guard is not theft (*steya*). Furthermore, even if an act is committed with a trace, if one denies it, that too is indeed theft. (8.331)
But the king shall fine that man who steals these prepared articles one hundred [paṇas], as well as whoever would steal the fire from the house. (8.332)

If anyone should forcibly steal these aforementioned items—such as thread and so forth—even if they have been prepared for use or are merely stored away in some way, the king, in order to prevent such recurrence, shall punish him with a fine of one hundred *paṇas* without distinction, whether the value of the object be small or large. The fire is mentioned separately for the sake of showing it special respect; furthermore, in the case of a group of items beginning with thread, a fine double their value is prescribed, but there is no buying or selling of fire. Therefore, the king shall punish with a fine of one hundred *paṇas* whoever steals fire from a house. "Prepared for use" (*upakḷptāni*): regarding these items, the first punishment applies to one who would seize them when they are intended for use, or to one who, having taken charge of the fire, should neglect it due to misconduct. Or, implements such as the *sruk*, *sruva*, mortar, and pestle are referred to by the word "fire" figuratively, because they serve the purpose of the fire. (8.332)
With whatever limb a thief commits an offense against men, that very limb the king shall take away as a deterrent. (8.333)

Whatever limb—whether hand or foot—upon whose strength a thief relies to commit theft, that very limb of his shall be cut off. For example: one who cuts a knot [of goods] has his hand cut off; one who uses the strength of his feet has his feet cut off. This amputation of limbs is prescribed for one who, even after being punished, persists repeatedly, disregarding the previous punishment. Thus it is said: "After this, the punishment of death. In this way, the rule of amputation becomes meaningful in certain cases, such as when there is cutting, his hands are to be severed. (8.333)
Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest—no one is exempt from punishment by the king who does not abide by his own duty. (8.334)

By virtue of the context, this is the punishment for stealing gold. However, if it were to apply elsewhere as well due to a similarity of the offense, then this punishment should be understood to apply to fathers and others in all transgressions according to the sequence of the topics, because of their great importance and the necessity of protecting them; thus, this statement regarding their punishment is intended to remove the doubt that they might otherwise be exempt from punishment. Others, however, consider this to be a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) concerning the punishment for theft which applies to other persons. That is incorrect, because it would contradict the royal punishment mentioned in the following verse. (8.334)
And so it is shown:
"Where the fine for an ordinary person would be one kārṣāpaṇa, there the king shall be fined one thousand; such is the established rule. (8.335)

If a king also practices a transgression of the law, his punishment shall be a thousandfold greater than that prescribed; he must be cast into water for Varuṇa, or this fine must be paid to learned Brāhmaṇas. He will describe these two modes of disposal for both other fines and gold. And it is fitting that the king’s fine should be great even for a minor offense, so that he, being a knower of dharma and the cause of its establishment, may not persist in a transgression of dharma. Thus they say: "In the case of a transgression by one who is ignorant, the punishment is more severe, even for a superior. (8.335)
For a Śūdra, however, the guilt in the case of theft becomes eightfold;
for a Vaiśya, it is sixteenfold, and for a Kṣatriya, it is thirty-twofold.
A Brahmin possesses sixty-four [qualities], for he knows their faults and virtues; or perhaps twice sixty-four, for he knows their faults and virtues. (8.337)

This punishment shall apply to the theft of those substances not previously mentioned; or it may apply to the repeated commission of these very offenses, or to the theft of gold. For one who is learned, there should be a greater severity of punishment for exceeding [the limit]. This same rule would also apply to the king. Thus, because it follows the preceding section, this is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) and not a mandatory injunction regarding punishment. If it is indeed an explanatory statement, then whatever gradations of punishment were mentioned for verbal and physical assault and so forth become consistent. If, however, on the strength of the direct Vedic text (*śruti*), this alternative of punishment is intended according to the specific instruction—just as in the case of public and secret penances (*prāyaścitta*)—then it possesses the character of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). And this being the case, the alternative punishments for a Brāhmaṇa are to be understood with reference to his age and his mastery of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), as is seen elsewhere. However, what is now stated is for the purpose of providing exceptions to the rules on theft. (8.337)
Manu has declared that wood from trees, roots and fruits, firewood for the sake of the sacred fire, and grass for the fodder of cows, are not theft. (8.338)

And because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of taking up the sacred fire (*agnigrahaṇa*), all this [acceptance of gifts] is for the sake of sacrifice and does not cause sin. Thus he will say: "He may accept three or two [kinds of gifts]. This [verse] was spoken for the purpose of punishment, in order to demonstrate that a Brāhmaṇa who knowingly accepts gifts from a thief and so forth is equal to a thief. (8.338)
A Brahmin who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given, even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching, is just like a thief. (8.339)
And thus, because he is equal to a thief, he should be punished like a thief; yet now, on account of a specific cause, he permits the taking of even a small amount from another. (8.339)
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose provisions are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be punished. (8.340)

And thus, this undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting royal punishment when theft is characterized by a specific motive, but it is not an authorization for robbery; therefore, there is no fault. By this, the taking of vegetables, fish, and so forth is explained. 8.340.
One who binds those who are unbound, and releases those who are bound, and who seizes slaves, horses, and chariots, shall incur the guilt of a thief. (8.341)
And the mention of "horse-chariots" should be understood as intended to illustrate camels and other such vehicles by way of a general reference to conveyances. || 8.341 ||
By this method, a king who carries out the suppression of thieves shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death. (8.342)
This verse serves as a summary. 8.342.
Now, rashness is being discussed:
A king who desires to attain the position of Indra and imperishable, undecaying fame should not overlook a man of rash deeds even for a moment. (8.343)
This verse is intended to present a bold proposition. 8.343.
One who is corrupt in speech, a thief, and one who causes injury by means of punishment—the man who commits such violence should be known as the worst among evildoers. (8.344)
And since this is so, therefore: "But that king who tolerates one engaged in violence quickly goes to destruction or incurs enmity. (8.345)
And this being so:
A king should not, for the sake of a friend or from the acquisition of vast wealth, release those who act with violence and bring fear to all living beings. (8.346)

This censure of the perpetrator of violence (sāhasika) is to be understood as intended to show respect for the restraint thereof. Taking up weapons by one belonging to a caste for which it is unjustified constitutes violence (sāhasa). He who acts through that [unjustified taking] is a perpetrator of violence. This being the case, this [rule] concerning the taking up of weapons by a twice-born man on account of a specific cause is commenced as an exception (apavāda) to that [general prohibition], for the purpose of precluding those faults. 8.346.
The twice-born may take up arms when their dharma is obstructed, or during a upheaval of the twice-born and the social orders caused by the exigencies of time. (8.347)
One who kills in self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, or in order to protect a woman or a Brahmin, does not incur sin, provided he acts according to dharma. (8.348)

Because the taking up of weapons serves a purposeful end, this is not a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). Rather, it is a restatement of what is already established by necessity (*arthaprāptānuvāda*), intended to prohibit punishment (*daṇḍapratiṣedhārtha*). Since the protection of subjects is enjoined for the Kṣatriya, the taking up of weapons is already implied; this instruction is therefore understood to apply to the other twice-born castes (*dvijāti*). By stating that "weapons may be taken up by the twice-born," the author now shows the occasion for such taking up: when the Dharma of those belonging to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*) is obstructed in a particular place or time. This constitutes the aphorism (*sūtra*); the following is its commentary (*bhāṣya*). In the case of a collapse among the twice-born castes—such as through the confusion of castes (*varṇasaṅkara*) or the breakdown of social order (*vyavasthābhaṅga*) caused by Time, or due to some misfortune of the king at any time—the obstruction of Dharma occurs. In such a situation, the taking up of weapons is blameless, because the punishment for a violent offender (*sāhasika-daṇḍa*) would otherwise be unjustly applied. Furthermore, it applies to the protection of oneself, one’s family, and one’s wealth from all sides; and it continues with the phrase "the protection against the seizure of sacrificial fees" (*dakṣiṇā*). The mention of "sacrificial fees" is intended to indicate all materials used in sacrifice. In battle (*saṅgara*), but not in deceit, one who has taken up arms for the sake of protecting women and Brāhmaṇas—having taken up arms to prevent the obstruction of Dharma—is not tainted by sin if he kills according to Dharma, and not by treacherous warfare, both in this world and the next, due to the authority of the scriptural teaching. And since Dharma and Adharma are characterized by their respective definitions, this matter is beyond doubt. The mention of "women" is intended to represent all those deserving of protection, such as children, the elderly, and the sick, because of the commonality of the objective (*kāryasāmānya*) of the rule; and the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is intended to represent all those worthy of honor, such as teachers and others. (MDh 8.347–348)
The statement that "one who seizes a weapon in order to prevent an obstruction to the Dharma incurs no fault by killing an assailant" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). [It is said:
"Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or even a highly learned Brāhmaṇa, one should certainly kill an approaching assailant without hesitation. (8.349)

Since it has been stated by such scriptural passages as, "The teacher, the expounder, the father, the mother, and the preceptor," that these persons beginning with the guru are not to be slain even if they commit extreme offenses, this [verse] is for the purpose of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) regarding the preceding injunction. For while even the gurus and others, though being among those who would otherwise be absolutely exempt from death, might be slain on account of this specific cause if they are *ātatāyin*s (aggressors), how much more so those other than them? This is an explanatory eulogy intended to show excellence, just as is common in the world. (8.349)
And thus it says:
"In the killing of an *ātatāyin* (one who comes to kill), there is no fault whatsoever for the slayer, whether done openly or in secret; rather, it is the wrath that reaches that wrath. (8.350)

*Manyu* is the anger of the one who is to be slain; that anger reaches—that is, turns back upon—the slayer. These two verses are intended to praise rashness (*sāhasa*), and that praise is for the purpose of exempting such a person from royal punishment. Thus, by this [text], it is understood that just as there is no royal punishment for killing an *atattāyin* (one who does not come with a weapon), there is likewise an absence of sin (*pratyavāya*). And so Vyāsa says in the dialogue between Bhīṣma, Jāmadagnya, and Rāma: "He who, enraged in battle, slays an opponent fighting without fleeing, incurs no sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*); such is the certainty in the *Dharma*."

Others hold that even teachers and the like, when they persist in such acts and cause slight harm, become liable to be killed; thus, the learned desire the killing of even such *ātatāyins*. Others consider the killing of an inferior *ātatāyin* to be without doubt, whereas in the case of an equal, there is an option, since for one who is superior—whether oneself or another—the act of abandoning one's own life is preferable due to the capacity to avoid the commencement of unwholesome action. This [point] has been answered as far as possible within the commentary on the preceding verse. Furthermore, in this context, only the prohibition of violence (*sāhasa*) is heard, not any rule regarding punishment; therefore, for the low, middling, and high offenses of a perpetrator of violence, the first, middle, and highest fines for violence should apply respectively, as previously defined. Alternatively, because of its similarity to theft, even for a perpetrator of violence, an option regarding the punishment for theft may apply by implication, even though it was not explicitly stated. (8.350)

Now, the offense of adultery with women, which has been reached [in the sequence], is discussed. Men who have engaged in the violation of another's wife, the king, having branded them with terrifying punishments, shall banish them. (8.351)

But for those who, even after being repeatedly warned, do not desist, this procedure of banishment with a mark [of infamy] applies to them. And so it has been stated in the *Aparādhasamuccaya*: "One should first administer a verbal punishment," and so forth. (8.351)
For it is because of that [adharma] that the intermixture of castes arises in the world;
by means of this, adharma becomes a destroyer of the very root, leading to total ruin. (8.352)
This verse is intended to praise the punishment of those who violate another's wife. 8.352.
If a man who has previously been accused of such offenses should engage in secret conversation with another's wife, he shall incur the first amercement. (8.353)
One who has been slandered—that is, one whose guilt is suspected—should not even converse for the sake of ordinary social intercourse. (8.353)
But he who, having not been previously accused, speaks out for a valid reason, shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part. (8.354)
For the sake of social intercourse, public conversation is permitted for one who is not suspected [of wrongdoing]. (8.354)
He who violates another man’s wife at a sacred bathing place, in a wilderness, or even in a forest, or at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery. (8.355)
If a man addresses a woman at sacred bathing places or other secluded spots, even for a valid reason, he shall be guilty of adultery, even if he has not been previously accused. (8.355)
Moreover:
"Performing services, playing together, touching her ornaments and clothes, and even sitting on the same bed—all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery). (8.356)

From the instruction regarding ornaments and garments belonging to women or men, and from touching them—this constitutes an offense against both. Furthermore, anything else such as casting affectionate glances or making gestures with the limbs should also be understood as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual solicitation). 8.356.
And this is another point:

if a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he allows himself to be touched by her when she touches him, it is declared in the legal tradition that all such acts constitute *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse) when there is mutual consent. (8.357)

All these cases should be understood as included within the category of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse), as the purposes of others and women have already been explained in four verses; however, it is not *saṃgrahaṇa* alone [that is meant here]. For there could be no punishment for these that is equal to the punishment for *saṃgrahaṇa*. As it has been said: "Having fully ascertained the offense. Now, if the punishment for *saṃgrahaṇa* were applied to all of these, what would it do when the offense is complete? It is not right to treat unequal things as equal. (8.357)
A non-Brahmin who commits adultery deserves a punishment ending in death;
for the wives of all four castes must always be protected most carefully. (8.358)

If a non-Brāhmaṇa—a Śūdra—engages in sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman who is self-restrained and unwilling, he deserves a punishment ending in death. However, in the case of Kṣatriya or Vaiśya women, the determination of the punishment should be proportionally less according to their respective castes. In the same manner, when a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engages in sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, the punishment must be determined by this same standard; and for a Vaiśya with a Kṣatriya woman, the same applies. Furthermore, when Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya women are willing and unrestrained, the punishment should be determined as previously stated. This [verse] is spoken for the purpose of providing an exception to the prohibition against conversation, with certain specific distinctions. (8.358)
Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice, and artisans may converse with women in the house without being forbidden. (8.359)

It is permitted for mendicants and others to converse with women in their homes even in the absence of a specific reason. However, in secluded places such as bathing ghats and the like, even when a reason exists, mendicants and others should not speak with them, as these are occasions for suspicion. (8.359)
One who is forbidden should not engage in conversation with the wives of others; however, if he converses despite being forbidden, he deserves a fine of one suvarṇa. (8.360)
Conversation with another man’s wife is forbidden by the scriptures; for its transgression, one deserves punishment. (8.360)
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers nor to those who live off their own labor;
for they entice women and keep them hidden away. (8.361)

This is indeed permission for conversation, not for approaching [them sexually]. For in this case, there is merely an absence of royal punishment, but not an absolute absence of invisible (adṛṣṭa) fault; since it is said that "there would be some slight fault for the one who approaches. Furthermore, this is not the subject of the previous prohibition, because these belong to a different class of courtesans (veśajāti). And for this reason, even in the absence of a specific motive, one who converses with them would not incur the charge of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct). || 8.361 ||
But he who engages in conversation with such women shall be made to pay a small fine;
as shall one who does so in secret with female slaves who have only one master, or with female ascetics. (8.362)
And this qualification "alone" (rahaḥ) applies to all [the preceding terms]. 8.362.
And because it concerns sexual union with women, this which pertains to virgins is also stated here:
"He who violates a virgin against her will deserves immediate execution; a man violating one who is willing, being equal [to her], shall not suffer execution. (8.363)
From this point forward, the rule being stated should be understood as pertaining to the maiden. (8.363)
One should not cause a maiden who is pursuing a superior man to give him anything at all;
however, one should keep her confined in the house if she is serving an inferior man. (8.364)
The meaning is straightforward. || 8.364 ||
But a man of lower caste who has intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves death;
one who has intercourse with a woman of equal caste should pay a fine, if her father so desires. 8.365.

Because the text states this without distinction, for a man of lower caste who has sexual intercourse with a woman of higher caste—whether she is willing or unwilling—the punishment is death alone. However, for one who has intercourse with a woman of equal caste who is willing, the fine is the payment of her nuptial fee (śulka) or a punishment equal to that amount. And the preceding verse in this section on adultery, which serves as the basis for this rule, is: "A non-Brāhmaṇa deserves the death penalty for adultery. (MDh 8.365)
But that man who, out of arrogance, should violate a maiden by force, shall have two fingers immediately amputated and deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas]. (8.366)

For one who has sexual intercourse with a woman against her will, the punishment is the cutting off of the fingers and a fine of six hundred [paṇas]. However, there is another reading: "But that man who, out of arrogance, defiles a maiden who is unwilling... (8.366).
But one who violates a willing woman shall not suffer the cutting off of his finger;
rather, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] to prevent a recurrence of such attachment. 8.367.
This may apply to the best [of men] regarding unmarried girls. || 8.367 ||
If a maiden should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod. (8.368)
He shall give double the nuptial fee, namely a pair of cattle, to the father of the maiden, and pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] to the king. || 8.368 ||
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head, or else the cutting off of two fingers, as well as being carried on the shoulder with the hand. (8.369)
There is an option between shaving the head and cutting off the fingers. || 8.369 ||
But that woman who, arrogant because of her kinsmen or her own virtues, should transgress against her husband,
the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public place crowded with many people.

If a woman, out of pride toward her kinsmen, commits adultery with a virtuous husband, she shall be devoured by dogs at the king's command. But for another woman, the punishment shall be that which applies to the man who approaches another's wife; and this is demonstrated in the rule for penance: "that which [is prescribed] for the man regarding another's wife. (8.370)
They should cause the sinful man to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they should pile wood upon it, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire. (8.371)
This rule applies specifically to one who has been captured by this [method]; for any other, however, the punishment shall be exactly as previously stated. (8.371)
And he demonstrates that:
"For a wicked man who has been cursed for a year, the fine is double;
likewise for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī* woman. (8.372)

If a man who has been convicted of a particular offense is again convicted of that same offense after a year has passed, a double fine shall be imposed upon him according to the prescribed rule. However, if he is caught again before a year has elapsed, his fine for the first month shall be twelvefold; in this manner, the calculation of the fine is adjusted by reducing the portion month by month until, after a year has passed, it becomes double. Likewise, beyond a year, the fine should be calculated month by month by reducing the portion by one-twelfth each month, until only a single portion remains. This same method of calculation is also reiterated for the fine prescribed for returning [to the crime]. Furthermore, regarding the offense of approaching a Caṇḍāla woman, the author will state the punishment later: "But a thousand [paṇas] for a woman of the lowest caste. (3.372)

A Śūdra who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the twice-born castes—whether she is guarded or unguarded—is deprived of one limb if she was unguarded, and of his entire property if she was guarded; in the case of a guarded woman, he is deprived of everything. (8.373)

And here, that single limb which is the primary means of committing the offense is to be seized; by means of it, his punishment shall be inflicted. But when the crime is concealed, he is deprived of both. Even though there is no specific statement regarding the castes, the punishment should likewise follow the hierarchy of superior and inferior, as is seen elsewhere. For treating the unequal as equal would be unjust, given the general nature of punishment. (3.373)
A Vaiśya shall be fined his entire property after being imprisoned for one year;
a Kṣatriya shall be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine. (8.374)
If the Brāhmaṇī woman does not consent, it should be understood by implication that both of these receive the same punishment. (8.374)
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman,
he should fine the Vaiśya five hundred and the Kṣatriya one thousand.

The purpose for the greater severity of punishment for a Kṣatriya has been stated: "In the case of transgression by one who knows better, the punishment must be more severe. In this context, this [greater severity] may also apply to him due to the persistence of repeated offenses. (8.375)
For both of them, having violated a protected Brahmin woman, should be punished like Shudras or burned in a fire of straw. (8.376)
But this burning with a fire of chaff is to be understood as an alternative punishment for a Śūdra. (8.376)
A Brahmin who approaches a guarded Brahmin woman by force shall be fined one thousand;
he who has sexual intercourse with a willing woman shall be fined five hundred. (8.377)

The word "by force" (*balāt*) is not intended [as a restrictive condition]. For he who approaches a protected woman does indeed become one who has committed the offense by force alone. Likewise, regarding the phrase "one who desires it" (*sakāmām*) and "one who does not desire it" (*akāmām*), elsewhere the designation of "protected" (*guptā*) and "unprotected" (*aguptā*) is intended [to apply regardless of her desire]. The rest is straightforward. (8.377)
Shaving the head is prescribed as the penalty for a Brāhmaṇa that ends his life;
however, for the other castes, the penalty shall be one that ends their lives. (8.378)

In all cases involving the death penalty, a Brāhmaṇa must have his head shaved; having been shorn, he should be banished from the kingdom with all his property intact and his body uninjured. Likewise, in all instances where limbs are to be severed, only the shaving of the head and exile should be carried out for a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, it is recorded without distinction in another Smṛti: "No corporal punishment is to be inflicted upon a Brāhmaṇa. (8.378)

Therefore: "One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is established in every kind of sin; rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving his entire wealth intact and his body uninjured. (8.379)
The explanatory praise for this is: "There is no unrighteousness greater on earth than the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even conceive of his killing in his mind. (8.380)
The explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning that which is prohibited serves the purpose of causing desistance. 8.380.
If a Vaiśya should approach a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya a guarded Vaiśya woman, both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman. (8.381)
"One should fine a Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas]," and so forth; this has been stated regarding an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman. (8.381)
A Brahmin should be made to pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas] for approaching those two when they are guarded;
however, for approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya shall indeed be one thousand.
In the absence of other statements, this same punishment shall apply to a Brāhmaṇa for having intercourse with a guarded Śūdra woman. 8.382.

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unprotected Vaiśya woman or a Kṣatriya woman, or a Śūdra woman, shall be made to pay five hundred [paṇas]; but if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyajastriyam), he shall be made to pay one thousand.

The *caṇḍāla* is the lowest of all castes and the outcaste among the social orders (*varṇa*). This punishment applies to sexual union with his woman. Since there is no specific rule [distinguishing between protected and unprotected women], this punishment would apply without distinction to both protected and unprotected women; or rather, by virtue of the context, it should apply only to the unprotected woman, whereas for the protected woman, a more severe penalty must be imposed. (8.383)
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words,
and no perpetrator of violence or one who strikes with a staff, shares the world of Śakra.
Since this is so, therefore:
"The suppression of these five within his own realm by a king brings about imperial sovereignty over his kinsmen and brings him glory in the world. (8.385)
The praise of Nigraha is expressed in two verses; furthermore, this other matter is mentioned here incidentally within the very section on Sāhasa. || 8.385 ||

If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—provided that each is capable of the rite and free from fault—the punishment for both of them shall be one hundred [paṇas]. (8.386)
The meaning of this verse is straightforward. || 8.386 ||
Neither mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son deserves to be abandoned. He who abandons these, provided they have not fallen from their caste, shall be fined six hundred by the king. (8.387)
When an occasion for expiation arises, those who fail to perform these [rites] should be abandoned, but not out of hatred or similar motives. (8.387)
When twice-born men in their hermitages dispute with one another over a matter,
a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to act righteously should not pronounce a judgment.
This verse has the purpose of explaining the meaning of "ascetic" (tapasvin). 8.388.
Having honored these men as was fitting along with the Brahmins, the king should first pacify them with gentle words and then establish them in their own duty.
If a Brahmin does not feed his neighbor or next-door neighbor when they are worthy and present at a virtuous rite for twenty Brahmins, he deserves a fine of one māṣaka.

The two houses on the sides should also be understood as being included by implication. However, another reading provides this meaning: "the *anuveśya* is one who follows him; the *prativeśya* is one who faces him. (8.390)
If a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) does not feed another virtuous *śrotriya* during auspicious rites—
even if the latter’s house is not nearby, provided they are in the same village—
he shall be made to pay double the value of that food and a *māṣaka* of gold. (8.391)

This is the penalty for transgressing against an Arhat or a Brahmin. Because of the expression "in rites for prosperity" (*bhūtikṛtyeṣu*) and by virtue of its commencement, this is understood to be greater than the previous [penalty] for auspicious acts. And these two penalties would apply when there is the failure to give to an Arhat. (8.391)
One who is blind, dull-witted, a cripple, or seventy years of age;
from seventy onwards, one is considered an elder (*sthavira*).
Furthermore, one who serves those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) shall not be made to pay any tax by anyone. (8.392)
Even those who are not Brahmins, or even those who are Brahmins, are unworthy [of offerings]. || 8.392 ||
The king should always honor one learned in the Vedas, those afflicted by disease or pain, children, the elderly, the destitute, those of noble lineage, and the virtuous. (8.393)

By the technical usage of the scriptures, the term *śrotriya* refers to a Brāhmaṇa; whereas those who are afflicted by disease, children, the elderly, the destitute, and even those who are not *śrotriyas*, as well as one born of a great family (*mahākulīna*)—meaning one born of a virtuous lineage—and an *ārya*, the king should always honor. This is because of the context of receiving taxes, providing food and clothing, or ensuring their subsistence. Since this follows the discussion on ascetics and *śrotriyas* in relation to the collection of taxes and so forth, this duty toward artisans is mentioned here within the midst of legal procedures. (8.393)
A washerman should wash clothes on a smooth *śālmalī* fruit;
he should not carry clothes with other clothes, nor should he let them remain together. 8.394.
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 8.394 ||
A weaver shall give back ten palas of thread with an increase of one pala;
if he acts otherwise, he shall be made to pay a fine of twelve paṇas. (8.395)

He shall be made to pay twelve times the value [of the severed part]. This applies to the cutting of all materials, such as iron and the like. And because of their similarity to those cases, these two verses are stated here in the section on violence (sāhasa-prakaraṇa). 8.395.
Experts at the toll-stations, skilled in evaluating all merchandise, shall fix the price according to the goods; from that, the king shall take one-twentieth.
Upon the importation or exportation of goods, a customs duty (śulka) of one-twentieth [of the value] shall be levied according to the fluctuation of prices in relation to place and time. 8.396.
If one, out of greed, exports those articles of the king that are renowned or prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire property. (8.397)

Whatever is abundant in one place and rare elsewhere becomes famous as a specialty of that king. Thus, thoroughbred horses are found among the northerners (*udīcya*), saffron in Kāśmīra, and aloe-wood, camphor, and so forth among the easterners (*prācya*); these are not to be exported elsewhere. For, being rare, they are not taken out. Among kings, there occurs an exchange of gifts due to the obstruction of their respective affairs. Furthermore, regarding a gift of dharma or wealth that produces merit or profit, the king shall prohibit its buying and selling, such as in the case of honey from bees; that must not be exported. If a merchant exports it, the king shall take the entire share. (MDh 8.397)

One who evades a customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time, or one who gives false statements regarding the quantity [of goods], shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty. 8.398.

"Who will be able to avoid the toll-station during the day?"—this merely restates a time that is established by its very nature; it does not, however, permit avoidance at any other time, nor does it mean there is no fault for one who avoids it during the daytime. [In such a case,] he should be made to pay eight times the toll. Likewise, whatever the amount may be, he should be made to pay eight times that amount due to his false statement. This is stated because the acquisition and the use of the goods are uncertain. (8.398)
Having investigated the arrival, departure, and storage [of goods], as well as both their increase and decrease, he should regulate the purchase and sale of all commodities. (8.399)
Having regard for the source of the goods and the profit or loss of both the buyer and the seller, he shall cause their purchase and sale to be conducted by fixing the price. 8.399.
Every five nights, and likewise at the end of every fortnight, the king should perform the offering of the guest-water (argha) in the presence of these Tathāgatas. (8.400)

Since the application of substances for traditional authority (*āgama*) and utility (*upayoga*) is not fixed, this is said: "The balance, the measure, and the weight—all marked by earth—one should examine these again at every six months. (8.401)
All three of these, when marked with the royal seal, become unassailable; the rest is straightforward. 8.401
A vehicle shall be made to pay one paṇa at a ferry; a man carrying a load, half a paṇa;
an animal and a woman, a quarter; and a man dressed in colored garments, half a quarter. 8.402.

For an empty vehicle, such as a chariot and the like, one should pay a *paṇa* as a fine; for a load carried by a person, half a *paṇa*. For an empty animal and an empty woman, one-fourth of the standard *paṇa*; for an empty man, one-eighth of a *paṇa*. (8.402)
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay a ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, and men without belongings, shall pay whatever little they can. (8.403)

They shall provide vehicles filled according to the nature of the goods and the labor performed; even those without such equipment shall give whatever they can. For one who is empty-handed, the fine is one half-pāda. (8.403)
On the long journey, one should cross at the proper time and in the proper place;
one should know that this applies to riverbanks, but there is no such fixed mark for the ocean. (8.404)

When the path to be traversed is long, one should employ a raft after considering the loss and gain; likewise, when crossing a river, one should do so by considering its breadth. Otherwise, it is straightforward. (8.404)
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a wandering ascetic,
a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll at a crossing.
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 8.405 ||
Whatever on a ship may be damaged through the fault of the boatmen, that must be paid by the boatmen themselves, having assembled together from their own respective shares. (8.406)
This verse has been explained by its very recitation. || 8.407 ||

This has been declared as the legal decision regarding those traveling by boat: in the case of water damage caused by the fault of the boatmen, there is no punishment; but in the case of an act of God (such as a storm), there is no liability. (8.407)
Nothing need be said, for the meaning of the verse is already clear. (8.407)
He should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, money-lending, and agriculture, as well as the tending of cattle; and he should cause the Śūdra to perform service for the twice-born. (8.408)

If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra fails to perform their own duties, such as trade and so forth, they must be compelled by the king to do so by force; and if they still refuse, they shall be punished with fines. This is the purpose for which this matter is undertaken once again among the duties of the king. 8.408.
A Brāhmaṇa should support out of compassion a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties.

But not by means of servile labor, such as washing clothes or cleaning utensils; for, since these two must be maintained with compassion, the phrase "having them perform" is intended to exclude servile work, meaning they should instead be made to perform their own duties. (8.409)

If a Brahmin, out of delusion, forcibly compels refined twice-born men to become his slaves against their will, he shall be made to pay six hundred [paṇas] by the king, since he possesses the power to do so. (8.410)

Because of the mention of "twice-born" (dvija) here, the Brāhmaṇa is also included by virtue of being equal [to the others]. Furthermore, these persons—whether they desire it or not—must not be made to perform servitude. However, this much is the distinction: this penalty applies to the performance of service against their will; but when performed with their consent, a different arrangement must be made. And it is for this purpose that this has been stated among the duties of the king. (8.410)
But one may cause a Śūdra to perform service, whether he was purchased or not;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa. (8.411)

There is no difference in the duties to be performed between one who is a slave by devotion and one who is purchased; and the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate the twice-born in general. (8.411)
And this being so:
even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that is innate to him—so who can remove him from it? (8.412)
Just as teaching and so forth are innate to the Brāhmaṇas and others, so too is servitude for the Śūdra; that this is what he must perform has been stated precisely in the scripture. 8.412.
In connection with that, these origins of slaves are stated:

one captured under a banner, one who is a slave for food, one born in the house, one purchased, one given, one inherited from a father, and one enslaved by way of punishment—these seven are the origins of slaves. (8.413)

One captured under a banner is one conquered in battle; a slave by food is one who has entered [the house] for the sake of sustenance; a slave born in the house is the son of a female slave; those who are "bought" and "given" are well known; a paternal slave is the son of a female slave who has come down through the succession of ancestors; a slave by punishment is one who, having no wealth, is fined and enters himself into slavery by means of that fine. These are the seven origins of slavery. Among these, even by being joined with any one of them, one receives the designation of "slave. However, a Śūdra who possesses wealth and lives by his own effort should not be understood as a slave in the ultimate sense; otherwise, this verse regarding the meaning of the origins of slavery would be rendered meaningless. (8.413)
A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong. (8.414)

The mention of the wife and son here is for the purpose of providing an illustration by way of analogy with the slave, because they are equal in this context; it does not mean that they lack property in an absolute sense. This being so, the lack of wealth belonging to these three should be understood as being for the sake of their transactions with property only when authorized by him [the head of the household]. For what reason? Because whatever is acquired by someone cannot be separated from him. Furthermore, if these—sons and the rest—were without property, there would be no connection between them and their own actions (*karma*); and this is not desired, since their actions are governed by the scriptures. Thus, their lack of wealth should be understood as figurative. And this is for the sake of what follows. (8.414)
Since this is so, therefore:
A Brāhmaṇa may confidently take property from a Śūdra;
for he has nothing that is his own, since his wealth is to be taken by his master. (8.415)

Because the context concerns slaves, he is a slave; [the gift] is from that Śūdra to his own master. One should not consider the option of acceptance for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, for the acceptance of one's own slave pertains only to a Brāhmaṇa. Or rather, this acceptance should be understood as being lighter than that from another Śūdra who is not a slave; for it would not be appropriate to speak of praise or abundance regarding that [gift] without cause. Nor is it proper for the twice-born to establish equality with a Śūdra even of such a kind. Therefore, this instruction must be understood as having precisely this intended meaning. (8.415)
He should cause the Vaiśyas and Śūdras to perform their own duties with diligence; for if they fall away from their respective dharmas, they would throw this world into turmoil. (8.416)
