The verse beginning with “the Vaiśya should be made to practice trade” is a concluding statement for what was specifically declared at the outset—that [the Vaiśya and Śūdra] must be made to perform their own duties with effort, based on the context of this verse. Alternatively, a Śūdra who performs the work of the twice-born creates great danger for the world through the confusion of dharma; likewise, even a Vaiśya, if he does not engage in agriculture and other such duties, causes the depletion of food and other necessities. Therefore, these two must be made to perform their respective duties with special care by the king. Nor does this imply that [these duties] are not taught for the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya, as they have already been prescribed for them. The specific mention of the Vaiśya and Śūdra should be understood as being for the sake of emphasis. (8.416)
Day after day, he should inspect the state enterprises and the vehicles, as well as the fixed income and expenditure, the mines, and the treasury itself. (8.417)

Having attended to the administration of justice for the sake of maintaining the world, for the purpose of the royal system, and in accordance with the various legal proceedings of the citizens and country folk—thus [he performed] the inspection of legal cases. 8.417.
Thus, by settling all these legal cases, the king, having cast off all sin, attains the supreme goal. || 8.418 ||

This is a rule regarding the fruit [of action] for a king who observes legal proceedings as prescribed, by virtue of the power of the treatise. And because of the commonality of its performance, this summary of legal proceedings applies to the former judges of law even when the bases of legal proceedings—beginning with the duties of women and men—among the four types, have not yet been fully concluded. (8.418)
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the work composed by Bhāruca.
The ninth chapter [concerns] the man and the woman abiding in the path of dharma.
In both union and separation, I shall declare the eternal dharmas.

I shall declare the duties of husband and wife—who abide on the path of dharma characterized by mutual non-deviation—whether they are in union while the husband is alive and present, or in separation because he is dead or away; these include the rules for the practice of *niyoga* and other regulations. The inclusion of the word "eternal" (*śāśvata*) is for the purpose of praising their performance. This much, at least, is already well known. (9.1)
For example:
"Women must be kept under control by their own men day and night; even when they are attached to sensual objects, they must be established under one's own authority. (9.2)
Surely, their lack of independence is established as the very nature of women in the fifth chapter.

True. Those [previously mentioned] were indeed the duties of women alone; however, these which are about to be described pertain to both women and men. And this being so, the formal proposition must be stated as: "of the man and of the woman. This very point has been stated in the *Śāstrānukramaṇī*: "The procedure for questioning witnesses, and likewise the law (*dharma*) of women and men. Furthermore, in the summary of legal procedures (*vyavahārānukramaṇī*) in the eighth chapter, there is a reference to both together: "the law of women and men, and partition. Alternatively, this may be for the sake of what follows. And this being so, since it was stated that their dependence (*pāratantrya*) exists among the duties of women, one might ask: "Whence does that [dependence] arise? It is for this reason that this is now stated in connection with that. (9.2)
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence. 9.3

This being the case, their lack of independence does not apply solely to the king or the husband; rather, it applies to the father and others according to their respective ages. Furthermore, since the statement is primarily concerned with their protection, the fathers and others are not restricted as protectors of women such as daughters-in-law based on distinctions of age. This being so, this instruction regarding their protection should be understood as applying by implication to all people at all times. In every instance, the present tense (*laṭ*) should be seen as having the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*), such as "he should protect" (*rakṣet*), because there is no difference in its Vedic character. That definition is appropriate here for a *smṛti* text. And since this is so, therefore: [9.3]
A father who does not give [a daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable;
and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable. (9.4)

Those who do not always protect her, as well as those who give away their daughters in marriage and so forth, should be censured as blameworthy whenever possible; for it is by these means that this fault may be avoided. (9.4)
Women must be guarded especially against even the slightest of attachments;
for if they are not protected, they will bring sorrow upon two families. (9.5)
Furthermore, subtle grounds for deviation from these [virtues], well known in the world as association with female ascetics and the like, exist even without being explicitly taught. (9.5)
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all castes, husbands strive to protect their wives, even if they are weak. (9.6)
How much more so, then, the others? And now, for all purposes, this is explained in detail regarding how that state of being the supreme dharma comes about through the protection of women. 9.6.
For by protecting his wife with diligence, he indeed protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma. (9.7)

For by protecting his own offspring—that is, the purity of his progeny—and his wife, he likewise protects his conduct and his behavior; he protects his wife as one who must be guarded, his lineage through his ancestors, and himself—both when deceased, by means of the offering of rice-balls and water from progeny that is not of mixed caste, and while living, by avoiding the confusion of his offspring. Thus says another Smṛti: "Worthy sons born in a noble family, endowed with learning and virtue, and good disciples, protect their mother, father, and teacher."

One’s own dharma is that which is prescribed by the Śruti, by means of which there arises the entitlement to perform the rites of conception (*ādhāna*) and so forth for the sake of producing unmixed offspring, or it is that which is secondary (*gauṇa*); this we shall explain later. And by performing the naming of the woman for the purpose of protection, he says this [in verse 9.7]: 9.7. "A man should give a name to his daughter at her birth, consisting of two syllables or four syllables, ending in a long vowel and containing a benediction; he should not, however, bestow a name upon women that is the same as his own. The author states this while performing the naming of the woman, which serves as an explanatory injunction (*arthavāda*) for her protection. He says: "A man should give a name to his daughter at her birth, consisting of two syllables or four syllables, ending in a long vowel and containing a benediction. The word *svadharmam* (his own dharma) refers to the primary or secondary duty. By this, the entitlement to the *ādhāna* and other rites is established so that the offspring remains unmixed. Alternatively, it may refer to a secondary duty. Furthermore, by performing the naming of the woman for the sake of her protection, he utters this [verse]. (Note: The provided text contains a mix of commentary and the root verse. The translation above focuses on the core commentary explaining the purpose of the naming rite.)
The husband, having entered his wife and become an embryo, is born here; for that indeed is the "wifehood" (jāyātva) of the wife, because he is born again from her. 9.8.

Furthermore, this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the protection of the wife is in contradiction with the Vedas, the Smṛtis, the Śāstras, and logic; such is the context. Moreover, this worldly proverb is observed to be for the purpose of protecting her. Another explanatory passage is now stated. (9.8)
For whatever kind of man a woman serves, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should seek such a woman as he wishes to beget. (9.9)

And because, through the purity of one's offspring resulting from its protection, there arises the qualification for all ritual acts—which has as its purpose ultimate excellence—for this reason, he is repeatedly told with great care to protect it. 9.9.
No one is able to guard women by force; however, they may be guarded by means of these appropriate expedients. 9.10

Inconsistency between earlier and later parts of a treatise is not logical even when they belong to different sections, much less when they belong to the same section. Therefore, the statement that "no one is able to forcibly protect women" is intended as a praise for the method that will be explained [later]. In this way, the previous instruction regarding the protection of women is not contradicted. (9.10)

What, then, are the means for her protection? For this reason, [the author] shows them: "He should employ her in the collection of wealth and in its expenditure; in purification, in the cooking of food, and in the supervision of household goods. (9.11)
Household goods, such as seats, beds, pillows, and coverlets, [belong to her], according to the Vedic revelation: "For the wife is the mistress of the household goods. (9.11)
Those women who, though confined at home and guarded by trustworthy men, protect themselves by their own efforts—they are truly well-guarded. (9.12)

Furthermore, by the means described in the immediately preceding verse, these women protect themselves by their own efforts; therefore, this [present verse] is solely for the purpose of praising them. It is not, however, a prohibition against the two causes of protecting women—namely, the employment of men obtained through the obstruction of the home—which follows from both the capacity [of the context] and the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*). Alternatively, this is intended as praise for the avoidance of corrupting women: those who protect themselves by their own efforts are well-protected. Since it is for the sake of avoiding that [corruption], he shows those [means] in the following verse (9.12).
Drinking, association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [independently], and dwelling in another's house—these six are the vices that corrupt women. 9.13.
The instruction regarding these [vices] is for the purpose of their avoidance by those men, since they remain engaged in the practice of deviant conduct such as drinking and so forth. (9.13)
They do not examine beauty, nor do they take account of age; whether he is handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply as "a man. (9.14)
Remaining in these states, they are as if unconscious, since they would abstain from drinking and other such activities. (9.14)

"Because of their proclivity for men, because of their fickle minds, and because of their natural lack of affection, these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world. (9.15)
In these states such as drinking and so forth; therefore, one should not neglect [the precepts] regarding drinking and the like out of prior trust. (9.15)
Having thus understood their nature as born from the creation of Prajāpati, a man should apply the greatest effort toward their protection. (9.16)

In their very nature, these women consist of infidelity; therefore, having understood this, they must always be guarded. They should not be neglected out of misplaced trust simply because they have been subjected to discipline. (9.16)
And because Manu assigned to women the following: beds and seats, ornaments, lust, anger, ignobility, a malicious disposition, and misconduct. (9.17)

Therefore, because they possess such a nature, it is proper to guard them with great effort. In this context, however, *śayyā* (bed) is a state (*bhāva*) and not a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as in the sense of "that upon which one sleeps. The same applies to *āsana* (seat), *alaṃkāra* (ornament), and *kāma-krodha* (desire and anger), even though there is no abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the word *māyā* (deceit). In the phrase "the ignobleness of being, the state of malice," the state (*bhāva*) is taught by the very word itself. *Caraṇa* means conduct (*caryā*); thus we have "bad conduct" (*kucaryā*) and "excessive conduct" (*utsitā caryā*). All these are states (*bhāvāḥ*). This is so because the subject under discussion is "having understood their true nature" (*svabhāvam jñātvāsām*). And this being the case, the statement censuring them is for the purpose of guarding against them. (9.17)

And because it is established in the Dharma that women have no ritual efficacy through mantras; for women are without [Vedic] authority and devoid of mantras, and are falsehood—such is the settled rule. (9.18)

It has been stated: "This entire cycle of rites for women must be performed without mantras. That which was said is now explained: "There is no ritual action for women with mantras. Furthermore, the sacrament of marriage (*vivāha-saṃskāra*) is dependent upon connection with a male through the use of mantras; it is not independent, nor is it common [to both]. Thus, there is no contradiction. This statement of censure is for the purpose of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). "Indriya" refers to wisdom, fortitude, and so forth. Because they lack these, women are called "without *indriya*" (*nirindriyā*); it is not otherwise. And thus they are well known as "the weak" (*abalā*). Since women are without *indriya* and without mantras, they lack the capacity for self-protection by their own power due to the absence of personal vigor. And because they lack mantras, they do not attain purity through a sacramental rite accompanied by mantras, as men do. Indeed, their purity must be sought through self-restraint. Therefore, being without *indriya*, without vigor, and—due to a lack of consciousness—without discernment, women are censured by the word "untruth" (*anṛta*), or else on account of their inherent nature characterized by infidelity. (9.18)
And likewise, many scriptural passages have been proclaimed even in the Vedas for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics; hear now their form.
Their specific characteristics are subject to deviation; therefore, hear this account of their deviant forms. (9.19)
"Whatever my mother, wandering unfaithful, lusted for, may my father take that seed"—this is the illustration of that [Vedic passage]. (9.20)

It is said that in a certain ritual, the sacrificer says this: "Even if my mother should become unchaste through desire for another man, may her seed nevertheless be taken up by my father alone. This is the illustration: even in the Veda, the natural tendency of women toward infidelity is observed; therefore, this Vedic scriptural citation is quoted for the purpose of protecting them. (9.20)
And he says another thing:
"Whatever undesirable thing one meditates upon in the mind of the bridegroom, this concealment of that transgression is rightly called [the atonement]. (9.21)

And this should be understood as referring to mental transgression: "In whatever manner a woman is united with a husband of such-and-such qualities, in that same manner [the concealment of] such a mental transgression is its purification—that is, its expiation—by means of this mantra. This is not merely an illustration of mental transgression; rather, it should be understood as the expiation specifically for transgression through action. (9.21)
Whatever the qualities of the husband with whom a woman is united according to the prescribed rule, such qualities she comes to possess, just as a river does when it joins the ocean. (9.22)

This is an instruction on another means: that these [women] can also be guarded by a man through self-restraint. It is not only that men destroy themselves through lack of restraint; rather, this verse is an illustration of the fact that one who behaves in such a manner brings about the ruin of women as well. 9.22.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained venerability through her union with Vasiṣṭha;
and Śāraṅgī reached the state of being worthy of honor through Mandapāla. 9.23
And because: "In this world, these and other women of lowly birth have attained excellence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives. (9.24)
Therefore, one must exert effort in self-restraint for the sake of protecting women from him. || 9.24 ||
Thus has been declared the auspicious conduct for men and women throughout their worldly life; now learn the duties regarding progeny, which yield happiness both in this world and after death.
To whom does the offspring belong—to the owner of the field, to the owner of the seed, or to both? || 9.25 ||
For the sake of procreation, these highly fortunate women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
between women and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) in houses, there is no distinction whatsoever. 9.26.

This is his intention: for even in the case of women who have been defiled by every fault, their abandonment is improper when they possess the capacity for procreation and when there is a great purpose [in keeping them], because they can be reclaimed through penance (*prāyaścitta*). And so he will say later: "One should cause restrained women to dwell in the house," based on the statement: "Whatever [penance] is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others, that same vow one should cause her to perform. Furthermore, since praise does not proceed without a basis, this must necessarily be accepted. (9.26)
For it is from this that the procreation of offspring, the protection of those already born,
and the daily course of worldly life are visibly dependent upon women. (9.27)
This other verse, intended as praise of women, should be understood as having the very same purpose as the one previously stated. 9.27.
Moreover:
"Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme delight—indeed, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself likewise depends upon the wife. (9.28)
And therefore, the meaning should be understood exactly as stated [in verse 9.27]. 9.28.
And this being so:
"She who does not transgress her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, attains the worlds of her husband and is called 'virtuous' by the righteous. (9.29)
But through infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by sinful diseases. (9.30)
Therefore, for this reason, she must not abandon her dependence upon her husband. || 9.29–30 ||
Listen to this meritorious discourse, beneficial to all people, which has been uttered by the virtuous and by the great seers of old concerning a son. (9.31)
Just as that [is] "beneficial for all," so too is this stated. || 9.31 ||
They recognize the son as belonging to the husband; however, there is a conflict in the sacred texts regarding the progenitor.
Some say he is the one who causes the birth, while others know him to be the owner of the field.
According to the view of others, it belongs to both. 9.32.
He states the cause of this misconception:
"The woman is considered the field, and the man is considered the seed;
from the union of the field and the seed, there is the birth of all embodied beings. (9.33)
For this reason, therefore, this disagreement is logical. || 9.33 ||
And regarding this disagreement, he shows his own position:
"But in some cases, a specific seed has been accepted by certain [authorities]."
However, in some cases, it is indeed the female womb;
this is the view of others.
But where both are equal, that offspring is distinguished [as superior]. (9.34)
Thus, this established position of the Teacher is to be understood. 9.34.
Here the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is presented:
"Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior; for..."
For the production of all beings is indeed characterized by the nature of the seed. || 9.35 ||
This being so:
"Just as whatever seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time, such a seed grows therein, manifested with its own specific qualities. (9.36)
And for this reason, seeds possess that preeminence. 9.36.
And by this, this ground is indeed called the eternal womb of beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any qualities of the womb during its growth. (9.37)
And for this reason, because it does not follow the properties of that [seed], the field is not the primary factor for the seed. 9.37.
For it is so: even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown at the proper time by farmers grow here in various forms according to their own nature. (9.38)
By way of conforming to the seed and not conforming to the nature of the soil. || 9.38 ||
And so it is shown:
"Rice, śāli rice, mung beans, sesame, beans, as well as barley, garlic, and sugarcane—these sprout according to their respective seeds. (9.39)
And this being so, it is not logically tenable that what is sown is one thing and what is born is another; for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts forth. (9.40)
This much has been the position regarding the primacy of the seed; now, the position regarding the primacy of the field is demonstrated. 9.40
Therefore, a wise and disciplined man, who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom and desires long life, must never sow [his seed] in the wife of another. 9.41

Because of the preeminence of the field, let there be no theft of the seed in another's field; for that which is born in another's field, established through beginningless succession, is not the offspring of the owner of the seed. (9.41)
And so it is;
regarding this, those who know the past recite a verse sung by Yama:
"Just as a seed should not be sown by a man in what belongs to another. (9.42)
Just as an arrow, once shot, vanishes from sight when one shoots after it while it is already in flight, so too does a seed sown in what belongs to another quickly perish. (9.43)
When there is appropriation by another, he subsequently demonstrates the absence of fruit due to the lack of ownership. 9.43
Those who know the past understand that even this earth was the wife of Pṛthu;
they say that a field belongs to him who cleared the stumps, and a deer to him who struck the arrow.

And therefore, the field belongs to the original owner who took possession of it; and it should be understood that the fruit of the field belongs to him whose field it is, not to the sower. Such is the traditional teaching (āgama). 9.44
"The Puruṣa is only this much: wife, self, and offspring—so the wise have declared; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as the woman. (9.45)
Since this is so, we know this to be the law established of old by Prajāpati: a wife is not released from her husband either through ransom or through repudiation. (9.46)

By this [verse], he shows that another man’s wife cannot, according to the law (*dharma*), be made one’s own by anyone through purchase or acceptance as a gift; for, because the field is primary, the destruction of the seed belonging to the other [owner] is inevitable. And so it is in the world. (9.46)
A share of inheritance falls but once; a daughter is given away but once;
one says "I give" but once—these three things happen but once among the virtuous.

The giver gives other objects of gift to the recipient besides the maiden. This being so, these three [acts] are performed by the virtuous simultaneously; and for this reason, there can be no further giving of her. Likewise, the seed does not hold primacy in the case of one who has been taken in marriage by another. How so? 9.47.

Just as one is not considered a sharer in the offspring of cows, mares, camels, slave-girls, goats, sheep, or female buffaloes merely by being the progenitor, so it is likewise with the wives of others. 9.48
Thus, they are like those who possess seeds but have no field, sowing them in another's field; they indeed never obtain the fruit of the crop that has grown. 9.49
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of another, they all belong to the owner of the cows; the bull's effort was in vain. (9.50)
Just as the seed of one who does not own the field, sown in another’s field, serves the purpose of the owner of the field and the sower does not obtain the fruit; || 9.51 ||

All these illustrative verses are for the purpose of elucidating the subject at hand: thus, because the womb is more powerful, those born in another’s field do not belong to the owner of the seed. (9.49–51)
But the fruit belongs to neither the owner of the field nor the sower without mutual agreement;
the benefit is clearly for the owner of the field, for the seed is stronger than the womb. (9.52)

And this being so, because of the statement "but the fruit [accrues] without intention," it is said: "But when seed is sown for the sake of a crop, having accepted the labor, both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen here as sharers in its fruit. (9.53)

And thus, through such mutual agreement, the sower obtains the fruit, and not otherwise. This third position, characterized by the instrument of mutual agreement, is to be understood; however, that case where there is no such mutual agreement between both parties is as follows: || 9.53 ||
If seed carried by the current of a flood sprouts in someone's field, it should be known as belonging to that owner of the field alone; the sower does not receive the fruit. (9.54)

And the mention of "being carried away by the flood or by the wind" is to be understood as illustrative; therefore, it is understood that if another person sows in a field or a pond [belonging to someone else] either through theft or by force, he has no share in it. (9.54)
This law regarding the offspring of cows, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes should be understood. (9.55)
Even for a donkey that has not been formally initiated, this same rule shall apply because it shares the common nature of a domestic animal. (9.55)
Thus has been proclaimed to you the essential and the worthless nature of seed and womb;
hereafter, I shall declare the duty of women in times of distress.
This verse is for the purpose of stating the summary and the presentation. 9.56.
The wife of an elder brother is the wife of a guru for the younger brother;
but the wife of the younger brother is considered the daughter-in-law of the elder. (9.57)
And this being the established rule:

"An elder brother who approaches the wife of a younger brother, or a younger brother who approaches the wife of an elder brother—even if they are authorized [to do so]—become outcasts, unless there be a calamity. (9.58)

The following two verses are for the purpose of praising the approach [to a teacher] in times of distress. Since it is stated that even those who are "appointed" (niyukta) are [treated as such] only by virtue of the word "even others," it follows that in times of distress, even those not appointed become fallen [if they do not approach]. This being the case, whether one is the eldest or the youngest, and whether appointed or not, the approach to the teacher must be undertaken in times of distress. (9.58)

Now, the case of distress is described: When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized may obtain the desired offspring from her husband’s brother or from a sapinda relative. (9.59)

This being the case, both the elder and the younger brothers-in-law (*devara*) are to be understood by that term. Therefore, it is understood that *niyoga* (authorization for procreation) applies to them without distinction. And so he will say: "The husband’s own brother-in-law (*devara*) may take [the widow]. "Calamity" (*āpad*) refers to the absence of progeny, either because no offspring has been born or because the son has died. Others, however, explain it thus: based on the statement, "If he should see the face of one who lives," the purpose of the lineage has already been fulfilled by him through his very birth. That is incorrect, because it contradicts the scriptures. For it is heard in the *Rahasyabrāhmaṇa* of the Vājasaneyins, in the section concerning the remedy: "Therefore, they say that a son who has been instructed wins that world; therefore, they instruct him. Likewise, another *Smṛti* states: "A virtuous son and a disciple save [one from hell]. Thus, there is *niyoga* even for one whose son has died. Accordingly, this scriptural rule regarding the destruction of the lineage applies without distinction. Just as there is a destruction of the lineage for one who has not yet produced a son, so too for one whose son has perished; this is what is meant. Since the time factor is common to both cases, *niyoga* is prescribed for both. This being the case, the statement, "Some say a second [procreation is permitted]," becomes appropriate. Now, the rule for approaching [the widow] is stated: 9.59. [The verse follows.]
But one appointed to a widow, being anointed with clarified butter and remaining silent, may procreate a single son during the night; he must by no means produce a second.

Since the mention of a "widow" is intended to be illustrative, it is understood that *niyoga* is not prohibited even for one who is not a widow; for he will say later: "If, however, there should somehow be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and others. And thus, the birth of offspring from Pāṇḍu through *niyoga* with a non-widow is recorded in tradition. Furthermore, because of the prohibition regarding the daytime, this [injunction for the husband to approach at night] is an instruction concerning darkness; and so too is Vyāsa’s approach [to his mother] recorded in tradition. (9.60)
Some who know the truth consider procreation with women to be the second [duty], seeing that the purpose of the appointment between those two has not yet been fulfilled according to dharma. (9.61)

Of these two traditional accounts, the one concerning the birth of the second son is superior, because it favors the continuity of the lineage. If it is argued that a specific cause is required here, then since a cause is mentioned in both cases, there would be no engagement [with the practice] at all. (9.61)
When the purpose of the appointment regarding the widow has been fulfilled according to the rule, the two should behave toward each other like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law. (9.62)

And from this, the appointment of the eldest (*jyeṣṭhaniyoga*) is understood. Accordingly, a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) has been stated: "The eldest [may take] the wife of the younger brother. Furthermore, it is appropriate that both [the husband's brother and the paternal kinsman] are included by the term *devara* in the passage: "From the *devara* or from a *sapiṇḍa*. This is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) for the prohibitory injunction that follows. (9.62)

If those two who have been appointed should act according to their own desire, disregarding the prescribed rule, they would both become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher. (9.63)

This explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning the transgression of all rules for the appointment of widows (vidhavā-niyoga) is to be understood as applying without distinction, and not merely to the prohibition occurring after the completion of the purpose of the appointment in the immediately following verse. Such is the reason why the appointment of widows exists; this is its prohibition. (9.63)
A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born;
for by appointing her to another, they would destroy the eternal dharma. (9.64)

Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is "authorization" (niyoga) mentioned, either by its characteristic mark or by explicit statement; nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the injunctions for the wedding ceremony. (9.65)
The meaning is that this is the ritual for marriage according to the scriptures.
Indeed, this practice, which is the law of beasts, was censured by learned twice-born men;
yet it was declared [as permissible] even for humans while Vena was ruling the kingdom. (9.66)
In former times, while enjoying the entire earth, that most excellent of royal sages,
his mind struck down by lust, brought about the intermixture of the social orders.
From that time forward, the virtuous censure any man who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of obtaining offspring. (9.68)

These five verses, including the ancient narrative (*purākalpa*), have the purpose of enjoining and prohibiting *niyoga*. Because *niyoga* has both been prescribed and prohibited, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them. Regarding these two Smṛtis, which one is more authoritative? What do we say? By this it can be said that in both cases there is prosperity (*abhyudaya*), since in one case there is offspring and in the other there is self-restraint (*saṃyama*). Moreover, both are especially consecrated (*saṃskṛta*), because even *niyoga* leads to prosperity. For there is no pleasure of the senses for the husband—whether dead or living—who would perform the *niyoga*, nor for the father and others. And from the force of the injunction, it is understood that even for the father and others, it is for their own appropriate prosperity. From the force of the teaching of the prohibition, there is no transgression even in the absence of *niyoga*. And because of its similarity to the *niyoga* of a widow, this *niyoga* of a maiden is taught in that very same context. (9.64–68)
If the husband of a maiden should die after the word of betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this rule.

The "rule" (vidhi) is the procedure for marriage as previously described, because of the scriptural statement that "he shall obtain [a wife]. Otherwise, for one who approaches an unmarried girl, the defilement of a maiden would logically ensue. And this undertaking is for the purpose of restriction. From this very indicative mark, there exists the giving of the word (vāk-pradāna) prior to the marriage; once that has been performed, if the husband dies, she may be given to another. (9.69)
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule—she who is clad in white garments and pure in her vows—he shall enjoy her in private once at each season until the birth of a child. (9.70)

Having approached her according to the prescribed rule after she has been wedded according to the rite—[the rule being that she is] dressed in white garments—and having observed pure vows, being restrained in mind, speech, and other faculties, he shall unite with her in private once at each menstrual period until the birth of a child. Because the physical body is common [to both], the same rule would apply even in the case of a widow’s appointment (*niyoga*). Furthermore, everything previously mentioned, such as being anointed with ghee and so forth, would apply here as well, since the nature of the appointment is the same. (9.70)
A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again to another;
for by giving her once more after she has been given, he incurs the sin of lying regarding a human being. 9.71.
"A thousandfold is the falsehood regarding men"—this is a restatement of a prohibition [against lying] made out of apprehension that someone else might offer a gift. (9.71)
Even after having formally accepted her, one may abandon a bride who is censurable, diseased, defiled, or one who was presented through deception. (9.72)

Even when she has been accepted [as a wife], she may be relinquished only when the specific grounds for relinquishment exist, and not otherwise, according to the statement: "except through redemption or formal renunciation. Therefore, in the absence of the grounds for relinquishment, there is no relinquishing her at will, just as one cannot discard substances that have become ritually impure by contact with food remnants. || 9.72 ||
But if one should bestow a daughter who possesses defects without having disclosed them, he should render that gift of the daughter void, for that evil-minded man. (9.73)

This is a restatement of the principle that "what is obtained through deception should be abandoned," intended to demonstrate the absence of fault in relinquishing it for a specific reason. || 9.73 ||
A man who has business abroad should depart after providing for his wife's livelihood;
for a woman, even one of steadfast character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of means. (9.74)

For the sake of his duties, he must invariably provide for his wife’s food and clothing. The second half of the verse is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding this rule of obligation. Furthermore, since it is taught that a man may travel abroad for the sake of his duties, this [verse] prohibits him from going elsewhere after leaving his wife except for such business. (9.74)
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live remaining steadfast in her observances;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for her, she should live by means of blameless crafts.

In this state, living by means of an irreproachable craft is permitted, such as the making of nets and the like. By this, the means of subsistence for a widow who has not borne a son is explained. Furthermore, reproachable acts such as the washing of clothes and so forth are forbidden. Now, with reference to her livelihood, he shows the variation in time depending on the specific purpose of her journey abroad. (9.75)
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of religious duties should be awaited for eight years;
for the sake of learning or fame, for six years; but for the sake of pleasure, for three years. (9.76)

"She should live by means of irreproachable [means]"—this is because of the governing context of "without [the husband] prescribing. This is a regulation of time for that very [period], namely, living by means of irreproachable crafts. But after this time, she may live even by a reproachable craft. And thus, this should be understood as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the prohibition of forbidden crafts. "Duties of dharma" refers to the words of the teacher and so forth. "For the sake of pleasure" refers to following the pursuit of a livelihood through beauty; however, it does not mean adultery, because of such statements as "she should wait for eight years," which implies that their transgression would contradict the scriptures due to the instruction of extreme self-restraint. Such being the case, even the practice of *niyoga* (appointment of a widow) is only with great difficulty permitted; how much less so adultery? But another says: "After this [time], there is no fault of adultery, owing to the force of the counter-exception. However, there is no instruction of adultery as a rule. For there is no connection with another man while the husband is away, since she proceeds for the sake of offspring when appointed by her superior. And this being so, for one who cannot survive at all, this should be understood as a counter-exception merely for the sake of subsistence or for the sake of secret offspring. The phrase 'she who has been abandoned by her husband' refers to the state of being remarried (*paunarbhava*) resulting from such means of abandonment. But that is improper, because it is in absolute contradiction with the scriptures. Others, however, explain this as a regulation of the period of absence specifically for men: "Beyond this, if the husband remains away, there would be sin even for the sake of dharma. That meaning which is reached through the force of the sentence in this other context cannot be assumed as the literal meaning of the word. (9.76)
A husband who hates his wife should wait for one year;
but after a year has passed, he may take back her property and no longer live with her. (9.77)

"He shall not cohabit with her" means the cessation of sexual intercourse, not banishment; for even in the case of a grave sin (*pātaka*), it is not appropriate to banish her, since the instruction for penance is given there with the words, "he shall confine her in a single room. Others, however, say that abandonment alone is intended. This being so, there is no great fault for one who abandons her because of the instruction regarding a specific cause; but this does not apply in other cases. Furthermore, some maintain that the abandonment of a wife is to be understood as occurring before the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), and not thereafter, because it is taught that he must perform the rites for offspring together with her. (9.77)
Whether she be intoxicated, negligent, or afflicted by illness, she who transgresses [the bounds] shall be abandoned for three months, stripped of her ornaments and belongings.
In this case, renunciation is non-enjoyment, for it is not the absence of latent tendencies. 9.78
There is no abandonment of a wife who is insane, fallen [from caste], deformed, barren, or afflicted with a foul disease; nor is there any revocation of the gift [of her hand]. (9.79)
In this circumstance, there is indeed no relinquishing of her [the vow]. || 9.79 ||
A wife who drinks liquor, is untruthful in conduct, or is hostile; one who is diseased, violent, or always wasteful of wealth—such a woman may indeed be superseded by another. 9.80.

On this point, someone says: Even though there is no distinction in the meaning of the word *jāti* (caste), the prohibition against drinking *surā* is understood to apply specifically to a male Brāhmaṇa because of the gender marker in the phrase, “while the gods eat the sacrificial offering” (*devānām aśnatā haviḥ*). From that same gender marker, it is known that for a Brāhmaṇī woman, there is no such prohibition, just as there is none for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. Furthermore, he will state later that for killing her, the penance is that for killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, which is a minor offense (*upapātaka*). And in the case of touching her [impurity], she is equal to a Śūdra; likewise regarding eating the leavings of women and Śūdras. Moreover, their sin is enumerated in another Smṛti: “A woman falls [from her caste] by killing an embryo or by serving a man of a lower varṇa. And in the Śruti, the gift of the *śatakumbha* spirituous liquor is prescribed. There is a specific rule regarding the *śrāddha* for women: “Even if she is prohibited, [she may drink] wine even at festivals,” according to which the drinking of wine is forbidden to all women, but not specifically the *surā* liquor. For women of the twice-born castes, it is like that of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. This being the case, when she has been prohibited—either by herself or by the husband’s own word—from the mere practice of drinking liquor, the taking of another wife (*adhivedana*) should be understood as the remedy for her. That is incorrect. For we see other Smṛti texts stating, “Half the body of him whose wife drinks *surā* falls [with her]”; and because the phrase “while the gods eat the sacrificial offering” is merely an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*). Thus, a Brāhmaṇī must also not drink *surā*. The term *adhivedana* means marrying another woman over and above her. Even on these grounds, there is no mandatory rule for supersession (*adhivedana*) when dharma is lost; for in those cases, the destruction of half the sin can be rectified through penances, since it is possible for them [the women] to do so. (9.80)

A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth; one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but one who speaks unpleasantly, immediately. (9.81)

This should be understood as the rule for supersession (*adhivedana*) when there is a failure in religious duty (*dharma*); by this, one who has fathered a son gains the right to perform the *śrauta* rites. However, supersession is not permanent in the case of a wife who speaks unpleasantly, because once a son has been born, she remains entitled to participate in the ritual acts alongside him. (9.81)
But she who is healthy, devoted to his welfare, and endowed with virtuous conduct—having obtained her permission, he may take another wife; for he should never treat her with disrespect.

And because of the prohibition against her being treated with contempt, the other wives are not only not to be superseded, but furthermore, they are to be instructed and admonished for the sake of discipline. 9.82.
But a woman who, having been given in marriage, should leave the house in anger, must be restrained immediately or abandoned in the presence of the family. (9.83)

When the aforementioned grounds for supersession have occurred, the husband may, out of anger, abandon a wife who has departed from him; provided this does not conflict with his entitlement to perform Vedic rites, he may abandon her in the presence of her family, or else refuse to cohabit with her, or impose a confinement upon her. Others, however, maintain that this statement regarding abandonment is intended to terminate her right to participate in domestic duties, while remaining consistent with her entitlement to perform Vedic rites. 9.83.
If a woman, though forbidden, should drink liquor even on festive occasions, or should go to a spectacle or a social gathering, she shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*. (9.84)

The prohibition concerns the drinking of intoxicants, not the act of going to public spectacles. Or rather, it is for the purpose of preventing excessive attachment (*prasaṅga*). This being the case, since the punishment is light, there is a slight allowance for non-prohibition when there is a motive such as prosperity and so forth. And that intoxicant should be understood as *asurā* (distilled liquor) among twice-born women. This being so, even in the previous case [regarding a wife who drinks], this same explanation applies to the drinking of intoxicants under the pretext of taking a second wife, as in the verse: "one who drinks intoxicants and is untruthful. Furthermore, this form of prohibition should be understood as referring to other castes (*varṇa*). (9.84)
If twice-born men should marry women of their own caste as well as those of other castes, seniority and honor in the household shall belong to them according to the order of their castes. (9.85)

The performance of marriage was taught according to the sequence "these others [wives] shall be in order. But here, by the sequence "having abandoned," seniority and so forth for those already married shall be determined solely by the order of their castes. The purpose of this is the distribution of inheritance. And honor is likewise [determined] by this very same order; thus, seniority among those of the same caste is to be understood as being according to this sequence alone, and not by birth. (9.85)
The personal service of the husband’s body and his daily religious duties must be performed by each wife herself; under no circumstances may one of a different caste perform them for any of them.

The religious duties that must be performed by a woman—such as the smearing of the fire-sanctuary and so forth—are what is intended here. For a man as well, only bodily service characterized by acts such as providing water for ritual sipping (*upasparśana*) and giving [food] is included, because of its association with religious duties; however, service consisting of washing the feet and the like is not included, as it does not share the same nature as a religious duty. (9.86)
But he who, out of delusion, causes it to be performed by another woman while remaining within his own caste—
just as a Brāhmaṇa-Caṇḍāla was seen before, so indeed is he.

This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) concerning the rule of service. This being so, it must not be performed in any other way. However, this is an explanatory statement of censure regarding anyone who persists in transgression, based on some general principle. (9.87)
To one who is distinguished, handsome, excellent, or suitable, he should give his daughter according to the prescribed rite, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age. (9.88)

To one who is superior to oneself by reason of learning and other such excellent qualities—whether he be a handsome suitor, or in his absence, one of equal status—the rest is straightforward. Although it was stated here [in verse 9.87] that "one should always form connections with the most excellent," this is now restated for the purpose of prescribing a gift to an equal; for thus, there is sin for one giving to one devoid of good qualities. This is what is being reiterated here. (9.88)
A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father’s house until death if she so desires;
yet he must never give her in marriage to one who is devoid of good qualities. (9.89)

By this mention of giving at an improper time, the acceptance of another’s daughter at an improper time is inferred; for one who accepts her when she has not reached [the proper age] will not accept her when she has reached it. And because the connection with the proper time is already implied by the sense, the mention of giving at an improper time is not made merely as a commendatory statement (arthavāda). (9.89)
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years; after this period, she may choose a suitable husband for herself. (9.90)

This is the instruction regarding the maiden; and it is recorded in the Smṛti that she reaches puberty at twelve years of age. Therefore, after this time, her taking [of a husband] may occur through self-choice (svayaṃvara) for three years. But after that—9.90.
If she should obtain a husband of her own accord when one is not being given to her, she incurs no guilt whatsoever, nor does he whom she obtains. (9.91)
Regarding the boon that a maiden herself obtains, the statement that she is faultless is for the purpose of declaring her freedom from defect. (9.91)

A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take for herself the ornaments belonging to her father, nor those belonging to her mother, nor those given by her brother; if she were to take them, it would constitute theft. (9.92)

Others, however, read this verse as follows: "A maiden should not take for herself ornaments belonging to her father at her own-choice marriage (svayaṃvara), nor those belonging to her mother or given by her brothers; if she should take them, she would be a thief. In the absence of such a reading, the verse refers to a male subject. (9.92)
One who carries off a maiden who has reached her menses shall not pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her menstrual periods, he would be overstepping his authority as master. (9.93)
This verse is found in other Smṛtis, but it is not recited here. 9.93.
A man thirty years of age should marry a charming girl twelve years old, or one twenty-four years old an eight-year-old; otherwise, his religious duty quickly comes to grief.
With the permission of his teacher, he may marry a younger girl after this much time has elapsed. || 9.94 ||
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
he should always support that virtuous woman and act in a manner pleasing to the gods. 9.95

Without her own effort, she becomes "given by the gods" (devadattā) when brought home by her parents, or she is obtained through her own agency. The purpose of this instruction is that one should maintain such a virtuous wife, even if she is hateful or disliked. For it is with such a partner in dharma that the oblation offered by the sacrificer is accepted by the deities. Furthermore, she who is pure in her lineage is the cause for discharging one's debts to the gods, the ancestors, and the sages; therefore, one should not abandon her on account of such reasons as being disliked. (9.95)

Women were created for the purpose of procreation, and men for the purpose of continuing the lineage; therefore, in the Veda, religious duty is declared to be common to both, performed together with the wife. 9.96

Thus, just as these two are remembered to share a common destiny regarding offspring, they are likewise remembered to share a common destiny regarding karma; therefore, one should not abandon her, so as to favor the fulfillment of one's duty.
If the giver of the bride-price should die after the bride-price has been paid for a maiden,
she should be given to the husband's brother, provided the maiden consents.

This section is commenced again for the sake of a specific distinction. This being so, the statement, "If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made," would be a rule concerning one for whom the bride-price has not yet been paid. Furthermore, from the mention of the brother-in-law (*devara*), the exclusion of other *sapiṇḍas* is understood; and that exclusion is indeed appropriate. For since she is purchased, she is properly permitted [to go] only to the brother-in-law who is connected with that wealth, because she is the commodity for which the bride-price was paid. (9.97)
Even a Śūdra should not take a bride-price when giving away his daughter;
for by accepting a bride-price, one performs a concealed sale of his daughter. (9.98)
By the statement "not even a Śūdra," he shows that the taking of a fee (śulka) is faulty; however, this is not a prohibition against a Śūdra [from marrying]. (9.98)
But this is what neither others have done, nor have other virtuous men ever done:
that having first given permission to one person, it is then bestowed upon another. (9.99)
By this [verse], it is shown that there is no such gift elsewhere; this refers to the subject under discussion. 9.99.
For even in previous births, we have never heard of such a thing:
the sale of a daughter concealed under the name of a "bride-price" (śulka). || 9.100 ||

This being the case, even the practice of *niyoga* with a *sapiṇḍa* is not permitted due to the defects associated with the bride-price (*śulka*). Therefore, in the absence of a brother-in-law (*devara*), the division of offspring is certain. (9.100)
Let there be mutual fidelity until the end of life; this is the auspicious dharma for a man and woman of equal status that should be known. 9.101

For a woman, non-deviation consists in abandoning union with another man; however, for a man, there is no prohibition against approaching another woman as there is for a woman. Thus says the Śruti: "Therefore, one man may have many wives, but one woman does not have many husbands at the same time. Furthermore, it has been stated that for a woman, deviation occurs even through the mere intention toward another man. This being the case: 9.101.
Likewise, once they have performed their rites, the woman and man should always strive so that, even when separated from one another, they do not transgress [their vows]. (9.102)
This restatement of the various kinds of duties prescribed for women and men in this section is made for the purpose of showing respect for their performance. 9.102.

This law concerning men and women, together with the rules for sexual pleasure, has been declared to you, as well as the acquisition of offspring in times of distress; now learn the law of inheritance.
This statement of summary and introduction regarding the two preceding sections is for the purpose of awakening the listeners. (9.103)
After the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled together, shall divide the paternal inheritance; for they have no authority over it while the two are alive. (9.104)

It follows by implication that even those whose father and mother are still living may divide [the estate] for the sake of religious duties with their parents' permission; thus Gautama says: "If the father is living and desires it. Furthermore, after the mother's death, her division of property should be understood as optional, to be shared together with the sisters. (9.104)
The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest shall depend upon him, just as they did upon their father. (9.105)

This non-distinction based on cause is to be understood as partial. [If that cause did not exist,] then he would have described the manifold distinctions among the superior, middling, and inferior in various ways. Furthermore, this explanatory passage (arthavāda) applies to the position that accepts the superior [as the cause]. 9.105.
By means of the first-born son, a human being becomes a father;
he is indeed freed from his debt to the ancestors, and therefore he deserves everything. 9.106
And because he pays off the debt to his ancestors and through whom one attains infinity—that alone is known as the son born of dharma; the others are known as born of desire. (9.107)
He would be considered disciplined. And this conduct of an eldest brother toward his younger brothers is described according to the view that [the property] is indivisible. 9.107.
As a father protects his younger sons, so should the eldest brother protect his younger brothers; and he should likewise behave toward his eldest brother as a son, in accordance with dharma. (9.108)

Because one who possesses such qualities as these—the eldest son—either causes the family to prosper or, conversely, causes it to perish; whereas one who lacks such qualities does not. For that reason.
He is the eldest and most worthy of honor in the world; therefore, he is the eldest, unreviled by the virtuous. (9.109)
This being so, he who is the eldest and behaves as an elder should be honored like a mother and like a father; but he who does not behave as an elder should be revered merely as a kinsman. (9.110)
This speech to his kinsmen was for the purpose of concluding his duties toward his teacher; and such being the case, [verse 9.110].
Thus they may dwell together or separately out of a desire for the Dharma; for the Dharma increases when practiced separately, therefore separation is consistent with the Dharma. (9.111)

The reason for this is stated here: If the eldest son is worthy of the entitlement to religious duties (*dharma*) due to his possession of virtues, while the others are neither entitled nor capable of performing those duties, then this non-division (*avibhāga*) is to be understood. However, if the eldest were to behave like one who is not the eldest—even though he possesses virtues—then this non-division would not apply among the younger brothers who are incapable of performing religious duties. For it has been said: "He who is the eldest and behaves like an eldest," and likewise, "But he who behaves like an eldest. This being so, when the younger brothers are capable of performing religious duties and are entitled thereto, this non-division must be regarded as prohibited by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), even if the eldest possesses virtues and behaves like an eldest. And thus it has been said: "Therefore, separation is consistent with *dharma*. Furthermore, when there is a separation consistent with *dharma*, non-division is not logical, because a specific cause has been taught. And that has already been stated. By this, the division between father and sons is explained, as the underlying reasons are the same. Nor should it be thought that such a division does not exist, because the division after the father's death is taught [in the verse]: "After the father... Since he will say, "One should not share [the estate] with their sons," from that indicative mark (*liṅga*), the division between father and sons is to be understood. And since there is a separation consistent with *dharma* among all those who are entitled and capable of performing religious duties, therefore this is stated: 9.111. [The verse follows.]

The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the goods; half of that shall be the share of the middlemost, while the youngest shall receive a fourth. (9.112)

The eldest shall receive one-twentieth of all the property, as well as the best item among them; the middle son shall receive half of that, which is a fortieth part; and the special allotment (*uddhāra*) for the middle son consists of the next best item after the best one. Likewise, the youngest shall receive one-eightieth part, which is the least of all the property; this is his special allotment. According to the reading "the best item from among the best items," the assignment of shares for the middle and youngest sons should be understood as corresponding accordingly. Thus, having set aside the special allotments, the remainder that is left must be divided equally. This rule of equal division applies to three brothers of equal merit, since special allotments are seen to be prescribed for three. This is another method of partition. (9.112)
Both the eldest and the youngest shall take their shares as prescribed;
the wealth of those others who are between the eldest and the youngest shall belong to the middlemost. (9.113)

In the case of a man with many sons, after setting aside for the eldest and the youngest as prescribed if they possess good qualities, that fortieth part which was mentioned in the immediately preceding verse for the one middle son who possesses good qualities—even among many middling sons—must be divided among all those middling sons. However, if all the middling sons are equal in merit, then a fortieth part must be set aside for each one individually, just as previously stated. (9.113)
Of all kinds of wealth, the eldest son shall take the best; and whatever is particularly excellent, he shall also receive as his choice portion from ten times [the remainder]. (9.114)

From each category of property, that which is the best and that which is the single most excellent item—one-tenth of all such property shall be set aside for the eldest. Having thus extracted this share, they should divide the remainder equally as before. This rule should be understood to apply by implication to cases where the eldest possesses great virtues while the others are devoid of merit; for the author will clarify this very point in the following verse. Others, however, read the second word as *varān* (accusative plural), meaning "he should receive ten excellent items"; these are either cows or horses, and this is specified in another Smṛti as referring specifically to ten animals: "A group of ten animals, but not of one-hoofed or two-footed creatures. (9.114)
There is no deduction for those who have performed their own duties well;
however, something whatsoever should be given to the superior as an increase for the man. (9.115)

The preferential share (*uddhāra*) for the eldest mentioned in the preceding verse is here set aside. There is no preferential share for the eldest even among ten head of cattle, much less in other cases such as the aforementioned types of wealth and so forth. He shows the reason why this exception to the eldest’s share is made: "among those brothers who are accomplished in their respective duties. Thus, since the phrase "accomplishment in duties" implies their study and specialized knowledge, this too is understood. Furthermore, it should be known that whatever little may be given to the elder as an honor to him is not the aforementioned preferential share. And thus, this division is to be understood as applying when the brothers possess equal qualities; this is stated in the case where the taking of a preferential share is permitted. (9.115)
Thus, when the preferential shares have been set aside, one should assign equal portions;
but if no preferential share has been set aside for them, this following shall be the allotment of shares. (9.116)
Thus, having extracted [the portion] without contradicting the aforementioned principle, there is an equal division of what remains. 9.116.
The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the next younger brother, one and a half shares; and each of those younger than him, one share each—thus is the law established. (9.117)

This distribution is understood by implication to apply respectively to: the eldest brother who is superior in qualities; his younger brother who is slightly inferior in qualities; those who are even lower than him in qualities; and those who are equal to them. Because of the statement, "The brothers, having come together," the giving of a share of the paternal estate to sisters is prohibited. Yet, their acquisition of it is desired on the ground of their being unmarried; therefore, this [following verse] is commenced as an exception to that prohibition. (9.117)
The brothers shall each separately give to their unmarried sisters portions from their own respective shares;
they shall give one-fourth part from each share, and those who refuse to give shall become outcasts.

This is declared to be the obligatory gift for unmarried sisters, similar to the gift for those seeking progeny (*sāntānika*) and others, based on the statement: "They would become outcasts if they were unwilling to give. And this is to be given from one's own share, not from the collective estate. It should be given solely for the purpose of their marriage, without obstructing one’s own religious duties; it is not a fourth part as literally stated. For if it were so, the wealth would result in being much greater than the number of daughters when there are many brothers, and in the case of two or one brother having many sisters, the consequence would be total poverty. Nor is this desired, because of the statement: "Separation [of property] is lawful. Alternatively, because of the word "separately" (*pṛthak*) in the verse-line "the brothers should give separately," these [brothers] who have different mothers should give to their uterine sisters as previously described. (9.118)
One should never divide goats, sheep, and single-hoofed animals unequally;
however, it is ordained that the goats and sheep themselves shall belong exclusively to the eldest.

But as for goats and sheep, if at the time of partition they cannot be divided by way of odd numbers, they shall belong to the eldest alone. One should not bring them to equality by distributing a portion of other property, nor should one cut their value into pieces. (9.119)
If a younger brother should beget a son upon the wife of the elder, the division of property there shall be equal; such is the established law. (9.120)

This section is commenced for the purpose of setting aside the special share (*jyeṣṭhāṃśa*) [due to seniority]. Thus, by virtue of being the eldest son, he shall not receive a portion exceeding that [of the others], because although he possesses good qualities, he was begotten by a younger brother and is a *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife). Nor does he receive half a share; rather, "the division there shall be equal. With whom? With the paternal uncle who begot him from the father's younger wife. And this son should be understood as a *kṣetraja* begotten on an appointed woman (*niyuktāsuta*). As for the son of one not so appointed, his lack of entitlement to a share will indeed be stated later. Furthermore, it is understood by implication that if the eldest son possesses good qualities, he receives a share of the property with the *uddhāra* (preferential deduction), just like the father himself. (9.120)
Subordination of the principal is not consistent with dharma; the father is the principal in procreation, therefore one should honor him according to dharma. (9.121)

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the meaning of the preceding verse. It is not consistent with *dharma*—that is, with the sacred scriptures—that the subsidiary (*upasarjana*), the subordinate younger brother of the father who is the progenitor of the *kṣetraja* son, should receive an equal share with the principal elder brother. For it has been stated that the allotment of shares belongs to the eldest. This being so, the father is the principal in the procreation of offspring; and thus he will later declare the preeminence of the *aurasa* (legitimate) son, whereas this *kṣetraja* son was not begotten by the father himself. Therefore, one should treat him according to *dharma*: *dharma* here refers to the scriptural rule of the preceding verse, namely, "In that case, the division shall be equal. Some read, "One should treat him with half a share" (*ardhena taṃ bhajet*). That is incorrect, because it would entail a contradiction with what was previously stated. Nor is an option (*vikalpa*) appropriate here, because this is not an injunction (*avidhitvāt*). And its non-injunctive nature follows from its being an explanatory statement for the preceding verse. Alternatively, the subsidiary—the *kṣetraja*—should not, according to *dharma*, receive an equal share with the principal *aurasa* son. For he will later state: "The *aurasa* son alone is the master of the paternal wealth. Since the father is the principal in procreation and this son was not begotten by him, it is therefore proper that he should receive only an equal share. The previous scripture [prescribes] the paternal gift as equal; hence [the former reading is correct]. Or else, it is not consistent with *dharma* that the subsidiary *kṣetraja* should receive an equal share with the principal owner of the field (*kṣetrin*). The rest is the same. (9.121)
If a doubt should arise as to how the division of property should be made in the case where there is a younger son born of an elder wife and an elder son born of a younger wife: || 9.122 ||
Whether seniority is determined by the order of the mothers' marriages or by the order of the birth of the offspring—such being the doubt, this sequence for the decision is prescribed. 9.122.
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share; thereafter, the others shall have bulls inferior to that, according to their respective mothers. (9.123)

One born first is called "pūrvaja," yet it is the younger one who is so designated here; for if it were simply "born first," this mention of "the eldest" would be inconsistent. Furthermore, [the rule applies to] those who are not the eldest, each individually, among those inferior to him. Therefore, "tadūnānām" (inferior to him) means those inferior to him, not taken separately, but rather in relation to their own mother. This being the case, seniority among sons here is determined by the mother, not by birth. 9.123.
But the son born of the eldest wife shall take a bull as the sixteenth [share];
the remainder shall then divide their own shares according to their mothers—this is the settled rule. (9.124)
The meaning of this verse is straightforward. This is the opinion of some, but the blessed Manu has said: 9.124.
Among sons born of wives of equal status, there is no seniority according to their mothers; rather, seniority is said to be determined by birth [from the father]. (9.125)
The explanatory passage (arthavāda) for this is: "Even in the Subrahmaṇyā liturgies, it is recorded that the invocation is made by the eldest by birth;
and even among twins born from a single womb, seniority is declared to be according to birth. (9.126)

Even though [the two cases] exist as being poured out at the same time, here someone thinks that because of the mention of a "similar wife," the preceding rule concerns a dissimilar wife. That is incorrect, because it would be improper to equate what is unequal. Furthermore, the mention of a "similar wife" here, being stated in connection with another rule, is not capable of showing that the preceding rule has dissimilar wives as its scope; for he will say later: "This rule should be understood to apply to the division among those of one womb, and among those born of many wives of the same caste, but not among those of different castes. Therefore, if this were so, an inconsistency would result due to redundancy. (9.126)

A sonless man may, by this rite, make a daughter his "appointed daughter" (putrikā), with the agreement: "Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the one who performs my ancestral rites. (9.127)

Just as in the section on the partition of inheritance, the mention of sons born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and others is for the purpose of obtaining a share in the absence of a legitimate son (*aurasa*), so too should the rule regarding the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) be understood. This rule concerning the son of an appointed daughter applies only to one who has no son at all. By this agreement—"Whatever offspring may be born of her, that shall be mine for the performance of ancestral rites"—the meaning is that he shall be the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and the water libation. An explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the form of a traditional narrative (*parakṛti*) is cited to illustrate this. (9.127)
In accordance with this very ordinance, Dakṣa, the Lord of Progeny, formerly fashioned those daughters himself for the sake of increasing his own lineage. (9.128)
For Prajāpati is indeed the knower of the method for creating progeny; therefore, he alone has been cited as the example. 9.128.
With a joyful heart, he respectfully gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kāśyapa, and twenty-seven to King Soma. (9.129)
And the word "satkāra" (hospitality) is a sign for all purposes, while for others it serves as an indicator in the ritual of appointing a daughter. || 9.129 ||
As is one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's very self, how could another take away the wealth? (9.130)
When the father has died, whether she has sons or is sonless, the appointed daughter shall take his wealth. (9.130)

Whatever may be the mother’s separate property (yautaka), that indeed is the share of the unmarried daughter; but the son of the daughter (dauhitra) alone shall take the entire wealth of a woman who has no [other] sons. 9.131.

The ownership of that [property] belongs to the father alone. However, if the maternal grandfather dies without a son, the son of the appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) shall take the entire estate, or the appointed daughter herself. When, after a daughter has been appointed, a son is somehow born to the maternal grandfather by chance, then the son of the appointed daughter becomes the owner of the brother’s share. But even if she has been appointed as an appointed daughter, she does not become an heir to her father's property before his death. (9.131)
For if a daughter’s son exists, he shall inherit the entire estate of one who has no son;
he alone shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his father and to his maternal grandfather. (9.132)

In that case where the maternal grandfather is sonless and the son of the appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) is the sole heir to the entire estate, in that case there is a rule for him to offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). But when, by chance, the maternal grandfather comes to have a son while the son of the appointed daughter exists, then even though he is the son of the appointed daughter, he shall not offer a cake to the maternal grandfather. "Should he take [the estate]"—this is the meaning of "in that case. And that offering of the cake is first for the father and the maternal grandfather. In this same manner, a cake must also be offered to each of the two subsequent pairs. For it is said: 9.132.
"In this world, according to the law, there is no distinction between a son's son and a daughter's son;
he states the reason for this:
for both their parents were produced from his own body. (9.133)
The praise of the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra) is for the purpose of the preceding injunction. 9.133.
But if, after a daughter has been appointed, a son is subsequently born, the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman. (9.134)
And this being the case, there is no giving of a share to sons because they are not the eldest. 9.134.
But if the appointed daughter (putrikā) should somehow die without a son,
her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation.

When the father of an appointed daughter (putrikā) has died without a son and all his wealth has been taken by her, if that appointed daughter should die childless, then that wealth shall belong to her husband; he is not to be challenged by her father-in-law’s sapindas or other kinsmen. (9.135)

Whether she has been formally appointed or not, if a mother obtains a son from a man of equal status, that grandson makes his maternal grandfather the recipient of the funeral cake; he shall offer the piṇḍa and inherit the wealth. (9.136)

Since the taking of wealth is for the purpose of offering the funeral oblation (*piṇḍa*), the inheritance of wealth and the offering of the oblation are mandatory [only when she has been formally appointed]. However, if she has not been made an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), the offering of the oblation and the inheritance of wealth by the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) would depend on his own choice. This would be the case whether one accepts an option (*vikalpa*) or a rule (*niyama*). Consequently, the purpose of the rite of the appointed daughter would be lost. Therefore, it is stated that the rule applies when she has been appointed, whereas elsewhere there is an option. As he says: 9.136.
Through a son one conquers the world; through a grandson one attains infinity;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.

This verse is for the purpose of praising the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*). How so? He is praised by treating this very grandson as a daughter’s son, on account of his special connection to benefiting the deceased. How so? For those who have sons, when they die and enter the company of the ancestors (*pitṛgaṇa*), they become worthy of worship like fathers; because of the efficacy of the ritual injunction, they remain there in that state until the fourth generation, subsisting merely by receiving and enjoying the *kavya* (food for the ancestors) offered according to rule by their sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. This is understood through the power of the scripture. For it is in this way that the praise—namely, that one conquers the worlds through sons and the rest—is rendered appropriate. And thus, he provides here an etymological explanation of the name [of the daughter’s son]. (9.137)
Because a son saves his father from the hell named Put, he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself. (9.138)

The authoritative status of the meaning-form residing in the name of that which is being traversed has been demonstrated here by means of the etymological derivation of the name. And since this is so, therefore, on account of the similarity of their effects. (9.138)
In this world, no distinction is found between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for even a daughter’s son saves him in the hereafter, just like a son’s son. (9.139)
This verse is for the purpose of summarizing the meaning already stated. || 9.139 ||
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to his own father. (9.140)
