"That same [son] should offer that funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his father and to his maternal grandfather"—though this has already been stated, it is repeated here. For what purpose? How indeed is there a redundancy? In that context, because the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) is the subject under discussion, it is appropriate for the offering by the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) to follow the sequence of the maternal grandfather. Therefore, this is another alternative rule regarding the offering of the funeral cake by the son of an appointed daughter: "He should first offer the cake to his mother," and so forth. However, the reading and meaning of this verse according to others is as follows: "The son of an appointed daughter should first offer the cake to his mother, but the second to his own father. And the meaning is: first the mention of the mother's name, then that of his own father; then those who follow, namely the maternal grandfather and the paternal grandfather. That, moreover, should be examined as to whether it is logical or not. (9.140)
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage. (9.141)

Because of the rule concerning those who have no son, a *dattaka* (adopted son) shall take the inheritance when there is no biological son. This should be understood as an illustration for the *kṛtrima* (artificially made) and other types of sons as well. Thus, it is logical that all substitutes for a son, without distinction, are entitled to share the wealth of one who has no son. As for the statement that the six types of sons beginning with the *kānīna* (maiden-born) are not heirs, that should be understood as being contingent upon certain circumstances. When a legitimate (*aurasa*) son is born later, he provides mere subsistence to the subsequent [sons]; at that time, he gives to the *kānīna* and others only optionally. It is in this sense that the status of the *kānīna* and others as non-heirs is stated. (9.141)
An adopted son shall not inherit the family name or the estate of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and the estate, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who holds them. 9.142

An adopted son (*dattima*) shall not take the lineage (*gotra*), the inheritance (*riktha*), or the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍadāna*) from his biological father. Rather, he belongs to the lineage and inheritance of the one to whom he is given, and the offering of the funeral cake is likewise connected to him; for the funeral cake follows the lineage. For this reason, the *svadhā*—of which the offering of the funeral cake is indicative—is excluded from the biological father, because it has been bestowed by him upon another. But another says: "Even though he is being given to another, he should not take the lineage or the inheritance of his biological father. In that case, he becomes a son belonging to two lineages (*dvyaumushyāyaṇa*). Gautama, however, having distinguished him, says: "Those related by funeral cake, lineage, or *ṛṣi* [ancestral seer] shall divide the inheritance"; thus, he alone shall take the lineage and the inheritance. (9.142)
The son of an unauthorized woman and the son obtained from a brother-in-law by a woman who already has sons—
neither of these two deserves a share, for they are born of an adulterer and born of lust.

"And even the son of one not authorized"—this means [a son] born by the king of gods (the brother-in-law) to the eldest wife. This being the case, it should be understood that the son of an authorized woman receives an equal share therein. And regarding the phrase "obtained from the brother-in-law by a woman who has sons," this establishes that the right to inherit belongs only to one begotten by the brother-in-law upon a woman who is childless, and not to one begotten by another. By the force of the context, the elision of the word "even" (*api*)—as in "from the brother-in-law *or* from another"—is to be understood. Furthermore, the mention of the "brother-in-law" (*devara*) serves as a qualifier for both. The explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for this is: "since those two are born of an adulterer and born of lust," they are in some way to be censured; thus, the statement of censure applies to both, because both were produced outside of the prescribed rule. (9.143)
Even if born of a woman duly appointed,
a son produced contrary to the prescribed rule is not entitled to his father’s inheritance, for he was procreated by one who has fallen from his status.

Even in the case of a woman who has been duly appointed, because of the injunction that she must be "anointed with ghee and remain silent," one born from a transgression of that rule shall not be an heir to the estate—namely, one begotten by an outcaste man or by two outcastes. Since restrictive rules are heard for both [the husband and the wife], this censure is understood to apply to the transgression of those rules. (9.144)
A son born to a woman duly appointed is indeed considered as one's own legitimate son; for, according to the law, that seed belongs to the owner of the field, and so does the offspring. (9.145)

The statement, "born like a legitimate son," is intended for the purpose of granting a share of the paternal estate to a *kṣetraja* son who possesses such qualities. This being the case, this [rule] should be understood as an exception to the previously mentioned principle of equal shares, because its commencement carries the force of establishing the status of a qualified offspring. Otherwise, since the meaning would already be established by implication from the preceding verse, this [present rule] would be redundant. Furthermore, in this context, the commendatory statement—"this seed belongs to the owner of the field, and according to dharma, the offspring belongs to him"—is appropriate as a means of praise. Moreover, this statement of praise cannot be made without cause; and thus [it is said]: 9.145.
"He who shall maintain the property and the widow of his deceased brother, having procreated offspring for that brother, shall give that very property to that offspring. (9.146)

This statement—that a son born of a widow [should be produced] by means of the *niyoga* procedure and so forth—is based on the maxim of "the stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikanyāya*) regarding the legitimate son. However, others say: "One may give the paternal estate even to one born of a woman not authorized [for *niyoga*]. This matter, however, must be examined as to whether it is logical or illogical. (9.146)

A son whom a woman, having been appointed by another, may obtain from her brother-in-law or another [relative], they declare to be born of lust, not entitled to the inheritance, and produced through improper means. (9.147)

This is a praise of offspring born according to the rule, by way of censuring offspring not born according to the rule, for the purpose of obtaining a share of the father's wealth. But another says: this is a prohibition against what was stated [in verse 9.146], namely that "the son of a woman authorized [to bear a child] shall inherit from the husband's brother or a sapinda"; and because it is both stated and prohibited, his inheritance of the estate should be understood as being optional. One should determine between the two alternatives based on the presence or absence of qualities. (9.147)
This rule for the division among sons born of wives of a single caste should be understood; now learn that which applies to those born of many wives of various castes. (9.148)
This verse serves as an introduction to the section that is about to be expounded. 9.148.
If a Brahmin has four wives in the prescribed order of castes, this is the rule recorded for the division [of the estate] among the sons born of them. (9.149)

The inclusion of the term *ānupūrvyā* (in succession) is for the purpose of restatement; and the inclusion of the word *yadi* (if) is for the sake of indicating that this is not mandatory. Thus it has been said: "But for those who proceed out of desire, these [penances] shall be the lesser ones in their respective order. (9.149)
The ploughman, the breeding bull, a vehicle, an ornament, and a dwelling—these are to be given to the Brāhmaṇa as his preferential share, along with one portion from the best of the property. (9.150)

*Kīnāśa* means a ploughman. Thus says the mantra: "Indra, the lord of a hundred rites, was the master of the plough; the bounteous Maruts were the ploughmen. *Govṛṣa* is the bull that impregnates cows. *Yāna* refers to a carriage and the like. *Alaṃkāra* refers to ornaments such as the father's ring and so forth. Likewise with the house. And that one share which is distinguished by its preeminence—this is the preferential portion (*uddhārika*) for the Brāhmaṇa. Having set this aside from the middle [portion], the rule by which the division of shares for the remainder is made is now stated. (9.150)
From the inheritance, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three parts, the son of a Kṣatriya two parts, the son born of a Vaiśya one and a half parts, and the son of a Śūdra only half a part. (9.151)

The determination of the shares has been explained by the preceding statements. Even when there are two or many [sons], they shall divide in this manner only if they are equal in number; thereafter, those of the same caste shall divide as before. However, when they are unequal in number, the allotment of shares must be inferred from the indications of the scriptures. (9.151)
Or, having divided the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts, one who knows the law should make a righteous distribution according to this rule:
dharmyaṃ vibhāgaṃ kurvīta vidhinānena dharmavit || 9.152 || One who knows the dharma should make a righteous division by means of this procedure.
Regarding this, because it is consistent with the Dharma, this distinction applies to all those who act as described; that very point is now stated: 9.152.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share. (9.153)
This is the conceptualization of the portions of the straight meaning. Here too, as before, the division among those with equal and unequal numbers is to be understood. (9.153)
Whether there be a virtuous son or whether there be no son at all,
one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman.

He whose sons are virtuous is a "man with good sons" (*satputra*). Even if he should be sonless, in his absence, the son of a Śūdra woman alone [may inherit]. Even so, more than a tenth part of the estate should not be given to him; the rest, the *sapiṇḍas* shall take. In their absence, they alone are the rightful heirs to that wealth. From this very indicative mark, the same applies to a Kṣatriya. Otherwise, the prohibition regarding the Śūdra would be meaningless. (9.154)
The son of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra woman does not inherit the estate;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth. 9.155

"The share of this [son] is dependent upon his father"—this is another alternative rule based on the connection with specific qualities (*guṇa*), which relates to the preceding injunction. This being the case, because there is a contradiction between the former and the latter, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between these two based on the connection with qualities. Alternatively, this rule should be understood as applying to the son of an unmarried Śūdra woman, whereas the former applies to the son of a married woman. And so Gautama says in the section concerning Śūdras: "If he is obedient, he may receive the means of subsistence according to the rule for a pupil (*antevāsī*). (GDh 9.155)
Or, sons born of wives of equal caste for those of noble birth should all divide the estate equally after giving a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the eldest. (9.156)

Or, those born of wives of equal caste shall divide the estate equally after giving something to the eldest for the increase of honor; this rule is to be understood by implication as applying to those of lower birth who are superior in qualities. 9.156.
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is prescribed, and no other;
those born of her shall share equal portions, even if there be a hundred sons. (9.157)

This is stated regarding a Śūdra woman who is pure; in the case of other women who are superior or inferior, the distribution [of the estate] should be determined with regard to merit and demerit. (9.157)
Of the twelve sons whom Manu, the son of the Self-Existent, has named for men, six are kinsmen entitled to inheritance, and six are kinsmen not entitled to inheritance. (9.158)

This instruction regarding sons is presented here with reference to the section on the division of inheritance; it serves as a commentary (bhāṣya) upon that which stands in the place of a sutra, for the purpose of defining its essential nature. 9.158.
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son—these six are both heirs and kinsmen. (9.159)

The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the son of a Śūdra woman—these six are kinsmen who do not inherit property. (9.160)

This classification of groups of sons is for the sake of legal duties, as he will explain later; it is stated so that, by virtue of being taught together with the *aurasa* son, the *kṣetraja* and other sons might not be thought to be equal to him. Therefore, this is said: [9.159–60].
Just as one who crosses water by means of bad boats suffers such a fate, so too does one who crosses over darkness by means of bad sons suffer such a fate. (9.161)

By this indicative mark, all [sons], beginning with the *kṣetraja*, shall perform the duties of a son for one who has no son, and they shall all receive the inheritance. It has been explained that the statement regarding the non-inheritance of the *kānīna* and others refers to a contingent possibility. (9.162)

If there should be two sons, one legitimate (aurasa) and one born of the wife (kṣetraja), who are co-heirs, each shall take that paternal inheritance which belongs to his own father, and not the other. 9.162.

[And] because of the force of the context, it must be stated that "if there is an *aurasa* [son], there is no *kṣetraja*," or "if there is a *kṣetraja*, there is no *aurasa*. This being the case, this [son] should be understood as an *aniyuktāsuta* (the son of an unauthorized woman) by virtue of his qualities. For instance, when a *kṣetraja* is born from a wife who already has a son, or when an *aurasa* is born after a *kṣetraja* has been produced, then this is the division of their wealth: "whatever belongs to the father [goes] to whichever [of them]. According to this view, since sons such as the *aniyuktāsuta* are not entitled to a share in the other case, they receive a share from the biological father (*bījī*). But another says: if a man who has already fathered a child performs the rites according to the *Atharvaṇa* school and produces more sons after having performed everything again, and if the wealth belonging to the woman were to belong to both the biological father and the owner of the field, then this is the division between those two. (9.162)
The legitimate son of the body alone is the master of his father’s wealth;
however, for the sake of compassion toward the others, he should provide them with a livelihood. (9.163)

Thus, when a son of the body (aurasa) has been born later than sons such as the son of the field (kṣetraja), their lack of entitlement to a share having been established, this rule is stated for the purpose of providing an alternative: that only a mere subsistence allowance should be given to the others, namely the son of the field and the rest. (9.163)
But when dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) shall give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), or even a fifth share. (9.164)

This third alternative regarding the son of the appointed woman (*niyuktā*) pertains to the *kṣetraja* son, because he is the primary [type]. And the alternative regarding the sixth or fifth share depends upon his qualities. (9.164)
The son begotten on one's own wife and the son begotten on the wife of another are both entitled to share in the paternal inheritance;
however, ten other types of sons, in their respective order, are entitled to share in the family lineage and the inheritance.

And thus, when each preceding one exists, each subsequent one is joined with a share consisting merely of the right to subsistence. And because of this, since each preceding one possesses seniority, belongs to the family lineage, and performs the duties of kinship—even those duties performed by the son born in adultery (kānīna) and others—now their defining characteristics are stated. (9.165)
But that son whom one should beget oneself upon one's own wedded wife, one should know him as the legitimate *aurasa* son, the foremost of all types. (9.166)

Whichever woman belongs to whichever man's lineage, she is his field; one born of her should be understood as a legitimate (*aurasa*) son of the first rank. However, those born of Kṣatriya or Vaiśya women do not possess the full characteristics of legitimate sons. Therefore, their distribution of inheritance must be determined in a manner that does not contradict justice. Others, however, consider only the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya to be legitimate sons who are superior to the *kṣetraja* and other types of sons. (9.166)
A son born on the bed of a man who has died, is impotent, or is diseased, from a woman duly appointed according to her own dharma, is known as a *kṣetraja* (son of the wife). || 9.167 ||
This verse has been explained by its very recitation. || 9.167 ||
When the mother and father, out of necessity, give a son with water to one who is similar and well-disposed, he is to be known as a "given" (dattrima) son. 9.168.

As for those who read, "The mother or the father may give him," that is said to be incorrect; because the rule regarding the giving [of a son] applies to both together, an adopted son (dattaka) should not be accepted if either one is absent. However, under this alternative view expressed as "the mother or the father," there is no requirement for the giving by both together. "Similar" means of the same caste (*savarṇa*), [in terms of] birth and so forth. (9.168)
But he whom one may make similar [to oneself], who is discerning of virtues and faults, and who is endowed with the qualities of a son—he is to be known as the "adopted" (kṛtrima) son. (9.169)
Even one who is adopted shall be of the same caste, provided he is destitute of father and mother. (9.169)
If one is born in a house but it is not known whose he is, he is one born secretly in the house; he belongs to him by whom he was begotten on the bed. (9.170)
One who possesses unknown seed, born of the mother's lineage, and produced in secret is to be known as such; and thus is the view of Vyāsa. 9.170.
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is called an *apaviddha*. (9.171)

When one of the two has died, the abandonment of the other is prescribed; for otherwise, if either parent were still living, his status as an *apaviddha* (cast-off) would not be appropriate. Furthermore, this [abandoned son] must also be of the same caste (*savarṇa*). 9.171.

If a maiden, however, should secretly give birth to a son in her father's house, one should call him by the name "Kānīna" (maiden-born); he is born from the maiden, but belongs to the man who marries her.

One born of a similar [woman] is for the sake of the same caste (*savarṇa*). Others, however, because of the mention of "in secret" (*raha*), say that even here, since the biological father (*bījī*) is not specified, the *kānīna* son belongs to the mother's caste alone. (9.172)
If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition be known or unknown, the child belongs to the man who marries her; he is called a *sahoḍha* (one taken with the bride).
This son born of a woman who was pregnant at marriage also belongs to the caste of his mother. || 9.173 ||
If one should purchase from someone else a son for the sake of his own offspring, he is that man’s *krītaka* (bought) son, whether he be of similar or dissimilar status. (9.174)

Others, however, say that the "purchased" [slave] is determined by his qualities as being either similar or dissimilar; for if the classification were based on caste, there would be a contradiction with legal reasoning in the case of accepting one of a different caste. But another [author] states that the contradiction with legal reasoning applies specifically to the case of a Brāhmaṇa. 9.174.
A woman who, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, produces offspring again by her own will after marrying once more, is called *paunarbhava*. (9.175)
Whether he be of the same caste as a son born of a remarried woman, or even of a different caste, yet one who is superior in qualities; 9.175.
If she has remained a virgin, or even if she has returned after having left,
she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with her husband from a second marriage.
Even if she has been defiled by the mere taking of the hand, if she returns from her husband's house with her virginity intact, she is to be consecrated again. || 9.176 ||
One who is bereft of parents, or has been abandoned without cause, and who offers himself to another—that is known as "self-given. (9.177)
He should be of the same caste, and not otherwise. 9.177.
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may father out of lust upon a Śūdra woman is indeed a corpse while still alive;
therefore, he is known as a Pāraśava.

He who was previously designated as a *śaudra*—the term "Brāhmaṇa" being used here for the sake of illustration, including the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya as well—is called a *pāraśava*. He is a corpse (*śava*) while still living (*pārayan*), because he lacks connection to those actions characterized by the purposeful pursuit of human goals; thus he is remembered as a *pāraśava*. (9.178)
If a Śūdra should have a son by a female slave or the daughter of a male slave, he may, with permission, take a share; such is the established law. (9.179)
Based on the statement regarding the father's permission with respect to a Śūdra, there is no permission for Brāhmaṇas and others to give an inheritance out of affection or passion. 9.179.
The wise declare that these eleven sons, beginning with the son of the wife (kṣetraja) as previously described, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites.

Because there is a general statement regarding substitutes for all eleven [types of sons], even the *kānīna* (maiden-born) and others are understood to be no different from the preceding ones. Therefore, it has been explained that what was stated regarding their status as non-heirs (*adāyāda*) and non-relatives (*abāndhava*) must be intended to mean that they may optionally receive a maintenance allowance. Is this, then, a substitute for the primary son in a specific function, as the Mīmāṃsakas say? No, it is replied, because it is improper to equate things that are unequal. And so it has been said: "By means of bad sons, one crosses over the darkness and attains such merit," and so forth. Thus, this deprecatory statement regarding them is for the purpose of negating their equality in strength [with the legitimate sons]. (9.180)
These sons who have been mentioned incidentally as born from the seed of others belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else. (9.181)

Having excluded the two types of sons born of remarriage (*paunarbhava* and *kānīna*), nine other sons born from the seed of others are mentioned. Among these, when the biological father (*bījī*) is available, those who have been superseded by the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*) are entitled to a share. However, in the case of those whose biological father is unknown—such as the secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*), the maiden-born (*kānīna*), and the one taken with the bride (*sahoḍha*)—since they have no claim to a share in either estate, only mere subsistence is given to them; and this is permitted for all of them because of the injunction against cruelty. Others hold that this verse is intended to praise the legitimate son of the body, as it neither enjoins nor prohibits anything else. Alternatively, this verse is intended to demonstrate that a substitute does not perform the same function as the primary. (9.181)
If among brothers of the same caste one should have a son, Manu has declared that they all become possessed of a son through that son. (9.182)

This is intended to mean that these substitutes should not be employed when a brother’s son exists. Alternatively, by this verse, the status of the [son of that brother] as a substitute is understood according to the principle applied to the *dattaka* and others; however, if a brother’s son is unavailable or does not exist, other alternatives are to be resorted to. (9.182)
If among many wives who have one husband only, one should have a son, Manu has declared that they all become possessed of sons by means of that son. (9.183)
From this it is understood that she must not be appointed [to perform religious rites]; nor should she, being alone, undertake the adoption of a son such as a *dattaka* and others. (9.183)
In the absence of a superior, one who is inferior is entitled to the inheritance;
but if there are many of equal status, all are sharers of the estate. (9.184)

This verse is the seed for the entire distribution of inheritance; and this being so, in accordance with it, one must describe the distribution of inheritance regarding those who have not yet arrived and those who have already passed away. (9.184)
Neither brothers nor fathers, nor sons, are the heirs to the father's estate;
rather, the father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, and so too shall the brothers. (9.185)

Those sons who have been mentioned here, beginning with the *aurasa* (legitimate son), shall be the heirs to the inheritance; so too shall those beginning with the *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife) [be heirs] in the absence of an *aurasa*. Why is this so? Because of the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Even though they are more closely related than the father or the brother, they would not be entitled to the inheritance [otherwise]. For it is said: "The father shall take the property of one who has no son; in his absence, the brothers. Thus, since the acquisition of the father's wealth by the *aurasa* is already established, this present section is commenced for the purpose of establishing the rights of the *kṣetraja* and other such sons. As he says in verse 9.185: [Verse 9.185 follows... Thus ends the section on the division of the estate among sons. Now, the author sets forth the rules regarding the partition of the estate among brothers. Among these, first, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers who were previously living together: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.114:** "Brothers who were previously united in household affairs, whether reunited after separation or not, are entitled to equal shares upon reunion. **Commentary:** The term "previously united in household affairs" (*pūrva-saṃsṛṣṭāḥ*) refers to those who, having once lived together as a single economic unit, have subsequently separated and then reunited. The phrase "whether reunited after separation or not" (*vibhaktā vāpi saṃsṛṣṭāḥ*) indicates that even those who were not previously united but have become so through subsequent reunion are included. The word "equal" (*samāṃśāḥ*) means they shall receive identical portions. This applies to all brothers, including those born of different mothers, provided they are reunited. This is because the right to a share arises from the fact of being a brother, and the status of being a brother is not lost by the act of separation. Therefore, when they reunite, they must divide the property equally. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers who were never united: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.115:** "The eldest alone takes the entire paternal estate, and the others live under him as they did under their father; or, with the consent of the eldest, they may divide the property. **Commentary:** In this case, the eldest brother takes the whole estate, and the younger brothers live under him in the same manner as they lived under their father. Alternatively, with the permission of the eldest, they may divide the property. The option is given because the eldest brother is entitled to a special share as the primary heir. However, this applies only when there is no specific agreement to the contrary. If there is an agreement, the partition proceeds according to that agreement. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers where some are capable of managing the estate and others are not: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.116:** "If the eldest or the youngest is deprived of his share, or if either of them dies, his share goes to the middlemost; or it goes to the one who is capable of maintaining the family. **Commentary:** If the eldest or the youngest brother is disqualified from inheriting due to lack of capacity or misconduct, or if he dies, his share does not go to his own offspring but goes to the middlemost brother, or to whichever brother among them is capable of supporting the family. This is because the estate must be managed by one who is competent. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers where some are learned and some are not: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.117:** "If the eldest or the youngest is devoid of learning, he shall receive a maintenance; the rest shall divide the remainder according to the prescribed shares. **Commentary:** If the eldest or the youngest brother is unlearned, he shall receive only enough for his subsistence. The remaining property shall be divided among the other brothers according to the standard shares prescribed in the scriptures. This is because the learned brother is entitled to a larger share as a reward for his knowledge and the burden of maintaining the family. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers where some have performed Vedic rites and some have not: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.118:** "If the eldest or the youngest is devoid of Vedic study, he shall receive a maintenance; the rest shall divide the remainder according to the prescribed shares. **Commentary:** This is similar to the previous rule. If the eldest or the youngest brother has abandoned Vedic study, he is entitled only to a maintenance. The rest of the estate is divided among the others. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers where some have defects and some do not: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.119:** "If the eldest or the youngest is an outcast (*patita*), insane, or impotent, he shall receive a maintenance; the rest shall divide the remainder according to the prescribed shares. **Commentary:** If the eldest or the youngest brother is an outcast, insane, or impotent, he is excluded from the inheritance. He is entitled only to a maintenance. The rest of the estate is divided among the others. This is because such persons are incapable of performing religious duties or managing the estate. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers where some are minors and some are adults: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.120:** "If the eldest or the youngest is a minor, he shall receive his share when he reaches majority; until then, it shall be held in trust by the others. **Commentary:** If the eldest or the youngest brother is a minor (under twenty years of age), his share shall be set aside and held in trust by the other brothers until he attains majority. This is to ensure that the minor's rights are protected. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers where some are absent and some are present: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.121:** "If a brother is absent, his share shall be set aside; when he returns, he shall receive it. If he does not return, his share goes to the others. **Commentary:** If a brother is away from home, his share shall be reserved. When he returns, he shall receive his portion. If he does not return within a reasonable time, his share goes to the other brothers. This is because the estate must be managed by those who are present and capable. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers where some have debts and some do not: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.122:** "If a brother has incurred debts, he shall pay them from his share; the rest shall divide the remainder according to the prescribed shares. **Commentary:** If a brother has contracted debts, he must repay them from his own share before the partition. The remaining property is then divided among the others. This is to ensure that the debts are cleared before the estate is distributed. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers where some have performed ancestral rites and some have not: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.123:** "If a brother has performed the ancestral rites, he shall receive a larger share; the rest shall divide the remainder according to the prescribed shares. **Commentary:** If a brother has performed the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) for the ancestors, he is entitled to a larger share as a reward for his service. The rest of the estate is divided among the others. This is to encourage the performance of ancestral rites. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers where some have performed sacrifices and some have not: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.124:** "If a brother has performed sacrifices, he shall receive a larger share; the rest shall divide the remainder according to the prescribed shares. **Commentary:** If a brother has performed Vedic sacrifices, he is entitled to a larger share as a reward for his spiritual merit. The rest of the estate is divided among the others. This is to encourage the performance of Vedic sacrifices. Now, the rule concerning the partition of the estate among brothers where some have performed penances and some have not: **Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.125:** "If a brother has performed penances, he shall receive a larger share; the rest shall divide the remainder according to the prescribed shares. **Commentary:** If a brother has performed penances (*prāyaścitta*) for past sins, he is entitled to a larger share as a reward for his purification. The rest of the estate is divided among the others. This is to encourage the performance of penances. Now, the
Water must be offered to three; the funeral cake proceeds for three.
The fourth is the giver of these; a fifth is not possible. (9.186)
This verse is intended to illustrate the proximity of that which has been under discussion. 9.186.
The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda; after him, it shall go to the sakulyas, or to the teacher, or even to the pupil. (9.187)

By the mention of "those belonging to the same lineage" (sakulya), those related by water (samānodaka) are included, as well as the teacher or the pupil; in their absence [the following applies]. 9.187.
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs to the estate; thus the law is not violated. (9.188)
From the phrase "even in the absence of all," it is understood that this applies even in the absence of those women who possess the aforementioned qualities; and such being the case, [verse 9.188].

The property of a Brāhmaṇa is always inviolable by the king; this is the established rule. But in the case of the other castes, the king may take their property when all [other heirs] are absent. (9.189)
The meaning of this verse is straightforward. || 9.189 ||
For one who has died childless, one should obtain a son from a member of the same lineage; whatever property there may be, that one should bestow upon him. (9.190)

Since the *kṣetraja* son has already been mentioned as being born from either the husband’s brother (*devara*) or a *sapiṇḍa*, the inclusion of the term “of the same lineage” (*sagotra*) here is for the purpose of ensuring that even one born from such a person obtains a share of the wealth. Otherwise, based on the statement “from the husband’s brother or from a *sapiṇḍa*,” a *kṣetraja* son born from a *sagotra* who is neither the husband’s brother nor a *sapiṇḍa* would be ineligible for a share. However, for a *klība* (impotent) man, the *dattaka* (adopted), *kṛtrima* (artificially made), and *svayaṃdatta* (self-given) sons may be [his heirs]. (9.190)
If two men, born of the same woman by two different fathers, should dispute over her property, he whose portion is the paternal inheritance shall take it, and not the other. (9.191)

Furthermore, regarding a woman who has remarried—having children and possessing wealth—and becomes a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) with another man, this is the division [of property]. And this is the view concerning the inheritance rights of the son of a *punarbhū*. (9.191)
But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally. (9.192)

Because of the scriptural statement [that they are equal], there is no preferential share for the eldest here. And "sisters" includes both those who are uterine and those who are married or unmarried; however, some maintain that only the unmarried ones are meant. But in the absence of sisters, however... [9.192]
Whatever daughters they may have, something should be given to them from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection. (9.193)
This has already been considered regarding those who are married and those who are unmarried; because of the expression "out of affection," this gift is understood not to be mandatory. (9.193)

That which is given before the nuptial fire, that which is received from the bridegroom, that which is given as a token of affection, and that which is obtained from her brother, mother, or father— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.

Because of the restriction regarding the sixfold [types of property], that which is obtained through friendship does not constitute "woman's property" (*strīdhana*). That which is given near the fire (*adhyagnīya*) is what is bestowed upon her while being led away from the fire. That which is given at the time of the wedding procession (*adhyāvāhanika*) is what is given to her as she is being brought to her husband’s home. (9.194)

Furthermore, that which was given as a post-nuptial gift (anvādheya) and that which was given by the husband out of affection—when she has passed away while her husband is still living, that wealth shall belong to her offspring. (9.195)
The meaning of this verse is straightforward. || 9.195 ||

Whatever wealth is acquired in marriages according to the Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Gandharva, or Prajapatya rites, it is ordained that, upon the death of the wife without issue, it belongs to the husband alone. (9.196)
In these five types of wives, the husband's property is permitted [to be used]. (9.196)
Whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others, it is ordained that upon her death childless, it shall belong to her mother and father.
In these cases, such as those involving Asuras and others who are virtuous, the wealth must be returned to those two. || 9.197 ||
Whatever wealth may belong to a woman, having been given by her father in any manner whatsoever, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her daughter, or to her offspring.

Since it is proper that the six kinds of *strīdhana* (woman’s property) be taken when she has died without a son, the phrase "given by the father" is to be understood here as an illustration for all types of woman’s property. Furthermore, he will state the division for one whose sons have died, based on the rule: "The Brāhmaṇī wife shall take it, as shall the maiden. This restriction applies to the maidens of the Kṣatriya and other castes. This refers to the Brāhmaṇas and others: when those who have married Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriyā, or Vaiśyā wives die without leaving wives of their own caste, the distribution of wealth to the maidens of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes is to be understood as follows. (9.198)
Women should not effect a withdrawal from the family property held in common, nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their husband. (9.199)

This is understood from the prohibition against withdrawal: if someone were to withdraw that property by virtue of being the mistress [of the household], then, having taken it back, it must indeed be divided by the brothers. (9.199)
Whatever ornament may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide it; those who do divide it fall from their status. 9.200.
This prohibition applies to heirs; however, the division of property among one's own legitimate sons is permitted. (9.200)
Those who have no share are the impotent, the outcaste, those born blind or deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs. (9.201)
By this [statement], those who crawl on their haunches, the lame, and others are also included by implication. 9.201.
However, it is right for the wise man to give to all of them according to his ability, providing food and clothing as long as they live; for by failing to do so, he would become an outcast. (9.202)
From the context, this is stated regarding eunuchs and others: they shall be given food and clothing for as long as they live. (9.202)
If, however, eunuchs or the wretched should somehow have a desire for wives, their offspring, having produced a lineage, shall be entitled to the inheritance. (9.203)

Regarding the phrase "of the impotent and so forth," by virtue of the context here, there is no *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (retention of the quality) in the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Thus, those other than the impotent are understood [to be excluded]. For one who possesses the capacity for which the taking of a wife is intended—namely, for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*) and progeny (*prajā*)—there is no such taking of a wife for the impotent man due to the absence of that capacity. Furthermore, because one who is sonless has no entitlement to the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires), the taking of a wife would be required only with respect to the duties prescribed by the *Smṛtis*. In that case, it would be appropriate to include the impotent man here as well, by means of a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi*. (9.203)
Whatever wealth the eldest son acquires after his father has died belongs to the younger brothers as well, provided they are observant of their studies. (9.204)

The meaning is that virtuous younger brothers are entitled to a share of what was acquired by the eldest, but the elder brother is not entitled to a share of what was acquired by the youngest; this is established by implication. (9.204)
But if all those who were ignorant should acquire wealth through their own efforts, the rule is that there should be an equal division of it, as it is not ancestral property. (9.205)

"From effort" means from exertion, such as agriculture and so forth. If all [the sons] exert themselves equally, then the division of the estate shall be equal; however, no method of division based on their respective merits should be adopted. (9.205)
Whatever constitutes the wealth of knowledge belonging to anyone shall be that person's own wealth;
this includes what is received from a friend, what is obtained at marriage, and likewise what is given with the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka).
By the mention of "that which is received at marriage," everything obtained from the father-in-law's house is included. (9.206)
But he among brothers who, though capable by his own labor, does not desire wealth, shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence. (9.207)
Moreover, there is no contradiction even in the case of those who do not give. || 9.207 ||
Whatever one may acquire through one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate, that which is obtained by one's own effort, he is not obliged to give away unless he so desires. (9.208)
That is to say, he permits the giving of what is desired. 9.208.
But whatever paternal property a father may acquire that was not previously obtained, he need not share that with his sons unless he so desires, for it is self-earned. (9.209)

The prohibition is based on the apprehension that others might also have authority over the grandfather’s wealth. By this view, when the division [of the estate] is established, all property must be divided; this is the view regarding the division of sons by the father. It demonstrates that there is a division for those whose fathers are still living. (9.209)
If those who were divided while living together should divide again, the division in that case shall be equal; there is no right of primogeniture in that situation. (9.210)

He who is the eldest among those who have reunited shall not receive the preferential share of the eldest; however, where the eldest reunites with the preferential share, there his preferential share is again extracted for him. (9.210)
If among them the eldest or the youngest should be deprived of his share by the distribution of inheritance, or if either of them should die, his portion is not lost. (9.211)
Having set aside the share for one who is away on a journey or for one who is deceased. || 9.211 ||
The uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally; so too shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters. (9.212)

Those uterine brothers who are not reunited shall divide that [property], not the half-brothers; but when there is a state of reunion, those who are reunited shall divide it, not even the uterine brothers if they are not reunited. (9.212)
If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers, he shall forfeit his status as the eldest, receive no share of the inheritance, and be restrained by the kings. (9.213)

The unjust distribution of property, the humiliation of the younger brothers, and the appropriation of wealth by deceiving them—since these things occur, it follows that even the youngest son must be strictly controlled for the sake of the estate. (9.213)

All brothers who are engaged in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the wealth; nor should an elder brother make a separate provision for himself without having given anything to the younger brothers. (9.214)

Those who are unskilled in family affairs and, through gambling and other such means, engaged in improper occupations (vikarma) are understood from the force of the context; it has been stated that those who have fallen [from their caste] are not entitled to a share. (9.214)
If brothers who have not yet divided their inheritance should undertake some enterprise together, the father must by no means allot unequal shares among them. (9.215)
But one born after the partition shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or, those who may have reunited with him, he shall divide it together with them. (9.216)

An unequal division of wealth must not be made among those who have acquired their respective fortunes through mutual effort, whether by the father’s affection or out of regard for their virtues. And this view applies only when the father has no specific intention; however, if there is a partition according to the father’s intention, the acceptance of that intention would be optional, but not otherwise. (9.216)
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies childless;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.

While the mother and the paternal grandmother are alive, the uterine brothers have no authority over the property of one who dies childless; nor do his father or his uterine brothers have such authority. (9.217)
When all debts and assets have been divided according to the rule, whatever may subsequently be discovered, all that should be brought into equality. (9.218)

The instruction is given again for the purpose that such [property] is not to be taken by the owner, or else for the purpose of prohibiting the share of the eldest; for it has been stated that "the first-born receives two shares," and therefore that [right] of the eldest would not apply here. (9.218)
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, and the management of property and security—they declare these to be indivisible. (9.219)

One may divide even these according to one's desire. This statement, "one who lacks desire is not entitled to give," should be regarded as a restatement (*anuvāda*). In every case, it is improper to prohibit giving based on desire, because in all instances of dividing property, such giving is already established. Clothing is well known. A "vehicle" (*patra*) is that by which one travels, such as a horse and so forth. An "ornament" (*alaṃkāra*) refers to whatever was personally appropriated by each while the father was still living—this follows from the context. "Prepared food" (*kṛtānna*) refers to rice and the like. "Water" (*udaka*) refers to wells and other sources that serve as its receptacle. "Women" refers to female slaves intended for personal enjoyment, who are specifically assigned. And "the management of acquisition and preservation" (*yogakṣemapracāra*) refers to that wealth by means of which they carry out the purpose of acquisition and preservation; "acquisition" (*yoga*) is the gaining of what has not yet been obtained, and "preservation" (*kṣema*) is the protection of what has been obtained. Alternatively, "acquisition and preservation" should be understood as even that which is granted by the king for that purpose. Furthermore, "means of livelihood" (*pracāra*) refers to fuel, firewood, and so forth produced from the land used for subsistence; these they declare are not to be divided. (9.219)
This division of yours and the procedure for the rites of the sons, beginning with the son of the wife (kṣetraja), have been declared in due order; now learn the law concerning gambling. 9.220.
This verse has the purpose of presenting a summary. 9.220.
The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his realm;
these two vices bring about the end of the kingdoms of those who rule the earth. (9.221)
Since this gambling and betting are such that they are openly practiced as theft,
therefore—
The king should always be diligent in preventing those two. || 9.222 ||
Now this is stated for the purpose of showing the distinction between gambling (dyūta) and betting with living creatures (samāhvaya):
"That which is performed with non-living things is called gambling in the world;
that which is performed with living beings should be known as betting. (9.223)
The king shall execute all those who engage in gambling or betting, or cause them to be done, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born. (9.224)

The masters of the gambling house (*sabhika*) who cause gambling to be played must also be beaten, not only the players themselves. Since the instruction regarding execution is intended for prohibition, those who oppose the royal administration must be restrained by some other means as well; for in such a case, there is no transgression of *dharma* whatsoever. This being so, it should be understood that "killing" (*vadhi*) here actually signifies "beating. However, Śūdras who violate the established order of *dharma* and assume the insignia (*liṅga*) of the twice-born (*dvija*) should indeed be put to death. Those Śūdras assuming the insignia of the twice-born include those who wear the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) and carry [the mendicant's] bowl, those who address others with the word "Bhoḥ," and those who wear the dress of wandering ascetics (*parivrājaka*) and the like. Furthermore, it can be said that even the study of grammar constitutes the insignia of the twice-born. (9.224)
He shall quickly banish from the city gamblers, actors, cruel men, those who adhere to heretical sects, those who follow improper occupations, and drunkards. (9.225)

The terms *krūra* (cruel), *abhinna* (unchaste), and *duṣṭa* (wicked) are used here by means of ellipsis (*varṇalopa*) and figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*). Another reading is *kelān*, which refers to those who are excessively lustful and live by means of amorous play (*kelījīvinaḥ*). Others read *kailān*, meaning those who act as intermediaries for secret assignations (*saṅketakāriṇaḥ*). Furthermore, he should banish from the city all men belonging to heretical sects (*pāṣaṇḍasthān*), those established in the outward signs of religious orders that lie outside the scope of the Vedas and the Law Codes (*śrutismṛti*). The term *vikarmasthaḥ*—meaning one who stands in opposition to his duty—is a self-contained compound; alternatively, it serves as an adjective qualifying the *śauṇḍika* (liquor-seller). He should expel all these from the city. Since there is no distinction in the act of banishment, they are effectively to be expelled from the kingdom as well. And in this context, following the mention of gamblers, the prohibition of actors (*kuśīlava*) and others is also established. By which... (9.225)
These, existing within the kingdom as secret thieves of the king, constantly afflict the virtuous subjects through their performance of improper acts. (9.226)
Since these, while residing in the royal capital, lead to great misfortune for the king, their banishment even from the kingdom is therefore prescribed. (9.226)
This gambling, seen in former ages, is a great cause of enmity;
therefore, a wise man should not practice gambling, even for the sake of amusement. (9.227)

Yudhiṣṭhira and the others belong to a later time. However, the gambling match witnessed by the gods and asuras is cited here because it occurred long ago, according to the Vedic text: "Those gods were on one side. Thus, this should be understood as an explanatory passage (arthavāda) intended to censure gambling. Since this is so, therefore... [9.227]
Whether it be done in secret or openly, whatever man should practice such [an act], there shall be a choice of punishment for him as the king desires. (9.228)
And this being so, by whatever kind of punishment he might be deterred from gambling, that specific kind of punishment he may prescribe according to his own discretion. (9.228)
But a member of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes who is unable to pay a fine shall discharge his debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, shall pay it gradually, little by little. 9.229.

As it has been stated, Kṣatriyas and others who, being penniless, are unable to undergo the aforementioned forms of punishment, shall perform services corresponding to the nature of their offense. A Brāhmaṇa, however, should be punished gradually in accordance with his own specific duty (*svadharma*). Although this has already been mentioned, it is now stated again for the sake of the subject of punishment; previously, however, that matter was addressed in the section on usury (verse 9.229).
The king should administer punishment with whips, split bamboo, ropes, and the like for women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, the helpless, and the sick. (9.230)

This flogging with whips and the like for those engaged in forbidden acts is to be carried out in accordance with the nature of their offense; however, it should not be understood as a mere act of capriciousness even toward those who have committed grave sins. 9.230.
But those who, having been appointed to duties, ruin the affairs of the litigants while being consumed by the heat of wealth—of them the king shall deprive of their property. (9.231)

They provide assistance to someone through their wealth by means of legal proceedings; they should be deprived of that wealth. Or rather, those officials who, having received money, perform their duties otherwise than they ought, should be deprived of that wealth. (9.231)
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the subjects, those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, as well as those who serve his enemies. (9.232)
For those who persist in opposition to the administration of the kingdom, execution is the rule; those who serve the enemy have no other recourse but death. (9.232)
Whatever has been settled and adjudicated, wherever it may have occurred, one should know that to be established by dharma; one must not reverse it again. (9.233)

And this being so, one should not turn back out of friendliness, compassion, or for any other reason; rather, one should turn back from that which is not established by the treatise. And such being the case: || 9.233 ||
Whatever legal matter ministers or presiding judges might decide otherwise than it ought to be, the king himself shall settle that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas]. (9.234)

The minister appointed by the king for the protection of legal proceedings is a Brāhmaṇa. As it has been said: "Then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee the affairs. However, the presiding judges (*prāḍvivākas*) are distinct individuals who are experts in the Vedas and the Śāstras. As it has been said: "In whatever place three Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas sit down... Whatever these [judges] might do otherwise than correctly, due to causes such as passion and so forth, when the king is not present, the monarch himself should perform that task. Furthermore, he should fine them one thousand [paṇas]. This refers to the technical definition of *paṇas* already mentioned. And this injunction regarding the punishment applies to the group collectively, just as in the expression: "Let the descendants of Gārgya be fined one hundred. (9.234)

The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—all these men are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin). 9.235.

There is another reading for this verse: "One should know these men— slayers of a Brāhmaṇa, drinkers of spirituous liquor, thieves, and violators of the Guru's bed— to be individually all great sinners (mahāpātakins)."

In this context, because of the connection with "sin" (pātaka), the term *taskara* refers to one who has committed the theft of gold. Regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, there is a transgression for all [classes]. Regarding liquor, we shall state the specific distinctions based on caste concerning the drinking of sweet intoxicants (*madhu-madya*). And in the case of theft, all castes have the capacity for the offense. That [is the same] regarding violating the Guru’s bed. 9.235.
And for these four who do not perform expiation, he shall prescribe a lawful punishment involving both their bodies and their wealth. (9.236)

By the statement "of all four," the fifth person related to them is included. For the killing of women, children, and Brahmins, corporal punishment has been prescribed. In the verse beginning "and of all these four," however, there is mention of both fines and monetary penalties. This should be carried out in accordance with the gravity of the offense. But for a Śūdra who fails to perform the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa, both types of punishment apply. (9.236)

For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ shall be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag; for theft, the mark of a dog's foot; and for killing a Brahmin, the mark of a headless man. (9.237)
Because of the mention of the forehead in the rule prohibiting the marking of the forehead. || 9.237 ||

For they shall be unfit for social enjoyment, unfit for marriage alliances, unfit for study together, and unfit for intermarriage; excluded from all religious duties, they shall wander the earth in misery. (9.238)
This alone is to be understood as their renunciation; he demonstrates that very point. 9.238.
But these, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives; they shall be without compassion and without the salutation—this is the instruction of Manu. (9.239)

Thinking, "These have not been punished by the king," they should not be taken under the protection of their kinsmen and relatives. This being the case, even when these individuals are afflicted by disease or other calamities, no compassion should be shown toward them; and even when they possess qualities such as seniority, they are not to be honored with rising from one's seat and other marks of respect. It is precisely this that must be understood here as the dharma by virtue of the force of the statement; it is not that compassion or humility are independently enjoined as previously taught. (9.239)
But those of the higher castes who perform the prescribed penance as declared shall not be branded on the foreheads by the king; rather, they shall be made to pay the highest fine. (9.240)
The "preceding castes" refers to the Brāhmaṇas and the others; and by implication, it is understood that for killing through negligence, the fine shall be five hundred. 9.240.
For insulting a Brahmin among these [offenses], the middle amercement shall be imposed; or he shall be banished from the kingdom along with his property and his belongings. (9.241)

"He did so unintentionally" will be stated in the following verse; that should be understood here as well. This being the case, for these very offenses, a Brāhmaṇa should be punished with the middle amercement, or at the king's pleasure, he may be banished from the kingdom. Thus, there shall be two options for his punishment, depending on his conduct and Vedic study. (9.241)
But others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the forfeiture of all their property; if, however, they did so intentionally, they deserve banishment. (9.242)

Kṣatriyas and others who have committed these very same mortal sins (mahāpātaka) unintentionally shall be fined the confiscation of all their property, or else be punished with the highest amercement as previously described. Likewise, for a Brāhmaṇa who does not perform penance, the punishment for doing so unintentionally is the middle amercement; for doing so intentionally, it is banishment. For a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, the punishment for doing so unintentionally is the highest amercement or the confiscation of all property; for doing so intentionally, it is death. But for a Śūdra, the punishment for doing so unintentionally is the confiscation of all property and branding; for doing so intentionally, however, it is death. (9.242)
A righteous king must not take the wealth of those guilty of mortal sins;
for by taking it out of greed, he is tormented by that very sin. (9.243)
Since this is so, therefore:
Having cast that staff into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa;
or he should present it to a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and good conduct. (9.244)
Regarding this injunction for practice, he states the reason:
"For Varuṇa is the lord of punishment; he is indeed the wielder of the rod among kings.
A Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world. (9.245)
Therefore, that property must not be seized by the king. Moreover: 9.245.
Wherever a king avoids acquiring wealth from evildoers, there men are born in due time with long lives. (9.246)
And the crops of the various classes of people ripen individually as described;
children do not die prematurely, and nothing deformed is born. (9.247)
Verses in praise of the application of punishment (daṇḍaviniyoga). 9.246–47.
But if one born of a lower caste oppresses a Brāhmaṇa out of desire, the king shall slay him with various means of execution that cause terror. (9.248)

In this case, for one who does not perform expiation, death itself by various means of execution is prescribed as a rule for his purification—such as beating, binding, and so forth, according to the offense, for a Śūdra; and some say it applies to the three [higher castes] as well, because of the following verse. 9.248.
As much demerit is seen for a king in killing one who should not be killed, so much is seen in releasing one who deserves to be killed; but merit accrues to him who restrains the wicked. 9.249.

Furthermore, for a king who is authorized to protect [his subjects], there is sin (*pratyavāya*) in releasing one who deserves execution. This is especially true for one who takes a sixth part as tax, since the removal of that fault must be accomplished through the very means prescribed in the scriptures, according to their literal injunctions—just like a penance (*prāyaścitta*). And thus it has been stated that the determination of what is *dharma* and *adharma* is based solely on the characteristics of the scriptures. Consequently, just as the authority of those [scriptures] lies in their origin, so too would their authority lie in the destruction of sin. This applies first to matters whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*). However, regarding matters with a visible purpose (*dṛṣṣṭārtha*), such as the instruction on the principles of statecraft (*rājyatantra*), the mention of execution—as in the statement, "And he should slay those who serve his enemies"—is not a mandatory execution, because the purpose of that instruction is a visible one. This being the case, there is no fault for one who restrains [the offender] by other means, such as imprisonment and the like. (9.249)
Thus has been set forth in detail the determination of legal procedure for two parties disputing with one another across the eighteen titles of law. 9.250
This verse summarizes all conventional discourse. 9.250.
Thus performing all his duties correctly, the lord of the earth should seek to acquire territories not yet won and protect those already acquired. (9.251)
The means by which the protection of subjects is achieved for a king is now being stated; in this way, the preceding summary should be understood. (9.251)

Having settled in a properly chosen location and having constructed fortifications according to the treatises, he should constantly exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns (the suppression of criminals). 9.252
This is a commendatory statement (arthavāda) in the form of an injunction regarding the fruit [of the practice]. 9.252.
By protecting those of noble conduct and by clearing away thorns, kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to the third heaven. 9.253.

It is fitting that kings who protect [their subjects] go to the third heaven, because they favor both [the living and the deceased]. Therefore, it is also appropriate that this [protection] extends even to those who do not take a side in the dharma that is to be protected. And thus, they must certainly be protected, both because their livelihood must be secured and because no such praise is found unless there is a connection to a fruit. Furthermore, since dharma and adharma are characterized by the scriptures, just as their origination is established, the commencement of their fruit must also be accepted on the basis of the fruit itself. Since this is so, therefore... (9.253)
But that king who collects taxes while failing to punish thieves, his kingdom becomes agitated and he is excluded from heaven. (9.254)
But that kingdom which is fearless and dependent upon the strength of its arms increases constantly, like a tree being watered. (9.255)
This is a praise of the unseen fruit by means of a connection with a visible object. (9.254–55)
The king, whose eyes are his spies, should recognize two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who are open and those who are secret. (9.256)

Theft should be understood as the misappropriation of another's property by kings who have spies for their eyes; this instruction is given at the outset for the sake of emphasis, so that it may be recognized as such from the very beginning. (9.256)
Those who live by various wares are open deceivers;
those such as thieves and forest-dwellers are concealed deceivers. (9.257)

In that regard, those who deceive by means of specific weights, measures, and scales in buying and selling—failing to consider the source and destination of goods—are open swindlers. Those who are concealed, however, are "night-sacrificers," which means thieves. And it is not only for this reason; rather, these and others whom we shall describe hereafter [are also such]. (9.257)

Bribe-takers, those who act by means of fraud, deceivers, gamblers, those who live by prescribing auspicious rites, fortune-tellers, and those who subsist on omens—these, along with the diagnosticians, [should be avoided]. (9.258)
High officials who act improperly, physicians, those skilled in the practice of crafts, and clever courtesans— (9.259)
One should recognize such people as manifest thorns to the world, as well as others who move in secret—ignoble men wearing the outward marks of the noble. (9.260)

Having identified them through secret agents who have conducted themselves well and performed their duties, and by means of spies in various disguises, he should encourage them and bring them under his control. (9.261)

Having publicly proclaimed their faults according to the truth of each respective deed, the king should duly administer punishment in accordance with the gravity of the offense and the essential nature of the crime. (9.262)

For what reason, then, is the application of punishment prescribed for the king in that regard? Because, indeed, without punishment it is not possible to effect the restraint of evildoers—those thieves of sinful intent who move about secretly upon the earth. (9.263)

This definition has been stated for the purpose of suppressing those who are thorns to the realm; this term "thorn" should be understood as being used by way of comparison to them. Now, the means for their apprehension is being explained. (9.263)
Assembly halls, water-stations, groves, taverns, shops for selling liquor and food, crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and places of execution. (9.264)
Dilapidated gardens, forests, and the workshops of artisans; empty houses, as well as groves and pleasure parks. (9.265)
The king should cause such regions to be patrolled by both stationary and mobile military outposts, as well as by spies, for the purpose of suppressing thieves. (9.266)
He should recognize and encourage them through clever former thieves who follow as companions and are skilled in discerning various types of work. (9.267)
And by means of the pretext of various foods to be chewed and eaten,
through sacrifices to Caṇḍikā and other deities for all occasions, and by the sight of Brāhmaṇas;

To those who possess the knowledge of the yoga of coming and going through spells, by whose power theft becomes easy and yields great fruit according to their desire, he should arrange a meeting under the pretext of deeds of valor. (9.268)
This applies to those of such character who engage in acts of excessive force. And this being so:
"The king shall forcibly slay those who do not submit there, as well as those instigated from the root, together with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives. (9.269)

Those thieves who do not come forward when summoned by the king's command, and those thieves who have been secretly instigated and do not appear at the sacrifices to Caṇḍikā and other such rites—having traced them back to their very source, he should have them executed. Thus should he proceed in the suppression of thieves. (9.269)
A righteous king shall not execute a thief without the stolen goods; however, he may execute one caught with the goods along with the implements [of theft] without hesitation. 9.270.

He would be seized together with that stolen property, and not otherwise. If, upon investigation through examination, the stolen property is proven pure according to the evidence, then the same should be understood regarding the implements used for breaking into holes and so forth. (9.270)
Moreover, whoever in the villages provide food to thieves or give them space for their goods—all of those as well he shall cause to be executed. (9.271)
Having investigated by means of the valid cognitions of direct perception, scripture, and inference, [one realizes] that even from the non-cognition of this, all of this comes to be. (9.271)
He should swiftly punish those appointed to protect the realms and the vassal kings who have been incited, if they remain neutral during attacks, just as one punishes thieves. 9.272.

In cases of emergency, one should not strike these [pupils] with a rod; however, through a conversation regarding thieves, or out of negligence, one might treat them like thieves. Furthermore, a difference in instruction should be understood to arise from a difference in the underlying signs (nimitta). || 9.272 ||
And even one who lives by the Dharma, if he has fallen away from the covenant of the Dharma,
he should indeed burn him with punishment, for he has strayed from his own duty.

A Brahmin lives by his dharma; for he indeed lives without performing services for others. Therefore, even for him, punishment proportionate to the offense must be administered for the sake of establishing him in his own duty. (9.273)

When a village is plundered, when a highway is obstructed, or when robbers and the like are seen on the road, those who are capable but do not come to the rescue shall be banished along with their belongings. (9.274)

Those who do not run [to help] due to laziness shall be banished; however, those who do not pursue [the thieves] because they are occupied with their own work shall be put to death like thieves. 9.274.
Those who steal from the royal treasury, those who stand in opposition,
and those who instigate enemies should be executed by various means of capital punishment.
Their punishment shall be in accordance with the offense, taking into account the independent suffering [inflicted]. || 9.275 ||
But those thieves who, having broken into a breach, commit their deeds at night—
the king, having cut off their hands, shall impale them upon a sharp stake.

And the mention of "breaking into a wall" (*saṃdhi*) is for the purpose of characterizing theft; thus, this same punishment would apply even to one who commits theft by entering right into the royal camp (*skandhāvāra*). "The cutting off of both hands, or impalement on a stake"—others say this refers to a single offense. However, both [options] are to be determined here with respect to the specific caste (*varṇa*) and the connection to the motive (*prayojanānubandha*), and not according to the literal text alone. And so he shows: 9.276.
In the first apprehension of a housebreaker, one should have his fingers amputated;
in the second, his hands and feet; in the third, he deserves the death penalty.

Even for one who has already been punished, there is the instruction for further punishment, as when someone whose hands and feet have been severed continues to practice theft by some other means. (9.277)
The Lord punished those who set fires, those who provided food, as well as those who gave weapons and shelter, and those who consigned stolen goods to them, just as one would punish thieves. 9.278.

Having identified them as thieves, those who assist them and act like thieves shall receive punishment (*śiṣṭi*) consisting of beating, imprisonment, verbal censure, and so forth; however, "punishment" does not mean the amputation of a limb or the confiscation of property. Furthermore, even if not explicitly stated, for the castes, the punishment for theft shall be the same as that for a thief, provided the offense is minor; this applies to a thief as well. (9.278)
One who destroys a water tank should be killed by drowning in water or by some other form of pure execution; or else, he should repair it and pay the highest fine.

For one who diverts the water by breaking the embankment of a tank, the punishment is death, whether the act occurs in the water or on dry land, provided he is incapable of repairing it; even for one capable of repair, there shall be corporal punishment. For in both cases—the owner of the tank and the breaker of the tank—merit alone is intended as the favor bestowed upon them. In the case where repair is undertaken, the highest amercement (uttama-sāhasa), which is ten thousand paṇas, shall be imposed. (9.279)
Those who break into storehouses, armories, or temples, as well as those who seize elephants, horses, or chariots, he should indeed put to death without hesitation. (9.280)

Except for the destroyer of a temple of the gods, for others, because the purpose of the instruction regarding execution is solely for the sake of independent protection, execution is not carried out as a mandatory rule. Furthermore, because there is the possibility of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), even when [the offense] ceases, there is no [automatic] prosperity [of the king]. For even the destroyer of a temple of the gods, if he is unable to repair it or pay the fine, execution would be the penalty. Thus it was stated in the preceding verse. And in this way, by virtue of the context, the punishment is the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*). In the verse to be cited later, "Of bridges, flagstaffs," etc., he will state a punishment for the destroyer of a divine image that is devoid of execution. This being the case, if execution were declared as a mandatory rule for the destroyer of a temple of the gods, then such an instruction would be contrary to logic and improper in form. Therefore, execution should be understood as being optional (*pākṣika*). 9.280.
But he who diverts the water of a tank already established, or cuts off the inflow of waters, shall be made to pay the first amercement. (9.281)

It is called the "first fine" because it destroys the deity [of the field], or else for another reason. In this regard, it has been stated: "He who steals standing grain, or who, while the water has not yet arrived, should break its embankment or the like, shall be fined the first amercement. This being so, that which was stated—that Kṣatriyas and others who are unable to pay a fine should attain freedom from debt through labor—that should be understood to apply here in all such cases due to the similarity of the underlying matter. (9.281)
He who, except in an emergency, should void excrement on the royal highway, shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately clean away that excrement. (9.282)
The measure of the kārṣāpaṇa has been explained. 9.282.
One who has fallen into misfortune, or an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child, deserve only a verbal reprimand; and that [offense] must be purified—such is the established rule. (9.283)
By the instruction "one who has fallen into calamity," it should be understood that this refers to one who is extremely aged, a pregnant woman, or a child. || 9.283 ||
For all physicians who practice deceitfully, there shall be punishment:
