the first amercement for offenses against non-humans, but the middle amercement for those against humans. (9.284)

These two should be understood as referring to the first and middle degrees of the *sāhasa* (violent crimes), respectively, even in the absence of a formal legal treatise (*śāstra*). Alternatively, this punishment applies to those who, despite having studied the *śāstra*, practice medicine falsely toward humans and non-humans. (9.284)
One who breaks the crossing-bridges, flagstaffs, or images shall repair all of that and pay five hundred [paṇas]. || 9.285 ||

Those by which people cross rivers, ravines, and so forth, are called "crossings" (*saṃkrama*). A "flagstaff" (*dhvaja*) refers to one at the palaces of kings or in temples of the gods; a "pole" (*yaṣṭi*) refers to one in a temple of the *nāgas*, or a sacrificial pole (*baliyaṣṭi*) in villages. This matter has already been considered. In the preceding verse, for the sake of providing an alternative, the punishment of death was prescribed here for the destroyer of an image due to certain reasons such as the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*). (9.285)
For the adulteration of unadulterated goods, as well as for the breaking [of vessels] and the boring of gems, the punishment is the first amercement. (9.286)

The defiling of substances such as saffron with something similar to them, such as artificial safflower (*māyākusumbha*), is what is intended; whereas piercing refers specifically to gems. In the case of piercing, destroying, boring through, or boring gems in the wrong place, the punishment for the gems themselves shall correspond to their value. This being the case, the mention of the "first amercement" should be understood as illustrative. For there are gems whose value is merely a *kākaṇika*, while others are worth many thousands. Therefore, a uniform punishment here would not be appropriate. For this reason, it is inferred that the mention of the first amercement is intended to be illustrative. (9.286)
He who exchanges equal goods for unequal ones, or does so even by way of price, shall incur the first or indeed the middle amercement. (9.287)

If a seller sells otherwise than it truly is—due to a defect in the substance—by concealing that the items are of unknown value or by failing to inform the buyer that they have specific uses, then for that seller, the first and middle fines shall be determined in proportion to the value of the goods. Alternatively, the first fine shall be imposed on the buyer and the middle fine on the seller. (9.287)
And he should place all the prisoners along the royal highway,
so that those who have committed evil deeds may be seen there in their suffering.
The instruction on the means for ordinary persons to turn away from evil. || 9.288 ||
One should swiftly banish anyone who breaks down a wall, fills up a moat, or destroys a gate. (9.289)

Regarding the city, the royal palace, or the fortress: in this context, exile is to be understood as being of two kinds, depending on whether it conflicts with the king's affairs or not. This being the case, since the king’s own protection is independent here, the instruction does not mandate the execution of those who commit transgressions. (9.289)
In all cases of malevolent sorcery, a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed; likewise for root-charms performed by those who are untrustworthy, and for various kinds of magical rites. (9.290)

This is stated regarding malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) that fall outside the scope of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, such as the burying of a needle made of *khadira* wood, the seizing of dust from the feet, and so forth. In these cases, no punishment exists for one who is subject to such malevolent rites. Likewise, he will later prescribe an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for performing malevolent rites against one who should not be subjected to them, stating: "One removes the sin of malevolent rites and the *ahīna* sacrifice by three *kṛcchra* penances. And [this applies] when a root-rite (*mūlakarman*) is performed by untrustworthy persons—not by mothers, sisters, and the like, because they lack the authority [to do so]. And regarding magical spells (*kṛtyā*), such as those involving *vaitāla* demons and others prescribed in the *bhūtatantra*, this applies only when they are performed by unrelated parties. Others, however, on the strength of the inclusion of the word "all," maintain that this punishment applies to all malevolent rites whatsoever. (9.290)
One who sells seedless grain, as well as one who extracts the best portion of the seed, and one who violates established boundaries, shall suffer the punishment of mutilation or death. (9.291)

He who sells what is seedless under the pretext that it is seed, or who, seeing prospective buyers, raises the price beyond the value of the seed; and he who breaks the boundaries pertaining to fields and plots—but not the boundaries of villages, districts, or assemblies, because of the association with seeds, buying, selling, and so forth—he deserves the mutilation known as the cutting off of the ears and nose. Because of the accumulation of offenses and their persistence, there may even be execution, since this punishment is appropriate for one who acts without any visible purpose. Furthermore, this penalty need not necessarily apply only to these specific offenses, because this instruction regarding punishment is intended for a visible purpose. (9.291)
The king, however, shall cut a goldsmith who is the most wicked of all thorns and who practices injustice, piece by piece with razors.

This is stated regarding one who is habitually addicted to the theft of gold from all castes, or specifically to the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, and who is engaged in fraudulent practices such as rubbing [the gold] on a touchstone, changing its weight, or manipulating the scales. According to the rule "by whichever limb and in whatever manner," he should be put to death limb by limb—such as the tongue, hands, feet, head, eyes, and so forth—for protecting the gold, depending on the repetition and persistence of the offense. Others, however, say that this refers to the theft of gold from all castes; and because the quantity of gold made by the artisan may be large or small, this instruction for cutting off limbs is intended merely as an illustration. Still others teach that even for a goldsmith, this is not a means of purification, just as in the case of the penance for drinking *surā* even when stealing what has been protected. (9.292)
In cases of the theft of Sītā-grain, weapons, or medicine, the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the specific circumstances of the act. (9.293)

"Sīta-dravyas" refers to the plough and other such implements; "weapons" refers to the sickle and so forth by association with them; "medicine" refers to garlic and the like contained therein. Alternatively, it is appropriate to take "medicines" in a general sense, since the offense is equal. Having considered the time and the purpose, the king may impose upon them whatever punishment he deems fit, as a means to prevent further offenses on the part of others as well. (9.293)
The sovereign, the minister, the capital, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these seven constituent elements (prakṛtis) together are called the kingdom. 9.294.
A king should understand that among these seven constituents of sovereignty, each preceding one is more important than the next in the event of a national calamity. (9.295)

The purpose of this instruction is that a king, having recognized that among the [seven constituents] beginning with the sovereign, each preceding one is more grievous in its calamity and more destructive to the administration of the kingdom, should avoid such calamities. 9.294–95.
Of this seven-limbed kingdom, which is supported like a triple staff, nothing excels another because of the specific excellence of their mutual qualities. (9.296)
For,
in each respective task, that particular factor is distinguished [as predominant],
just like a sense organ due to its restriction to its own specific object. This being so,
Whatever means by which a task is accomplished is said to be the most excellent for that purpose. || 9.297 ||

For there is indeed such a task for a king wherein even a minor constituent element (*prakṛti*) becomes more significant. Therefore, all of these, as well as their subordinates (*tatpuruṣa*), must always be scrutinized. This instruction regarding the king's constituents is given here again for this purpose: because, for the most part, the thorns of the kingdom are those who rely precisely upon the ministers and other constituents. For they, having taken refuge with the king’s favorites, ministers, queens, princes, and so forth, become entirely fearless through the king’s influence and plunder the countryside all the more effectively. (9.297)
"By means of his movements, his application of energy, and the very execution of his deeds, the lord of the earth should constantly ascertain his own strength and the strength of others. (9.298)

Therefore, these are taught again here in the section on the removal of thorns (*kaṇṭakoddharaṇa*). Just as this [instruction] is taught by relying upon that, so too is the mention of "permanence" [included]. And thus, like the protection against a foreign army, the countryside must also be protected from oppression by one's own forces. This repeated statement of the king’s duty (*rājadharma*) here should be understood as being for the sake of showing respect for the removal of thorns. (9.298)
Having understood all forms of oppression as well as calamities according to their relative gravity, one should then carry out one's duty.

Having understood the afflictions of the worlds—such as lightning strikes, famine, and the like—as well as the three types of calamities caused by one's own actions, which lead to the destruction of the body, fate, and the self, according to their relative gravity for the world, the king should then administer punishment with corresponding severity or leniency, and not without distinction. And thus abiding in the duties of a king for as long as he lives... (9.299)
One should indeed undertake actions again and again, even when exhausted; for prosperity attends the man who perseveres in his undertakings. 9.300

And thus, one should not desist from undertaking actions due to fatigue or laziness. One should not think, "I must act in accordance with the age," because: "The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages—all these are the modes of conduct of the king; for the king is said to be the age. (9.301)

And thus, considering it to be the Kali age, he should not remain indifferent. He now demonstrates that royal conduct by which a king is designated as belonging to the Kali age and so forth: || 9.301 ||
When asleep, he is the Kali age; when waking, he is the Dvāpara age;
when risen for action, he is the Tretā; but when moving about, he is the Kṛta age. (9.302)

One who lacks the habit of exertion is as if asleep; he who, knowing the means for advancement, applies himself to it, is awake. The application of determined action constitutes the Tretā Yuga. And by performing all actions according to the scriptures, through the excellence of the fruits of one's deeds, the Kṛta Yuga is realized. Thus, since all undertakings have the king as their cause, praise of his conduct is appropriate. (9.302)
A king should practice the conduct of splendor belonging to Indra, Arka, Vāta, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, and the Earth. (9.303)

For a king who conducts himself in this manner, by removing the thorns [of his realm], generates both majesty and affection within himself and is endowed with the sovereignty over the entire circle of the earth as his final goal. The conduct of the king is shown to share some commonality with that of Indra and the other world-protectors. (9.303)
Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season, so should one practicing the vow of Indra shower his own kingdom with the fulfillment of desires. 9.304
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays for eight months, so should the king draw taxes from his realm; that is the eternal solar vow. 9.305.
Just as the wind enters all beings and moves through them, so too should one enter by means of spies; for this indeed is the "wind-like" vow.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come, so must subjects be restrained by the king; for that is the vow of Yama. (9.307)
Just as one is seen bound by Varuṇa with his nooses, so too should he bind himself for sins; for this is the Vāruṇa vow.
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do the subjects rejoice in that king who observes the lunar vow. 9.309
One who is endowed with majesty, radiant, always intent upon evil deeds,
and a slayer of wicked vassals— that is remembered as the Agneya vow.
Just as the earth supports all beings equally, so too is the vow of a king who sustains all beings. 9.311
Employing these and other means, the king, ever vigilant, should suppress thieves both within his own kingdom and in those of others. (9.312)

Although the conduct of kings has already been stated in eight verses, it is repeated here for the sake of clarifying the meaning. It is stated again in this section on punishment (*daṇḍaprakaraṇa*) out of respect, so that by inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it according to their offense, he may be equal toward his subjects like a guardian of the world (*lokapāla*). (9.304–12)
Even when fallen into the greatest calamity, one should not provoke the Brahmins;
for if they are angered, they can instantly destroy him along with his army and his mounts. (9.313)
[He is protected] from malevolent magic and curses; and thus he demonstrates his majesty. 9.313.
By whom was fire made to consume all things and the great ocean rendered undrinkable? By whom was the waning moon made to wax full? Who would not perish by provoking them? (9.314)
Moreover,
who could prosper while harming those who, when provoked, might create other worlds and world-protectors, or turn gods into non-gods? (9.315)
Those upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend, and for whom Brahman is their sole wealth—who, desiring to live, would harm them? (9.316)
Nor is he to be despised as being ignorant, because:
"Whether ignorant or learned, a Brahmin is a great deity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, just as fire is a great deity. (9.317)
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled;
when oblations are offered to it in sacrifices, it increases all the more. 9.318
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of unworthy actions,
Brahmins are to be honored in every way, for they are the supreme deity.
When the Kṣatriya power becomes excessively overbearing in every respect toward the Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇical power alone must be its restrainer; for the Kṣatriya was born from the Brāhmaṇa. (9.320)
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
the all-pervading heat of these is extinguished within their own sources. (9.321)
The Kṣatriya power does not prosper without the Brāhmaṇa power, nor does the Brāhmaṇa power flourish without the Kṣatriya power;
when the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya powers are joined together, they both prosper in this world and the next. (9.322)

In ten verses within the section on the restraint of those deserving punishment, Brahmins are praised. Even though there exists a legal treatise [prescribing their punishment], this [passage] is for the purpose that, out of consideration for them, their restraint should be mild and undertaken with patience, so as to establish them in their own proper conduct. (9.313–22)
Having given all the wealth arising from fines to the Brahmins,
and having entrusted everything to his son, he should seek his end in battle.

And the departure of the king according to the first rule is the primary option; therefore, in its absence, other options may apply so that there is no contradiction with his own desire for departure, as has been explained. (9.323)
Acting thus and always disciplined in the duties of kingship, the monarch should employ all his servants in what is beneficial for the world. 9.324
This eternal rule of action for the king has been declared in its entirety;
one should likewise know this rule of action for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra in due order. (9.325)

The conclusion of the duties of kings with these two verses should be understood as having the specific purpose of introducing the duties and conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras; and thus he demonstrates that distinction: "That for which this [section] is commenced again" (9.324–25).
But a Vaiśya, having undergone the sacraments and taken a wife, should be constantly engaged in agriculture and commerce, as well as in the protection of cattle. (9.326)
This teaching has the sense of immediacy and the sense of distinction; this is its explanatory praise (arthavāda). 9.326
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya; and he entrusted all creatures to the Brāhmaṇa and the King. (9.327)
A Vaiśya should not have the desire, "I will not tend cattle";
if the Vaiśya so desires, they must by no means be tended by anyone else. (9.328)
This is the instruction for the king, as well as for other non-royal men such as Brahmins; and this is another specific [duty] for the Vaiśya, consisting of his professional occupation. (9.327–28)
One should know the relative value and worth of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven textiles, perfumes, and liquids. (9.329)

One should know the method of sowing seeds, as well as the qualities of the field and the seed; one should also understand the application of measurement and all the applications of the balance. (9.330)
He [should know] the worth and worthlessness of goods, the merits and defects of regions, the profit and loss of merchandise, and the increase of livestock. (9.331)
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the methods of storing goods, as well as their purchase and sale. (9.332)
One should exert the highest effort to increase one's wealth through righteous means, and one should diligently provide food for all living beings. (9.333)

Although the occupation of a Vaiśya has already been stated in eight verses, it is mentioned again for the sake of specific detail. And this is the specific detail: "A Vaiśya should not have the thought, 'I will not tend cattle. This being so, it is understood that among his other occupations, the occupation of tending cattle is his specifically *dharmya* (righteous) duty. Furthermore, the mention of gems, pearls, and so forth is intended to represent all types of goods; thus, it is understood that there is nothing whatsoever that he may not sell. Moreover, setting aside the gift of gold and such, one should especially give food, because of the statement, "to all beings. It is not only for virtuous Brāhmaṇas [that this applies]. Now, the righteous occupation of the Śūdra is also being stated. (9.329–33)
For a Śūdra, however, the service of Brahmins—those who are learned in the Vedas, householders, and illustrious—is indeed the highest dharma leading to supreme beatitude. (9.334)
A Śūdra, especially through service to Brāhmaṇas who possess such qualities as these, attains the highest good. || 9.334 ||
Pure, devoted to excellent service, gentle in speech, and free from egoism—
one who conducts himself thus and always takes refuge in Brahmins attains the state of one whose birth is transcended. (9.335)

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the fruit of relying on that [Brahmin] for a Śūdra who has taken refuge with a Brahmin; or rather, this is a rule concerning the fruit (*phalavidhi*), which is appropriate as it does not contradict the principles of the science of logic (*nyāyaśāstra*). (9.335)
This auspicious rule for the righteous livelihood of the social classes in times of non-distress has been declared;
now learn that which pertains to them in times of distress, respectively. (9.336)
The twofold nature [of the self] is for the sake of establishing both its function and its dharma. 9.336.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Commentary on the Code of Manu composed by Bhāruci.

The Tenth Chapter: "The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study; but among them, it is the settled rule that only the Brāhmaṇa may expound this, not the other two. (10.1)

Following the treatment of the Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the possibility of the mixed castes (*saṃkīrṇa*) must now be discussed in accordance with the sequence of the treatise. For this purpose—as an introduction to that subject—it is stated here, "they should study," with reference to the study prescribed in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*). Thus, in this context, the verb *iṅ* preceded by the prefix *adhi* is understood to have the Veda as its object, since it is a verbal action involving the word "Veda"; the meaning is that they should study, i.e., recite the Veda. Although such an injunctive statement was not explicitly heard there, it is to be inferred from the force of the restatement (*anuvāda*). Furthermore, in the very section on the religious student, this was stated for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), such as: "The entire Veda is to be mastered. And by the force of the phrase "established in their own duties," one understands that these refer to the duties regarding the vow of study, such as approaching the teacher and saluting him, which were already mentioned in the section on the religious student. Since teaching would naturally accrue to all three [castes], this is stated as a restriction: "But a Brāhmaṇa should teach them. Thus, because the meaning "not the other two" is already established, this statement—which was not previously commenced—is made for the sake of a specific qualification. We interpret "not the other two" as a prohibition concerning times when there is no distress. This is what is being said: in times of distress, however, even the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya may teach. By doing so, that which was stated—that the study of the Veda is enjoined for a Brāhmaṇa in times of non-distress—becomes consistent. Alternatively, it is for the purpose of prohibiting the study of the Veda by a Śūdra in times of distress; "not the other two" refers to those other than the Śūdra. Thus, in times of distress, only the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya may teach, but not the Śūdra. Even though this statement is general, it is made after considering that the Śūdra’s acquisition of study comes from a non-Brāhmaṇa, and not from the scripture itself. And thus it becomes appropriate, as stated in the section on those excluded from the *pañcayajña* feast: "The Śūdra disciple and the [Śūdra] teacher... Alternatively, "not the other two" means they should not teach the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*); however, teaching other subjects such as political science (*rājaśāstra*), Dharmaśāstra, the Atharvaveda, elephant-training, and Āyurveda is not forbidden for them. That is incorrect, because in the restatement of study, it is for the purpose of connecting it with the section to be explained hereafter. Or rather, the meaning should be understood as: "A Brāhmaṇa should teach them, but not the other two. And thus it has been explained. Others, however, say: this very injunction for Vedic study applies to all three castes. That, moreover, should be examined as to whether it is logical or not, and it has already been stated. Since this is the case, therefore... [10.1]
A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all [classes] according to the rule;
he should declare them to the others and should himself likewise abide by them. (10.2)

One should know the means for subsistence; or rather, one should know both the mode of subsistence and the means for attaining dharma. And the inclusion of the word "all" refers specifically to the two castes, by virtue of the context. Or else, this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of both these points. 10.2.
Due to his distinction, the excellence of his origin, his observance of the rules, and the particularity of his refinement, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes. (10.3)

Because of his distinction, he is superior to others by virtue of his knowledge. Or rather, this is a formal proposition (*pratijñā*). He then states the reason for this: "The excellence of his origin" refers to his birth from the mouth, as stated in the first chapter during the praise of the Brāhmaṇa in the phrase "because of his birth from the highest limb. Furthermore, "because of his adherence to the rule" means that the instruction regarding the entire study of the Veda—characterized by the practice of memorization—is taught as being performed exclusively by the Brāhmaṇa. Thus, this [superiority] is to be understood as distinct from the others due to these specific excellences. Moreover, "because of his [exclusive] cause for refinement"—that is, because the sacraments (*saṃskāra*), such as the initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth, ending with the funeral rites (*śmaśāna-karaṇa*), which pertain to the twice-born, have the Brāhmaṇa as their primary cause, his distinction is established. Alternatively, this is said in view of the performance of even minor rites, such as the accomplishment of the hundred-and-one-fold fires of the *agnihotra* and so forth, or the performance of the rites of other castes, such as the *aśvamedha*. Such a distinction of refinement belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone. By the word "and" (*ca*), the "eldest status" (*jyeṣṭhatva*) taught in the first chapter within the context of the praise of the Brāhmaṇa is included in this conjunction. And since the Brāhmaṇa, characterized in this way, possesses sovereignty over all castes, he is entitled to duties such as teaching; this is the meaning of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). 10.3.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are the twice-born;
the fourth is the once-born Śūdra, and there is no fifth. (10.4)

In the passage, “the three castes (*varṇa*) should study,” the word *varṇa* is used specifically because, apart from those [three], the Śūdra is not included therein, yet it is desired that he [be included]. Therefore, this verse is commenced for his sake, so that it may apply to him as well. Alternatively, this instruction in the treatise regarding the designation of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of technical usage (*vyavahāra*). And thus, their usage by means of these [names] is seen everywhere in the treatise. Or rather, he first shows this [usage] in order to indicate the absence of that [designation] among the mixed castes (*varṇāpaśada*) which will be mentioned later, stating: “but there is no fifth. This being the case, these same four castes are established by themselves. How? Like tastes (*rasa*). Just as the six kinds of tastes are established by themselves, and whatever specific taste is perceived through their mutual contact does not constitute a different genus (*jāti*) from them, even so, although a Caṇḍāla or others are perceived through the mutual contact of the castes, he cannot, according to the treatise, be a different genus from them. A Caṇḍāla receives that name when a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra, being joined in reverse order (*pratiloma*), produce offspring. Even for those who hold the view that a different genus arises from the contact of two castes, since that [genus] does not exist inherently, the prohibition of the designation “caste” for the mixed castes is logical. However, there is this much distinction: because their relative superiority and inferiority, as well as their connection to ritual duties, are based on Smṛti, these two are understood according to the scriptures. Now, one might object: “Is it not already established that the Śūdra has only one caste simply because no purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are prescribed for him? If that is so, then this mention of “one caste” for the Śūdra is for the purpose of prohibiting the purificatory rite of initiation (*upanayana*) even without mantras. Thus it has been said: “Excluding mantras, they do not incur fault and they obtain praise. That being the case, this mention of the Śūdra’s single caste is appropriate for the purpose of prohibiting the purificatory rite of initiation whose means—such as time and so forth—are unrestricted, lest there be the possibility of its application to him without mantras, as occurs in the case of the *pākayajña* sacrifices. This is a restatement of what has already been said for the purpose of completing the meter. Thus, since this reference to “one caste” is intended for another purpose, there is no room for objection. Alternatively, it is for the sake of what follows. And so he demonstrates this: || 10.4 ||
Among wives of equal caste who have not lost their virginity, those born in the direct order [of castes] are to be known as belonging to that same caste. (10.5)

"In all castes" (*sarvavarṇeṣu*) means not only among those [castes] authorized [for Vedic rites], such as the twice-born (*dvijāti*). "Among equal women" (*tulyāsu nārīṣu*): by whom? By husbands. How? Among women who are equal in terms of caste (*jāti*), meaning they have been married according to the scriptures as "virgins" (*akṣatayoni*). But is it not already established that they are virgins simply by the use of the term *patnī* (wife)? For only those who are fit for sacrifice are *patnyaḥ*, and they alone are virgins, not others. This objection does not apply when the word *nārī* is used; however, even when *patnī* is used, this mention of "virginity" serves as a reason: why is she a *patnī*? Because of her virginity. Furthermore, the word *patnī* is seen to be used based on qualities (*guṇataḥ*); therefore, the expression "virginity" should be understood as its primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*). By the phrase "among all castes, among equal women," the inclusion of the *anuloma* (natural order) marriages here is rendered redundant; thus, it should be understood as serving the purpose of the subsequent verse. Therefore, those castes produced by these two [parents] are to be known as being of that very caste (*jāti*). By the words "those very [castes]," the inclusion of the father's caste is stated: just as a caste produced by parents belonging to the Brāhmaṇa caste becomes that caste, so too those produced from Kṣatriyas and others are to be known as belonging to those respective castes, like cows and other animals. But if this is so, this definition of caste (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) would be unnecessary to state. It must indeed be stated in order to exclude other causes for Brāhmaṇahood. Likewise, explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) serve as grounds for confirming the vision of reality, such as: "The gods know even a Caṇḍāla who stands firm in his conduct to be a Brāhmaṇa. Since one is not a Brāhmaṇa by virtue of sacraments (*saṃskāra*), study, or conduct, but rather by both lineages (*abhijana*), as we have said, caste should be understood as the foundational cause (*adhikaraṇa-kāraṇa*) of the sacraments and so forth. Nor is conduct alone the cause of excellence. And since no difference in caste among Brāhmaṇas and others is perceptible or inferable—given their lack of distinction as human beings and the non-perception of any specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*) distinct from that—just as in the case of cows, buffaloes, horses, and donkeys. This being so, this scripture (*śāstra*) should be understood as meaningful because it provides knowledge regarding what cannot be obtained through perception or inference, just as there is a connection between wholesome and unwholesome actions and human activity. Thus, examples such as cows should be understood merely as illustrating the nature of producing offspring of a similar kind. And in this way, it is accepted that this connection with the caste of Brāhmaṇahood and so forth occurs in conjunction with the production from a single caste. If you think that offspring is similar to the caste of the progenitor, then this is precisely the definition of caste for the progenitor, because that definition is common [to both]. But if this is so, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Let it be so. What is the fault? This definition is effective only in an infinite regress, not otherwise, as in the case of cows and the like. And this being so, there is no contradiction with observation (*dṛṣṭa*) or with scripture (*śāstra*), because this is nothing at all [new]. (10.5)
Sons begotten by twice-born men upon women born in the next lower caste are said to be similar [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers. (10.6)

For what purpose is this? It is for the sake of praising those born in the natural order (*anuloma*), by virtue of the context. For the twice-born—namely the Brāhmaṇas and others—have declared that the sons begotten upon women of the next lower caste, such as Kṣatriya women and so forth, are indeed "similar" (*sadṛśa*) to them. By whom? By the father. However, this does not mean they are of the same *jāti* (caste), because the word "similar" is used; just as one says, "the *gavaya* is similar to a cow. Here he states the reason: because they are censured due to the defect of their mother. And we have already stated the definition of *jāti*: "among all castes, when [the parents] are equal," and so forth. This contradicts those who claim they are similar to the mother: for it would follow that they are "censured due to the defect of their mother," whereas in the case of those born in the reverse order (*pratiloma*), they are censured due to the defect of the father. Since this [definition] applies only to those born in the natural order, it is understood that they are slightly inferior to their fathers and superior to their mothers. Thus, the statement regarding the natural order mentioned in the preceding verse should be understood as being for the sake of the present context (*adhikāra*), and not for the sake of the meaning of that specific verse itself, due to the force of the immediate sequence and the use of the plural "by the twice-born. (10.6)
This is the eternal rule for those born of women one degree lower;
one should know this righteous rule to apply to those born of women two or three degrees lower. (10.7)

Because this section concerns the *anuloma* [order], this righteous rule (*dharmya vidhi*) regarding women separated by one or two intervening generations should also be understood as being as before, by the force of the statement itself. This very rule is now set forth for those separated by one generation. (10.7)
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of a Vaiśya is born one named Ambaṣṭha; from a Śūdra woman, he who is called a Pāraśava is born as a Niṣāda. (10.8)

Not by name, but by caste; he who is named Bhṛjyakaṇṭha in another Smṛti. But in the case of a woman of two intermediate castes, from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother, [the son] is a Niṣāda. (10.8)

From a Kṣatriya and the daughter of a Śūdra is born a creature named Ugra, whose body partakes of both Kṣatriya and Śūdra characteristics and who is characterized by cruel conduct and pastimes. (10.9)

The practice of cruelty is prescribed for one whose nature is that of a Kṣatriya. This being the case, because of the force of the single governing authority stating that they are "born in the direct order" (*anuloma*), it is not only those born from an immediate caste difference who are *anuloma* and superior; rather, by such statements as "in women born from an immediate caste," it should be understood that those separated by one or two intervening castes are also similar to the father, since the defects of the mother are censured. Thus he shows: "In three castes for a Brāhmaṇa, and in two castes for a King (Kṣatriya). (10.9)
Within the single caste of the Vaiśya, these six are recorded as base-born (apasada).

Those who are censured due to defects in their mothers are called *apaśada*s. They are degraded compared to other human beings belonging to the mother’s caste. This being the case, this term *apaśada* is to be understood as relative among them; however, they are *apaśada*s specifically because of the inferiority resulting from the three types of inverse (*pratiloma*) unions. The word *apaśada* means "fallen away" (*apaśīrṇa*), for the root *śad* signifies falling. The meaning is that they are deficient in the duties of a son. They are spoken of in comparison with the sons of women of the same caste (*savarṇā*). Thus, immediately after the *anuloma* [sons], he now speaks of the *pratiloma* [sons]. (10.10)
From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa maiden is born a Sūta by birth;
from a Vaiśya father, the sons of a Kṣatriya’s wife are the Māgadha and the Vaideha. (10.11)

In the inverse order, according to the sequence: from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, a Sūta is born; from a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriyā mother, a Māgadha; and from a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, a Vaidehaka. 10.11.
From a Śūdra [beget on women of the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa castes] are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men; thus arise those of mixed caste (varṇasaṃkara). 10.12.

Thus, in the inverse order (*prātilomya*), from a Śūdra with a Vaiśya woman an Āyogava is born; with a Kṣatriya woman, a Kṣattṛ; and with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Caṇḍāla. In this verse, however, because the Vaiśya and Rājanya are mentioned by their generic class names (*varṇa*), the feminine gender is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). This lack of significance is due to the requirements of the metrical composition; otherwise, had the feminine gender not been used, there would have been a break in the meter (*ślokabhaṅga*). Having thus described these inverse castes, this is now stated for the purpose of specifying their particular distinctions. (10.12)
But when there is an interval of one caste [between the parents], they are known as Ambaṣṭha and Ugra through natural order;
likewise, Kṣattṛ and Vaidehaka arise in birth through the reverse order.

Just as the Ambaṣṭha and Ugra, born from the inverse order (*pratiloma*), are to be avoided in social dealings such as physical contact because they are separated by one intervening caste (*ekāntara*), so too should the Kṣattṛ and Vaidehaka, born from the inverse order, be understood in the same way. As for the Sūta, Māgadha, and Āyogava, since they are born from the immediate inverse order (*anantara*), their superiority over the Kṣattṛ and Vaidehaka is established by the maxim of the "stick and the rice-grains" (*daṇḍāpūpika*). Thus, it is the Caṇḍāla who is intended here as the exception; as it has been stated: "The Divākīrti and the Udakyā," and so forth. (10.13)
Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women of successive castes have been described in order; indeed, they are called "intermediate" because of the defect of their mothers' status. (10.14)

The Kṣatriya woman is immediately following the Brāhmaṇa. A son born of her is named according to the caste immediately following his father's; he is designated by the mother’s caste, using the term "Kṣatriya. The purpose is so that he may be included in the legal transactions prescribed for the Kṣatriya caste. How might this not be the case? Because those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) are said to be superior to the mother’s caste, as stated in the preceding verse: "Sons procreated by the twice-born on women born of castes immediately following them are declared to be equal [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers. Therefore, since there would be no application of either caste designation for those born from two castes, he says this. Likewise, a son born of a Vaiśya woman by a Kṣatriya man receives the name "Vaiśya"; the purpose of this has already been explained. But if this is so, since there is no immediate succession between the Brāhmaṇa and the Vaiśya, the designation "Vaiśya" would not apply to one born of her. The same would apply to one born of a Śūdra woman by a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa. There is no fault here, because "immediate succession" is not intended to be the sole criterion. Rather, those born of women of other castes receive the name of the woman’s caste. This being the case, this rule should be understood as providing for the sacraments, such as initiation (*upanayana*), for the three *anuloma* sons born of the two castes from Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya fathers. Consequently, the three born of a Śūdra woman from Brāhmaṇas and others, though bearing those names, are not to be consecrated like Śūdras due to the defect of their mothers. Thus Gautama, having stated, "But those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) are devoid of duty" (GDh 4.25), immediately adds: "And [those born] of a Śūdra woman" (GDh 4.26), implying even the *anulomas*. Now, where the status of the mother’s caste is not desired even for those of a superior birth, he begins this prohibition: 10.14. "A son born of a Brāhmaṇa on a Śūdra woman is called a Caṇḍāla; he is excluded from all rites. A son born of a Vaiśya woman by a Brāhmaṇa is called a Vaidehaka; he is fit for service. A son born of a Kṣatriya woman by a Brāhmaṇa is called a Māgadha; he is fit for praise and the like. (GDh 4.25–27) In this context, the term "excluded from all rites" means that he is unfit for the sacraments and other duties of the twice-born. The phrase "fit for service" means he is fit for menial labor. "Fit for praise and the like" means he is fit for singing praises and similar tasks. Since these are born of women of lower castes, they are not entitled to the sacraments even if they bear the names of the higher castes. Thus, the prohibition against the sacraments for those born of a Śūdra woman is established. Furthermore, regarding the sons of the Vaiśya and Kṣatriya women, although they are not explicitly mentioned in this verse, the same principle applies because they are also born of women of lower castes. Therefore, the prohibition of sacraments for those born of a Śūdra woman extends to all three. As for the sons of the Vaiśya and Kṣatriya women, they are not entitled to the sacraments because they are born of women of lower castes, even though they are named after their fathers. This is the meaning. And thus Gautama, having stated, "Those born in the inverse order are devoid of duty," immediately thereafter says: "And [those born] of a Śūdra woman," implying that even the *anulomas* are included. Now, where he does not accept the mother’s caste even for those of superior birth, he begins this prohibition: 10.14. "A son born of a Brāhmaṇa on a Śūdra woman is called a Caṇḍāla; he is excluded from all rites. A son born of a Vaiśya woman by a Brāhmaṇa is called a Vaidehaka; he is fit for service. A son born of a Kṣatriya woman by a Brāhmaṇa is called a Māgadha; he is fit for praise and the like. (GDh 4.25–27) The meaning of "excluded from all rites" is that he is unfit for the sacraments and other duties of the twice-born. "Fit for service" means fit for menial labor. "Fit for praise and the like" means fit for singing praises and similar tasks. Since these are born of women of lower castes, they are not entitled to the sacraments even if they bear the names of the higher castes. Thus, the prohibition against the sacraments for those born of a Ś
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra, one called an Āvṛta is born;
he does not belong to the mother's caste, but rather belongs to a different caste entirely:
an Ābhīra from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha.

He should be known as "born. The term "from a Brāhmaṇa" carries over [from the previous verse]. Thus it is first with respect to women born in the natural order (*anuloma*), because of their superior status. And just as there is a different caste among women born in the natural order, he shows that the same applies to women born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*): "But from an Āyogavī woman, a Dhigvaṇa is born. (10.15)

One is born as a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone; it does not depend on the mother's caste. Just as those born in the natural order (anuloma) from Brāhmaṇas and others upon Kṣatriya women and so forth are designated by the mother’s name in order to censure the mother’s inferiority, likewise, those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) from Śūdras and others upon Vaiśya women and so forth are not of that [mother’s] caste even because of the censure of the father’s inferiority; rather, they belong to a different caste altogether, being excluded from both [parental] castes. For this reason, he points them out [in the following verse]. 10.15.
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men—these three outcasts are born from a Śūdra woman through the reverse order of castes. 10.16.

And just as these three [castes] arise from a Śūdra in relation to the [first] three [higher castes], so too do the Māgadha and Vaideha arise from a Vaiśya in the two higher varṇas respectively as pratiloma offspring.
But from a Kṣatriya, only a Sūta is born. And thus, these others are also born in the inverse order; they are the three outcastes (apaśadas). 10.17.
And likewise, he shows others as well for the sake of illustration:
"One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by birth a Pulkasa;
excluded from both [castes], he is a distinct caste. In this very same way:"
But one born from a Śūdra upon a Niṣāda woman is indeed known as a Kukkuṭaka. || 10.18 ||

This Niṣāda mentioned in this verse is not the one born from a Brāhmaṇa on a Śūdra woman as previously stated; for that is established by the context of the section concerning inverse (pratiloma) unions. Otherwise, since the Niṣāda born from a Brāhmaṇa on a Śūdra woman is born in the direct (ānulomya) order, it would be improper for one born from a Śūdra woman [by a Niṣāda] to be a Pulkasa, because the Pulkasa caste belongs to the inverse order. In the same way, one born from a Kṣattṛ on an Ugrā woman is proclaimed to be a Śvapāka;
and one begotten by a Vaidehaka on an Ambaṣṭhī woman is called a Veṇa. (10.19)

The increase and decrease of these [castes] are to be determined according to the scriptures. Furthermore, in the section concerning the mixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), it must be stated that even those born from non-pratiloma unions—those of mixed origin who are *vrātyas*—are to be mentioned; for this reason, the following is said: 10.19.
Those whom twice-born men beget on wives of equal caste who have not observed their vows, one should designate as *vrātyas*, fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*. (10.20)

From one who has fallen from the *Sāvitrī* is born a *vrātya*; however, one who has fallen from the *Sāvitrī* does not himself become a *vrātya*. And thus, the expiation of the *vrātyastoma* applies to one who has fallen from the *Sāvitrī* and becomes a *vrātya*. Consequently, the expiation of the *vrātyastoma* does not apply to one who has already fallen from the *Sāvitrī*, for another expiation must be devised for him. From this point forward, these [others] are born as *vrātyas*; some say that their sons and grandsons are *vrātyas*. That is incorrect, because the definition of a *vrātya* was already stated in the section on initiation (*upanayana*) with the words, "From this time onward, all three of these," and so forth. Therefore, this is not the definition of a *vrātya*. It was stated that he who is born from one who neglects his vows (*avrata*) is a *vrātya*; rather, it was said that one who is himself without vows (*avrata*) is a *vrātya*. Since this contradicts that [previous statement], it is meaningless. Moreover, this is contradictory: if they are twice-born (*dvijāti*), how can they be without vows? If they are without vows, how can they be twice-born? How then is this passage to be read: "Those whom twice-born men beget upon wives of equal caste, but who are without vows—those who have fallen away from the *Sāvitrī* (i.e., those deprived of the purificatory rites such as initiation)—one should designate them as *vrātyas*"? This is a restatement of the previously mentioned definition of a *vrātya*, intended to connect it with the subsequent sections and so forth. That is precisely this [point]. 10.20.
From a Vrātya Brahmin is born the evil-natured Bhūrjakaṇṭhaka, as well as the Āvantya, the Vātadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha. (10.21)

From a *vrātya* Brahmin, [a son is born] only from a woman of his own caste (*varṇa*), because she was the subject of the preceding verse and is not mentioned here; [the son] born of her is named Bhūrjakaṇṭha and has the *vrātya* as his lineage. In another *smṛti*, one born from a Brahmin and a Vaiśya woman is recorded as a Bhṛjjakaṇṭha. Since he is born in the natural order (*anuloma*), he is not inherently wicked. Therefore, this qualification is stated with reference to him: "His wickedness arises from being born of a *vrātya* whose self is unrefined. Even more wicked than that is the Āvantya born of a Brahmin woman, but not the Bhūrjakaṇṭha; for he is called "of no caste" (*avarṇa*) because he was born of a woman who is not of his own caste. Thus, this is specified: "only from a Brahmin woman. By this, the subsequent cases are explained: likewise, from an Āvantya comes a Vātadhāna, who is more wicked; from him a Puṣpadha, and from him a Śaikha. This enumeration is made because there is only a slight difference, or rather, it is intended as an illustration of the five types born of *vrātya* Brahmins. The same should be understood for the following two cases as well. Now, those born from a *vrātya* Kṣatriya and a Kṣatriya woman are described. (10.21)
From the Vrātya of the Rājanya caste arise the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Licchavi;
as well as the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khasa, and the Draviḍa. (10.22)
And these are to be explained as before. || 10.22 ||
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa, the Nijaṅgha, the Maitra, and the Sātvata. (10.23)

From a *vrātya* Vaiśya, those such as the Sudhanvas are to be understood as before; and there is a purpose for the mention of these names. Those who, in a certain region, are called by these names and are of low caste (*avarṇa*)—even though their origins are unknown—they are to be recognized as being of this same type. But why are those born from *vrātyas* of the Brāhmaṇa and other classes mentioned here in the section on the designations of those born from intermediate castes? Because: [10.23]
Through adultery, through a man knowing a woman who should not be known, and through the abandonment of one's own duties, the mixture of castes arises. (10.24)

The primary transgression of the castes (*varṇa*) consists in taking a woman from a lower caste (*pratiloma*); even in the case of a *anuloma* union, it is described with reference to the primary caste. Furthermore, "knowing one who should not be known" refers to the acceptance of women such as those who have gone astray (*vilomacārinī*) or remarried widows (*punarbhū*). And the "abandonment of one's own duties" refers to the loss of the initiatory rite (*upanayana-saṃskāra*) for those who are eligible for it. This being the case, this statement is rightly made both to demonstrate the causes of the intermixture of castes and to serve as a remedy for these [transgressions]. (10.24)
I shall now describe exhaustively those of mixed birth who are born from inverse (pratiloma) and natural (anuloma) unions, as well as those who are mutually intermingled.

In this manner, those who are mutually intermingled through both inverse and direct orders should be understood as being likewise of the direct order. This is for the purpose of directing the mind by way of introducing the subject matter that is about to be explained; for this is a restatement of the inverse order mentioned in the preceding verse, intended for the sake of what follows. (10.25)
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, and the Caṇḍāla, the lowest of men;
as well as the Māgadha, the Kṣattṛ caste, and likewise the Āyogava. (10.26)
These are mentioned again for the purpose of what is to be said hereafter; that is now stated: || 10.26 ||
These six produce offspring of similar caste within their own wombs; they also procreate children born of the mother's caste when united with women of superior castes. (10.27)

These, such as the Sūta and others, produce offspring similar to themselves only within their own wombs (*svayoni*). For example: an Āyogava produces an offspring similar to himself only in an Āyogavī; and an Ambaṣṭha produces a Vaiśya only in an Ambaṣṭhī who is similar to him and inferior to himself—that is, in a Vaiśya woman—and not in another. The same applies to the other *anuloma* castes, such as the Pāraśava and so forth. And although there is a distinction for these, such as the Ambaṣṭhas, by virtue of their superiority over mere Vaiśyas and the like, nevertheless this "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is stated because, on account of it, there is no distinction between these two groups regarding the duties of the Vaiśyas and so forth. For it is said: "He produces offspring similar to himself in his own womb and in the mother's caste. And so it has been stated: [The verse follows: *sadṛśān janayaty eṣāṃ svayonyāṃ mātṛjātiṣu |* *putrān sādhūṃs tathaivāśubhān anyatra jātiṣu ||* *(YDh 1.92)* "These [castes] produce sons similar to themselves in their own wombs and in those belonging to the mother’s caste—sons who are virtuous if born in their own kind, and likewise unworthy if born in other castes. Thus it is said.

"The sons born of women immediately following [the mother's caste] in the sequence prescribed for the twice-born are designated by the name of the mother's [caste], on account of the defect of the mother. As for the Āyogava and others, however, being born in the reverse order (pratiloma), they procreate those even more devoid of dharma upon women of their own caste and upon women of higher castes. In this same way, the Ambaṣṭha and others born in the natural order (ānulomya) are also to be understood. (10.27)
Just as for the three castes, the offspring of two [castes] is born from this [mother], so too is the sequence among the outsiders, due to the immediate proximity of their own species. (10.28)

Just as when a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya is born from Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya progenitors, his self attains the status of being twice-born (*dvijatva*); and having been so born, he becomes a twice-born by virtue of his qualification and capacity—exactly so, even among those outside [the fourfold order] who act in the inverse direction (*prātilomya*), the self of a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa becomes twice-born through two [progenitors], namely a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya respectively. And since the status of being twice-born exists, the author will later state that there is no prohibition against sacraments such as initiation (*upanayana*), saying: "These six possess the duties of the twice-born. However, this much is the distinction: just as those born in the natural order (*ānulomya*) do not belong to the caste of their mothers due to the mother's deficiency or inferiority, so too those born in the inverse order do not belong to the caste of their fathers due to the father's deficiency or inferiority. Thus, the attribution of commonality to the Māgadha and Sūta born in the inverse order from a Kṣatriya and a Brāhmaṇa is for the sake of praise; and such praise is for the sake of practical application (*vyavahāra*). Alternatively, the praise is intended to exclude the Caṇḍāla and others born in the inverse order. (10.28)
And they, moreover, procreate upon the wives of one another many outsiders who are even more corrupted than themselves and are held in contempt. (10.29)

And these six, beginning with the Āyogava, by procreating upon one another’s wives—just as the Āyogava begets upon a Kṣattrī woman a son called a Kṣattrāyogava—produce further descendants who are even more degraded than themselves. For instance, the Āyogava begets upon a Kṣattrī woman a son more excluded and inferior to himself; and upon a Caṇḍālī woman, one even more excluded than that. Likewise, the Kṣattṛ begets upon an Āyogavī woman a son more excluded than himself, and upon a Caṇḍālī woman, one even more so. Similarly, the Caṇḍāla begets upon a Kṣattrī woman a son more excluded than himself, and likewise upon an Āyogavī woman. By this same principle, the Māgadha begets upon a Vaidehī woman a son more excluded than himself, and upon a Sūtā woman, one even more excluded. Likewise, the Vaidehaka begets upon a Māgadhī woman a son more excluded than himself, and upon a Sūtā woman, one even more so. And the Sūta begets upon a Māgadhī woman a son more excluded than himself, and upon a Vaidehī woman, one even more so. Thus, by this sequence, producing offspring again and again through mutual intermarriage, they generate many descendants of fifteen types. Having thus explained the case of mutual intermarriage, he now speaks regarding the "fourfold caste system" (*cāturvarṇya*). (10.29)
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcaste being upon a Brāhmaṇī woman, so does an outcaste beget one even more outcaste within the fourfold caste system. || 10.30 ||
This is now stated:
acting in opposition to their own kind, those who are outsiders beget yet more outsiders; being inferior, they give birth to even more inferior castes—fifteen in total. (10.31)

These same six, when procreating within the four-fold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*), produce offspring who are even more external to themselves. For example, a *Caṇḍāla* produces from a *Śūdra* woman an offspring inferior to himself; one even more external than that from a *Vaiśya* woman; one even more than that from a *Kṣatriya* woman; and one even more than that from a *Brāhmaṇī*. In this very way, a *Kṣattṛ* produces four types of offspring from the four castes, each mutually more external to himself. Likewise, an *Āyogava* produces nine increasingly inferior types from the four castes in the same manner. From these *Caṇḍālas*, *Kṣattṛs*, and *Āyogavas* born of *Śūdra* origins, twelve distinct caste-divisions arise within the four castes. Including the three original types—the *Caṇḍāla*, *Kṣattṛ*, and *Āyogava*—there are thus fifteen caste-divisions originating from the *Śūdra* through the inverse order (*pratiloma*). These fifteen caste-divisions born of the *Śūdra* repeatedly produce offspring who are even more external and nearly extinct within the four-fold caste system. Now, the fifteen castes originating from the *Vaiśya* in the inverse order are described. A *Vaiśya* has two offspring in the inverse order and one in the natural order (*anuloma*). The *Māgadha* and *Vaidehaka* are born from a *Kṣatriya* and a *Brāhmaṇī* respectively; his offspring in the natural order is born from a *Śūdra*. When these, born of a *Vaiśya* by a *Śūdra* woman, procreate within the four castes, they produce from a *Śūdra* woman an offspring even more external than the *Śūdra* himself; one even more inferior than that from a *Vaiśya* woman (the *Āyogava*); one even more inferior than that from a *Kṣatriya* woman (the *Kṣattṛ*); and one even more inferior than that from a *Brāhmaṇī* woman (the *Caṇḍāla*). These, however, should be known as superior to the previously mentioned ones born solely of the *Śūdra*. Thus, a *Māgadha* producing from a *Śūdra* woman produces an offspring even more inferior than the *Śūdra* born solely of a *Vaiśya*. Likewise, he produces a *Māgadha* even more inferior to himself from a *Kṣatriya* woman. Similarly, from a *Brāhmaṇī*, he produces one even more inferior than the *Vaidehaka* born solely of a *Vaiśya*. In this way, the *Māgadha* produces four types from the four castes. We shall speak similarly of the *Vaidehaka*. The *Vaidehaka* producing from a *Śūdra* woman produces one even more inferior than the one born solely of a *Vaiśya*. Likewise, from a *Vaiśya*, a *Kṣatriya*, and a *Brāhmaṇī*, he produces offspring even more inferior than those born solely of a *Vaiśya* or those of the *Māgadha* type. Thus, the *Vaidehaka* also produces four types from the four castes. Thus, from these three born of the *Vaiśya*, there are twelve in the four castes. Including the three original types, there are likewise fifteen caste-divisions to be understood as originating from the *Vaiśya*. Now, for the *Kṣatriya*: [two are born in the natural order from a *Vaiśya* and a *Śūdra*], and one is born in the inverse order from a *Brāhmaṇī*. One born of a *Kṣatriya* by a *Śūdra* woman, when procreating within the four castes, is named *Ugra*; he produces from a *Śūdra* woman an offspring even more inferior to himself, yet superior to the *Śūdra* born solely of a *Vaiśya*. Likewise, from a *Vaiśya*, a *Kṣatriya*, and a *Brāhmaṇī*, he produces the *Āyogava*, *Kṣattṛ*, and *Caṇḍāla* in progressively inferior order. These, however, should be known as superior to the *Āyogava* and others born of the *Vaiśya*. Thus, these are the four sons of the *Ugra*. A son born of a *Kṣatriya* by a *Vaiśya* woman, when procreating within the four castes, produces from a *Śūdra* woman an offspring even more inferior to himself. But when producing from a *Kṣatriya* woman, they produce a *Māgadha* superior to the *Māgadha* born solely of a *Vaiśya*. Likewise, producing a *Vaidehaka* from a *Brāhmaṇī*, they produce one superior to the *Vaidehaka* born solely of a *Vaiśya*. Thus, the sons of the *Ugra* are four. Likewise, one born of a *Kṣatriya* by a *Brāhmaṇī* woman, when procreating within the four castes, produces from a *Śūdra* woman an offspring even more inferior to himself, yet superior to the *Ugra* born of a *Kṣatriya*. Thus, these are the four sons. Likewise, one born of a *Kṣatriya* by a *Brāhmaṇī* woman, when procreating within the four castes, produces from a *Śūdra* woman an offspring even more inferior to himself, yet superior to the *Ugra* born of a *Kṣatriya*. Likewise, producing from a *Vaiśya* woman, he produces one even more inferior to himself, yet superior to those born of a *Vaiśya* or a *Kṣatriya*. Likewise, producing from a *Kṣatriya* woman, he produces one even more inferior to himself, yet superior to one born solely of a *Kṣatriya*. Likewise, producing a *Sūta* from a *Brāhmaṇī*, he produces one even more inferior to himself, yet superior to the previous *Sūta*. Thus, there are four born of a *Kṣatriya* from a *Brāhmaṇī*. Thus, from these three born of a *Brāhmaṇa*, there are twelve, and including the three original types, there are fifteen caste-divisions originating from the *Brāhmaṇa*. Thus, from the four castes, there are sixty castes. Including the four original types, these forty-six caste-divisions should be understood according to their broad outlines. When these are divided again and again, the caste-divisions become innumerable. Therefore, this should be understood as the detailed exposition of the verse: "Those of mixed origin, born in the inverse and natural orders, and mutually intermingled. Even though they are outcasts of the castes (*varṇāpaśada*), they are treated as if they were castes. By the elision of the word "like" (*iva*), they are called "caste-like" (*vārṇāḥ*). And so it has been said: "The Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya are the three twice-born castes; the fourth is the once-born Śūdra; there is no fifth. (10.31)
From a Dasyu and an Āyogava is born a Sairandhra, who knows how to apply ornaments and cosmetics, who is not a slave yet lives like a slave, and subsists by means of nets.

"Skilled in the art of adornment and service" is an instruction regarding his livelihood; it means that though he was not a slave, he lived the life of a servant by virtue of his skill in adornment and service. He was one who lived by the work of others, which is why he is described as a *sairandhra*. However, another says: "The author of the *Granthi* [text] states that Sairandhra was so called because of his seeing Draupadī. The practice of using snares (*vāgurā-vṛtti*), known as the killing of wild animals, is appropriate for the noble ones when performed for the sake of the gods and ancestors, for medicinal purposes, or for the mere maintenance of life when one has reached a state of extreme distress involving the loss of wife and children. (10.32)
The Vaideha, however, procreates the Maitreyaka, who praises men incessantly and strikes a bell at the break of dawn. (10.33)

He begets a Maitreyaka—or, according to another reading, a Maireyaka—by means of a Vaidehaka; this refers to the one born from a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother who was previously mentioned. He further characterizes the Maitreyaka by his quality as a *mādhūka*, meaning one who speaks sweetly. He is procreated specifically upon an *Āyogavī* woman who has been authorized for the task. His livelihood is indicated as follows: "He constantly praises men at the break of dawn, ringing a bell, while singing in the morning with salutations and the like. (10.33)
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgara, a fisherman who lives by the work of boats; those dwelling in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta. (10.34)

The Niṣāda should be understood as a *pratiloma* (inverse-caste) offspring born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother, by virtue of the context concerning *pratiloma* castes; however, he is not a Brāhmaṇa-born son of a Śūdra woman, because that would constitute an *anuloma* (direct-caste) union. That Niṣāda, upon marrying an *āyogavī* woman, begets a son of the Mārgava caste, known by the name Dāsadvitīya. His prescribed livelihood is living by boat-work (*naukarma*). Those who dwell in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta by his third name. The *āyogavī* should be understood as even more excluded than the [mother of a] Niṣāda, and she is not one born of a Vaiśya woman by a Śūdra. Thus it is shown. 10.34.
Among women who wear the clothes of the dead and eat despised food—
these Āyogava women— there arise three distinct classes of those deprived of their caste.

From the three castes as previously taught—the Dasyu, the Vaideha, and the Niṣāda—those who read the final quarter of the first verse as "the Sūta is born from the Dasyu and the Āyogava," for them, the Sūta is stated there to be a Kṣatriya-born son from a Brāhmaṇī mother. Thus, from such [mixed] Sūtas, Vaidehas, and Niṣādas, those castes designated by name as Āyogavas are born according to the teaching of the three verses. (10.35)
From a Niṣāda, however, a Kārāvara is born, who is a leather-worker;
from a Vaidehaka are born the Āndhra and Meda, whose dwellings are outside the village.

[The offspring] is born from a Vaideha woman alone, according to the indicative marks of the verses to be cited later. From a Niṣāda, a caste named Kārāvara, whose occupation is working with hides, is born from a Vaideha woman. [Regarding the statement that] "from a Vaidehaka [are born] Andhra and Meda": since these cannot possibly be born from other women, and because the two castes taught in this very verse are present here, and because it is impossible for the Andhra and Meda castes to be born from a Vaideha man and a Vaideha woman, we must by process of elimination take them as being born from the women of the Kārāvara and Niṣāda castes respectively. For thus, in the case of different female castes, it is logical that the Andhra and Meda are of distinct castes born from a Vaidehaka man, and not from a Vaideha woman. (10.36)
From a Caṇḍāla and a Niṣāda woman, a Pāṇḍusopāka is born, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. || 10.37 ||

From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī is born the Ekajātīya; these two castes, characterized by the names Pāṇḍusopāka and Hiṇḍika, are produced. Thus, in this section concerning those of inferior caste (varṇāpaśada), one should understand that there is a distinction either due to the difference of the mother—even between those born of the same caste—or due to the difference of the father, even within the case of a single woman. 10.37.
But from a Caṇḍāla, by a Pulkasī woman, is born the sinful Sopāka, who subsists by the occupation of root-thievery and is always censured by virtuous people. (10.38)

The "fundamental vice" means a livelihood involving killing; that is, the killing of those condemned to death, carrying out the corpses of the destitute by order of the king or the state, taking their clothes and other belongings, eating the funeral offerings (piṇḍa) intended for the deceased, and so forth—such is the livelihood born of a Caṇḍāla from a Pulkasī woman. 10.38.
But from a Caṇḍāla, a Niṣāda woman gives birth to a son called an Antyāvasāyin, who frequents cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the caste system. (10.39)

He frequents cremation grounds, subsists on their products, and dwells in those places; and this being so, he should be known as even more sinful than a *caṇḍāla*. This should be understood as merely an illustration of the endlessness of such intermixture (*saṃkara*). || 10.39 ||
These castes resulting from intermixture have been shown according to their fathers and mothers;
whether they are concealed or manifest, they are to be known by their own actions. (10.40)
One's birth, as taught in the scriptures, is to be inferred from one's actions; and by indicating their birth, these people are to be assigned to their respective duties. (10.40)
Six sons born of women of their own caste or of those immediately below it possess the dharma of the twice-born;
however, all those born of a Śūdra woman are considered outcasts (apadhvaṃsa). || 10.41 ||

Those born of their own caste from the three twice-born men—namely, those born of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya woman—are eligible for the sacraments (*saṃskāra*). Likewise, those born immediately after (in the inverse order) from a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya father and a Kṣatriya and Vaiśya mother—these six sons possess the status of the twice-born. In this way, the mention of "those born immediately after" is intended for the sake of including those born of their own caste, not for its own sake. Now, one might object: since only two types of offspring are produced by a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya father from the two immediately following castes—the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya women—a son born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya mother would not be "born immediately after. Yet he too is indeed "born immediately after," because the term refers to the *anuloma* (natural/regular) order. The phrase "possessing the status of the twice-born" excludes those who do not follow that rule; for it is stated: "But all those born of a violation of the law (*apadhvaṃsaja*) are declared to have the same status as Śūdras. Thus, even though they are born of Brāhmaṇas and others, they are excluded. Therefore, this mention of "six" does not refer to these [violation-born sons], but rather to those born of their own caste together with those born immediately after. Accordingly, Gautama says: "But those born in the reverse order (*pratiloma*) are devoid of dharma, as are those born of a Śūdra woman. Now, one might ask: is this verse not a repetition of the meaning already stated in the passage, "Those sons who are born of women in the immediate sequence"? It is not a repetition. For in that [previous] passage it was said: "They call them by the name of the mother's immediate [caste] because of the mother's defect. The designation "by the name of the immediate [caste]" applies in two ways: for the sake of social convention (*vyavahāra*) and for the sake of sacraments (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, this statement—that these three possess the status of the twice-born—is made to remove doubt. Alternatively, this verse serves as a reason for the preceding verse. How so? In the passage, "They call them by the name of the mother's immediate [caste] because of the mother's defect," it states the reason why "the six sons possess the status of the twice-born. In this way, the non-redundancy of this verse in relation to the previous one should be understood. (10.41)
And by the power of the seeds of their asceticism,
they undergo increase and decrease among human beings here, birth after birth, in age after age.

And this verse is to be understood as a praise of the sacramental rite prescribed in the preceding verse for those born from Brāhmaṇa and other castes through women of the Kṣatriya and other castes. Thus he will say later: "Born from a Brāhmaṇa on a Śūdra woman," and so forth. This being the case, this classification of castes and its connection with superiority and inferiority should be seen as pertaining only to human beings, not to cows and the like. Consequently, there is no avoidance [of the rules] regarding one born of a cow or a female buffalo, whether by her mother or her sister. || 10.42 ||
But through the gradual neglect of sacred rites and by the absence of Brāhmaṇas, these Kṣatriya tribes have become Śūdras in this world. (10.43)

This is an elaboration of what was stated [in MDh 10.24]: "The intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) arises through adultery, by a man knowing a woman who should not be known, and by the abandonment of one's own duties. This passage explains that, like a Śūdra, there is no entitlement to perform rites; and here, the cause for the omission of rites is both the lack of sight of a Brāhmaṇa and the aforementioned factors. Because of their absence, he declares the absence of penance (*prāyaścitta*). Alternatively, the lack of sight of a Brāhmaṇa serves both purposes: it is the cause for the omission of rites and the cause for the absence of penance. Furthermore, the demonstration of the causes of degradation is for the sake of providing a remedy, since those causes are being pointed out. (10.43)
The Puṇḍrakas, the Coḷas, the Dramiḷas, the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, the Śakas, the Pāradas, the Pallavas, the Cīnas, the Kirātas, and likewise the Daradas. (10.44)
The Puṇḍrakas and others, who were originally Kṣatriyas from Darada, became Śūdras due to the neglect of their religious duties. || 10.44 ||

Those castes in the world who are outside those born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet—whether they speak the speech of barbarians or the speech of the Aryas—are all traditionally known as Dasyus. 10.45.

This exclusion from the community due to the neglect of rites applies not only to Kṣatriyas, but to all social classes (varṇas) alike, as well as through the failure to see Brāhmaṇas. Since this is so, therefore all three causes of degradation must be avoided with effort; these include the Barbaras, Maṇḍikas, and others. This same principle should also be understood in the case of the verse: "A Dasyu begets an Āyogava on a Vaiśya woman. (10.45)
Those who are considered outcasts among the twice-born, as well as those born of degraded unions,
should subsist by means of those despised occupations belonging to the twice-born themselves.

Among the women of the twice-born castes, those born in the reverse order (pratiloma) by Śūdra men—such as the Āyogava and others, with the exception of the Caṇḍāla—as well as those born of transgression (apadhvaṃsaja), even though they are born in the direct order (anuloma) from Śūdra women by twice-born men; regarding them it has been said: "All those born of transgression in a Śūdra woman are declared to share the same duties [as the Śūdra]. They should maintain themselves by means of despised occupations. This instruction is intended to prescribe their livelihood. And so he shows: 10.46.
The management of horses and chariots belongs to the Sūtas; the *ciktisita* (craft) belongs to the Ambaṣṭhas.
In this context, by implication, it is the one born from a *pratiloma* union with an Ambaṣṭha woman who is intended; or [it refers to] one born from a *pratiloma* union with an Ambaṣṭhī woman.
The work of women belongs to the Vaidehakas.
In the protection of women, within the inner apartments, and so forth, the path of the Magadha merchants lies through the office of chamberlains. (10.47)
Those known as the path of birds and the path of water; thus [it is]. 10.47.
The killing of fish is the occupation of the Niṣādas; that of the Āyogava is carpentry; and the slaughter of wild animals is the work of the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus.
Those born of Niṣādas who are excluded [from the caste system] are understood by the term "Niṣāda" through the force of the context; and this has already been explained previously. 10.48.
For the Kṣattrugras and Pulkasas, there shall be dwelling in holes, execution, and imprisonment;
for the Dhigvaṇas, the work of tanning leather; and for the Veṇas, the playing of musical instruments.
These wise ones should dwell at shrines, under trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in caves, subsisting by their own prescribed duties. 10.50
The dwelling for Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas shall be outside the village;
they must be made outcaste from the community, and their only wealth shall be their own donkey.
Their garments shall be the clothes of the dead; their food shall be from broken vessels;
their ornament shall be black iron; and they shall always lead a life of wandering mendicancy.
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them; their mutual dealings and marriages are only with their own equals. 10.53
Their food should be given by others in a broken vessel;
they must not wander at night through villages or cities. (10.54)

They may go about during the day for the sake of their business, having been authorized by the king’s edicts; and they shall carry out a corpse that has no kinsmen—such is the established rule. 10.55.
They shall constantly execute those condemned to death according to the scriptures and by the king’s command;
they shall take the clothes, beds, and ornaments of the executed. (10.56)

This section concerning their livelihood and residence applies specifically to those of inferior caste (varṇāpaśada). In the absence of traditional authority (āgama), they are inferred from reasoning: they say that such a person is one born in the reverse order (pratiloma), whose arrival is unknown due to the capacity for the habitual practice of censurable actions. || 10.56 ||
One should discern by their own actions a man who is devoid of proper caste, unrecognizable, and born of a defiled womb—an ignoble man appearing in the form of a noble one. (10.57)

"Un-Aryan" means devoid of the [proper] conduct of the castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others; the meaning is that it is inconsistent with the actions corresponding to one's own defiled womb. What, then, are those [actions]? For this reason it is said: || 10.57 ||
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty, and a lack of virtuous action reveal in this world that a man is born from a defiled womb. (10.58)

"Let this ignoble, outcaste, and ignoble wretch experience ignobility, cruelty, harshness, and a lack of virtuous action"—these words are intended as illustrations of the signs of birth from a defiled womb, not for the purpose of excluding others. And this being so, such qualities manifest here in this world the person born from a defiled womb, even if he is descended from a preeminent family. For what reason? Because effects conform to their cause. Thus he demonstrates: 10.58.
He inherits either the character of his father, or that of his mother, or indeed both;
for in this world, it is observed that effects conform to their causes. Since this is so, therefore:
"In no way does one born of a low womb suppress his own nature. (10.59)
Thus, it is logical to employ inference for the sake of understanding what is not known from scripture. And he demonstrates this:
