"Even though born into a preeminent family, there may be a confusion of his lineage, which remains unknown due to its being concealed."
A person indeed resorts to that conduct, whether it be slight or great.

Just as a mule (*aśvatara*) is born from a donkey, therefore that inference regarding it must be understood as non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*). Just as, O noble lady, there is a comprehension of specific species among those mixed with other animals through inference based on the characteristics described in the treatises (*śāstra*), so it is here as well. And this is the purpose of the instruction: just as one does not engage in social interaction with those of low caste (*varṇāpaśada*) known through scripture (*āgama*), so too [one should not do so] with those known through inference. Since this is so, therefore the mixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) must be guarded against by the king with great effort. For it has been said: || 10.60 ||
But where these corrupters of the castes are born through promiscuity, that kingdom, along with its inhabitants, perishes very quickly. (10.61)

This censure should be understood as being for the sake of protecting the king, intended as a praise by way of contrast. Now, this cause of purification is stated for those who are not entitled to [Vedic] rites, for the purpose of their elevation. (10.61)

The unconditioned sacrifice of one's body for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, and for the protection of women and children, is the cause of success for those outside [the Vedic fold]. (10.62)

The "outcastes" (*bāhya*) are understood here as those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*). "Unadorned by wealth" means not purchased with money. This is a qualification regarding the renunciation of the body; it is stated because "attainment" (*siddhi*) refers to the attainment of one's entitlement (*adhikāra*) in another birth, by virtue of that entitlement’s efficacy. Alternatively, the attainment of heaven is indeed mediated [by this process]. Some maintain that this treatise on penance (*prāyaścitta-śāstra*) is intended solely for the purpose of the appointment (*niyoga*) for outcastes. Others, however, by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), accept this as applying without distinction to all. Since this renunciation of the body is taught for the sake of penance, this is stated for the purpose of the duties of men belonging to the outcaste classes. (10.62)
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, purity, and restraint of the senses—Manu declared this to be the summary of the dharma for the four castes. (10.63)

And thus, by the force of the context, it should be understood that even for those born from the intermixture of the four castes (*cāturvarṇa*), non-violence and the other duties of man (*puruṣadharma*) are to be known [as applicable]. In this way, this [latter set of duties] is the cause of their gradual perfection; however, it is understood that the former [set], by virtue of its inherent capacity, leads to perfection immediately—this being because of the previous [text] which defines the characteristics of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes, such as [the verse beginning] "among all castes, when they are equal," and so forth. Otherwise, the status of being a Brāhmaṇa and the rest would not be attained; yet these are desired [to exist] through both superiority and inferiority. Therefore, this [next section] is commenced. (10.63)
If one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother procreates with someone of a superior caste, the inferior offspring attains the superior caste within the seventh generation. (10.64)

The caste born from a Brāhmaṇa on a Śūdra woman is characterized by female traits and is called Pāraśava; if he is procreated again and again by a superior Brāhmaṇa of male name, then in this manner that inferior Śūdra caste attains the superior Brāhmaṇa birth at the end of the seventh generation—that is, by birth—due to the predominance of the seed. And thus, by this sequence of the revolution of the ages (yuga). 10.64.
A Śūdra attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa, and just as a Śūdra does, so too a Brāhmaṇa attains the state of a Śūdra.

The one called *pāraśava* is so designated through his connection with a Śūdra man; thus, there is a degradation from the status of a Śūdra man. The Śūdra-nature of the *pāraśava* caste should be understood to persist for seven generations.
One should know that [the same applies] to one born from a Kṣatriya, and likewise from a Vaiśya. (10.65)

One should understand the upward and downward movement [of status] in the case of a Śūdra woman; this occurs after five cycles of the *yuga*. Here too, the upward movement is from the female side, and the downward movement is from the male side. Even one born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother should be understood—by implication—to attain [the status of] a *varṇa* through such upward and downward movements in the third birth. By this same logic, even one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother should be understood to belong to the Kṣatriya *varṇa* in the third birth, by virtue of his connection with the Kṣatriya. And likewise, for one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya mother, the upward and downward movements are understood by implication to occur in the fifth birth. This same logic applies when a Kṣatriya fathers a son by a Vaiśya woman who is not a woman of the immediately lower caste, just as it does for a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother. This is not explicitly stated in the text but must be explained as established by implication, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the first verse. Alternatively, this instruction is based on observed facts: just as a man of Brāhmaṇa *varṇa*, being drawn down by the defect of the womb through his connection with a Śūdra woman to become a Pāraśava, remains a Śūdra until the seventh *yuga*; so too the Pāraśava *varṇa* called "female," while remaining connected to a Brāhmaṇa womb, becomes a Brāhmaṇa *varṇa*. For him, the Brāhmaṇa sacraments (*saṃskāra*) and the entitlement to perform *śrauta* and *smārta* rites are appropriate, just as in the previous case of memory. But another says: he has no entitlement to the *śrauta* rites. That is incorrect, because the preceding and succeeding cases are governed by the same scriptural authority. As was stated previously. Having heard this principle of the predominance of the seed, [the author] says: "If a Śūdra attains Brāhmaṇahood through the predominance of the seed, and a Brāhmaṇa falls to Śūdrahood through the predominance of the soil. This being the case, [verse 10.65 follows].
If one should ask: "Wherein lies the superiority between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa father upon a non-Aryan mother, and one born from a non-Aryan father upon a Brāhmaṇī mother? (10.66)

Or, regarding the superiority [of offspring] from a non-Aryan: if one born from a Brāhmaṇa father to a non-Aryan Śūdra woman—even if she is not married to him, let alone if she is—does not incur reproach, and is even more highly esteemed than those born from purely Śūdra, Vaiśya, or Kṣatriya lineages, then likewise, for one born from a non-Aryan Śūdra to a Brāhmaṇa woman, there would follow the absence of reproach, just as in the case of the *pāraśava*, because of the predominance of the field (*kṣetra*). Furthermore, his superiority over those born from Kṣatriya and Vaiśya lineages would follow by virtue of the power of the field. Thus, this verse should be understood as intending to refute the predominance of the seed (*bīja*), based on the scriptural teaching that sons are produced from the field; it is not intended as a question arising from doubt. As some have said: "In some cases the seed [is primary], in others the womb," and thus, due to the instability of the predominance of either seed or womb, a state of confusion arises. This being so, the section concerning the predominance of the seed is upheld. Here is the answer to this [objection]: 10.66.

A son born to a non-Aryan woman from an Aryan father may possess the qualities of an Aryan; however, it is certain that one born to an Aryan woman from a non-Aryan father is a non-Aryan, such as a Pāraśava, even through the performance of domestic sacrifices (pākayajña) and other rites. || 10.67 ||

[This applies] to those such as Cāṇḍālas, because they lack even the qualification for the duties of a Śūdra. His intention [is this]: for who is capable of determining the goodness of the Lord’s Dharma through logical reasoning? For in that case, due to the instability of reasons, the instability of Dharma itself would follow as a consequence. And this has already been rejected previously in the passage beginning with "of the inconceivable and immeasurable. This being so, one must accept the predominance of the seed and the womb according to the scriptural instruction, and not by means of inference. This is also the case elsewhere than in the scope of scriptural instruction, such as in the production of merit and demerit from pleasure and pain. And having established this... (10.67)
The law is established that both of these are ineligible for the sacraments (*asaṃskāryau*).
It is not only the *caṇḍāla* and others; rather, the *pāraśava* and others are also included. And so it has been said:

"Due to the deficiency of their birth, the former [the *pāraśava*] is excluded from the sacraments, while the latter [the *caṇḍāla*] is excluded because of being born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*). (10.68)

In some cases, such as the *pāraśava* and others, although the seed (*bīja*) is predominant; and in other cases, such as the *caṇḍāla* and others born from inverse unions (*pratiloma*), although the womb (*yoni*) is predominant due to the defect of the father. However, according to worldly perspective, he further praises those born of their own caste (*svajāti*) and those born of intermediate castes (*antaraja*). || 10.69 ||
Just as a good seed, when grown in a fertile field, reaches fulfillment;
such is the worldly illustration, and likewise one born noble deserves every refinement within the noble [lineage]. 10.69

By the power of instruction, both Śrauta and Smārta rites [are permitted]. Who, then, is this [eligible person]? One born of his own caste and one born of the next lower caste, with the exception of the Śūdra. However, even though the *pāraśava* and others are *anuloma* (born in the natural order), they are entitled only to the Smārta rites such as the *pākayajña*, and not to the Śrauta rites; for it has been stated [in the scriptures] that "this is due to the reproach of the mother's defect. Furthermore, those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), such as the *āyogava* and others, are excluded even from human duties such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth, and from taking refuge in Brahmins and others by sacrificing their lives. This being the case, it is improper for some to praise the seed (*bīja*) alone as the sole factor in all instances while maintaining a one-sided adherence. Thus, as for that which...
Some wise ones [hold that liberation comes from] the field;
others [hold it comes from] both, because faults are seen in each extreme.
Likewise, others [hold it comes from] the seed and the field; however, the settled conclusion in this matter is as follows. (10.70)

Even that which they state with absolute certainty is incorrect; for even when there is a defect in the field, we observe that among Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, and among Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, three [classes] are seen to be censurable and yet authorized for their respective duties as far as possible. Thus, since faults are seen even in these three absolute positions, this very rule as previously stated should be understood. Alternatively, the statement "only good seed in a good field" expresses a regulation based on excellence; whereas the former [rule] is to be understood according to the specific context through the power of the instruction. And it is precisely by accepting the primacy of both that these two positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are stated. (10.70)
A seed sown in a non-field, such as upon stone and the like, perishes right there within.
The meaning is that its fruit is not obtained; or else, it perishes right there within the layers [of the soil] and so forth. Even a field that is seedless would become merely a barren plot. (10.71)
Even a well-prepared plot of ground, if it is devoid of seed, will be fruitless. Furthermore, the predominance of both is stated in some places:

"Because by the power of the seed (*bījaprabhāveṇa*), those born as animals became seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*). Regarding "the seed and the power" (*bījaṃ ca prabhāvaś ca*): this is a dual compound (*dvandva*) treated as a singular neuter noun, *bījaprabhāve*. The "seed" is as previously described; "power" (*prabhāva*) is the manifestation of one's own nature through specific, firmly established qualities (*dharma-viśeṣa*). By that "power of the seed," even while being born as animals, they became seers.
Since those beginning with Ṛṣyaśṛṅga were honored and praised, therefore the seed is praised. 10.72.

Thus they say; and this [statement], while being subject to the aforementioned fault if taken as an absolute rule, serves to indicate through its conclusion that, between the seed and the womb, the caste produced from a superior seed is praised. And so, while this is true, he praises those born in the natural order (*anuloma*)—specifically those born of Kṣatriya and Vaiśya mothers, excluding Śūdras—as being indeed superior. And this is the nature of both the seed and the womb. (10.72)
Having carefully considered the non-noble who performs noble deeds and the noble who performs non-noble deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal. (10.73)

First, a non-Aryan is a Śūdra; even if he performs the work of an Aryan—that is, the work of the twice-born—he is not equal to the twice-born. Why? Because he lacks the qualification for that [work] and because there is no excellence [in him]. Not only is there a lack of excellence, but there is also further transgression due to his engagement in what is forbidden. A Brāhmaṇa, even if he performs the work of a Śūdra, is not equal to a Śūdra, owing to the greatness of his birth, even when engaging in what is forbidden. Thus, because of this inequality between the two, they are not "unequal" in the sense that both would fall by engaging in what is forbidden. And so Gautama says: "In the case of a mutual exchange of work between an Ārya and a non-Ārya, there is equality of action. This is understood through the force of the praise of action. This being so, one should not neglect one's duties by relying on the power of caste alone, since it is when caste and action are conjoined that they accomplish the unseen result known as the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Now, this is introduced for the purpose of presenting the section on rules for times of distress (*āpadkalpa*) regarding the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. (10.73)
Those Brāhmaṇas who abide in the womb of Brahman and are established in their own duties should properly subsist by means of the six occupations in their proper order.

The phrase "those established in the womb of Brahman" he himself explains: those who remain steadfast in their own duties and not in the duties of other castes, they should properly subsist by means of the six duties. And so he will say later: "not following the livelihood of a Vaiśya," and so forth. "In due order" means the commencement of conduct according to the sequence prescribed by the scriptures and following the traditional succession. By this, the word "subsisting" (*upajīvana*) should be understood as referring either to the performance of such duties alone—as in the case of [the statement] "he studied the lineages of the ancestors according to the sequence of the *Śruti*," and so on—or to the connection with the acts of livelihood itself. These, moreover, are... (10.74)
Teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts—these six are the duties of the first-born (the Brahmin). 10.75.

The instruction regarding these [rules] here is for the purpose of injunction (*vidhi*). In the first chapter, it was stated for the purpose of praising the scripture. However, if their injunction could have been understood from the previous scripture alone, then their instruction here should be understood as being for the purpose of the section on emergencies (*āpad-prakaraṇa*). Now, the division of these into two groups is established because they serve visible and invisible purposes (*dṛṣṭa-adṛṣṭārthatva*). (10.75)
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons. (10.76)

This acceptance [of gifts] is said to be from one who is pure, because it is investigated here: "Who, moreover, is pure in this world? [The answer is: "He who is [pure] by birth and by action. Now, if this were the case, the Brāhmaṇa alone would be the pure recipient. However, in another Smṛti it is stated: "A Brāhmaṇa may eat and accept [gifts] from twice-born men who are praised for their own duties" (GDh 17.1–2); thus, both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya are also included. But here, if the word "pure" (*viśuddha*) is conceived as including even the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, then what jealousy could there be toward the Śūdra, since he too is pure by birth and by action? If there is a distinction, then there is also a mutual distinction between the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya compared to the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, either the Śūdra should be accepted if he is established in his conduct, or the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya should be excluded while accepting the Brāhmaṇa. It is replied: Even though this is so, considering Vedic study and connection with Vedic rites, the purity of action is declared to be without distinction for all three, due to the equality of their entitlement. And thus, without distinction, acceptance from all three is permitted in another Smṛti when they are established in their own duties; however, not from a Śūdra. This being the case, it should be explained in the same way here as well. Furthermore, the mention of "purity" (*viśuddha*), although connected to acceptance, should be understood by implication as being for the purpose of officiating at sacrifices and teaching, for otherwise—since these two are not connected [to the Śūdra]—this would apply only to the Śūdra, because of his entitlement to officiating and teaching. (10.76)
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts. (10.77)

And here, the word *dharma* should be understood as referring specifically to the duties of one's station (*vṛtti*), because of the force of that specific designation. This being the case, sacrifices, study, and giving—which have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*)—are not prohibited for him; indeed, he will mention those later. And here, by virtue of the context, it is the teaching of the Veda that is prohibited for the Kṣatriya, along with its auxiliary branches, but not the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) and so forth. (10.77)
It is the established rule that these [duties] should likewise cease with respect to the Vaiśya;
for Manu Prajāpati did not prescribe those duties for them. 10.78

The prohibition of the occupations [of the twice-born] applies to Vaiśyas. It should be understood that, as before, there is no prohibition here regarding sacrifices and other such duties; and he will state those [duties] accordingly. (10.78)
Bearing weapons and missiles is the livelihood of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya. But their true dharma consists of giving, study, and sacrifice. (10.79)

"The study of the Vedas is for the Brāhmaṇa, the protection [of subjects] for the Kṣatriya, and the occupation of trade for the Vaiśya; these are the distinguished duties within their respective spheres. (10.80)

In this context, by the term "practice of the Vedas" (*vedābhyāsa*), both personal study and teaching are intended by implication, but not merely recitation (*adhyayana*), because that would be redundant and because of the statement that [these duties] are "distinguished among their respective occupations. Furthermore, among these modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*), that of the Brāhmaṇa alone is superior, as it serves the purpose of human goals both seen and unseen. Likewise, the protection of subjects by the Kṣatriya should be understood as serving both his livelihood and his duty (*dharma*). Similarly, the Vaiśya’s management of wealth must necessarily be performed for the sake of supporting the Brāhmaṇas and others; for his specific duty (*dharma*) is indeed the distribution of wealth. Alternatively, from the statement that they are "distinguished among their respective occupations," another point is understood: just as a Brāhmaṇa becomes purified by the mere practice of the Vedas even without performing sacrifices or accepting gifts, so too a Kṣatriya is exalted by the mere protection of the people even if he does not study or perform sacrifices; and a Vaiśya, even in the absence of sacrifice and study, is exalted by his own livelihood (*vārtā*) directed toward the needs of the twice-born and others. Thus, these [occupations] are prescribed for the Brāhmaṇas and the rest for the sake of their livelihood and for the sake of *dharma*. (10.80)
But if he cannot subsist by his own prescribed duty as a Brahmin,
he may live by the dharma of a Kshatriya, for that is the one immediately next to him.

If the family’s livelihood is jeopardized due to the king being devoted to righteousness (*dharmātman*), he would be unable to survive; therefore, in such a state, setting aside his own duty, it would be his task to protect villages, cities, and the country through the conduct of a Kṣatriya. Others, however, maintain that kingship arises from a single individual. Thus, from the statement of the immediately preceding cause, it is understood that there is only slight transgression [in this case]; yet, if the order of succession is violated, the gravity of the transgression increases. (10.81)
But if he should find it impossible to live by either of these two, how should he act?
He should subsist by the livelihood of a Vaiśya, engaging in agriculture and cattle-rearing. 10.82.

The mention of agriculture and cattle-rearing is for the purpose of illustrating all the occupations of a Vaiśya. This Vaiśya occupation is stated here in the case where the Brāhmaṇa performs the work himself; however, when not performed by himself, it was previously mentioned in such passages as, "He shall live by ṛta and amṛta. In this way, the distinction between the contexts of the Vaiśya occupation is justified. Now, these [occupations] are being discussed in detail. 10.82.
Even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which consists mostly of violence and depends upon others. || 10.83 ||
They consider agriculture to be a good thing, yet that livelihood is despised by all;
for the wooden plough with its iron mouth destroys both the earth and those who dwell within it.

This deprecation of agriculture is for the purpose of praising the other occupations of a Vaiśya; this is understood from the force of the instruction regarding agriculture. Otherwise, it would follow that it was not fit to be taught at all. This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serves to prohibit the scratching of the earth by means of the principle that "one should not perform what is censured. Nor is this [censurable] because of the earth itself, as is the case with those who lie upon the ground. Others, however, say: "For this very reason, one must not scratch the earth even with the tip of a fingernail. (10.84)
But for one who, due to a lack of livelihood, abandons skill in the Dharma, this may be sold as merchandise to increase wealth—provided that the choice pieces have been extracted. (10.85)

From the statement regarding the renunciation of skill in dharma, its inferiority is understood even when compared to cattle-rearing. This being the case, trade is superior to agriculture; nevertheless, by implication, it is understood that cattle-rearing is better still. Now, this removal of the merchant's wares is described for one who is selling his goods: 10.85.
One should exclude all liquids, prepared food along with sesame seeds, stones, salt, animals, and human beings. (10.86)

And here, substances such as jaggery (*guḍa*) and the like, which have taste as their primary quality, are referred to by the word "taste" (*rasa*) through implication. This is just as a collection of *tagara*, *uśīra*, and sandalwood, which has fragrance as its primary quality, is referred to by the word "fragrance. Cooked food refers to rice and the like; others say it refers to what is cooked. "Stones" (*aśman*) means all rocks. The mention of "salt" (*lavaṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding non-stone salts; it is not for the sake of rock-salt (*saindhava*), since that is included under the term "stone. Furthermore, in the interpretation of "taste," the mention of salt is for the purpose of making it obligatory. "Beasts" includes both humans and animals: domestic and wild beasts, as well as humans who are likewise considered beasts. (10.86)
And all woven cloth that is dyed, as well as garments of hemp and linen—even if they should be undyed—as also fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs. (10.87)
The undertaking [of this rule] regarding hemp and other such materials is for the purpose of not dyeing them; likewise, medicinal herbs are not to be sold. 10.87.
Water, weapons, poison, meat, Soma, and all kinds of perfumes;
milk, alkaline salt, curd, clarified butter, oil, honey, molasses, and Kuśa grass. (10.88)

The mention of milk, curd, and ghee here is for the purpose of illustrating all products derived from milk; thus, whey, *kilāṭa* (half-coagulated milk), and so forth are also not to be sold. Furthermore, the mention of milk and the others is appropriately intended as an illustration (*pradarśanārtha*) due to their primacy, and not for the sake of an exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyārtha*). It is stated in another *Smṛti*: "Milk along with its derivatives. Since molasses was already prohibited by the word "flavor" (*rasa*) in the preceding verse, its specific mention here is for the sake of making it obligatory. In this case, there is an optional prohibition regarding other flavors. However, if molasses is not included under the word "flavor," then there is no such optionality regarding these flavors. By this, honey is also explained. (10.88)
All wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds; liquor, indigo, lac, and likewise all one-hoofed animals. (10.89)

Others read the word as *bahūn* (many). The prohibition regarding wild animals is for the sake of establishing a permanent rule (*nityārtha*). And thus, in the verse "those animals which are human," a choice (*vikalpa*) regarding domestic animals is understood. Furthermore, because of the mention of "single-hoofed animals" here, there is no option regarding horses, mules, and donkeys, nor regarding camels. However, for those who read "and all many single-hoofed animals," this repetition is for the purpose of specification: that many single-hoofed animals are not to be sold. This being the case, [verse 10.89].
Having generated a desire for agriculture, the farmer himself may sell pure sesame seeds that have not been kept for long, for the sake of dharma.

Because the sale of sesame seeds is generally prohibited, this [verse] constitutes a specific exception (*viśe�ṣāśraya*) that permits their sale under certain conditions. The use of the word "pure" (*śuddha*) is for the purpose of prohibiting sesame mixed with other substances. Alternatively, it shows that the word "sesame" (*tila*) has a restrictive sense; thus, this is not intended to illustrate other items, since the underlying reason is the same. [The sale is permitted] for the sake of dharma, when one is engaged in obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), or upon the loss of children or wife. The phrase "not kept long" prohibits waiting for a higher market price. This is the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for this rule. (10.90)
If one performs with sesame seeds any act other than giving them as food or as an ointment, he becomes a worm in a dog's excrement and sinks there together with his ancestors. (10.91)
One falls immediately by selling meat, lac, or salt;
a Brāhmaṇa who sells milk becomes a Śūdra within three days.
But by selling other commodities here out of desire, a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights. (10.93)

The demonstration of the gravity or lightness of meat and other substances by means of these two verses should be understood as being for the purpose of penance, so that there may be heavy penance for grave offenses and light penance for light ones. (10.93)
Condiments may be bartered for condiments, but salt must never be exchanged for sesame seeds;
prepared food may be exchanged for unprepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equal.

Because the exchange of salt for sesame seeds is forbidden, sesame seeds must be bartered for other liquids. Sesame seeds may be exchanged for grain such as rice and the like, but a *prastha* measure of them must be exchanged for exactly an equal *prastha* measure of that grain, and not for less on account of its lower value. (10.94)
A Kṣatriya who has fallen into misfortune may live by all this, even by everything;
by the phrase "by all," there is a counter-exception to the prohibition of forbidden goods for one who cannot subsist by the previous means.
However, he must never at any time consider his own livelihood to be superior [to that of a Brāhmaṇa]. 10.95.

This is a restatement of the prohibition against the higher mode of life; it is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) intended to censure that which was stated as "one must never [resort to] the higher mode of life. (10.95)
If one who is low by birth should live through superior occupations out of greed, the king, having deprived him of his wealth, should banish him immediately. 10.96.

Having confiscated all his property, a righteous king shall impose exile as a mandatory penalty. Although this teaching pertains specifically to a Kṣatriya by virtue of the context, nevertheless, because the underlying reason is the same, it should be understood to apply to Vaiśyas and Śūdras as well. 10.96.
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the well-performed duty of another; for by living according to the duty of another, one falls immediately from one's caste. 10.97

This is another declamatory statement (arthavāda) intended as a censure regarding the prohibition of practicing the livelihood and duties of a higher caste. [The verse states: "One's own duty (svadharma) or the duty of another (paradharma). However, on account of the context, the word *dharma* here refers specifically to the subject of livelihood (*vṛtti*). 10.97.
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may live even by the occupation of a Śūdra;
provided he does not perform forbidden acts, he should desist from it as soon as he is capable.
By implication, this is also intended for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. || 10.98 ||
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born, having fallen into distress regarding his children and wife, may live by the work of artisans. (10.99)
And from this it is understood that the crafts of artisans are far more degraded than the occupations of Śūdras; such is the livelihood of those who have fallen from their caste (varṇāpaśada). 10.99.
Those crafts and various arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served— these are the works of artisans.

The crafts of artisans include carpentry, blacksmithing, and so forth; the various arts include painting and so forth. These two verses should be understood as pertaining to times of distress for the sake of livelihood, according to the force of the context. || 10.100 ||

A Brāhmaṇa who does not follow the occupation of a Vaiśya, yet remains on his own path and is distressed by the lack of means of subsistence, should practice this dharma when he is suffering. || 10.101 ||

From the indicative mark (liṅga) that he "stands on his own path," it is understood that he does not even adopt the livelihood of a Kṣatriya. And thus, the acceptance of gifts from unworthy persons by a Brāhmaṇa is understood to be optional when the livelihoods of a Kṣatriya and others are unavailable; it is not, however, to be practiced in conjunction with them. (10.101)
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone; that the means of purification should become defiled—this is not tenable according to the Dharma. 10.102

Just as it has been stated that the performance of the duties of other castes immediately follows [the failure of one's own], so too, in the absence of the lightest among the censurable objects of acceptance—due to their relative gravity—the acceptance of what is improper (*asatpratigraha*) may occur from the heaviest of sources. Thus, in the absence of what is praiseworthy, one may accept from what is censurable; in its absence, from what is more censurable; and in the absence of even that, from what is most censurable. And so the author will say: "Or he should bestow his entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas. If this were not the case, it would not be desirable. Therefore, the meaning of the scripture is exactly as stated. The statement that "it is pure and does not incur sin" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to commend the duty in times of distress (*āpaddharma*), or it is made on the grounds that it is a cause of only slight transgression. Alternatively, it may be intended to show the superior purpose of sustaining life, by which this person, remaining alive, will be able to avoid further transgressions and remove his unwholesome state. (10.102)
“No fault arises for Brahmins from teaching, from officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts—even if they are censurable—for they are like fire and water. (10.103)

In this context, there is no permission for the reprehensible acts of teaching and officiating at sacrifices, because the mention of those two is intended as praise for the acceptance of gifts from the unworthy. And it is only one who is qualified [for receiving gifts] who is addressed by the rule, "He may accept gifts from all"; however, one is not qualified for the reprehensible acts of teaching and officiating at sacrifices. Thus, being so, this too is explained as a mere explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), just like the previous one. 10.103.
He who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, eats food from whatever source it may come, is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud. 10.104
Ajīgarta, driven by hunger, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not tainted by sin, as he was merely acting to counteract his hunger.
Desiring dog-meat in his distress, yet discerning between dharma and adharma, Vāmadeva did not defile himself for the sake of preserving his life. (10.106)
Afflicted by hunger in the lonely forest, the great ascetic Bhāradvāja, together with his son,
accepted many cows from Bṛhadtakṣṇu.
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.

The five verses [10.104–108], which authorize the consumption of all kinds of food when life is at stake, should be understood as commendatory statements (*arthavāda*) regarding the actions of others.
From receiving gifts, from officiating at sacrifices, and likewise from teaching—receiving gifts is the lowest of these and is censured for a Brahmin after death. (10.109)

On account of the context, this is a censure of accepting gifts from the unworthy; by implication, its purpose is to praise the livelihood of officiating at sacrifices and teaching when these are only slightly censurable. This being the case, it is understood that one should not engage in accepting gifts from the unworthy for the sake of a livelihood when slightly censurable officiating or teaching is available. Otherwise, the censure of accepting gifts from the unworthy—which is prescribed as a rule for times of distress—would result in a contradiction with the preceding scripture, which is not desired. Therefore, it should be understood that the praise of engaging [in officiating or teaching] is achieved through that censure. And it has been stated that this is for the sake of establishing the proper sequence. Here, he states the reason: || 10.109 ||
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed by those who have been refined through sacraments;
however, the acceptance of gifts may be performed even from a Śūdra of the lowest birth.
Since this is so, therefore the sequence as it has been taught should be practiced. || 10.110 ||
Sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings;
however, that caused by accepting gifts is removed by renunciation and by austerity alone. (10.111)

From the context, this "acceptance" (pratigraha) should be understood as the acceptance of what is improper; the word *asat* is not explicitly read here as a modifier for "acceptance" due to the fear of violating the meter. Furthermore, the instruction here regarding recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), renunciation (*tyāga*), and austerity (*tapas*)—which were taught in the section on expiation—is for the purpose of praise, not for the purpose of an injunction. || 10.111 ||
A Brahmin who cannot subsist otherwise may gather grains from various sources even by means of *śiloñcha*;
for gathering by *śila* is better than receiving gifts, and gathering by *uñcha* is praised even more than that. (10.112)

Regarding the alternative of accepting gifts from the unworthy, [the livelihood] is by means of *śila* (gleaning) and *uñcha* (gathering ears of grain). These two are to be understood as "difficult to maintain. Some say they are [difficult to maintain] compared to accepting gifts from the worthy; for it is argued that praise for the virtuous is not appropriate in the case of *śila* and *uñcha* due to their being forms of accepting from the unworthy. However, because accepting from the unworthy is extremely base, these two are superior to it. As for the statement, "For those two are difficult to maintain by those who have not disciplined themselves," that is to be disregarded. Because even if one who subsists by *śila* and *uñcha* possesses self-restraint (*ātmanigraha*), there will nonetheless inevitably arise in him a deficiency in his ritual duties regarding the gods, guests, and dependents. Furthermore, self-restraint is prescribed specifically regarding accepting from the unworthy, based on the scriptural injunction: "One should not satisfy oneself with that [gift]. Moreover, self-restraint is more intense when the substance is already present; likewise, there is a restriction of effort in the acquisition, preservation, and distribution of wealth. Furthermore, even for one who subsists by *śila* and *uñcha*, there is the taint of accepting from the unworthy through *śila* and *uñcha*, because of the phrase "from that" (*tatas*), which refers without distinction to all cultivators. These two are what are here called *śila* and *uñcha*. This is known from the fact that one lives by gleaning and gathering as a means of avoiding acceptance from the unworthy, and from the mark (*liṅga*) of the phrase "from that. Thus, these two—*śila* and *uñcha*—belong to the category of accepting from the worthy. In this way, neither the entitlement (*adhikāra*) nor the mark is abandoned. It is understood that the praise for the virtuous is used in a figurative sense (*guṇavṛtti*). In the absence of that [virtue], there would be acceptance from the unworthy, as was stated regarding officiating at sacrifices and teaching. (10.112)
A king should be entreated by learned *snātaka* brahmins who are perishing, desiring base metals or wealth; however, if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned. (10.113)

And this acceptance of gifts is to be understood as being from a king who is not a Kṣatriya—that is, from one outside the royal caste—or even from a Kṣatriya king, provided he is free from greed and abides by the scriptures. But the Teacher says: this is the primary rule regarding acceptance only from a Kṣatriya king. One may accept base goods made of wood, such as beds and seats, which are of little value; or wealth such as cattle and gold, when requested, if there is no other means of procuring property, and for the sake of maintaining one's family, children, and religious duties during times of distress or famine. (10.113)
From a cultivated field, one may take unprepared grain, as well as cattle, goats, sheep, gold, grain, and food; among these, each preceding item is less blameworthy than the one following it.
In the renunciation of each subsequent [stage], there is spiritual advancement. || 10.114 ||
There are seven righteous ways of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, professional labor, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous. 10.115

Inheritance (*dāya*) refers to ancestral property or the wealth of a relative. Gain (*lābha*) is the discovery of a treasure-trove or a distribution [of property] resulting from some mutual assistance. Purchase (*kraya*) and victory (*jaya*) are well known. Lawful investment (*prayoga*) is interest-bearing lending (*kusīda*). Application to work (*karmayoga*) refers to agriculture and trade not performed by oneself. Acceptance of gifts from the virtuous (*satpratigraha*) has already been explained. Among these, inheritance and gain are common to all four castes because there is no prohibition against them. Regarding purchase, they dispute: some say it belongs to all four, others say it belongs only to the Vaiśya, on the grounds that it is not fitting for Brāhmaṇas and the others to receive benefit through the means of purchase. If that were so, then Brāhmaṇas and the others could not even consume vegetables after purchasing them. Others, however, considering that the prohibition applies to making a living through buying and selling, maintain that Brāhmaṇas and the others may use purchased goods for consumption, giving, and so forth. As for victory, because of the mention of its being "lawful" (*dharmya*), it is distinguished for the Kṣatriya over the others. Investment and application to work, when the Vaiśya’s livelihood is engaged in, are indeed more lawful for the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya. For agriculture, trade, and lending are permitted without distinction for the Vaiśya. Yet, because of the mention of their being "lawful," we consider that for him too, the accomplishment of a specific prosperity through non-self-performed work is not contradictory. This being the case, since these means of livelihood such as inheritance are designated as lawful, Brāhmaṇas and the others who possess wealth through these specific livelihoods like inheritance would not necessarily be restricted to occupations such as officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*). It is like the alms of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). Now, this verse has another meaning: just as for a Brāhmaṇa in his normal state acceptance of gifts and so forth are lawful, so too other optional acts taught for times of distress (*āpad-kalpa*) should be understood as lawful for Brāhmaṇas and the others in the absence [of their primary duties]. And that being so, the praise of performing prescribed acts is for the purpose of maintaining oneself and one's family, as it demonstrates an excellence of purpose achieved. And thus he says: 10.115. A Brāhmaṇa, unable to subsist by his own duty, may live according to the duty of a Kṣatriya; if he is unable even by that, he may resort to the duty of a Vaiśya, provided he does not engage in what is forbidden. (10.115) A Brāhmaṇa, unable to subsist by his own duty—that is, by teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts—may live according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, which consists of protecting the people and wielding the sword. If he is unable even by that, he may resort to the duty of a Vaiśya, which consists of agriculture, trade, and lending. Provided he does not engage in what is forbidden, such as the sale of salt and the like. But how can there be a lack of subsistence for one who possesses the knowledge of the Veda? Because of the rule: "One should not give instruction to one who does not offer a fee" (2.241), and because of the rule regarding the teacher's fee: "He should not refuse a pupil who has come for instruction" (2.240). Also, because of the rule: "If he is unable to maintain himself, he may seek wealth from kings, from persons who do not offer sacrifice, and from those who have not drunk the Soma juice" (4.33). Furthermore, because of the rule: "When the teacher is dead, the pupil should wait for him as long as life lasts" (2.242). Therefore, the inability to subsist arises from the failure to obtain pupils, or from the death of the teacher, or from the pupil's departure to his own home. Or, if he is unable to subsist by his own duty, it is because of the non-availability of pupils or the non-existence of the aforementioned objects of acceptance.
