Learning, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury—these are the ten means of livelihood. 10.116.

Whatever is prohibited for someone due to their specific duty (*dharma*) is permitted for that person in this particular state. For example, "teaching [the Veda] for the sake of wealth is [permitted] for a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth, in the case of one who has reached a state of distress regarding his son or wife. And having done so, it is said that there are ten means of livelihood. Others, however, consider the mention of knowledge (*vidyā*) and the rest to be for the purpose of demonstrating steadfastness (*dhṛti*); because knowledge and the other means do not become causes of livelihood without steadfastness. When followed by steadfastness, these are sufficient for livelihood. Therefore, since steadfastness must be practiced in every situation, this instruction is intended for the sake of steadfastness. (10.116)
Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor even a Kṣatriya should ever practice usury;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may indeed give a small amount out of compassion to a person of evil character.

The meaning is: "even in times of distress. This being so, by the logic of the "stick and cake" (the principle of the obvious), there is an absolute prohibition against a Brāhmaṇa’s engaging in usury even in the case of the primary rule (*prakṛti*), and even under the alternative view that he may not perform the work himself. Likewise, in the Mantra, a censure of usury is heard: "What do your cows do among the Kīkaṭas? and so forth. Alternatively, this verse may be intended to praise other modes of livelihood, or for the sake of establishing the proper order. This being so, even while other modes of livelihood permitted in times of distress exist, he should not practice this one himself; rather, he should do so only in their absence, because of its gravity. And thus it has been said regarding the wording of the Mantra. (10.117)
Even when taking a fourth part as his share during times of distress, a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is released from sin.

Even when taking a fourth part unjustly during times of distress, a Kṣatriya king who is appointed to protect the subjects is liberated from sin arising from such unjust appropriation of shares and the like, provided he protects the subjects. This being the case, the king’s taking of a fourth part from the Kṣatriyas is a commendatory statement (arthavāda) for the purpose of protecting the subjects. By this... [10.118]
Victory belongs to him who follows his own duty; he must not turn his back in battle.
Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapon, he may collect the lawful tribute.
While protecting his subjects, he is thus described as follows: || 10.119 ||
The toll for grain from the Vaiśyas shall be one-eighth; for other goods, it shall be one-twentieth, with a minimum of one kārṣāpaṇa.
Likewise, Śūdras who provide labor, as well as artisans and craftsmen, [shall pay this].

The king should take an eighth part of the grain from the subjects, according to his own circumstances; and from those engaged in monetary transactions, a twentieth part of the profit as a toll. This should be understood as a restatement of what was previously mentioned. Śūdras should be the laborers for the work, as well as the artisans and craftsmen; and the designation "artisan" and "craftsman" follows the maxim of the cow and the bull (where the specific is included within the general). 10.120.
But a Śūdra, seeking a livelihood in times of distress, may serve a Kṣatriya if he so desires.
A Śūdra who desires to live should seek to serve a Kṣatriya; in his absence, he should indeed seek to serve a wealthy Vaiśya. || 10.121 ||
And this being the case, the propitiation of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is the sole means of livelihood for the Śūdra. 10.121.
For the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both, one should serve the Brāhmaṇas.
For a Śūdra, this service to the Brāhmaṇas is both a means of livelihood and a source of dharma. This being the case, this praise of him is appropriate:
"For one who has attained the name of 'Brāhmaṇa,' that indeed is his fulfillment of all duties. (10.122)
Since this is so, therefore:
"Service to Brahmins alone is proclaimed as the distinguished duty of a Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs beyond this," [is not his true duty].
The propitiation of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas becomes fruitless for him. 10.123.

Alternatively, whatever else he performs besides this—such as the *pākayajña* and other rites—that becomes fruitless for him. And this being the case, it is understood through the force of the instruction that this censure of prescribed acts is intended as a praise of service to Brahmins. 10.123.
He should provide for his livelihood from his own family estate as is appropriate, having regard for their capacity, their skill, and the number of dependents they support. (10.124)

Even when the service of a Brahmin is for the sake of dharma and artha, his livelihood must be provided by them; this follows as a matter of course even for one who has resorted [to service] for the sake of livelihood, let alone for a Śūdra who has no other means of subsistence. Furthermore, his service should be like that of a son, not by way of a hired wage, since he has approached him for the sake of dharma. And this applies even to such a Śūdra. (10.124)

"Leftover food should be given. This is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the prohibited matter, namely that which was stated: "One should not give instruction to a Śūdra, nor leftover food. This being the case, this prohibition should be understood as referring to a Śūdra who is not dependent [on a Brāhmaṇa]. On the other hand, this counter-exception must refer to a Śūdra who is dependent on a Brāhmaṇa, by virtue of the force of the context. [The phrase] "worn-out garments" [is explained as follows].
Those things consumed by Brahmins are taken [as examples];
this refers primarily to the teaching on the essenceless substances, such as the shriveled grains of corn.
And his belongings have become worn out. || 10.125 ||
Seats, beds, coverings, pillows, and so forth—even such things as these. || 10.125 ||
There is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra, nor does he deserve any sacramental rite; he has no entitlement to dharma, yet there is no prohibition against him from dharma. (10.126)

The statement, “There is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra,” implies by its force that he is not prohibited from acts such as killing a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, as far as they are possible. What, then, is prohibited? It is the eating of garlic and similar things, because the prohibition of eating those constitutes the duty (*dharma*) of the twice-born. And thus it has been said: “This has been stated in its entirety regarding what may and may not be eaten by the twice-born. This restatement is for the sake of what follows. Why, then, is there no such sin arising from eating forbidden food for a Śūdra? Because he does not deserve the sacraments, such as initiation (*upanayana*), as the author states by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*): “The fourth is of a single birth (*ekajāti*); this is a restatement of that fact. This being the case, due to the absence of those sacraments, he has no entitlement to religious duty (*dharma*), such as the *agnihotra* and other Vedic rites. But how is this specific prohibition to be understood, given that he says: “There is no prohibition from dharma”? It is understood to mean that there is no prohibition from the *smārta* (tradition-based) *pākayajña* and other such rites. And thus, these are prescribed for him. Vyāsa has likewise stated: “It is certain that a Śūdra does not fall [from sin] here; nor is it that he does not deserve the sacraments here; nor does he fail to enjoy the dharma enjoined by the Vedas; nor is there a prohibition against his performing dharma in the *smṛtis*. Alternatively, all of this—namely, that “there is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra,” “he does not deserve the sacraments,” and “he has no entitlement to dharma”—is not to be spoken of, as it contradicts previous scriptures. However, the following is commenced for the sake of what follows: “There is no prohibition from dharma. And thus he will say later: “But those seeking dharma, knowing dharma...,” and “In whatever way one follows the conduct of the virtuous... Or rather, this commencement is for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*). For certain rites, such as the *pākayajña*, are permitted for a Śūdra even without mantras. By the performance of these, this Śūdra has an entitlement to dharma by necessity, depending upon a Brāhmaṇa. And there is no prohibition against this. Such being the case, since there is both a prescription and a prohibition, the performance of these acts would be optional. Thus it is established that for him, there is spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) from performing them, and an absence of transgression (*pratyavāya*) from not performing them. By the force of the context, this refers to one who depends on a Brāhmaṇa, or perhaps to another. And so, with this in mind, he says: [Verse 10.126]
But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous, do not incur blame for omitting the sacred mantras; rather, they receive praise. (10.127)

"Practicing what is not forbidden"—by the context, this refers to Śūdras who have taken refuge with Brāhmaṇas. Nor does this prohibition regarding mantras imply that he is permitted to participate in the Agnihotra and other such rites; for it has been stated: "They do not incur sin, provided they exclude the mantras. Since the Śūdra is excluded from the Agnihotra and other Vedic rites by direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*), it is therefore said that those seeking merit (*dharmepsavaḥ*) have an optional right (*pākṣika-adhikāra*) to perform those matters prescribed in the Smṛtis—namely, the fixed purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) and the *pākayajñas*, such as the establishment of the domestic fire (*āvasathya-ādhāna*), the *pārvaṇa* and *vaiśvadeva* sacrifices, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), and so forth. And thus says another Smṛti: "Some say that one should sacrifice himself by means of *pākayajñas*. And so it is [in verse 10.127].
For in whatever measure one who is free from malice abides in virtuous conduct, in that same measure he, being blameless, attains both this world and the next. (10.128)
The praise of Śūdra-like conduct regarding the rites prescribed by the Smṛtis is intended to encourage their performance. 10.128.
For even a Śūdra who is capable should not amass wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves. (10.129)

A Śūdra who has acquired sufficient wealth through highly profitable crafts and other means of livelihood might, especially by means of giving gifts, cause great Brahmins to fall from their own duty (svadharma) through the inducement of accepting gifts from a Śūdra. This, however, is not the intended meaning; for there is no fault whatsoever in one who performs what is enjoined by the scriptures, even if it results in injury to others. If such were the case, then there would be fault even for one giving at the *nava-śrāddha* and other rites, since that too causes injury to another. Indeed, he who honors virtuous Brahmins with wealth and honor does not cause them injury. Therefore, this is not the meaning. Nor can it be accepted that a Śūdra, out of an excess of wealth, should engage in the oppression of Brahmins; for in that case, everyone—Brahmins and others alike—would be subject to such restrictions. What specific distinction is there in the Śūdra alone, such that his accumulation of wealth is thus forbidden? This, then, is the other meaning: it is not only constant giving that is permitted for a Śūdra, but rather, he must also perform giving for the sake of spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Thus, the prohibition is for this purpose: that he should not accumulate wealth. Or, as it has been said: "Their livelihood should be provided by him from his own family according to what is appropriate," and so forth. This being the case, this instruction is for a Śūdra who is dependent upon a Brahmin. For even a capable Śūdra should not accumulate wealth. Likewise, another Smṛti states: "He whom an Ārya may depend upon must support him even if he is impoverished; and the latter [the Ārya] must support the former; his accumulation of wealth shall be for that purpose. (10.129)
These duties for times of distress have been proclaimed for the four social classes;
by properly following them, they attain the supreme goal. 10.130

Because one perceives a superior purpose in maintaining oneself, one’s family, and one’s life, and because such acts are connected to the system of Dharma, it is logical that there must be a firm adherence to obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) such as the *agnihotra*, which are performed for that purpose—as expressed in passages such as "those who perform these correctly," and so forth. Alternatively, this statement of praise is appropriate in view of the fact that actions yielding great fruits involve only a slight attachment to transgression; it is intended to summarize the duties pertaining to times of distress (*āpaddharma*). 10.130.
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter I shall declare the auspicious rule for penance.
In this context, the first half-verse is for the purpose of summarizing all the rules, while the latter half is for the purpose of introducing the expiations. || 10.131 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the work composed by Bhāruci.
The eleventh chapter:
[One should give] to one seeking offspring, to one intending to sacrifice, to a traveler, and to one who has given away all his property.
For the sake of one's guru, mother, father, or servants, or for the sake of Vedic study, one may approach those who are afflicted. || 11.1 ||

One should know these ten types of *snātaka* Brahmins who live as beggars for the sake of dharma; gifts should be given to them from those who possess nothing, according to the excellence of their learning. (11.2)

Here an objection is raised: Since it was stated immediately prior to the conclusion of the tenth chapter, "Henceforth I shall proclaim the auspicious rules for penance (*prāyaścitta*)," should not the section on penance itself have been introduced here with the verse beginning, "One who fails to perform the prescribed duty," and so forth? Otherwise, the introduction of an irrelevant topic and the interruption of the subject at hand would be improper; for all this ought to have been taught within the sections on the duties of the *snātaka* and the duties in times of distress (*āpad-dharma*), and not here. To this it is replied: Because these two [topics] find no place even in the two aforementioned sections due to their association [with the subject of penance], their mention here is appropriate. Let there be no inconsistency arising from a division of the sections, where one of two mutually connected topics is assigned to a different section by being mentioned elsewhere. This [verse] is an explanation of the purpose of the commencement already indicated, concerning the two verses. Furthermore, one should not beg for an object already in one's possession, because of the statement: "Gifts should be given to these who are destitute. Here, giving (*dāna*) is enjoined, not begging. For begging is not to be prescribed, as it is already implied by the context of the occasion (*nimitta*). He shows this by stating that "there is no difference in the fruit for those who are destitute, because the instruction is equal"; he says "from both" because of the rule (*niyama*) and the specific nature of the gift. If there were no distinction in the fruit based on the specific nature of the gift, no one would exert themselves toward excellence in giving, disregarding the scripture. Alternatively, since the rule dependent upon giving has been enjoined, and because of that rule, excellence in the gift must necessarily result in excellence of merit through the performance of the rule according to one's ability. Thus, even though the instruction is equal, it is impossible to deny that a distinction in the fruit arises from the distinction in the gift. And so it has been said.
"Indeed, it is specifically because of the recipient and through faith that one obtains the fruit of a gift after death, whether it be small or great. (11.1–2)
For food, together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), must be given to these foremost of the twice-born;
for others, unprepared food is not prescribed outside the sacrificial altar.

This is a restatement of a rule regarding a specific kind of food: cooked food alone must necessarily be given to other guests outside the sacrificial altar. This reiterates the aforementioned gift of food to guests; as for their ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), there is neither a prescription nor a prohibition. (11.3)
The king, however, should bestow all kinds of jewels upon the Brahmins learned in the Vedas as is appropriate, and likewise provide sacrificial fees for the sake of the sacrifice. (11.4)

But for the king, there is no such restriction because of his great wealth. Thus, apart from those seeking to establish a lineage and so forth, the king must necessarily grant land to other *snātakas* for the purpose of maintenance and enjoyment; and that it may be for the sake of sacrifice is understood from the force of this opening statement. "It should not be given to one who does not intend to sacrifice"—it is with reference to this connection that the following is said. (11.4)
If one who has already taken a wife obtains another wife by begging for her, his reward is merely pleasure; however, the offspring belongs to the giver of the wealth. || 11.5 ||

Regarding a wife who is endowed with both virtue (*dharma*) and offspring (*prajā*), this [rule] does not permit a second wife with one's own property. For when a second wife is already endowed with virtue and offspring, there is no occasion for obtaining another. And so says another *Smṛti*: "When a wife is endowed with virtue and offspring, one should not take another. This being the case, this is a prohibition against acquiring a second wife for one who has already fulfilled the duties of a householder. The censure is based on the side of begging. In that regard, just as the lineage of the giver of wealth is the fruit for one who becomes a part of that [marriage], so too is the lineage of the girl’s father the fruit even upon the acquisition of his own property; from this also, such censure can be inferred. Since the word "property" (*dravya*) applies to both cases, a maiden can indeed be designated by the word "property," because this verse is intended to prohibit the acquisition of a second wife for one who has already fulfilled the duties of a householder. However, in this sense, the context is not supported, since this [verse] supports a different context. The meaning of the verse is stated: for one who has fulfilled the duties of a householder and is begging for the sake of acquiring a second wife, [wealth] must not be given as a rule. And here, a declamatory censure (*arthavāda*) has been stated. This being the case, it should not be given even to one who is begging. And thus, this is an exception to the previous [rule]: "It should not be given to one who lacks lineage," as stated in the verse concerning lineage and so forth. It should be understood that the restriction regarding giving is prescribed for begging for the sake of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*); but for begging for the sake of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), there is neither a mandate nor a prohibition for giving. And so he shows: 11.5 ||
He who possesses enough food for three years to maintain his dependents,
or even more than that, is not entitled to drink the Soma.

This being the case, this instruction should be understood as referring by implication to the *soma* sacrifice performed for specific desires (*kāmya-soma*), because it is the performance of the obligatory (*nitya*) *soma* that is permitted even when it causes an obstruction to one's livelihood, precisely because it is obligatory. And that being so, the rule regarding giving at that very time is appropriate here, namely, "one should give to one who is about to sacrifice," as previously stated. This mention of *soma* is intended to indicate all ritual acts performed for specific desires, since the underlying reason is the same. (11.6)
Therefore, that twice-born man who drinks Soma when the substance is very small— though he may have drunk Soma before— he does not obtain its fruit.

By transgressing the rule of necessity (*niyama*), not only does his performance of that rite become fruitless, but there is also further sin (*pratyavāya*). This transgression would result in fruitlessness and sin even for one who has not previously drunk the *soma*; how much more so, then, for another? This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended as a censure. Furthermore, by the statement "even for one who has not previously drunk the *soma*," which is an expression of excellence for the sake of praise, it is not possible to infer a non-observance of the obligatory (*nitya*) drinking of *soma*. Such being the case, from this very mark (*liṅga*) of the excellence of praise, the non-cessation of the obligatory is understood. Thus, for the sake of the obligatory, it must be given as a rule; in other cases, however, there is no such rule. Now, the rule for a capable donor is stated. (11.7)
One who is capable of giving to strangers while his own people live in misery—this is a mere semblance of dharma; it is like the taste of honey followed by the taste of poison.

This being the case, it follows by implication that one should not give to others at the expense of one's own kin. He will later mention "one's own kin" as consisting of sons, wife, and so forth. For otherwise, if one gives by transgressing against one's own kin, that constitutes a "falling into the middle" for the donor; like honey, its "falling"—that is, its taste—is pleasant upon contact; it is fame. Although such fame may bring happiness to those who seek it, it should nevertheless be understood as being like the taste of poison, because of the arising of demerit (*pratyavāya*) due to its bitter flavor. Thus he shows that this is a semblance of dharma (*dharmapratirūpaka*), meaning it is actually non-dharma (*adharma*) for the donor. Why? Because of the transgression of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to effect desistance from such an act. (11.8)
Whatever one performs for the sake of the afterlife by oppressing one's dependents results in unhappiness both while living and after death. (11.9)
One's parents, children, wife, and dependents [must be supported]. As it has been said: "Desiring to uplift one's teachers and dependents. And likewise, another Smṛti states:
"Even if they have committed a hundred improper acts, an aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son must be maintained; so Manu declared."

Therefore, whatever else one performs for the sake of the afterlife—whether sacrificial rites (*iṣṭa*) or charitable works (*pūrta*)—by obstructing them, it is proper that its result be unpleasant both here and in the hereafter, due to the arising of demerit (*pratyavāya*). Others, however, read the quarter-verse of the preceding śloka as "madhvāsvādo viṣāpātaḥ," but the meaning remains exactly as stated above. 11.9.
If the sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by even a single limb—especially in the case of a Brahmin while a righteous king is ruling—[he must perform expiation]. || 11.10 ||

He will state that even for one who is begging for that purpose, there is the giving away of the sacrificial implements when they are incomplete. "By a single part" means by any small amount whatsoever that completes the sacrificial implements; the meaning is that this applies especially to a Brāhmaṇa. "On that account": this being so, the giving away of even a single [implement] is permitted for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are frequent performers of sacrifice (*yāyajūka*), because of the statement "especially for a Brāhmaṇa. When the king is righteous, he who knows the Dharma—indeed, he who knows this—[is the one concerned]. By this, two occasions are introduced in the scripture; when such a king exists here, this giving away is taught. But why is that so? Because he says the following (11.10).

If there should be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but lacks the means for sacrifice and has no water, one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice. (11.11)

And one who has few sacrificial rites should possess many cattle; he may be deficient in ritual action. Even if one’s sacrificial rites are not deficient, if he does not drink the Soma juice, then one should take that wealth from his household; and this applies when such [wealth] is unavailable [to others]. 11.11.

He may take three or two [grains] at will from the house of a Śūdra; because of the context of the "limbs" (aṅga), three or two limbs are connected [to the act]. And his taking [of these] is due to the abundance of limbs and his being of a lower caste. There is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) regarding this:
"For there is no entitlement whatsoever for a Śūdra in sacrifices. (11.12)
And thus Vyāsa said: "Wealth was created by the Creator for the sake of sacrifice; the sacrificer and the protector were likewise created as man.
Therefore, all wealth should be employed solely for sacrifice; it is not praised to use it for the sake of personal desire."

But will it not be stated that there is a prohibition against performing a sacrifice with the wealth of a Śūdra, by such passages as, "One should not [accept] wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice"? [Response: In that case, the prohibition applies to what is obtained through begging; however, this present act of taking from another is a distinct matter. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Alternatively, the prohibition in that other case refers only to the wealth of a Śūdra taken alone, whereas here, when two or three auxiliary requirements are lacking and wealth is impossible to obtain otherwise, it is proper to perform the sacrifice after taking it from him. Or rather, this shall be so in this very instance due to a specific scriptural statement, since the distinction in the occasion [for the rule] exists. There is no excessive burden on a scriptural statement, because the scripture is intent upon providing instruction. Now, this act of taking is prescribed from Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, as it is impossible [to obtain it] from a Śūdra. (11.12)

If there is one who possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, and another who possesses a thousand cows but does not perform sacrifices—one may take [wealth] from the households of both of them without hesitation. (11.13)
This verse has been explained by its very recitation. || 11.13 ||
One may take from a non-giver who is constantly taking [from others];
in this way, his fame spreads and his merit increases. 11.14

And this person is called a *brāhmaṇa* who is constantly engaged in taking. He is one who, having taken wealth, does not employ it as a means for performing sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) or works of public utility (*pūrta*). Therefore, this is called "taking" even when he does not give it away; however, this is not the case for one who is constantly engaged in taking yet is habitually devoted to sacrifice. This being so, the preceding verse should be understood as referring specifically to the *kṣatriya*. Others, however, consider the one "constantly engaged in taking" to be a usurer—one who takes interest prohibited by the scriptures and is not disposed toward sacrifice. Under this interpretation, caste (*jāti*) is not intended to be significant; thus, there is the mantra: "The cows produce milk for you among the Kīkaṭas," and so forth. (11.14)
In the same way, having fasted for six meals during the seventh meal-time,
one may take from a person of low conduct for the sake of not providing for tomorrow.

Taking from another is permitted as before, even on the grounds of distress caused by hunger for oneself or one's family; this applies especially to a Brāhmaṇa, as the preceding rule continues. Because of the statement "for the sake of not providing for tomorrow," the amount to be taken is authorized as sufficient for one day and night, and no more. Furthermore, the phrase "from one of inferior occupation" is stated for the purpose of establishing the proper order. Thus, another Smṛti states: "One should first take from an inferior; if that is unavailable, even from an equal;
but if these are impossible, one may take even from a superior who is righteous."

This being the case, this same sequence should be understood to apply to the former [the father] as well. And thus Gautama says: "The taking of property from a Śūdra for the purpose of accomplishing a marriage, and in connection with the performance of religious duties, [is permitted]; likewise, even from a Śūdra in other circumstances. (11.15)

Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be obtained—since the mention of the threshing floor and so forth is made, this grain should be understood as intended for food; likewise, it is stated in the seventh meal [rule] that if he asks, it must be told to him if he inquires. 11.16.

If the owner of the property asks while [the thief] is asleep, he should wake him up and answer once he has awakened; or rather, it should be told to that owner of the property who asks, provided he asks while awake about the thief who stole the wealth—it should not be told by waking him up by force. Or else, if the king or the king’s men, acting on behalf of the owner of the property, have brought him before the king and ask, then he should speak. Thus Gautama says: "He should speak when questioned by the king. This rule regarding the reporting of the theft of another's property is to be understood as applicable even in cases of withholding food or obstructing a sacrifice, since the underlying reason is the same. (11.16)

The property of a Brāhmaṇa must never be seized by a Kṣatriya—not even under any circumstances whatsoever, including those states already described. By this same principle of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikā*), the prohibition should be understood to apply to Vaiśyas and Śūdras as well. There is no prohibition against seizing the property of a Brāhmaṇa who is not a Brāhmaṇa-possessor (*brahmasva*); as it has been said: "And from one who is constantly taking from those who do not give" (MDh 11.14).
But when two Brāhmaṇas are both robbers or devoid of religious rites, one may take property from them for the sake of subsistence. || 11.17 ||

This should be understood as a counter-exception (pratiprasava) to the previous prohibition for a specific reason; and thus, even for a Brahmin who is superior, this is permitted by a [younger] Brahmin. 11.17.
He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a boat and carries both of them across. 11.18

[The king] is both the owner of wealth and its protector. This is said regarding the king who, by the pretext of obstructing sacrifices, seizes the one who has already taken wealth and does not punish him, but rather honors him—because he is favoring others. Furthermore, this wealth being taken from the wicked for the sake of sacrifice becomes as if given by the king himself through his indifference toward the virtuous. For it is said: "He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous... (11.18).
The wise know that the wealth of those who are devoted to sacrifice is the property of the gods;
but the riches of those who do not sacrifice are said to be the property of the asuras.
Therefore, it is appropriate for the king to maintain equanimity toward that matter, having considered this technical definition from the treatise; and such being the case: 11.19.
A righteous lord of the earth should not inflict punishment upon him;
for it is through the folly of the Kṣatriya that the Brāhmaṇa perishes from hunger. (11.20)
And this characteristic of a minor offense (kṣudra-liṅga) is to be understood as applying to both cases, because they belong to the same context. || 11.20 ||

Having ascertained his circle of servants and his own family members, and having understood their learning and character, the lord of the earth should provide them with a righteous means of livelihood.
This is stated specifically regarding a servant whose very nature is to be exhausted by hunger. 11.21.

Having provided for his livelihood, the king should protect him on all sides—even from mere talk of bravery and such qualities, let alone from thieves; for the king obtains a sixth part of the merit from that which is protected by him. (11.22)
The taking of a one-sixth share of the dharma should be understood as a figurative statement (arthavāda) for the sake of protection. || 11.22 ||
A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not beg for wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of performing a sacrifice.

Even if he is a Brahmin, being destitute, a deficiency of two or three limbs is indeed commendable; however, one who lacks wealth should not take two limbs from a Śūdra. Alternatively, it is begging from a Śūdra that is prohibited here, not the acquisition of what is obtained unasked. Thus it is understood that what is received unasked is superior to begging. And so it has been said: "The acceptance of goods that have come unasked is superior to gleaning ears of grain (*śila*) and picking up single grains (*uñcha*); one should know that to be a form of non-acceptance. But for one who possesses no wealth at all, even everything required for sacrifice may be taken from a Śūdra.
For a sacrificer who begs becomes a Caṇḍāla after death. || 11.23 ||

This is a deprecatory explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended to prevent the performance of prohibited acts. How so? So that he might not practice what is censured. Alternatively, regarding the acceptance of gifts from all sources mentioned for one who has neglected obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), this is a prohibition against accepting such gifts for the sake of Vedic (*śrauta*) or traditional (*smārta*) sacrifices. In such a state, while the acceptance of forbidden things might be permitted, begging from a Śūdra is not. However, begging even from a Śūdra is not prohibited when it is for the purpose of maintaining dependents. Furthermore, for the sake of optional sacrifices (*kāmyayajña*), there is no such thing as accepting gifts from an improper source; therefore, why would there be a prohibition of it? This being the case, he who begs from a Śūdra for the sake of an optional sacrifice transgresses both rules: the rule against accepting improper gifts and the rule against begging. Alternatively, this is a praise of taking [gifts] from others (i.e., from those other than a Śūdra): "A Brahmin should not beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice, O knower of Dharma. How so? It is thus: even taking [gifts] from a Śūdra is permissible, but begging is not. (11.23)
That Brahmin who, having begged for wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, does not bestow it all,
goes to the state of a crane or a crow for a hundred years.

This statement has been commenced for the purpose of explaining the utilization of everything—whether begged for the sake of daily requirements or for the sake of optional rites—from Śūdras and from other twice-born (dvijāti) classes according to the rules. Now, this [next section] is commenced for the purpose of praising the prescribed dharma. 11.24.
He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of Brahmins—
that evil-souled man lives in the next world on the leavings of vultures.

That which is set aside and established for the sake of a deity is "the property of a god" (*devasvam*). By the force of the context, this refers to what is begged for the purpose of a sacrifice, and nothing else. The property of a Brāhmaṇa (*brāhmaṇasvam*) should likewise be understood as that which is accepted for the purpose of feeding Brāhmaṇas at *śrāddha* ceremonies and the like. Its inclusion here alongside the property of a god is for the sake of making a parallel statement. This being the case, that which is commonly known in the world as "the property of a god" is not what is intended here, because it would contradict the context. Furthermore, deities possess no sense of ownership, as they lack the capacity for agency (*anadhikārāt*). Moreover, regarding that which is designated as "the property of a god" according to the scriptures, it can only be called such at the very moment of its dedication, by virtue of the power of the intent (*uddeśasāmarthyāt*). That period of enjoyment by the deity is momentary; once that enjoyment by the deity has ceased, it is impossible to designate it as "the property of a god. Thus, everything begged for the purpose of a sacrifice must be employed solely for the sacrifice. Nothing at all should be set aside for one's own personal enjoyment. As for one who, out of delusion, does not employ it all [for the sacrifice], this is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning his violation of the rule. Alternatively, the mention of the well-known "property of a Brāhmaṇa" is for the sake of providing an illustrative example. (11.25)

One should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice at the end of each year for the purpose of expiating any failure in the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed. || 11.26 ||

If, however, due to incapacity, one should be unable to perform the animal and Soma sacrifices enjoined by the scriptures, then one should perform this Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the sake of expiation, in the event of being unable to perform the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*). This being the case, since there is no contradiction in the omission of an obligatory rite, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the Vedic expiation and the Vaiśvānara substitute. [Objection: But surely, because they serve the same purpose, there should be an option (*vikalpa*) between them. [Reply: No, for their identity of purpose is not directly perceived; rather, one is Vedic (*śrauta*) and the other is Smṛti-based (*smārta*). And thus, there is no option between two things that differ in their source of authority (*pramāṇa*). An option would be logical only if they were based on a single source of authority. Others, however, maintain that there is indeed an option; and so he will later state an option between the Vedic and Smṛti-based expiations for killing a Brahmin. This present rule, however, applies to the contingency (*āpadkalpa*) of omitting an obligatory rite. And this being so... 11.26. If a twice-born man performs a religious rite according to the rules for times of distress when he is not in distress, it has been determined that he does not obtain the fruit of that act in the hereafter. (11.27)

And this being so, one who possesses wealth should not perform the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice—which is optional with respect to animals or Soma—or a substitute for an expiation, by which [he might incur sin]. || 11.27 ||
By all the gods, the Sādhyas, the Brahmins, and the great seers,
who were terrified of death in times of calamity, this substitute rule was established.
And so it is said:
"He who is capable of following the primary rule, yet conducts himself according to a secondary rule, for that person of evil intellect there exists no fruit pertaining to the future life. (11.29)

Therefore, for one who exerts effort with supreme diligence for the sake of the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), this [penance] should apply in the event of incapacity; it does not apply when there is capacity. Furthermore, if someone, while engaged in the seizure of another's property and so forth during an attachment to worldly affairs (*dharmatantra*), should somehow be restrained by some royal officer, then even while being thus restrained— || 11.29 ||
A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not report anything to the king;
rather, by his own power alone, he should deal with those offending men who are his pupils. 11.30
Since one's own valor is more powerful than both one's own strength and the strength of a king, therefore a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own valor alone. (11.31)
But by what means? For this reason, he says: || 11.31 ||
"One should employ the Atharva-Angirasa hymns; this has been declared without hesitation.
For the word is indeed the weapon of a Brahmin; with that, the twice-born man may slay his enemies. (11.32)

This [section] is commenced for the purpose of permitting *abhicāra* (malevolent rites). How so? For he who stands as an obstacle to one intent on the practice of dharma is an enemy; yet, such an enemy becomes bound by his own good deeds (*sukṛta*). If that person has committed an offense and is not fit to be reported to the king, then for that reason, *abhicāra* is permitted. And this being the case, *abhicāra* must not be performed out of mere anger alone. Furthermore, as for what is stated in another *Smṛti* regarding the impurity-inducing nature of *abhicāra*—"*Abhicāra* and false accusation cause impurity"—that refers to one who performs *abhicāra* out of mere anger, because such a person lacks the qualification [to perform it]. And this being the case, this [text] will also prescribe an expiation for performing an *abhicāra* that should not have been performed: "One removes [the taint of] *abhicāra* by three *kṛcchra* penances. Others, however, explain this expiation as referring to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) whose duties have not been abandoned. Thus there is a contradiction between these two *Smṛtis*. First, a Brāhmaṇa who has thus studied the Veda and mastered the scriptures and rituals should overcome the situation where their performance is obstructed. But how should the other castes proceed? This is what is being said: [11.32]
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune by the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra by wealth; but the best of the twice-born by recitation and burnt offerings.

And here, the mention of "the best of the twice-born" (dvijottama) should be understood for the sake of providing an illustration, since it has already been stated that this [rule] applies to him. And thus, this is stated while remaining within the very context of the Brāhmaṇas. 11.33.
One who is a provider, an instructor, a speaker, and friendly is called a brahmin; one should not do anything unwholesome for him, nor should one utter harsh words toward him. 11.34.

This is the instruction for the king: when a Brahmin is thus intent on practicing the Dharma and is engaged in countering those who oppose him, the king must not say anything at all to him. Or, this is the instruction for those men who would harm a Brahmin: he must not be oppressed by relying on the king's power; for he is capable of destroying his enemies through magical incantations even while the king looks on and cries out. Therefore, one should do no evil toward him, nor should one utter harsh words. (11.34)

Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool; neither one who is afflicted by illness, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, should be the officiating priest of the Agnihotra. (11.35)

This prohibition concerns those things not yet obtained, such as a maiden and the like; its purpose is to praise the performer of all rites, such as the Agnihotra and others. That, moreover, should be examined for its propriety or impropriety. And this being so, he says the following: || 11.35 ||
For those who offer oblations [in this manner] fall into hell, as does he for whom they perform them;
therefore, the officiating priest (hotṛ) should be one skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas. || 11.36 ||

From this it is understood that the mention of the *agnihotra* is intended as an illustration for all ritual acts (*karman*). Therefore, priests endowed with such qualities are required for all [rites], not merely for the one who offers the *agnihotra*. Others say that this prohibition concerns the subject of substitutes (*pratinidhi*); just as the statement, "The fire-altar must not be built in the intermediate space nor in the sky," is a prohibition of what is otherwise impossible, intended to praise the connection with the gold plate (*rukma*), so too is this [prohibition]. Another says: This *agnihotra* belongs to the domestic fire (*gṛhya*); and in that case, there is the possibility of women and others [performing it], because of the scriptural injunction: "At will, the wife may offer the evening and morning oblations in the domestic fire. And this being so, even though she is married, as long as she remains a maiden, she should not offer the *aupāsana* fire; and a married woman remains a maiden for a year or three nights. Since there is thus a prohibition against her when [the possibility] has arisen, there is likewise a prohibition against young women and others when they have attained [that status]. However, this contradicts the latter half of the verse: "The *hotṛ* priest should be skilled in the sacrificial fires (*vaitāna*) and a master of the Vedas. Through the connection with the *agnihotra*, the rules regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) are stated. (11.36)

If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, does not give a horse as the sacrificial fee for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), he remains one who has not established the fires (anāhitāgni). (11.37)

And because of the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," there is no restrictive rule regarding the gift of a horse for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. Furthermore, even for a Brāhmaṇa, the gift of a horse is shown to be non-obligatory, as it depends upon one's wealth. Moreover, by the principle of cumulative application (*samuccaya*), the horse is included among the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). This other matter is stated in connection with the giving of the sacrificial fee at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*): sacrifices should have complete sacrificial fees. And this being so, he declares the fault that arises from a deficiency in the sacrificial fee. (11.37)
One who possesses faith and has conquered the senses should perform other meritorious deeds;
however, one should never, under any circumstances, perform sacrifices here with meager sacrificial fees.
This is the rule regarding the sacrificial fees for optional sacrifices; however, for obligatory rites, even those with small sacrificial fees are permitted. || 11.38 ||
A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys one's senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who lacks wealth should not perform a sacrifice.

For when there is a doubt regarding the undertaking of commenced obligatory (*nitya*) rites—given that their performance can somehow be accomplished—this prohibition concerning the purpose of optional (*kāmya*) rites is restated in these two verses. Indeed, by logic alone, the non-performance of defective optional rites is already established. Thus, this is not a prohibition of the obligatory rites, precisely because they are obligatory. The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that even defective obligatory rites lead to results. This further [point] is stated in connection with the context of the *agnihotra* sacrifice. (11.39)
A Brāhmaṇa who, out of desire, neglects the sacred fires of the Agnihotra shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.

This penance, the Cāndrāyaṇa, is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa who intentionally abandons the Agnihotra; however, if it is unintentional, this general penance applies. Furthermore, although this prescription of penance occurs outside of a specific ritual context, it is intended as a praise for the performance of even those obligatory rites that have been neglected. 11.40.
Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice, become his officiating priests (ṛtvij) and are censured among those who discourse on Brahman. || 11.41 ||

The establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) must not be performed with wealth acquired from a Śūdra. Thus, the prohibition concerns the *agnyādheya* itself; it does not, however, pertain to the obligatory performance of rites for one who has already commenced them. Accordingly, it is said: "One should not perform the execution of a sacrifice after begging from a Śūdra. But there is no fault in obtaining wealth without asking. Likewise, while self-satisfaction through the acceptance of gifts from the unworthy is prohibited, the obligatory rites (*nitya*) are permitted. Therefore, because the statement applies equally to wealth from a Śūdra whether obtained through solicitation or otherwise, this prohibition should be understood as applying specifically to the *agnyādheya* alone. If this prohibition were intended for all ritual acts, then begging from a Śūdra would have been prohibited by that very rule, such as the statement: "Wealth for the sake of a sacrifice [must not be taken] from a Śūdra," and so forth. Furthermore, because of the specific exception regarding the fires of a Vṛṣala, this is understood to be a prohibition of the *agnyādheya* alone. And thus [the author] demonstrates: 11.41.
Treading with his foot upon the heads of those who are constantly ignorant and who serve the fire of the low-born (vṛṣala), the giver shall cross over all difficulties. 11.42.

When this entire section was concluded, it was stated right there: "Therefore, I shall now proclaim the auspicious rule for expiation. Since he intends to describe expiation, the causes thereof are first stated in general terms. (11.42)
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured, and remains attached to the objects of the senses, becomes liable to penance. (11.43)

A man who performs prescribed rites—whether Vedic (*śrauta*) or Smārta—such as sacrifices and study, or who practices what is censured and forbidden, such as violence, falsehood, theft, and the like, and who is addicted to the objects of the senses (sound and so forth) which are intended means for achieving human goals, becomes liable to perform penance (*prāyaścittīyate*). By the inclusion of the word "man" (*nara*), it is understood that this applies to the duty of all social classes (*varṇa*). Now, one might object: since addiction to the objects of the senses is already included by the mention of "censured" acts, its separate mention here is not appropriate. This objection is answered as follows: It is proper to mention this separately in order to prohibit excessive attachment even to those sense-objects where it is not explicitly forbidden, such as in the case of eating meat or the improper taking of wives from the Kṣatriya and other classes. How so? Because it is said: "he becomes liable to perform penance. For this reason, the following is stated [in verse 11.43].
The wise know that expiation is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;
however, some, citing the evidence of the Vedas, say it applies even to what is done intentionally.

The wise know that when a sin has been committed unintentionally, or when there is a transgression for the sake of a sinful act, the expiation (prāyaścitta) to be described hereafter applies as stated. For what reason? Because the instruction on expiation is appropriate only through the authority of the Smṛti; it is not [appropriate] even in the case of a transgression committed intentionally. For one who proceeds by transgressing the rule of the Smṛti’s authority, the instruction on expiation is useless, since he will transgress it regardless of his resolve. For what purpose would this instruction be to him? Thus, the instruction on expiation would be meaningless. When this first section concerning expiation has been established, this second section on expiation is now stated: "Some say that [expiation applies] even to what is done intentionally, based on the evidence of the Śruti. For thus it is heard in the Śruti: "Indra gave the Yatis to the hyenas; an unseemly voice spoke to him; he ran to Prajāpati; therefore, he gave him this Upahavya sacrifice. This passage from the Brāhmaṇa, which is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) regarding the Upahavya, shows that there is expiation even for intentional acts. It was previously stated that the expiation prescribed in the Smṛtis applies only to unintentional acts, as it is mentioned without qualification merely as a cause. And so they say: "In both the Veda and the world, expiation is seen for a transgression in either way; therefore, this [Smṛti rule] must be inferred accordingly. Thus, he demonstrates both sides of the argument. (11.44)
A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas;
but that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of expiatory rites.

Furthermore, we shall demonstrate the distinction between these two later on with the verse: "No expiation is ordained for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa. This verse is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) regarding such cases: namely, that for unintentional [sin] there is the study of the Veda, whereas for what is done intentionally, various other forms of penance (*prāyaścitta*) apply. For he will state both of these for both types of cases later on. However, this is the difference between the two: when a transgression is committed unintentionally, the retribution is small; when intentional, it is great. And so it has been said: "But what is done intentionally out of delusion [is removed] by various kinds of penances. Another, however, says: "The performance of penance is not even possible. For an action is not destroyed without the commencement of its effect, just like the humors of wind, bile, and phlegm. Since this is so, it must simply be performed due to the authority of the instruction in the Smṛti scriptures. For just as in the determination of the attainment or avoidance of merit and demerit, scripture alone is the authority and not logical reasoning, why then is the destruction of action not likewise believed to occur through scripture? This being the case, penance is a teaching based on logic. Otherwise, there would be a partial contradiction. In this way, the purposefulness of the scripture is established, because through penance—which is a light means and a swift demonstration—there is the destruction of great demerit characterized as an evil. Moreover, there is very great suffering consisting of self-restraint in it; for here too, we understand the destruction of this demerit, which is characterized as suffering resulting from a transgression, to occur precisely through the performance of the task. Just as for the humors of wind and so forth, medicine is the antidote and consists of both [elements], so too for demerit, penance and the experience of suffering in hell and so forth would be the cause of its destruction. By this, the case of scorpion venom is explained. Scripture also states that through penance, unwholesome actions—such as the burning of a house and the like—are the causes for occasional rites whose fruit is heaven, just as in the case of the *Kṣāmavatī* sacrifice. To this we reply: Penances are prescribed for occasions involving prohibitions, because they are understood to be solely for the purpose of removing faults (*doṣa*). Just as in the case of illness, when faults such as fever and the like arise, treatments such as fasting are prescribed. Furthermore, the Smṛti will clearly state later on: "Therefore, penance must always be practiced for the sake of purification," and so forth. Others, however, say they are for the purpose of restoring eligibility (*adhikāra*). Thus Gautama says: "Falling away from the duties of the twice-born is degradation. This refers specifically to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. It is heard in a statement defining the term "sinful act" (*pātaka*), but not in any other statement regarding transgressions. And it should be understood that eligibility for other rites arises only from the exhaustion of the fault, not for one whose fault is not exhausted—as in the case of a sick person. As for what some say—that penance is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the rite when a specific occasion arises—that is not possible here, because penance is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*). Now, the cause of the transgression for which penance is required is stated: [Verse 11.45] "If a Brāhmaṇa intentionally sheds the blood of a Brāhmaṇa, or kills a woman or a fetus, he becomes an outcast (*patita*) and must perform the penance prescribed for killing a Brāhmaṇa. (11.45) In this verse, the word "intentionally" (*kāmatas*) is used to distinguish this from the previous case. The phrase "becomes an outcast" indicates that he falls from his caste status. The mention of "prescribed for killing a Brāhmaṇa" implies that the penance is equal to that for killing a Brāhmaṇa, and thus it applies to all four types of penances mentioned for that crime. The mention of "woman" and "fetus" is for the purpose of excluding those who have already undergone the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa. The word "fetus" (*garbha*) here refers to one still in the womb, not one already born. Because the fetus is not yet distinct from the mother, the penance is the same as for killing a Brāhmaṇa. If it were born, the penance would differ according to the caste of the child. The word "blood" (*śoṇita*) here refers to the vital essence (*ojas*) located in the heart, not merely the physical fluid. Therefore, shedding blood from a wound or the like does not incur this penance. The word "sheds" (*sravayet*) is used in the sense of causing to flow out. The word "outcast" (*patita*) is used here to indicate the gravity of the offense, not to establish a new status, since the status of an outcast is already defined elsewhere. The penance is to be performed for twelve years, as it is the most severe among the options. The word "prescribed" (*vihita*) is used to indicate that this is a mandatory rule (*nitya*), meaning it must be performed until the end of life, just as in the case of the *Prājāpatya* penance. The word "Brāhmaṇa" is repeated to show that this applies even to a Brāhmaṇa who is a sinner. The repetition of "Brāhmaṇa" serves to exclude Kṣatriyas and others, as the penance is more severe for a Brāhmaṇa than for others. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where blood is shed unintentionally, such as by striking him with a stick. In that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is also used to exclude the case of a Brāhmaṇa who is a thief or otherwise wicked; for in such cases, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya out of anger; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Śūdra out of anger; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of anger; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of greed; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of delusion; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of fear; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of pity; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of ignorance; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of necessity; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of duty; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of sport; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of curiosity; for in that case, the penance is different. The word "intentionally" is used to exclude the case where a Brāhmaṇa is killed by a Brāhmaṇa out of pride; for in that case, the penance is different

Having incurred the state of requiring expiation, whether by fate or by his own prior actions, a twice-born man must not associate with the virtuous as long as the expiation has not been performed. (11.46)

Although the word *daiva* (fate) is common to all [causes], it should be understood here through the force of the context as referring specifically to *adharma* (demerit). Why? Because the effect corresponds to the cause of the transgression. In the phrase "or by what was done previously," *moha* (delusion) is connected [as the cause], acting as the reason for the transgression; it is not *adharma*, because that has already been mentioned, and it is observed in the world that a transgression occurs through the delusion of one who is confused. Therefore, this is the meaning of the words here: the acquisition of *adharma* occurs for some from the remainder of *adharma* performed previously, and for another from delusion. By stating this, it is established as a matter of course that the acquisition of wholesome action (*kuśalakarma*) occurs from the remainder of previous *dharma* and from the absence of delusion, which is characterized by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Since one must strive in the performance of *dharma* while remaining undeluded, one should not remain indifferent under the assumption that *dharma* and *adharma* are not the motivators of a person's action. In this way, the instruction of the scripture becomes meaningful; otherwise, if human effort (*puruṣakāra*) were non-existent, the scriptural instruction would be fruitless, since the activity of a person is caused solely by *dharma* and *adharma*. [Objection: But is this not already established by the prohibition of association with the wicked for the virtuous? [Response: It is not so established, because the actions are different. Here, by the prohibition of association with those who perform sinful acts, the association of the virtuous with those who perform sinful acts is not necessarily prohibited, since these two actions are distinct. This being the case, expiation (*prāyaścitta*) would apply only to the transgression of that specific rule for whom it is prescribed, because there is no such restrictive rule here. Therefore, the formulation of this prohibition is appropriate, just like the prohibition against a Śūdra having relations with the wife of a twice-born man. There is, however, another reading: "Having incurred [the state of] requiring expiation through delusion by what was done previously... The meaning remains the same. This is now stated to demonstrate the capacity for the performance of expiation. (11.46)
In this world, certain evil-minded men undergo a transformation of their appearance due to their own misdeeds, as well as those committed in previous lives. (11.47)

Thus, what the Sāṃkhyas assert—that prosperity and adversity arise solely from previously performed karma—is refuted. Now, this manifold diversity of physical deformities caused by unwholesome karma is described as a supplement to the performance of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta). 11.47.
A thief of gold suffers from deformed nails; a drinker of liquor, black teeth;
a killer of a Brahmin, consumption; and one who violates the teacher’s bed, a skin disease.
The slanderer [suffers from] a foul-smelling nose; the informer, a foul-smelling mouth; the stealer of grain, a deficiency of limbs; and the mixer [of goods], an excess of limbs. (11.49)
One who steals food suffers from chronic disease; one who steals speech becomes mute;
one who steals clothing suffers from leprosy; and one who steals a horse becomes lame.
Thus, by the remainder of their karma, they are born despised by the virtuous—dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, and likewise deformed in appearance. (11.51)

Since this is so, even for those who have experienced the sufferings of the places of torment and possess various kinds of deformities because they did not perform penance, there remains a residue of karma. (11.51)
Therefore, penance must always be performed for the sake of purification, neither for the sake of gaining further eligibility nor for any other purpose; for it has been said:
"Those whose sins have not been expiated are born endowed with censurable physical marks. (11.52)

This being the case, it should be understood that this selection of evil deeds by means of six verses is intended for the purpose of praising the performance of expiatory rites. Now, however, the expiations for the aforementioned causes are being stated. 11.52.
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of intoxicants, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife—they call these great sins (mahāpātaka), as does association with those who commit them. 11.53

The designation of these as *mahāpātaka* (great sins) is for the purpose of conventional usage. The word "greatness" (*mahattva*) is intended to convey their gravity; among all sins, these are the most serious. This being the case, a *pātaka* is simply a transgression, derived from the root *pat*, meaning "that which causes one to fall. Furthermore, these are called "great sins" because by avoiding them one will remain steadfast, whereas regarding association with those who have fallen, the text will later state: "One falls [from caste] in a year. The drinking of *surā* applies specifically to the Brāhmaṇa. Whatever is prohibited for a particular person constitutes a *pātaka* for that person. However, other acts such as killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*) are to be understood as *pātaka* for all castes (*varṇas*), because they are prohibited for everyone. Theft—specifically defined as the stealing of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold—is a *pātaka*, and nothing else. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "The theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold is a *mahāpātaka*," so says Āpastamba (11.53).
Falsehood regarding one's own excellence, malicious talebearing directed toward the king, and the persistent attribution of falsehood to a teacher—these are equal to the killing of a Brahmin. 11.54

Each individually, not collectively; the same applies to what follows. Falsehood regarding the excellence of one’s birth is when one who is not a Brāhmaṇa says, “I am a Brāhmaṇa,” in matters pertaining to Brāhmaṇas. This should likewise be applied to the castes of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. Or, falsehood regarding the excellence of one’s actions is when one says, “This sacrifice was performed by me. The same applies to study, austerity, and so forth. Falsehood regarding the attainment of a bride or similar matters for the purpose of self-exaltation is perjury in the presence of the giver, which the author will describe in the following verse. Malicious talebearing directed toward the king is equal to drinking liquor. Cruelty is well known. False persistence toward a guru: *alīka* means mental agitation; *nirbandha* is persistent insistence on a false matter. When such insistence is repeatedly carried out toward a guru after having approached him out of malice and the like, it is called *alīkanirbandha*. It is equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. Or, false accusation against a guru is *alīkanirbandha*. Thus says Gautama: “False accusation against a guru. These are equal to mortal sins (*pātaka*). 11.54.

Abandoning one’s Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, and eating forbidden food or the food of those unworthy of offerings—these six are equal to the drinking of spirituous liquor. 11.55.
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, silver, land, diamonds, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold.

They know that the emission of semen into women of one's own lineage, into virgins, into those born of other lineages, or into the wives of a friend or a son, is equal to violating the Guru's bed. (11.57)

The instruction regarding those acts equal to the *mahāpātaka*s (great sins) by means of four verses is for the purpose of making known their gravity, so that there may be a cause for the penance prescribed generally for a grave offense (*guru*). It is also stated in another *Smṛti*: "In cases of great sins, the penances are great; in cases of minor sins, they are small. Now, an objection is raised: when something is said to be equal to another, it is logical that the penance belonging to the latter applies to the former. To this it is replied: it would not be logical if this were intended solely for the prescription of penance, as you suggest; for if that were the case, [the author] would have stated it in the very section on the extension of penances (*prāyaścittātideśa*). Furthermore, he would not have later prescribed the extension of the penance for killing a Brahmin to false testimony and the killing of a friend—both of which are here equated with drinking liquor—and he would not have again prescribed the penance for killing a Brahmin for the "obstinate falsehood regarding a teacher," which is here equated with killing a Brahmin. Likewise, since the emission of semen in a maiden and similar acts, which are here equated with violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*), are again treated there under the penance for violating the Guru’s bed, it is understood that this equation is not for the purpose of prescribing penance. Others, however, think: because they are equated separately, the penance belonging to that with which it is equated is inferred for the one in question. For if only the gravity were intended to be indicated, he would have simply pointed out the equality with the *mahāpātaka*s in general. As for false testimony and the killing of a friend being equated with drinking liquor, the extension of the penance for killing a Brahmin is for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*). And "obstinate falsehood regarding a teacher" is indeed a different matter from [the actual sin of] falsehood. Furthermore, regarding the performance of penance, since there is no study of the Veda for these [offenses], the penance prescribed generally is also inferred for them. However, where only the extension of a specific penance is heard and no equation is made—as in the case of "having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown"—there is no option. Therefore, we consider that for those acts equal to the *mahāpātaka*s, either that specific penance or the one prescribed generally applies. Having thus described the *mahāpātaka*s and those equal to them, he now speaks this [verse] for the sake of the *upapātaka*s (minor sins). 11.57.
Killing a cow, officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, adultery, selling oneself, abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, sacred study, the sacred fires, or one's son; 11.58.
Being superseded by a younger brother, and likewise the act of superseding;
the giving away of a daughter to those two, and officiating as a priest for those very two. (11.59)
Defiling a maiden, usury, falling away from one's vows, and the sale of a tank, a garden, a wife, or a child. (11.60)
The state of being a *vrātya*, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for a fee, receiving instruction for a fee, and the sale of goods that ought not to be sold; 11.61.

Superintending mines, operating large mechanical contrivances, living by the use of harmful herbs, subsisting on women, performing malevolent incantations, and performing rites for the destruction of enemies. (11.62)
Felling trees that are not yet dry for the sake of fuel, undertaking actions for one's own sake, and likewise eating food that is censured; 11.63.
Not maintaining the sacred fires, devotion to women, failure to discharge debts, studying improper scriptures, dishonesty, and the pursuit of vices; 11.64.

The theft of grain, silver, or cattle; consorting with a woman who drinks liquor; the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these constitute secondary sins (upapātaka). 11.65.

This exposition on minor offenses (*upapātaka*) consists of eight verses. Within this category—beginning with the killing of a cow—some acts, such as approaching the wife of another, are taught among the *snātaka* vows; some, such as marrying before an elder brother, are mentioned in the section on the monthly *śrāddha*; and others, such as the sale of a pond, a garden, a wife, or a child, are mentioned right here. This exposition defines the minor offenses (*upapātaka*) arising from these three types of contrary actions. The purpose of this [exposition] is the penance for minor offenses, so that there may be a general rule applicable to them, while specific rules will be stated according to the instruction, such as: "A killer of a cow, joined with a minor offense, shall drink barley-gruel for a month," and so forth. Furthermore, fasting is prescribed as the penance for violating the *snātaka* vows, and likewise, the purification of those excluded from the company (*apāṅktya*) mentioned in the section on the meaning of the *sāṃsikā*. As for those acts already included in this very list of cow-killing and so forth that are mentioned again for the sake of penance, both types of penances may apply by virtue of their being recorded in both places, as an option. By this, the principle of repeated mention is explained everywhere. As for those acts mentioned here, such as the sale of a pond, which are understood through inference to be matters requiring the prescription of penance: since there is no instruction regarding a restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is no spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) in avoiding them, but there is penance upon their transgression. However, for those cases where there is both an instruction regarding the description [of the act] and a prescription of penance—such as the prohibition, "One should not bathe naked," and the penance, "And having bathed, a Brahmin [should not remain] naked"—for those, there is spiritual merit in avoiding them and penance upon transgression. But if the prohibition is inferred solely from the prescription of penance, then in that case, there is no distinction between the two. (11.58–65)

Causing pain to a Brahmin, killing a cow, eating the food of those two (a Śūdra and a woman of ill-repute), crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male are recorded as acts that cause loss of caste. 11.66.

The killing of donkeys, camels, horses, deer, and elephants, as well as goats and sheep, and likewise of fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as causing mixed-caste status (saṃkīrṇakaraṇa). || 11.67 ||

Accepting wealth from those who are censured, engaging in trade, serving a Śūdra, and speaking with vulgar or uncivilized persons should be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa). || 11.68 ||
The killing of worms, insects, or birds; eating food accompanied by liquor; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity. (11.69)

The designation of the groups of acts that cause loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), those that cause mixture of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), those that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), and those that cause defilement (*malinīkaraṇa*) is set forth by means of four verses. The purpose of this is so that the instruction regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*) may be given according to these specific groups. For he will say: "Having committed an act that causes loss of caste," and so forth. (11.66–69)
Now learn correctly those various vows by which all these aforementioned sins, each individually, are expiated. (11.70)
This verse is intended to introduce the expiatory rites that will be described hereafter. || 11.70 ||
A killer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having constructed a hut;
he shall subsist on alms for his own sustenance, carrying the skull of a corpse as his banner.

Later in this very section, he will state a rule regarding its specific qualities: "Having shaved his head, he shall dwell at the edge of a village or in a cow-pen," and so forth. In the phrase "having made a skull-topped banner," the primary meaning is intended, because there is no reason to take it in a figurative sense. Just as the donkey-skin is taken in its primary sense in the penance for a *avakīrṇin*, the skull must likewise be understood in its primary sense. The application of the scriptures is diverse, like the penance for drinking *surā* liquor; moreover, there is no excessive burden in such a statement. Furthermore, logical reasoning is not the proper means here, since dharma and adharma are defined solely by the scriptures. (11.71)

Or he may become a target for weapon-bearers at the will of learned men; this second optional penance is an alternative to the former one. "By learned men" means by those who know, "This man is one who requires expiation. Or [he may do so] for those skilled in missiles and weapons, that is, those studying the four-part science of archery (*dhanurveda*).
He should throw himself into a kindled fire three times with his head downward. (11.72)
And some say that this third [type of cognition] is the unadulterated desire itself. (11.72)
Or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.
Or one may travel a hundred yojanas toward Japan or any other [holy place], eating sparingly and with senses restrained, in order to expiate the sin of killing a Brahmin. (11.74)
Or he should bestow his entire property upon a Brahmin learned in the Vedas;
or else, wealth sufficient for a livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings. (11.75)
Or, eating only sacrificial food, he may follow the Sarasvatī upstream;
or, with his diet restricted, he may recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times a day.

The thirteen penances for killing a Brahmin are to be understood as optional alternatives for all four castes according to their respective capacities, since an explicit option is heard here through three uses of the word "or" (*vā*). Even in the absence of capacity, this option applies when a combination [of all] is impossible. One possesses the capacity for performing one's own intended [penance], even if it is prohibited by Śruti, provided it is other than the [specific] penance [prescribed]. Now, the section concerning the twelve-year penance is commenced for the purpose of prescribing its specific qualities. (11.75–76)
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village, or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage,
or at the root of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
