Regarding that which has been stated [in such passages] as, "A slayer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years having constructed a hut," some optional rules for that purpose are taught here, while others are entirely new. The rule concerning the qualities—"being devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins"—is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the person just mentioned. (11.77)
One who immediately gives up his life for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow,
or one who protects a cow or a Brahmin, is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin.

The meaning of "abiding" (sthiti) is like "destruction" (vināśa). And this is taught for one who has already commenced the twelve-year penance (*prāyaścitta*). Thus, even if the time [for the original vow] is not yet completed, he is purified by death; likewise, even if he dies while protecting cows or Brahmins, he is purified—this is the meaning. And so, this is not a separate penance, but rather an ancillary injunction (*guṇavidhi*) for this very one. For if this were a separate penance, then because they are optional (*vaikalpika*), one who has commenced the twelve-year penance would not be eligible for this one. Just as when one is eligible for one among several optional penances, one is not eligible for another penance precisely because they are optional. Otherwise, there would be a combination (*samuccaya*). And in that case, its direct scriptural hearing (*śravaṇa*) as an option would be contradicted. Nor is this logical: it would involve the abandonment of the heard meaning and the assumption of what was not heard. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. 11.78.

Or he may be one who attempts to obstruct even the lowest [of the castes] in the seizure of a Brāhmaṇa’s property; the meaning is that he is not released if he does not restore it. Or he may be one who proceeds in an unlawful manner, having plundered all the property [of others].

Even one who has not resisted [an attack] is liberated by the very first application [of effort] for the sake of releasing the seizure of a Brāhmaṇa's property, provided it is at least threefold; or he is liberated if the Brāhmaṇa recovers his life on account of that [effort]. (11.79)
This has been explained; now follows its summary: the appropriate penance must be applied accordingly. 11.79.
[Thus, one who is firm in his vows, constantly practicing celibacy, and composed in mind, removes the sin of killing a Brahmin upon the completion of twelve years. || 11.80 ||
Or, having confessed his own sin in an assembly of gods on earth (brahmins) and kings, he is liberated from it after bathing in the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.

The separate mention of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is for the purpose of indicating that this is an expiation not undertaken within another [prescribed penance]. Otherwise, since the *avabhṛtha* of the horse sacrifice is traditionally taught, one who has begun the twelve-year penance might become pure by bathing in the *avabhṛtha* in the midst of it. However, because of this separate mention, it is proper that this expiation of the horse-sacrifice *avabhṛtha* is independent and applies specifically to one who has not undertaken another expiation. Nor is this an instruction directed toward the performer of other optional alternatives, such that some other optional alternative would have been accepted by him. Someone says: "That is incorrect, because the *avabhṛtha* bath of the horse sacrifice is not independent, as it is not taught among the optional expiations. [The author replies: Because, although the context is concluded, this is an injunction regarding a subsidiary (*guṇavidhi*) for one who has already commenced the twelve-year penance. Or, there may be an expectation that this twelve-year penance has its conclusion reached [by this bath]. Even so, among all the optional alternatives, this *avabhṛtha* bath of the horse sacrifice serves as a cause of purification through its subsidiary quality for the sake of cessation [of the sin], according to the possibility of each case. This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is for the purpose of praising the performance of the rite. (11.80–81)
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be the root of Dharma, and the Rājanya is its summit; therefore, by confessing one's sin in their assembly, one becomes purified. 11.82

"Or, having instructed the gods of the earth in the assembly of the king of men, the sacrificer and the officiating priests, upon bathing at the *avabhṛtha* rite in the horse sacrifice, are released from their own sin"—this is the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for this injunction. (11.82)
By his very birth, the Brahmin is the deity even of the gods;
he is the authority for the world, for Brahmā himself is the cause in this matter.
This was said for the purpose of praising the rule that immediately follows what has been taught. 11.83.
Those three who know the Vedas should declare for them a complete expiation for their sin;
that shall serve as their purification, for the word of the learned is indeed purifying.

For he will say: "Or whatever law ten other members of the assembly might determine," and so forth. This being the case, some hold that one should perform the penance authorized by them after sitting with the Brahmins of the penance-assembly, even if one knows the transgression, on the grounds that this is a penance. That is incorrect; for in that case, the instruction of secret penances would be rendered impossible, since there is this Smṛti rule: "A secret [penance] for a secret [offense], and a public one for a public [offense]. Where, then, does this [rule] apply, given that its purpose is not understood? Alternatively, this should be understood as referring to cases where no penance has been specifically mentioned. And thus he will say: "But for the removal of sins for which no expiation has been stated, one should determine the penance after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the gravity of the sin. Alternatively, just as a specific benefit called *dharma* arises from those [Brahmins] due to their favor because of the excellence of the recipient (*pātra*), so too there must be a specific form of *adharma* resulting from the injury [to them], precisely because of that distinction. This being the case, it is in this context that it is begun: "one should tell them who are knowers of the Veda. And this being so, the relative gravity or lightness of the penances for killing a Brahmin is logical based on that distinction. Otherwise, because of the teaching of a light [penance] while bypassing the heavy ones, there would be a total lack of instruction. As in common worldly usage: "A wise man does not buy what can be obtained for a *paṇa* for ten *paṇas*"; so it would be here as well. (11.84)
Therefore, by adhering to one of these rules with a concentrated mind, a Brahmin,
through self-mastery, casts off the sin committed by killing a Brahmin.

This is a concluding verse for all penances for the killing of a Brahmin. The mention of the "Brahmin" here is intended to indicate all social classes (*varṇas*). This being the case, by implication, the eligibility for these penances must be understood as applying to Brahmins and others according to their respective circumstances. (11.85)
Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow; as also in the case of killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who knows [the Veda], or a woman who is an Ātreyī.

This extension of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa applies to those who kill a fetus and so forth. And the "fetus" should be understood from the context to be specifically a Brāhmaṇa fetus. An *ātreyī*, however, is a menstruating Brāhmaṇa woman; for since a male may potentially be conceived in her, one becomes a killer of a Brāhmaṇa by killing her. Others say that an *ātreyī* is defined by her lineage (*gotra*), because from the fact that one becomes a killer of a Brāhmaṇa by killing an *ātreyī*, it is understood that by killing another Brāhmaṇa woman who is not an *ātreyī*, one does not become a killer of a Brāhmaṇa. However, since in the cases of cows and others only the genus is intended, the penance applies without distinction to both female and male. Furthermore, as he will state in the subsequent verse, "and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend," the mention of "woman" there also refers specifically to a Brāhmaṇa woman. Since the term "woman" is present in the rules regarding cow-slaughter and other such acts, this penance might optionally apply to a Brāhmaṇa woman. And an option is appropriate depending on secondary qualities, or based on the presence or absence of certainty regarding the gravity of the offense. In this way, the specific mention of the *ātreyī* becomes meaningful. Having killed a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a Soma sacrifice, the same [penance] applies. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "Whoever performs a sacrifice, he sacrifices indeed becoming a Brāhmaṇa. (11.86)
Having given false testimony, likewise having obstructed a funeral procession for a teacher, having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend; 11.87.
This verse has already been discussed previously in the section concerning those acts equal to the great sins (mahāpātaka). || 11.87 ||
This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, no atonement is prescribed.

The deliberation as to whether [the act was] intentional or unintentional has already been made. Therefore, this does not indicate an absence of penance for what is done intentionally; rather, this is formulated for the purpose of praising the case of negligence (*pramāda*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction between the preceding and following passages. Alternatively, this is intended to teach the severity of the penance in the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa intentionally on account of his qualities. And thus, the penances for killing a Brāhmaṇa are to be determined according to the circumstances, having regard for all specific qualities, as well as for whether the killing was committed with or without conscious intent, and in accordance with the application of the facts. Other cases of equal significance are to be treated in the same way. (11.88)
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, drinks liquor, he should drink liquor that is red-hot like fire;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin.

And thus the purification of one who has died [drinking it] is to be understood; by this, the state of being fire-colored is attributed to *surā*. Furthermore, as for what was stated here regarding "through delusion" (*mohāt*), that is an indicative mark for the explanation of the meaning in the preceding [verse], because in the statement, "Having incurred the necessity of penance through delusion or by what was previously done," delusion is taught by its own specific term. (11.89)
Or he should drink cow’s urine that is fire-colored, or water alone;
or milk, or ghee, or the liquid from cow dung, until death. (11.90)

This [penance] has been undertaken for the purpose of distinguishing the mere substance; thus, the quality of heat here is the same as in the previous case regarding the substance. And the state of being fire-colored is the common remainder. Likewise, it was stated "until death"; this is the penance ending in life for intentionally drinking *surā* in its primary sense. 11.90.
Or he may eat grains for a year, or consume oil-cake once at night, wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks and carrying a flag, in order to remove the sin of drinking liquor. (11.91)

And this penance is understood to apply specifically to the unintentional drinking of *surā* (grain-liquor). For in this way, a distinction between heavy and light penances becomes appropriate based on the difference between intentional and unintentional causes for such transgression. Accordingly, Gautama prescribes a light penance for unintentional drinking of *surā*, which is lighter than the penance for intentional drinking of *surā*: "If one drinks [it] unintentionally, he shall consume milk, clarified butter, water, or air, each heated, for three days; that constitutes a *kṛcchra*, after which his initiation is performed again" (GDh 23.3). Alternatively, this light penance should be understood to apply to the drinking of the other two types of *surā*. And so says another Smṛti: "In the case of drinking non-*surā* liquor (*madya*), one should practice the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. (11.91)
Surā is indeed the dregs of food, and evil is called a dreg;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink surā. 11.92

Some here recite the verse beginning with “*gauḍī*” first, and afterwards this one beginning with “*surā vai malam annānām*. Even by them, these two verses must be explained in reverse order according to the sequence of their meaning; however, for those who recite this verse beginning with “*surā vai malam annānām*” first, the sequence of meaning is already correct. Therefore, this is recited by us first. *Sura* is well-known in the world, like cows and other such things. Its being the “dirt of food” (*annamalatva*) is an *arthavāda* (an explanatory or declamatory statement); therefore, its purpose is to instill an aversion toward drinking it. It is not a logical reason (*hetu*) for the prohibitory injunction (*pratiṣedhavidhi*), because if it were a reason, then everything that is the dirt of food—such as the scum of boiled rice (*maṇḍa*) and so forth—would have to be inedible, and there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress of reasons. [Objection: “*Sura* is undrinkable because it is the dirt of food; but why should the dirt of food be undrinkable? [Reply: In this case, a further reason would have to be stated. Since this is an *arthavāda*, it is not a reason. This being the case, even though *prasannā* (unfermented spirit) is also a type of *sura*, it is censured as being the dirt of food. Furthermore, “dirt” (*mala*) is said to be sin (*pāpman*). This *arthavāda* is also solely for the purpose of turning one away from the act. Thus, the fact that it is the dirt of food is not the cause of the sin; rather, it is the drinking of *sura*. For that reason, it is undrinkable by the twice-born (*dvijāti*). And thus, once the undrinkability of *sura* is established, the rule for penance (*prāyaścitta*) beginning with “Having drunk *sura* through delusion, a twice-born man... is appropriate. In this way, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the dirt of food, the *paiṣṭī* (grain-based) *sura* is primarily prohibited for the twice-born. Now, however, this [next section] is commenced for the purpose of prohibiting non-*sura* liquors (*asurāmadya*) for Brāhmaṇas. (11.92)
Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, and mādhvī are to be known as the three kinds of liquor;
just as one is so are all—none of them should be drunk by the best of the twice-born.

*Gauḍī* is a derivative of molasses (*guḍa*), or that which has molasses as its material cause. Since the formation of *taddhita* derivatives is not explicitly stated [in this context], even where liquor is a derivative of sugarcane juice, the sugarcane juice is referred to by the word "molasses" because it is the cause of molasses. Thus, in both ways, it is *gauḍī*. *Paiṣṭī*, however, is a derivative of flour (*piṣṭa*), or [it means] "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*). Since the formation of *taddhita* derivatives is not explicitly stated, the previously mentioned [meaning] is primary. And *mādhvī* is derived from the word *madhu* (honey) in the sense of a derivative. Thus, *mādhvī* is a derivative of honey, not *mādhavī*; for if it were *mādhavī*, this grammatical maxim—"A rule conditioned by a specific technical name (*saṃjñā*) is eternal"—would serve as its indicator. Regarding the statement "one should say *or od*," the mention of the *guṇa* vowel is for the purpose of indicating that the heavy vowel remains unaltered. This being so, because the *guṇa* substitution is not universal, the form *mādvī* is established. And thus, the form *svāyambhuva* is also established. In this way, this [liquor] is of three kinds, and it is well known that "just as one [is forbidden], so are all. Since the liquor made from flour (*paiṣṭī surā*) was prohibited in the preceding verse, in this verse the other two—*gauḍī* and *mādhvī*—which are actually *asurī* (non-liquor), are rendered *surī* (liquor) for the sake of censure. Therefore, the others are equal to the flour-based liquor, but they are not liquor itself; just as a minister similar to a king is called a "king. Just as one is forbidden, so are all; "the best of the twice-born (*dvijottama*)" should not drink them. The plural number used for *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* refers to the plurality of their varieties, or to the collective group. These, along with the flour-based liquor, are all undrinkable. Otherwise, if this plural were not explained in this way, the reading would have been: "Just as one, so are both not to be drunk by the best of the twice-born. Thus, in this verse, there is a prohibition of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* for Brāhmaṇas, whereas in the previous verse, the primary liquor (*mukhyasurā*) was prohibited for all three [classes]. This is understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*), and the context consists in the commencement of two separate statements. For if all three classes were prohibited in this verse, the commencement of the previous verse would be redundant. But since it was commenced, and to avoid redundancy between the two scriptural statements, the primary liquor was prohibited for all three in the previous verse, while in the subsequent verse, the prohibition of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* applies specifically to Brāhmaṇas. This being the case, the statement "just as one, so are all" becomes logical. As for the mention of "best of the twice-born" (*dvijottama*) here, for those who read "by the twice-born" (*dvijātibhiḥ*) in the [previous] passage, the meaning of "twice-born" should be understood as referring specifically to the "best of the twice-born," even though it is common to all three, due to the force of the context. Furthermore, we shall show in the three subsequent verses that the mentions of "Brāhmaṇas" are indicative marks (*liṅga*) of this very meaning. (11.93)
Wine, meat, and spirituous liquors are the food of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the oblation for the gods must not consume them.

Thus, from this indicative mark (*liṅga*), it follows that even though there is a specific distinction regarding caste, there is no prohibition for women. This being so, by virtue of this observation of non-prohibition, Brāhmaṇa women drink [Soma] in certain instances. And just as there is a difference in penance for a woman and a man despite their belonging to the same caste, so too should this particular prohibition be understood. Just as in the case of the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, where they "consume the *āśvin* cup," there is no fault because it is an integral part of the ritual—just like meat—and as it is said, "so too in the *vājapeya*," this is another explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the injunction prohibiting liquor. (11.94)
Intoxicated by liquor, a Brāhmaṇa might fall into impurity, or he might recite the Veda, or he might perform some other improper act, being deluded by intoxication. (11.95)

This is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*), not a logical reason (*hetu*). For if it were a reason, one would drink only a very small amount—just enough that it does not produce intoxication—and it would not incite one to perform improper acts such as falling into impurity. Alternatively, since drinking [wine] together with meat-eating possesses a counteragent, it does not produce the state of intoxication along with the faults of falling into impurity and so forth; therefore, one may drink in such a manner. (11.95)
He whose Brahmanical nature, residing within his body, is once drenched by intoxicating liquor—his status as a Brahmin departs and he descends to the state of a Śūdra. (11.96)

Since that which is called the meditation on Brahman resides within the self (*ātman*), this statement—that it is "situated in the body"—is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" in these three verses is for the purpose of memorization, because in the following verse there is a prohibition against Gauḍī and Mādhvī wines specifically for Brāhmaṇas; thus, they are mentioned in relation to him. Alternatively, since they depend upon the prohibitions of the preceding verses as well, these explanatory praises of the three verses apply generally to both the preceding and subsequent prohibitions. On this view, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended as an illustration and should be understood accordingly. Others, however, considering that [the drinking of] Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas has already been addressed and prohibited, believe there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the prohibition of Gauḍī and Mādhvī wines. Whether this is correct or incorrect must be deliberated; however, it is not written here for fear of making the book too voluminous. What follows from this? If the prohibition is based on caste (*jāti*), then it is never to be drunk under any circumstances. If, on the other hand, it is based on the quality of intoxication (*mada-guṇa*), then when that quality has vanished, one might drink a small amount of it. For it is said that this prohibition is based on the quality [of intoxication]. This being so, Brāhmaṇas sometimes consume the two [wines] when their intoxicating quality has subsided. Thus it is said: "Or he may fall into impurity while intoxicated," and so forth; from such passages, it is understood that the prohibition of wine (*madya*) is indeed based on the quality of intoxication. Consequently, Mādhvīka that has not yet produced the quality of intoxication and is not stale is drunk, precisely because the prohibition depends on the quality. Moreover, others do not consume wine even when its intoxicating quality has vanished; as the author will say later: "Likewise, that which is situated in a vessel of *surā*," and so forth. (11.96)
This manifold expiation for the drinking of spirituous liquor has been declared;
hereafter I shall proclaim the expiation for the theft of gold.
This verse is for the purpose of presenting a summary. 11.97.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king and made his own deed known, should say: "May your majesty punish me. (11.98)
Taking up a club, the king himself shall strike him once;
by this execution the thief is purified, or else a Brāhmaṇa is purified through austerity alone.
But a twice-born man who, desiring to dispel through austerity the fruit born of stealing gold,
shall wear rags and perform the penance for killing a Brahmin in the forest.

The rule for the expiation of stealing gold is set forth in three verses. Since no specific rule for expiation has been prescribed for Kṣatriyas and the other castes, it should be understood that the mention of the term "Brāhmaṇa" in the phrase "the Brāhmaṇa who steals gold" is intended to indicate all castes. Likewise, regarding what was stated [in verse 11.74], "or a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone," this is now addressed: for austerity cannot be prohibited for those of the Kṣatriya and other castes. Others, however, believe from this effort that austerity applies only to the Brāhmaṇa and not to the other castes. Furthermore, although approaching the king is already established among the duties of a king, its re-statement here is for the purpose of expiation; in that context, it serves as the basis for royal punishment, or it is mentioned again because of the desire to prescribe austerity. And it has been stated in that very place that there is no killing of a Brāhmaṇa. The rest is explained by the literal reading of the text. (11.98–100)
By these vows, a man may remove the sin of those who commit theft;
however, he should expiate the sin of approaching the wife of a guru by means of these same vows.
The presentation of the summary [is made] between the preceding and subsequent sections. 11.101.
Having addressed the sin of violating the teacher’s bed, he should lie down upon a red-hot iron bed;
or he should embrace a blazing iron image of a woman, and by death he is purified. (11.102)
Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms, he should walk straight toward the direction of Nirṛti until he collapses. (11.103)
Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard and dwelling in a solitary forest,
he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind.
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) or barley-gruel (yavāgū), in order to expiate the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.

In these four verses, this expiation for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) is presented as an exceptional case (*vaikṛtika*). The "Guru" has been explained as both the teacher of knowledge and one's own paternal kinsman. One who approaches his wife is a "violator of the Guru’s bed"; thus, by way of secondary indication (*guṇataḥ*), the word *talpa* should be understood as referring to the Guru’s wife. And the mention of both "sacrificial food" (*haviṣya*) and "barley-gruel" (*yavāgū*) follows the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). The rest is straightforward. (11.102–105)

By these vows, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their impurities; likewise, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) may do so through these various observances. || 11.106 ||
One who has committed the minor offense of killing a cow shall drink barley-gruel for a month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
He should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at every fourth mealtime;
for two months, with his senses restrained, he should perform his bath with cow urine. (11.108)
By day he should follow the cows, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having served and paid homage to them, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night. (11.109)
One should stand when they stand, follow when they walk, and likewise sit when they sit—self-restrained, free from envy. (11.110)
One should liberate by every possible means a woman who is afflicted or accursed, or threatened by fears such as tigers and the like, or one who has fallen or become mired in the mud. || 11.111 ||
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently, one should not seek protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability. (11.112)
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor of a calf drinking. (11.113)
But he who, following this rule, tends cows, removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months. (11.114)

Some, however, read "in three years. That is incorrect, because in this very section on penance (*prāyaścitta*) below, a period of three months is prescribed; and he will state that for all minor offenses (*upapātaka*), one should perform this same vow as an alternative to the *cāndrāyaṇa*, with the exception of the case of the student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*). Thus, since a three-year period would not be consistent with the rules for these [other] offenses, this interpretation is unjustified. (11.106–114)
One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.

When no subsequent sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is available for one who has performed the penance, his "entire property" (sarvasva) is the fee; and by implication, it is understood that this "entire property" is less than eleven cows. This may consist of cows, other items, or both. (11.115)
Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin),
with the exception of one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin), should perform this very same penance for the sake of purification, or else the Cāndrāyaṇa.

This very expiation for killing a cow is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to all minor offenses (*upapātaka*). And as an alternative to that, there is the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance itself. This being the case, the *cāndrāyaṇa* would not apply to the killing of a cow [as a specific rule], because of its capacity to serve as an alternative, just as it does with other minor offenses. For this very reason, there is a separate mention [of the cow-killing]. By the prohibitive indicator (*pratiṣedhaliṅga*) in the phrase "excluding the *avakīrṇin*," it is understood that the vows prescribed for cow-killing and so forth are to be applied to the *avakīrṇin* as well. (11.116)
But one who has spilled his seed shall, at night, sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*.
Having performed the oblations in the fire according to the rules, and finally having joined together with the *ṛc* verse,
he should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Agni.
He determines the meaning of the term *avakīrṇin* as the cause for a penance. (11.117–118)
The knowers of dharma, the exponents of the Veda, declare that for a twice-born man established in a vow, the emission of semen through lust constitutes a transgression of his vow. (11.119)

Thus, for one whose organ has discharged involuntarily during the day or night, the penance would be even lighter; and lighter still in the case of a dream. Accordingly it is said regarding the emission of semen by a celibate student in a dream: "He should mutter the verse beginning with *punar mām*. (11.119)
For the fourfold splendor of Brahman belongs to the student who has broken his vow: that of Māruta, Puruhūta, Guru, and Pāvaka. || 11.120 ||

Since this is so, therefore one who has broken his vow of chastity, having incurred this sin, shall wear the skin of a donkey and go about begging for alms at seven houses while proclaiming his own deed. (11.121)
Subsisting on food obtained from them only once a day, and performing ablutions at the three times of the day, he becomes pure in one year. (11.122)

This penance is to be understood as applying to a Vedic student (*brahmacārin*) for sexual intercourse with a woman. And thus, because their purpose is the same, such a penance for the emission of semen would likewise apply to those who have renounced the world (*pravrajita*), as it would be contrary to their state of renunciation; for no other penance has been prescribed for them in the event of such a lapse. (11.121–122)

Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance; if done unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance. (11.123)
He will describe the Sāntapana, the Kṛcchra, and the Prājāpatya penances.
For acts causing mixture of castes or unworthiness to receive alms, a month-long lunar penance (aindava) is the purification;
for acts that cause defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days.

The term "anyatama" (one or another) carries over [from the previous rule]. Thus, because the instruction of heavy penances is given for each case according to one's own wish, its lightness when there is no such determination is established by implication from the earlier scripture itself. 11.124.
The fourth part of the penalty for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part for a Vaiśya who abides by his duty, and it should be known as a sixteenth part for a Śūdra. 11.125.

There is another optional rule for penance for Kṣatriyas and others, distinct from the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance prescribed for minor offenses (*upapātaka*), by which the killing of women, Śūdras, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas is taught to fall within the category of minor offenses. Furthermore, with regard to the distinction between what is right and wrong, this other optional penance for Kṣatriyas and others is different from that previously mentioned. As it has been said: "For a Vaiśya who is established in good conduct, the penance is an eighth part. Now, this subsequent penance for the killing of Kṣatriyas and others is specifically taught for Kṣatriyas and the rest, serving as an alternative to the penance prescribed in the preceding verse. (11.125)
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born should give one thousand cows and one bull for the sake of his own purification.

And this expiation is prescribed for one who possesses wealth; previously, penance was prescribed for one without wealth. Furthermore, he will state that giving is an alternative to that penance, as in: "If one is unable to effect the purification of the killing of snakes and the like by means of giving," and so forth. The phrase "unintentionally" is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended to praise negligence, because it has been stated previously that no heavier expiation is applicable for what is unintentional. Thus far, this is the expiation for one who possesses available wealth; for the poor man, the previously mentioned alternative is reiterated as an option for him. (11.126)
Or, being self-restrained, with matted hair, he should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin for three years,
dwelling far away from the village and making his abode at the foot of a tree.

The statement regarding the matted-hair ascetic (jaṭila) is for the purpose of restriction, in order to exclude others such as those carrying a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅgin) and so forth. || 11.127 ||
The best of the twice-born should perform this very same penance for one year after killing a Vaiśya who is established in his proper conduct; alternatively, he should give one hundred and one cows.

This [rule] regarding one who possesses wealth is optional, as before. The mention of the "best of the twice-born" is for the purpose of indicating the other castes as well, not for the purpose of restriction. 11.128.
Having killed a Śūdra, one should perform this very same vow for six months;
or else, one should give ten white cows and a bull as the eleventh to a Brāhmaṇa.

The meaning of this verse has already been explained. The mention of the "white color" here is due to its commonality with purity. Thus, these three penances are to be treated as alternatives for the killing of a Kṣatriya or others. The previously mentioned Cāndrāyaṇa and the gift of a cow (*godāna*) in this context are both options for the expiation of Brahman-murder when committed intentionally. Some, however, believe that the expiation taught in this section consists of the combination (*samuccaya*) of these two. They recite the verses in combination: "He shall perform [the penance] for three years, self-restrained," and likewise, "Having killed a Vaiśya established in his duty, he shall give one hundred cows"; and similarly, "as well as ten cows and a bull. This is incorrect, because it contradicts the logic of the scriptures; furthermore, under such an assumption, the Cāndrāyaṇa—which is a lighter penance for minor offenses (*upapātaka*)—would become untenable in light of the instruction for a heavier penance consisting of a combination of gifts and austerities. As the worldly saying goes: "A wise man does not buy what can be obtained for five coins for ten coins. If these two were merely taught as optional alternatives, the Cāndrāyaṇa would already be rendered redundant; how much more so if they were combined? Because of this extreme heaviness, there is no combination; therefore, the word *vā* (or) must be read in the sense of an option. (11.129)
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay,
or even a frog, as well as a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.

This expiation applies to the killing of these [beings] when they are killed collectively. And so it will be stated: "But for the slaughter of a thousand vertebrate creatures. Others, however, because of their low status, maintain that this refers to the killing of all Śūdra-born castes born in the inverse order—namely, the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—and that this is the expiation for their collective killing. But for the killing of each individually, another expiation, lighter than the former, is prescribed. (11.130)
Or he should drink milk for three nights, or he should travel a distance of one yojana;
if he is incapable of traveling the road due to extreme old age, he should touch the water of a flowing river or mutter the hymn addressed to the waters (the Ābdavatam Sūkta). || 11.131 ||

The meaning is that one should bathe in a distinguished river flowing to the ocean. By implication, this is taught as being superior because it is intended to prescribe bathing with all its necessary accessories. Alternatively, one should mutter a *sūkta* dedicated to the waters. And in all these cases, by implication, there is the drinking of milk or fasting for three nights, depending on whether the transgression was intentional or unintentional. (11.131)
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
for killing a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead.

The combination of this [act] with the stealing of a *māṣaka* coin should be understood as resulting in immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) due to its inherent gravity; it does not apply to [the theft of] a plowshare. And the straw, by implication, refers to that belonging to a cow or an ox for the sake of a Brahmin. (11.132)
For killing a boar, one should give a jar of ghee; for a partridge, a drona of sesame; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and for a curlew, a three-year-old calf.
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or even a peacock, as well as a monkey,
a hawk, and a vulture, one should touch a cow and offer it to a Brāhmaṇa.

This expiation applies to the killing of all [three] together, because no division [of the penance] has been taught and because the cow is a large animal; as in the case of [the rule], "Having killed a cat and a mongoose," and so forth. Where, even when all are mentioned together, one intends [the penance] for each individually, there the author makes a separate mention. We shall demonstrate this further below. (11.133–134)
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; and for killing a goat, a sheep, an ox, or a donkey, a one-year-old calf.

This verse has been explained by its very recitation. Furthermore, the killing of goats and sheep is said to cause mixed-caste status (*saṃkīrṇakara*). Thus, the penance for that [killing] would be optional with the penance for killing a goat or a ram, according to the force of the instruction in the verse beginning "a goat, a ram, or a bull" (MDh 11.138). This same principle should be applied elsewhere as well. || 11.135 ||
Having killed carnivorous wild animals such as tigers and the like,
one should give a milch cow as a gift.
Milk is already established by the very instruction regarding the cow; thus, the instruction concerning that which is already established should be understood as being for the sake of excellence.
"But having killed a non-carnivorous animal, a heifer, or a camel, one shall give a *kṛṣṇala* [of gold]. (11.136)
For the purification of all four castes who have killed women of unstable character, one should administer the bowstring, the hide of a black antelope, and the bladder separately. 11.137.

He should give a lizard, that is, a leather pouch, to a Brāhmaṇa at a place where it may be used by him. Having killed an unchaste Brāhmaṇa woman, he should give a bow to a Brāhmaṇa; this is for the purpose of protecting the Brāhmaṇical order from the theft committed by her servants. For having killed a Vaiśya woman, he should give a goat; for a Śūdra woman, a sheep. Because they are mentioned separately here, it should be understood that in other cases involving groups, the penance is not performed separately for each individual. Some say [the word] "having gone" (*gatvā*) is implied; however, that is not correct, because this belongs to the section on injury (*hiṃsā-prakaraṇa*), and the reading is "having killed women who are unchaste. Furthermore, the author will provide a summary at the end of the section: "By these vows, the sin arising from injury may indeed be removed. (11.136–137)
If a twice-born man is unable to expiate the killing of snakes and other such creatures through gifts,
he shall perform a Kṛcchra penance for each individual creature in order to remove the sin.
And by this it is understood that, among penances, giving gifts is the primary rule, since the text prescribes the *kṛcchra* penance here for its absence. (11.138)
But for the killing of a thousand vertebrate beings,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.

Having fully understood the injury to a collective body and the injury to those possessing bone, one should perform that penance which is prescribed for the injury of a Śūdra who has not returned [to the fold]. Now, the penance for the injury to each of these individually is being stated. (11.139)

But for the killing of each individual creature possessing bones, one should give something to a Brahmin; this is understood from the force of the commencement of the rule. And for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control (prāṇāyāma). 11.140.

The killing of worms, insects, and birds is declared among the acts that cause defilement; this being the case, their penance is an alternative to this [present rule] because they share a common basis. 11.140.
Upon cutting trees that bear fruit, one must recite a hundred Ṛg-verses;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
And this is the expiation for their cutting when not used for sacrifice; for he will say later: "In the case of killing an animal in vain, one should follow a cow," and so forth. (11.141)
For all beings born from food, born from moisture,
and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the complete purification.

The rule concerning *asthimada* (bone-marrow) and *asthimaṇḍa* (bone-juice) mentioned previously is to be understood as applying to things other than those produced from food and so forth, because of the force of the commencement of this [present] rule. || 11.142 ||
For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.
By these vows, indeed, the sin arising from violence—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—is entirely removed; now hear [the rules] regarding the eating of forbidden food.
This verse is for the purpose of presenting a summary. 11.144.

Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the sacramental rite alone; but for intentional drinking, it is beyond prescription—the established rule is that it ends with life. (11.145)

It is understood from Gautama that one is purified by a rite of re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) accompanied by the *taptakṛcchra* penance, and not by the rite of re-initiation alone, because the latter by itself is extremely slight. Thus says Gautama: "If one drinks liquor unintentionally, he shall consume hot milk, ghee, water, or air for three days each; this constitutes the *kṛcchra*, after which his re-initiation takes place" (GDh 23.2). Here too, in the section on forbidden foods (*abhakṣya-prakaraṇa*), the *kṛcchra* is mentioned: "If one intentionally consumes semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the *kṛcchra*" (GDh 23.1). And that *taptakṛcchra* is indeed derived from Gautama’s text. In this context, however, the rite of re-initiation is understood as an auxiliary to the penance. This being the case, this penance does not apply to the unintentional drinking of the primary *surā* (the *paiṣṭī* variety made from flour), but rather to the unintentional drinking of the *gauḍī* (made from molasses) and *mādhvī* (made from honey), due to their close proximity to the primary type. Accordingly, regarding the intentional drinking of the *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*, a penance of eating grain-particles and oil-cakes for a year is prescribed, and not the *paiṣṭī* penance which is an alternative ending in death. Otherwise, if they served the same purpose, who—unless cursed by fate—would abandon the lighter penance and perform the life-ending one involving the consumption of grain-particles and the like, which is so utterly destructive? Likewise, another Smṛti states: "In the drinking of *asurā* and *madya*, one should practice the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. This being so, since there is an extreme disparity between this light penance and the life-ending penance prescribed for the drinking of the primary *surā*, this penance applies only to the unintentional drinking of the *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*. Furthermore, a distinction between the penances for intentional and unintentional transgressions is logical, as they cannot be identical in scope, just as in other cases. And thus, by implication, the penance for the once-only drinking of *asurā* and *madya* is understood. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: [a]surāmadyapāne cāndrāyaṇam abhyaset. And so it is. Thus ends the section.
"An excellent twice-born man who, through negligence, has drunk even once liquor or spirituous wine, becomes pure after ten nights by subsisting on cow's urine and barley-gruel. Thus it is said.

However, for one who habitually drinks the Gauḍī and Mādhvī liquors intentionally, this expiation is indescribable; rather, another expiation ending only with death must be prescribed for him due to the greater severity of the fault arising from intentional repetition, just as in the case of *paiṣṭī* liquor. And by this very implication, even in the drinking of the primary *surā* unintentionally, another expiation slightly less than that for intentional drinking should be inferred. Thus he will say: "Having considered the capacity [of the offender] and the sin, one should determine the expiation. (11.145)
Having drunk water that has stood in a vessel for spirituous liquor or likewise in a container for intoxicants,
one should drink milk infused with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.

Having drunk water contained in a vessel that held *surā*, for whom is there a prohibition? For a twice-born man (*dvijāti*), according to the circumstances. He should drink milk infused with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights; and thus, other food is prohibited for him. This expiation applies when the essence (*rasa*) has not been taken up; if the essence has been taken up, the expiation for drinking *surā* itself is proper. However, having drunk water that stood in a vessel containing non-*surā* liquor, a lesser expiation is proper. And so, since the division of expiations was established previously regarding the primary and secondary types of *surā*, by implication here too, the distinction between heavy and light expiations should be understood as before, according to that same method of division. (11.146)
Having touched or given liquor, or having accepted it according to the rules,
or having drunk water left over by a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.

The word "according to rule" (*vidhivat*) is connected specifically with the act of receiving, such as by pronouncing blessings (*svastivācana*) and so forth; or rather, this same rule should be understood to apply to the act of giving as well, regarding a Brāhmaṇa’s acceptance of liquor. For practicing what is forbidden in that regard, one should drink *kuśa*-grass water for three days. As before, there is a prohibition against food. And for drinking water that has been left over by a Śūdra, this very same penance shall apply. However, for food that is the leavings of a Śūdra, he will state another penance: "One should drink barley-gruel for seven nights. Since this matter is based on the authority of sacred tradition (*āgama*), there is no room for logical reasoning here; therefore, this alternative penance for the leavings of a Śūdra is not to be doubted. (11.147)
But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor, becomes pure by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter. (11.148)

One who drinks *surā* should perform this expiation after smelling the odor of *surā*, and not for any other [odor]. It refers specifically to the odor of that [liquor’s] body. And thus, by this very implication, it is understood that even when the *surā* is located elsewhere, if its odor is perceived, this same expiation applies. Furthermore, because of the specific qualification "drinker of *soma*," there would be a lighter expiation here for those Brāhmaṇas who do not drink *soma*. (11.148)
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything touched by liquor, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite once again. (11.149)

And when liquor has been touched [by another substance], it should be understood that it is still subject to the same rules regarding the perception of its taste. In the case of this transgression, however, for the twice-born, there is a purification consisting of a *satapta-kṛcchra* penance, based on the authority of other Smṛtis. Thus, Gautama’s rule—"In the case of consuming urine, feces, or semen" (GDh 23.3)—should be applied here as well. This being so, the *taptakṛcchra* and the *punar-saṃskāra* (re-initiation) are to be performed together as the expiation, and not the re-initiation alone. Because it is extremely light [in nature], it is stated here in the section on forbidden foods: "Having intentionally consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform a *kṛcchra*. Therefore, one might object: "In that case, a *kṛcchra* was prescribed for the intentional drinking of urine and so forth, whereas here it is for unintentional [contact]. This is true; however, because they belong to different ritual systems (*kalpa*), there is no contradiction between the transgressions involving intentional and unintentional acts. Furthermore, since all the duties pertaining to that [initiation] would otherwise apply, this [rule] is commenced for the purpose of restriction, because of the censure attached to the *punar-saṃskāra*. (11.149)
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are dispensed with for the twice-born upon the performance of the rite of re-consecration.
This verse has been explained by its very recitation. || 11.150 ||
But having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women and Śūdras,
or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.

Since the acceptance of gifts from such persons already implies the acceptance of their women by the force of the reference to the twice-born, the explicit mention of "them" (tat-) is to be understood as including all castes. In these cases, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights. Here, because of the instruction regarding drinking, a barley-soup made with ground barley is prescribed; for the act of drinking is accomplished by means of a liquid substance. Furthermore, that which is unfit to be eaten has been explained in the chapter on the observances of a Snātaka. (11.151)
Even after drinking fermented acids or astringent decoctions, though they are purifying, a twice-born man remains impure as long as that [substance] has not passed downward. (11.152)
Regarding those things that are otherwise forbidden but are pure [in this context], the expiation here consists solely in their removal; there is no other [penance required]. 11.152.
Having consumed the urine or excrement of a village pig, a camel, a cow, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

The ministers' consumption of these [forbidden substances] is permitted because of their specific office; as such, the author will observe in the following verse: "And even that which is unknown while situated in a slaughterhouse. However, if their consumption is intentional, the assembly (pariṣad) must determine a more severe penance for them. 11.153.
Having eaten dried meats, mushrooms from the earth, or anything from a slaughterhouse that was not known [to be such], one should perform this very same penance. (11.154)

Because of the mention of the term "twice-born" (*dvija*) in the rule "the twice-born shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance," and because of the context, there is no penance for a Śūdra’s transgression here. For a Śūdra who has taken refuge with a Brāhmaṇa, penance might occur only occasionally due to the prohibition [of such penance], based on the statement: "In whatever way they follow virtuous conduct, being free from envy... (11.154).
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, and cocks,
as well as that of hell-beings, crows, and donkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.

"Meat-eaters" refers to vultures and the like; "sūkara" refers to the village pig (*viḍvarāha*), as is understood from its association with donkeys and other such animals. Similarly, the "cock" (*kukkuṭa*) should be understood as the domestic cock, either because it was prohibited in the preceding verse or due to its association with donkeys and the like. In this way, the prohibition regarding the eating of meat is to be understood. In that context, within the verse concerning the village pig, the urine and excrement [of all these] are prohibited. Even for those meat-eaters and others whose urine and excrement were not previously prohibited, it should be understood here that they too are prohibited due to their association with donkeys and the like. (11.155)
If a twice-born man who has not yet returned home from his teacher's house should eat food given on the monthly Śrāddha occasion,
he shall fast for three days and remain in water for one day.

This expiation applies to eating food for a month when one has been requested by one's own request; for it is said, "One may eat at will when invited," and so forth. Otherwise, there would result a prohibition of what has already been enjoined. Thus it is also said: "One may, at will, engage even a daughter’s son who is observing a vow in the Śrāddha. This being the case, this should be understood as a specific prohibition based on this instruction regarding expiation, not an absolute prohibition. (11.156)
But he who, while observing a vow, should eat honey or meat in any way whatsoever,
having performed the ordinary *kṛcchra* penance, should complete the remainder of his vow.
At a funeral feast (śrāddha), or on other occasions. || 11.157 ||
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a mouse, or those of a dog or a mongoose, or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.

[The penance lasts] for one day because the instruction is given without distinction. This expiation applies to the eating of the remnants (ucchiṣṭa) of these [animals]. And thus, in the three verses of the Dharmaśāstra, the consumption of the remnants, urine, excrement, and meat of crows and other such animals is prohibited: in the verse concerning the village-pig (*viḍvarāha*), there is a prohibition against urine and excrement; in the verse concerning the carnivorous boar (*kravyādasūkara*), there is a prohibition against eating meat; and in the phrase "the remnants of cats, crows, and mice," there is a prohibition against the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*). This being the case, those such as the cock (*kukkuṭa*) and others who are mentioned in one place but not mentioned in another verse should be understood to be included in all three verses by virtue of their association with the aforementioned. And this is so for the following reason: || 11.158 ||

One who desires purity for oneself should not eat food that is unfit to be consumed; if it has been eaten unknowingly, it should be vomited up or quickly purified by means of purificatory rites. (11.159)
This has been declared as the various rule for the vows regarding the eating of forbidden food;
now hear the rule for those vows that remove the fault of theft.
This verse has been explained by its very recitation. || 11.160 ||
Having committed thefts of grain, food, or wealth out of desire from the house of one of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year. (11.161)

*dhānya* refers to rice and other grains; *anna* is that same grain when prepared as food; *dhana* refers to gold or other things such as clothing. Since the term *dhana* already includes everything, the specific mention of *dhānya* and so forth is like the expression "cows and bulls," where the general term implies the specific. What is meant is: "having stolen anything whatsoever. Furthermore, the phrase "out of desire" (*kāmāt*) is not intended to be restrictive, for there is no application of this elsewhere, as is the case with the penance for drinking *surā*. The word *dvijottama* (best of the twice-born) is for the purpose of specifying a Brāhmaṇa; and here, by virtue of the context, the word *api* (even/also) should be understood as elided, meaning: "even a Brāhmaṇa, having stolen from the house of a Brāhmaṇa. This being the case, the rule regarding the *apūpa* (cake) is explained by the penalty. This penance applies to Kṣatriyas and others as well. Otherwise, if it were restricted to "from the house of one's own caste," this penance would apply to Kṣatriyas and others only from the houses of Kṣatriyas and so on, whereas from the house of a Brāhmaṇa, a different penance prescribed generally, such as the *Cāndrāyaṇa*, would apply. But this is not desired, because the *Kṛcchra-ābdika* penance is more severe. Therefore, this penance should apply to all—Brāhmaṇas and others alike—for stealing the property of a Brāhmaṇa, just like the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*). The same should be understood for other cases as well. (11.161)
For the abduction of human women, as well as for [the theft of] fields, houses, wells, tanks, and water, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the means of purification. (11.162)

The taking of water for one's own personal use is forbidden; however, the taking of water from wells, tanks, and the like is permitted even for the sake of others' use. Therefore, because those two cases involve only a connection with one's own property, they incur the fault of theft; since this case differs from them, it is mentioned separately. Or else, another solution must be stated. (11.162)
Having stolen articles of small value from another's house, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of self-purification after returning that property. 11.163.

This refers to things of little essence, little value, or little utility; since other types of substances such as food and drink have already been mentioned, this mention of tin, lead, and so forth should be understood to apply to such items. (11.163)
For the theft of food that is chewed or swallowed, as well as vehicles,
beds, and seats, and for flowers, roots, and fruits, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.

And here, the number [of repetitions] regarding foods such as those to be chewed or swallowed depends either on the frequency of repetition or on whether they are prepared with or without ritual consecration. 11.164.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
clothing, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast for three nights.

The penance for grass and similar items is determined by their quality (*sāra*). Furthermore, although milk and the like are indeed drinkable, they should be understood as being included within the categories of "eatable" (*bhakṣya*) and "food" (*bhojya*). "Dry food" refers to items such as *parpaṭaka* (wafers) and the like. The mention of "molasses" (*guḍa*) is intended to include all products derived from molasses. The mention of "cloth" (*cela*) is intended to include hemp, linen, silk, and so forth; however, a different penance for cotton and other such materials will be stated later. (11.165)
For [stealing] gems, pearls, corals, copper, silver, iron,
bell-metal, or stones, one must subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
In this case as well, depending on whether the matter is essential or non-essential, there is [the rule] regarding holding [the breath] once or repeating it. || 11.166 ||
For cotton, silk-worms, and worn-out items; for animals with cloven hooves and solid-hoofed ones; and for birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope—one must drink milk for three days.

In this case as well, the requirement [of the preceding rule] is to be applied as before; furthermore, for elephants and the others, another [penance] prescribed generally should be observed. || 11.167 ||
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he should expel the sin of approaching those who should not be approached by means of these very vows.

Having discharged semen into women of his own lineage, or into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, he shall perform the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed. (11.169)

Furthermore, he will prescribe other penances for approaching even non-maidens, such as women of the Caṇḍāla and other lowest castes, in passages beginning with: "Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes... (11.168–169).

Having approached a daughter of his father’s sister, a daughter of his own sister, or even a daughter of his mother’s sister, as well as a daughter of his mother’s brother, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (11.170)
A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives; they are not to be approached because of their kinship, for by marrying them he falls low. (11.171)

Regarding the daughters of the mother’s sister and the maternal uncle, since their prohibition is already established by the rule “and those who are not *sapiṇḍas* of the mother,” their mention here again is for the purpose of prohibiting the daughter of the father’s sister (*paitṛṣvasreyyā*). Alternatively, this verse should be explained as being for the sake of restatement (*anuvāda*), because [the prohibition] is already established by the rule “and she who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother. (11.170–171)

Having discharged semen into non-human females, into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper place for conception, or even into water, one shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance. (11.172)

Another reading for the second half of this verse is: “...in non-human females, in a eunuch, and in a female Piśāca. Others read “and in the air” (*khe ca*). “Non-human females” refers to mares and the like; “a eunuch” refers to a man; “*udakyā*” is well known [as a menstruating woman]; and “in a non-vagina” means having discharged semen into water. Regarding “obstructed” places, he will mention in the following verse those such as boats and so forth. One should perform the *Sāntapana Kṛcchra* penance, which he will also describe. This rule does not apply to a cow in the same way it applies to a mare and others. Therefore, since that has not been mentioned here, it must be explained from another Smṛti: “. . . in the case of a daughter-in-law and a cow, it is equal to violating the Guru’s bed. (11.172)
But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or a woman, a twice-born man shall perform a bath with his clothes on in a bullock cart, in water, or during the daytime. (11.173)

The expiation mentioned in the preceding verse applies when a male is the one to be enjoyed; however, this other, lighter expiation applies in another context. Or, in the case of a woman, the mention of the term "twice-born" (dvija) is for the sake of distinction; it specifically qualifies the sexual intercourse of those two, the man and the woman. In a bullock-cart, in water, while traveling by vehicle, or even during daytime travel, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on. Because of the instruction to bathe with one's clothes on, this occasional (naimittika) bath is said to be distinct and superior to the obligatory (nitya) bath. || 11.173 ||

Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, having eaten [their food], or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his status] through ignorance; through knowledge [of the transgression], he becomes equal [to them]. (11.174)

Those for whom the Caṇḍāla is the lowest—namely the Āyogava and others who originate from Śūdras—they are these "Caṇḍāla-lowest" (caṇḍālāntyāḥ). For them, there is a prohibition against [intercourse with] women. However, we shall explain the penance later. What is the distinction between "falling" (patana) and "equality" (sāmya)? It should be understood that in the case of "falling," there is a recovery through penance, whereas in the case of "equality," there is an absence of penance. (11.174)
A husband shall confine a corrupt wife in a single room;
she must perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man who has committed adultery with another’s wife.
If, however, she should become corrupted after being solicited by one of equal status,
the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed for her purification.

The meaning of this verse is straightforward. However, there is this distinction: whatever [penance] applies to a man in connection with a woman, that same [penance] applies to that woman in connection with a man. For example, whatever [penance] applies to a Śūdra for approaching a Brāhmaṇī wife, that same [penance] applies to a Brāhmaṇī as well for contact with a Śūdra. In this manner, it should be explained for all forms of contact. (11.175–176)
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by serving a Vṛṣalī for a single night, he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting prayers for three years. (11.177)

Since no penance is prescribed for approaching a Caṇḍāla woman or a woman of the lowest castes (antyastri), and since a Śūdra woman—a Vṛṣalī—is in some cases considered a permissible partner while in others she is not entitled [to such status], this penance should be understood as applying to the approach of a Caṇḍāla or an Antya woman, because she is indeed entitled [to it]. Others, however, say that the non-angry Śūdra woman is the Vṛṣalī. They also provide an alternative reading: "in three months. But others maintain that this is not correct, because she is not entitled [to it]. (11.177)
This expiation has been declared for all four types of evildoers;
now hear these expiations for those who associate with outcasts. || 11.178 ||

By associating with an outcast for a year—through officiating at his sacrifices, teaching him, or forming a matrimonial alliance—one becomes an outcast; but not by sharing a vehicle, food, or a seat. (11.179)

[The text says] "not by means of vehicles, food, or seats for a year; rather, immediately. Beyond that time, or within a year, [the rule applies] "by means of vehicles, food, or seats"—this must be stated by implication. Alternatively, another meaning is stated based on another Smṛti text: through the assumption of a mediated connection, one falls after a year due to [using] vehicles, food, or seats; but not due to officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or matrimonial alliance. Rather, one falls immediately because of these acts such as officiating at sacrifices, as seen in another Smṛti text. Furthermore, the fall should be understood to occur through contact and similarity [to the outcaste], and his penance is the same as theirs. Thus it shows. (11.178–179)
Whichever person among these one associates with after he has fallen,
that person shall perform the very same vow as that individual for the sake of purification from that association.

Moreover, this expiation would apply only in the case of association with those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin); however, in the case of association with a cow-killer or similar offenders, an expiation prescribed in general terms should be devised. || 11.180 ||

The sapinda relatives and kinsmen must perform the water-libation for one who has fallen from his caste outside the village on an inauspicious day, in the evening, in the presence of agnates, officiating priests, and teachers. (11.181)
The meaning is "while he is still living. This rule for him is now stated. || 11.181 ||
A female slave should always overturn a water-pot full of water as if for a deceased person;
the kinsmen, together with her, should observe impurity for a day and a night.
But from that point on, there shall be a cessation of conversation and shared seating, as well as the giving of inheritance and even ordinary worldly intercourse. (11.183)
The status of being the eldest shall cease, as well as the wealth obtainable by the eldest;
however, a younger brother who is superior in virtue shall receive the portion of the eldest. (11.184)
But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe and then cast a new pitcher full of water into a sacred body of water along with that very person.
Having thrown that jar into the water and entered his own home,
he should perform all the ancestral rites for his kin as he did before.

These [penances] for removing the reversal of the vessel (*pātraviparyāsa*) would also apply only in connection with a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), as stated in the six verses; and that has been declared in such passages as, "Water-libations (*udaka*) must be performed for one who is fallen (*patita*)," and so forth. However, in another Smṛti, such as "One should abandon the father," and so forth, they apply only to certain [specific cases]. (11.182–186)
One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen from their status;
however, they should be given clothing, food, and drink, and they should dwell near the house. 11.187.
This verse has been explained by its very recitation. || 11.187 ||
One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins until they have been purified; yet once they have performed the rites of purification, one should never despise them. (11.188)

Because of the permission granted for the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) in the statement, "all duties toward kinsmen," this [rule] is formulated for the purpose of killing a cow. In both cases, association is possible to be understood by the statement, "one should not enter into association with the virtuous as long as the penance has not been performed. However, regarding the killer of a child and others, it is once again excluded. (11.188)

One should not live together with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who has sought refuge, or those who have killed a woman, even if they are pure according to the Dharma.
This undertaking is for the purpose of censuring [his] contact; or rather, it is for the purpose of making known the excellence of the transgression. 11.189.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
There are three *kṛcchra* penances; because they are the first [of their class], they are called *prājāpatya*. Others say they are the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*, the *parāka*, and so forth. (11.190)
This same penance should also be prescribed for those twice-born men who, being engaged in improper acts and abandoned by the Veda, desire to perform an expiation. || 11.191 ||

This expiation applies both to those who have not studied the Vedas and to those who, though having studied the Vedas, are engaged in forbidden acts (*vikarman*). That which is prohibited for someone constitutes their forbidden act; for example, serving Śūdras is a forbidden act for Āryas. (11.191)
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a reprehensible action, they become pure by relinquishing it, as well as by silent recitation and austerity. (11.192)

Since the twice-born were authorized in the preceding verse, the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" in the phrase "whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire by reprehensible action" is understood to indicate all twice-born persons. Because recitation and austerity are mentioned generally among reprehensible acts, whatever is specifically prescribed for a particular person should be understood as applying to that person. And although both of these [recitation and austerity] are already established [as means of expiation], they are mentioned here for the purpose of relinquishing the wealth. (11.192)
Having recited three thousand repetitions of the Sāvitrī mantra with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
The specific rule regarding the acceptance of improper gifts. 11.193.
When he has returned from his cow-vow, emaciated by fasting and bowing before them, they should ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity? (11.194)
But having spoken the truth before the Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for the cows;
when the ford has been established by the cows, they should perform his formal reception there.
The meaning of these two verses is straightforward. 11.194–195.

Having performed sacrifices for Vrātyas, having performed funeral rites for others, and having practiced malevolent magic (abhicāra) or the Ahīna sacrifice, one is purified by three Kṛcchra penances. || 11.196 ||

The meaning is "of others who are unrelated. And so it has been said: "A disciple, performing the funeral rites for a deceased teacher, becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who consume the food offered to the deceased."

Because of the qualification regarding officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), this statement regarding *abhicāra* (malevolent rites) and *ahīna* (sacrificial sessions lasting more than one day) refers to performing them for the sake of others. It is not, however, a prohibition against performing them for one's own sake. Thus, the revealed scripture (*śruti*) states: "Officiating at an *ahīna* sacrifice is an improper act. And this expiation applies specifically to the performance of malevolent rites against those who should not be subjected to such rites. Accordingly, the performance of malevolent rites against those who may be targeted has been declared: "Speech is indeed the weapon of the Brāhmaṇa; with it, the twice-born man should slay his enemies. (11.196)
Having abandoned one who has come for refuge and having caused the Veda to be corrupted, a twice-born man removes that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.

This being the case, the learned should not abandon one who has sought refuge for the sake of penance; rather, the penance prescribed by the scriptures must indeed be granted to him. Alternatively, "one who has sought refuge" refers to what is well-known in the world, and [the offense applies] in abandoning either that person or both. "Corruption of the Vedas" means teaching those who should not be taught, or providing instruction for the sake of wealth. Thus, another Smṛti states: "Manu declared that those who provide instruction for the sake of wealth are outcasts. (11.197)
One who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals,
as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*,
as well as daily *Śākala* oblations, are the means of purification for those unworthy of sitting in the same row at a meal.

Those unworthy of the company at a meal (*apāṅktya*) include thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, and so forth; as it has been said: "Those who are thieves, outcasts, or eunuchs," and so on. For those acts of theirs for which no expiation has been prescribed—namely, acts that cause one to be excluded from the company at a meal—in cases such as officiating at a sacrifice for a group, this [following] expiation applies. There is no option between this and the previous rule regarding the *śākala-homas*, because the former is stated as being mandatory. (11.198–199)

If one intentionally mounts a camel vehicle or a donkey vehicle, then by the logic of the "stick and cake" (daṇḍāpūpikā), this same penance applies even when there is no interval between the camel and the donkey, or perhaps slightly more.
And having bathed, a Brahmin who is naked becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma). 11.200.
If one has no need for water, or if one is in the midst of water, having touched the body [with earth], then by immersing oneself in water and touching a cow, one becomes pure. (11.201)
And the mention of "water" is for the purpose of bathing according to the prescribed rule.
Upon the omission of obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas, and upon the violation of the vows of a Snātaka, the penance is fasting. (11.202)

If one fails to perform the obligatory principal rites such as the Agnihotra and others, fasting is required; and because they serve different purposes, both the Vedic (śrauta) and Smārta rites are to be combined. Or, it may apply to the omission of subordinate rites (guṇakarma). Furthermore, in the case of violating the vows of a Snātaka, this very penance shall apply when no specific expiation has been prescribed. || 11.202 ||
Having uttered the sound "huṃ" to a Brahmin, or the word "thou" to one who is superior,
he should bathe, fast for the remainder of the day, and seek their favor by offering salutations.
This injunction for a distinguished bath should be understood as being occasional (*naimittikī*), superior to the obligatory (*nitya*) one. || 11.203 ||
Having struck him even with a blade of grass, or having bound him by the neck with a garment,
or having defeated him in a dispute, one should propitiate him by prostrating before him.
And "dispute" (vivāda) should be understood as worldly quarreling, not anything else, because the latter is designated as "debate" (vāda). || 11.204 ||
But by threatening a Brahmin, one enters hell for a hundred years; and by striking him with intent to kill, one enters hell for a thousand years. (11.205)
Not out of jest. || 11.205 ||
As many particles of dust as the blood gathers upon the surface of the earth,
for that many thousands of years shall the perpetrator dwell in hell.
Now, wishing to state the expiation for that act, he says this: "Having threatened [to strike] a Brahmin, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance; in the case of striking him down, an *atikṛcchra*.
One should perform a *kṛcchra* and an *atikṛcchra* after causing blood to flow from a Brahmin. (11.207)

"All" refers to the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, this act—"causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa"—is taught below as causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), because for that offense, the *Kṛcchra* and *Atikṛcchra* penances are prescribed as alternatives. (11.207)
