But for the removal of sins for which no expiation has been stated, one should prescribe an atonement after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin. (11.208)

For the killing of those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), such as Caṇḍālas and others, no expiation has been stated; or rather, no expiation has been stated for killing when it was done for a specific purpose or with permission, or for one who kills a Brāhmaṇa and others for the sake of pleasing the killer by providing weapons and so forth. In these cases, having considered the capacity [of the offender], as well as the gravity or lightness of the sin based on the means used, age, stage of life, physical strength, and the distinction between intentional and unintentional acts—meaning that even in the case of an intentional act, one should prescribe penance according to the persistence of anger and other factors—the assembly (pariṣad) shall consist of at least ten or at least three members; or else, as he will state later, "even a single person learned in the Veda may declare the dharma. (11.208)
I shall describe to you those very means by which a human being may cast off his sins—means practiced by the gods, the seers, and the ancestors. (11.209)

The mention of "human" is intended to include all social classes (*varṇas*); and the mention of "gods" and so forth is for the purpose of praising the means for the destruction of demerit (*adharma*). || 11.209 ||
For three days he should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days he should eat food that has not been asked for;
for the final three days he should not eat at all—this is the Prājāpatya penance performed by a twice-born man. (11.210)
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass, followed by a fast for one night—this is known as the *sāntapana* penance. (11.211)
It is called *kṛcchra* because it is difficult to accomplish, or because of the scriptural statement regarding the *kṛcchra-pratimocana* (expiation through hardship). 11.210–211.
A twice-born man performing the Atikṛcchra penance should eat a single morsel for three periods of three days each as before, and should fast for the final three days. (11.212)
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air, each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed in mind. (11.213)
For one who is self-restrained and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is this penance called Parāka, which removes all sins. (11.214)
And this Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance according to Gautama has thus been described. || 11.212–214 ||
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
touching water at the three times of the day, this is known as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. (11.215)
One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, being self-restrained and beginning with the bright fortnight, should carry out this entire procedure in its entirety during the Yavamadhyama variety. (11.216)
One who practices the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa, being self-controlled and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), should eat eight morsels when the sun has reached its meridian. (11.217)
A composed Brahmin should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set;
this is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
By eating, with a concentrated mind, eighty-three morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in some manner or other for one month, one attains the same world as the Moon. || 11.219 ||
The Rudras, as well as the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Maruts, together with the great seers, observed this vow for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.
He himself should perform the fire-oblation daily with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
he should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness. (11.221)
Three times during the day and three times at night, he should enter the water with his clothes on;
and he should never speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts.
He should pass his time standing or sitting; if unable to do so, he may lie down on the ground.
He should remain celibate and observant of vows, honoring his guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
And he should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory texts according to his ability;
thus, in all vows, he should be diligent for the sake of expiation. (11.224)
The twice-born whose sins have been made public shall be purified by these vows;
but those whose sins are not made public shall be purified by mantras, burnt offerings, and purificatory rites. (11.225)

The seventeen verses concerning purification through *kṛcchra* and other penances have not been explained because their meaning is straightforward. The phrase "in whatever way" (*yathā kathaṃcit*) is a restatement of what has already been introduced; it is not an instruction for a different rule. He will later describe the mantras and oblations for those whose sins have not been disclosed (11.215–225).
By confession, by remorse, by austerity, and by Vedic study, as well as by giving in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from that evil. (11.226)

This verse states the rule for the two expiations consisting of confession (*khyāpanā*) and remorse (*anutāpana*). Such being the case, the mention of austerity (*tapas*) and the other methods here is for the sake of illustration, not for their own sake. Thus, by the phrase "and by giving in times of distress," it is shown that those such as the elderly, women, children, and the sick—who are incapable of performing expiation over a long period—are purified through austerity or giving; and just as they are so purified, they are likewise purified through confession and remorse. This being the case, confession is combined with public expiation by virtue of its inherent capacity, and not alone. Remorse, however, is combined with both. In this regard, there is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) concerning confession. (11.226)
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act, confesses it, to that same extent he is released from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its skin. || 11.227 ||

The person residing in the body is designated by the word "body" due to its location, just as in the case of [referring to] a bed. This is why the self is the locus of merit and demerit; and so it is said: 11.227.
Having committed a sin, one is indeed liberated from that sin by feeling remorse; a person is purified by the resolve, "I shall not do this again," through such abstention. (11.228)
And this being so, it is established that even the cessation [of the act] is a penance, as previously stated. || 11.228 ||
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the arising of the fruits of action after death, he should constantly perform virtuous deeds through his thoughts, speech, and physical form. (11.229)

Both [are required]: cessation and expiation; by the former, there is simply the non-arising of sin in one case, while in the other, there is the destruction of what has already arisen. And since this is so, therefore... 11.229.
Whether through ignorance or knowledge, having performed a censurable deed, one who seeks liberation from it should not perform it a second time. (11.230)
By this he shows that there is purification through the cessation of even unwholesome action committed intentionally, let alone that committed unintentionally. || 11.230 ||
In whatever action he has performed that causes unease in his mind, he should perform penance for it until it becomes a source of satisfaction. (11.231)

The commencement of this [treatise] is for the purpose of practicing expiation according to specific causes; it is to be understood as applying to both cases, the secret and the public. And so it has been said that the clarity of one's inner disposition (*bhāvaprasāda*) is the cause of wholesome action (*kuśalakarma*). (11.231)
All this happiness of gods and men has austerity as its root;
it is declared by the wise that austerity is its middle and austerity its end, according to the vision of the Vedas.

For the gods, the state of being the cause is austerity alone for [the attainment of] the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, as well as for the human enjoyment of sound and other objects, and for the happiness of the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and others. 11.232.
For a Brāhmaṇa, austerity is knowledge; for a Kṣatriya, austerity is protection;
for a Vaiśya, austerity is trade and agriculture; and for a Śūdra, austerity is service. (11.233)

Since this is taught in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*), it is understood that even in matters concerning visible purposes, restraint (*niyama*) is a cause of purification, let alone for those who perform the prescribed penances. Thus, the fact that knowledge is a cause of purification has been stated: "Knowledge, austerity, fire, and food [purify]," and "The intellect is purified by knowledge. And its teaching here for the sake of purification should be understood as referring to that [knowledge] which is already obtained through the context of the subject matter. (11.233)
Sages who have purified their souls, subsisting on fruits, roots, and air,
behold the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving through austerity alone.

They perceive through austerity for the purpose of performing penance (*prāyaścitta*). This praise of penance as penance is to be understood from the force of the context. The same applies to the subsequent verses (11.234).
Medicines, antidotes, sciences, and the various states of the gods—
all these are accomplished through austerity alone, for austerity is their means of achievement.
Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to perform—
all this can be accomplished through austerity, for austerity is indeed hard to surpass.

Calamities caused by the irregularity of planets and constellations are difficult to overcome; likewise, the power of invisibility, possession, and traveling through the air is difficult to attain; and heaven and other such realms are difficult to reach. Furthermore, whatever is difficult to perform—such as drinking the entire ocean or reviving the dead, as accomplished by Agastya, Jamadagni, and others—all that is possible through austerity (*tapas*). Therefore, by the force of what has been stated, this should be understood, according to the context, as a praise of austerity as a means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). (11.235–236)
Even those who have committed great sins, as well as others who have performed forbidden acts, are liberated from that transgression by means of well-performed austerity alone. (11.237)

And for those whose sins have been destroyed, because of the absence of obstacles, the aforementioned perfection is attained through the performance of prescribed duties and austerity for every purpose. Furthermore: 11.237.
Insects, moths, animals, birds,
and even stationary beings go to heaven by the power of austerity.

Insects and moths go to heaven by the power of their austerity through entering fire; beasts, by nourishing and rearing their offspring, and by providing transport, milk, and the like; birds, by rearing their young; and virtuous men, by benefiting others with their own flesh; and stationary beings (plants), by providing benefit through flowers, roots, fruits, shade, and so forth. This is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) in praise of austerity. Alternatively, because they are released from the connection with the karma that caused their birth as insects and so on through expiation (*prāyaścitta*), this is said accordingly. Thus, this is another way of praising expiation. And this being the case... (11.238)
Whatever sin people commit through their mind, speech, or body,
those whose wealth is austerity quickly burn it all away by means of austerity alone.
And because it is only from a Brahmin purified by austerity that the gods accept sacrifices and fulfill their desires. (11.240)

Because it is to be accomplished through rites performed for specific desires, it belongs to those who practice them; therefore, it is right to perform this. And behold this other great power of asceticism!
The Lord Prajāpati created this scripture through austerity alone;
likewise, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity. (11.241)
"If even Prajāpati, when it was his duty to take refuge in austerity, acted thus, how much more so should human beings?"—in this way, its nature as a praise is to be understood. (11.241)
Thus do the gods proclaim the great majesty of austerity,
perceiving the supreme merit of this entire austerity.

From the verse beginning with "All this has austerity as its root" up to this [present] verse, whatever praise is found here refers primarily to the austerity of public penance (*prakāśaprāyaścitta*). Alternatively, starting from the verse "But he whose sin is unmanifested," because of the context of the section on secret penances (*rahasyaprāyaścitta*), that praise is for the austerity of those [secret ones]; or rather, both may apply without contradiction. Or else, the praise of austerity is intended for the destruction of non-virtuous actions performed unconsciously by those established in austerity. (11.242)
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices, and forbearance quickly destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes. (11.243)

Why is the praise of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) appropriate in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*)? Because it should be understood that these [obligatory duties] are also causes for the destruction of sin, and not merely for the sake of spiritual excellence. Others, however, say: "This is the penance for those sins (*enas*) for which no specific penance has been prescribed—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally. Regarding this, he provides an illustration. (11.243)
Just as fire consumes whatever fuel it encounters in an instant by its heat, so does the knower of the Veda burn away all evil with the fire of knowledge. 11.244

It is not merely the study of the Vedas, but rather the knowledge of them as well, for the purification of those who know the meaning of the Vedas. Otherwise, this praise in the section on penances would be purposeless. Others, however, consider this to be a praise of the knowledge required for performing penances; that is incorrect, because the knowledge of the practical application is already implied by the subject matter itself. Therefore, what is to be understood here is a different kind of knowledge, namely the true nature of the deities and so forth. As it has been said: "The knower of the Veda burns away everything. Now, the secret penance is being taught. 11.244.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava, performed day after day, purify even the slayer of an embryo within a month. (11.245)
Having declared [the penance] for killing a Brahmin, he now states the secret [penance] for one who has drunk liquor. 11.245.

Having recited the Kautsa hymn beginning with "apaḥ," the Vasiṣṭha verse beginning with "prati," the Māhendra hymn, and the Śuddhavatī verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified. (11.246)

The Kautsa hymn is that characterized by eight verses beginning with "apa naḥ śośucad agham. The Vāgdaivika is the Vāsiṣṭha hymn beginning with "prati stomair uṣasaṃ vasiṣṭhāḥ. The Māhendra is the hymn of forty-eight verses beginning with "mahām indro ya ojasā"; however, others read it as "Māhitra," reciting this mantra: "māhitrīṇām avo 'stu" and so forth. The Śuddhavatī verses are well known. (11.246)
By reciting the Āsyavāmīya and the Śivasaṃkalpa even once,
one becomes stainless in an instant after having stolen gold.

The hymn characterized by fifty-two verses beginning with "asya vāmasya palitasya hotuḥ" is the Āsyavāmīya; the Śivasankalpa hymn, characterized by six verses beginning with "yaj jāgrato dūram udaiti daivam," is also [to be recited]. And the word "once" (sakṛt) should be understood from the context as meaning that this act of recitation is to be performed every day for a month. For it has been said: "[Even] the killer of a fetus [is purified] within a month. (11.247)
By practicing the *Haviṣpāntīya* and the hymn beginning with "na tam aṃhaḥ," and by reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the Guru's bed is liberated from sin.

The term "monthly" (māsī) and "once" (sakṛt) continue to apply here. "Haviṣpāntam" consists of nineteen verses; "Na tam aṃho na duritam" consists of eight verses; "Iti vā itime manaḥ" consists of twelve verses; and the Pauruṣa Sūkta, beginning with "Sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ," consists of sixteen verses. || 11.248 ||
Desiring the removal of gross and subtle sins, one should mutter for a year the verse beginning with "Having known" (avet) and that which begins with "Whatever this" (yat kiṃcedam). (11.249)

Sins that are minor compared to the great sins (mahāpātaka) are called gross and subtle, such as the secondary sins (upapātaka) and so forth. Desiring to remove these, one should mutter the verse beginning with "ava" for a year: "Ava dvake ava trikā divaś caranti. Others, however, recite the Sāvitrī here instead. And as for the phrase "yat kiṃ cedam," it refers to the hymn beginning with: "yat kiṃ cedaṃ varuṇa daivye jane. 11.249.
Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
The *Taratsamandīya* is well known. || 11.250 ||
But by practicing the *soma-raudra* [hymn] many times for a month, one is purified;
or by performing the ritual bath in a flowing river while reciting the three verses beginning with "aryamṇām. (11.251)

In that context, there are two mantras dedicated to Soma and Rudra: the one dedicated to Rudra is "May we not provoke you, O Rudra, with our prostrations," and the one dedicated to Soma is "Soma flows, the progenitor of thoughts. Regarding these [verses] beginning with "of Aryaman," the mantra is to be sought from the Ṛgveda. (11.251)
One who has committed a sin should mutter the seven verses beginning with "indram" for half a year;
but having performed a blameworthy act, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.

For half a year or six months, one should mutter this group of seven verses beginning with "Indram id gāthino bṛhat," without distinction for any sin whatsoever. But having committed an act of sexual intercourse in water—an act not to be praised—one should subsist on alms for a month while remaining standing.

Having offered clarified butter for a year with the mantras used for the Śakala-homa, a twice-born man destroys even a very heavy sin; or he does so by reciting the verse beginning with "ima". (11.253)

The eight mantras beginning with "devakṛtasyainasaḥ" belong to the Śākala-homa. Having offered clarified butter for a year with these, one destroys even sin; the meaning is that one destroys all mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) as well. Or, having recited for a full year this mantra, "imā rudrāya tavase kapardine kṣayadvīrāya," this act of recitation serves as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in place of the preceding Śākala-mantra offering. Others, however, read: "or having recited the verse beginning with *manaḥ*"; that [verse] should be learned from the learned (*śiṣṭas*), namely: "mano nv āhuvāmahe. (11.253)
One who has committed a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by reciting the Pāvamānī verses for a year while subsisting on alms, he becomes purified.

The *pāvamānya* verses begin with "Sing forth to him, O men" (*upāsmai gāyatā nara*) and extend as far as the verse "He who studies the *pāvamānī*s. And the service of cows, as well as the expiation for killing a cow, has been mentioned; here too, that which remains [of that discussion] should be understood to apply. (11.254)
Or, having recited the Veda-saṃhitā three times in the forest while self-restrained, one who has been purified by three *parāka* penances is released from all sins. (11.255)
"Because of the statement without distinction, [it means] any Vedic collection whatsoever. (11.255)
One who, being self-controlled, fasts for three days and approaches water three times a day, is released from all sins after reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times. || 11.256 ||
And because this expiation is so brief, he says the following in order to encourage those who lack faith:
"Just as the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, removes all sins, so too does the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn remove all sins. (11.257)
Even if he has slain these three worlds and eats food from anywhere at all, a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever. (11.258)
The mention of the *Ṛgveda* may also be intended to indicate the other Vedas; and thus he shows: 11.257–258.
Having recited the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā three times, or the Yajurveda, or the Sāmaveda along with its secret portions, with a concentrated mind, one is liberated from all sins. (11.259)
This praise of him is for the purpose of inciting activity. 11.259.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake perishes,
so does all evil conduct sink away when immersed in the threefold Veda.
And this demonstrates that the purpose of the Veda is threefold. 11.260.
The Ṛg verses, the Yajus formulas, and various other Sāman chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.

The *ṛcas* are well known. The *yajūṃṣi* are those found in the *saṃhitās*, but not those studied in the *brāhmaṇas* accompanied by the *pada* and *krama* recitations. The *sāmans* are of various kinds, such as those belonging to the *grāma-gēya*, the *āraṇya-gēya*, the *arcika*, and the *stobhika*. (11.261)
That which is the primordial Brahman of three syllables, in which the Triple Veda is established—that other secret threefold Veda, he who knows it is a knower of the Veda. 11.262.

That which consists of three syllables is the *oṃkāra*, a collection of the three phonemes (*varṇa*) that constitutes Brahman. He who knows it is a knower of the Veda. And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "Just as by means of a pin [all the leaves are held together]," and so forth. Furthermore, its meditative worship (*upāsanā*) has been described previously; thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*. (11.262)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the Commentary on the Law of Manu, composed by Bhāruci.
The Twelfth Chapter:
O sinless one, you have fully declared this dharma of the four social orders;
now tell us truly and in its highest form the production of the fruits of actions.

[Objection: But surely, because of the mention of the four *varṇas* here, there is an exclusion of the duties of the *āśramas*. [Reply: There is no exclusion; since the *jāti* (birth-status) does not perish and does not depart, the duties of the *āśramas* are indeed included within the duties of the *varṇas*. And having established this, it was said: "The Blessed One [taught] for all *varṇas* duly and in due order," and so forth. The response to this is: "Learn the duties of the *varṇas*. Furthermore, the use of the word "entirety" (*kṛtsna*) here is with reference to the exposition of expiations (*prāyaścitta*), by means of which this Dharmaśāstra becomes the accomplisher of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*). In these three statements, the completion of the unseen human goals is seen: namely, "this is to be done," "this is not to be done," and "if, through delusion, one should ever transgress the prohibitory scriptures on account of unwholesome action, this expiation is to be performed. Here, the completion of the human goal has a visible purpose, like Āyurveda. Therefore, it is correct that he stated the inclusion of the "entirety" with reference to the exposition of expiations, and not what was previously stated: "This fourfold duty of the Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you," and so forth. And the phrase "the production of the fruits of actions" is to be understood primarily with reference to unwholesome duties, by the force of the context, meaning "this [result] occurs when the expiation is not performed. This being the case, this description of the torments in places such as hell—the ripening of unrighteousness (*adharma*) characterized by great misfortune—will be construed as a supplement to the performance of expiations. Since the destruction of merit/demerit can be accomplished by easy means, the instruction on expiation becomes conducive to the human goal. Thus, this verse should be understood as being solely intent upon introducing that [topic]. 12.1.
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire yoga of action."

This is the verse of the thesis. Although the word *karman* is common [to both merit and demerit], it should be understood from the context as primarily signifying unrighteous action (*adharma*). As it was stated previously: || 12.2 ||
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, bears fruit that is auspicious or inauspicious;
the destinies of men—superior, inferior, and middling—are born of action.

Furthermore, action—consisting of volition, speech, and physical movement, and appearing in the form of intention, utterance, and deed—is twofold according to its being wholesome or unwholesome; it is the cause of the various destinies that are distinguished by these two qualities. This being the case, it should be understood that the mention of "dharma" here, following the inclusion of "auspicious," is also part of the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*), albeit by way of indirect implication. (12.3)

One should know that for this embodied being—who possesses these three types [of action], who has three bases, and who is endowed with ten characteristics—it is the mind that is the instigator. (12.4)

It is the impeller of the threefold [action]—whether superior, middling, or inferior; it is the impeller of the three bases, namely those characterized by body, speech, and mind; for by means of it, a person is unable to speak or act with a mind that has not formed an intention. 12.4.
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and adherence to falsehood—this is the threefold mental action. (12.5)

The intent to seize the property of another; another, however, says: "May this also be mine"—this is covetousness regarding the property of others. And this is "paripelava" (frivolity). The desire to kill living beings, which is mentally undesirable; and false dogmatic adherence to such things as the existence of dharma—these are the opposites. And so Vyāsa says:
"Non-covetousness toward the property of others, friendliness toward all beings, and the recollection of the threefold nature of action—that there is a fruit for actions. (12.5)
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every respect, and incoherent prattle—this constitutes the fourfold nature of speech. (12.6)

That which involves a contrary designation of truth and falsehood is called "such-like" (tathākhyā); however, the opposite of this—namely, that which is pleasant, truthful, beneficial, and sacred study—is auspicious. 12.6.
Taking what has not been given, injury caused by improper means, and adultery with another's wife—this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action]. (12.7)

This is unrighteousness (*adharma*), which is the opposite of that which is called righteousness (*dharma*): namely, taking what is not given, lack of protection, and lack of restraint of the senses. This activity, accomplished through mind, speech, and body, is of ten kinds; however, when divided according to the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome, it is of twenty types. Thus, it has been demonstrated in both ways. (12.7)
This person experiences the mental [karma], whether auspicious or inauspicious, by means of the mind itself;
verbal karma through speech, and bodily karma through the body alone. (12.8)

One who causes mental distress to another incurs mental suffering itself; likewise, in the case of verbal misconduct, there is suffering characterized by muteness, stammering, and so forth. This same principle applies to the body as well. Such a demonstration of undesirable results, corresponding to the specific means employed, is intended either to bring about their cessation or for the sake of what follows. (12.8)
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of birds or wild animals; and through those of the mind, to the status of a low-born caste.

In the face of a contradiction with the principles of the scriptures, this is not a demonstration of the relationship between cause and effect; rather, it is a demonstration of the relative gravity or lightness of the threefold unrighteousness mentioned in the preceding verse. It should be understood as intended specifically for the avoidance of the most serious forms of unrighteousness. Alternatively, it may be regarded as a supplement to the section on expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) due to the context. Furthermore, the mention of "deer" is intended to represent all species of lower animals. (12.9)
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and the restraint of body—these three are his; he whose intellect has these under control is called a "triple-staffed" ascetic (tridaṇḍin). 12.10.
The three staffs have indeed these three foundations. || 12.10 ||
Having laid down this triple staff among all living beings and having restrained desire and anger, a person then attains perfection.

The intended meaning is that by casting aside this triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*), having withdrawn it into oneself—that which resides within all beings as the cause of injury—a human being attains perfection (*siddhi*). This [verse] demonstrates the means for withdrawing the triple-staff. The withdrawal of the triple-staff is accomplished through the prior restraint of desire and anger. And because of that withdrawal, one immediately thereafter attains perfection; this is the statement of its fruit. Furthermore, by the use of the term "human" (*mānava*), it shows that the withdrawal of the triple-staff is a duty of man. Now, wishing to demonstrate that person who possesses the qualification for all duties—one who attains perfection through the withdrawal of the triple-staff by means of the restraint of desire and anger—he says this: 12.11.
That which causes this self to act is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
but that which performs the actions is called the elemental self (bhūtātman) by the wise. || 12.12 ||

The knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is the instigator of the activity of this body. Furthermore, the word "self" (ātman) is used figuratively for the body because it exists for the sake of the self. However, that which is called the "body"—a collection of elements characterized by the head, hands, and so forth, consisting of the essence of food—is termed the "elemental self" (bhūtātman), the agent, because it is an effect of the elements. || 12.12 ||
There is another inner self, distinct from the body, known as the *jīva*, which is innate to all embodied beings;
by means of it, one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births. (12.13)

By the instrumental case in the word *yena* ("by which"), there is an instruction regarding the cause; therefore, this must be understood as the mind (*manas*), because it is an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "by the word *jīva*": the term *ātman* (self) is used [here] because until the attainment of liberation and until the final dissolution (*pralaya*), there is no separation from that [mind]. And thus, its status as a cause is indicated by the statement: "by which the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) experiences pleasure and pain. Others say it is the intellect (*buddhi*). Still others say it is the aggregate of the senses, such as hearing and the vital breaths, known as the subtle body (*liṅga*). And in the view that it is the internal organ, there is no disagreement that this is indicated as the instrument for the perception of the Knower of the Field. 12.13.
Both of these—the Great Principle (mahat) and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)—are joined with the elements;
they remain pervading that which resides within high and low beings.

By the word "Great" (mahat), that very internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is understood, which is a synonym for terms such as *liṅga* and so forth. The "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*), however, is the person subject to desire, the enjoyer of pleasure and pain. "In high and low beings" means among those established in a hierarchy of superior and inferior; or, this word *uccāvaca* is a synonym for "many," meaning "among many. "Established in Him"—referring to that Supreme Self who is distinct from the conscious and unconscious and will be described later—means "having pervaded, He abides," that is, He is their support. And thus Vyāsa says:
"There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
The perishable consists of all beings; the one who stands at the peak is called the imperishable."
But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self;
He is the immutable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them. (12.14)
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set in motion all beings, both high and low.

It has been stated that those innumerable forms which constantly impel high and low beings issue forth from the body of that Supreme Self as the Pradhāna. These forms are the effects and causes, the instruments of experience for the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). However, the followers of the Upaniṣads refer to the Supreme Self itself by the word "body. 12.15.
After death, for men who have committed evil deeds, another body certainly arises from those very five elements for the purpose of undergoing torment. 12.16.

From the five mere elements, another gross body capable of undergoing torment arises in the hells and other realms. From what is it different? It is different from the subtle *liṅga* (subtle body). 12.16.
Having experienced those torments in the body by means of that [karmic force],
they dissolve part by part back into those very same elemental constituents.
Having experienced those faults born of attachment to sense objects, which result in future suffering,
he approaches those same two of great splendor with his impurities removed.
The Great One (Mahat) and the Supreme Self (Paramātman). || 12.17–18 ||
Together with him, those two unweariedly perceive his merit and his sin—
by which, when joined with them, he attains what is auspicious or inauspicious both here and after death.
And they, having seen the course of dharma brought about by him. || 12.19 ||
If one practices dharma for the most part and unrighteousness only to a small degree,
one enjoys happiness in heaven, enveloped by those very same elements.
But if one generally practices unrighteousness and righteousness only slightly,
abandoned by those beings, he undergoes the torments of Yama.
Due to the predominance of unrighteousness,
having undergone those torments of Yama, that living being, freed from stain,
returns again to those very five elements, part by part. (12.22)
Furthermore, for the sake of experiencing this body born of karma, those very same five elemental constituents enter it; for without them, the experience of the person is not possible. 12.22.

Having observed this course of the living being by means of one's own mind— that is, by means of a mind refined through the scriptures— one should always fix the mind upon righteousness, both in terms of what is righteous and what is unrighteous. (12.23)

And this section should be understood as supplementary to the rules on expiation (*prāyaścitta*); or rather, it should be understood as supplementary to the entire treatise. For herein, the demonstration of desirable and undesirable fruits serves, by implication, for the avoidance of unrighteousness (*adharma*) and the adoption of righteousness (*dharma*). (12.23)
One should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the Self, by which the Great One (*mahat*) stands pervading all these states without exception. (12.24)

He will state that *sattva* and the other qualities are attributes of the Self (*ātman*), as in "sattva is knowledge, tamas is ignorance," and so forth. Since knowledge and the rest are properties of the *puruṣa*, the status of *sattva* and the others as attributes of the Self is stated with reference to the dharma and adharma under discussion. Others, however, say: although *sattva* and the others are not attributes of the Self, they are called attributes of the Self because they exist for its sake; and here the word "Self" refers to *pradhāna*. (12.24)
Whichever of these qualities predominates entirely within the body at any given time, it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality. (12.25)
Due to the influence of past karma as a basis, for someone at some time there occurs an excess in this regard. || 12.25 ||
Goodness is knowledge, darkness is ignorance, and passion is said to be attachment and aversion.
This is their pervasive nature, which rests within all beings. (12.26)
This is the characteristic of sattva and the other qualities in all living beings.
In that regard, whatever he perceives within himself as associated with joy—tranquil and possessing a pure luster—he should understand that to be the quality of *sattva*. (12.27)
In brief, this engagement in action, which is the activity of sentient beings, is said to be self-cognized. || 12.27 ||
But that which is conjoined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, know that to be passion (rajas), ever carrying away embodied beings without resistance. (12.28)
Here too, the application of the meaning is as before. 12.28.
But that which is joined with delusion, unmanifest, consisting of sense-objects, beyond reasoning, and unknowable—one should understand that to be *tamas*. (12.29)
The functioning of darkness (tamas) is also to be understood as before. || 12.29 ||
And I shall explain in its entirety the arising of the fruit of each of these three qualities— whether it be supreme, middling, or inferior.
The verse of the thesis: 12.30.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses, performance of dharma, and contemplation of the Self—these are the characteristics of the quality of sattva. 12.31.
Delight in undertaking tasks, lack of fortitude, engagement in improper actions, and constant indulgence in sense objects—these are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa). 12.32.
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct,
mendicancy, and negligence— these are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
The arising of the fruit for those beginning with *sattva* is described by these three verses (12.31–33).
Furthermore, for these three qualities residing in the three [states],
this should be known as the summary definition of their characteristics in their respective order.

Whatever action one feels ashamed of after having done it, while doing it, or even intending to do it—that should be known by the wise as entirely characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas). 12.35.
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world,
yet does not grieve over its failure to be accomplished, should be known as rajasic.
That which he desires to know in its entirety, that which he does not feel shame in practicing,
and that by which his own soul is satisfied— this is the characteristic of the qualities of a true being.

Through these four verses, this definition of the qualities—the subject matter of the preceding verses—is stated again for the sake of clarifying the meaning. This very same definition is further expressed in this manner in another way. (12.34–37)
Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
the characteristic of *sattva* is righteousness (*dharma*). Their respective degrees of excellence follow this sequence.
It is indeed due to the qualities [of the elements].
Those qualities by which one enters into these various transmigrations—I shall describe them all in their proper order, in brief. (12.39)
This is the introduction to what is about to be said; it is now being stated: || 12.39 ||
Those characterized by sattva attain the state of gods; those characterized by rajas, the state of humans;
and those characterized by tamas, the state of animals eternally—such is this threefold destiny.
This is a concise description of the destiny characterized by its qualities.
This secondary course of existence is to be understood as threefold and of three kinds—
namely, inferior, intermediate, and superior— according to the distinction between action and knowledge.

Being threefold, it is further divided into three types through application to action and knowledge; even within these nine modes of livelihood, an infinite number of subsistences are conceived solely through the combination of action and knowledge.
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes, reptiles, domestic animals, and wild beasts constitute the lowest state of darkness. (12.42)
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas;
as well as hyenas, tigers, and boars—this is the middling state of darkness (tāmasī gati). || 12.43 ||
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, and hypocritical men,
as well as Rākṣasas and Piśācas— this is the highest destination among those belonging to the quality of darkness (tamas).
Jhallas, mallas, and naṭas, as well as men of evil conduct, and those addicted to gambling and drinking—this is the first state belonging to rajas. (12.45)
Kings, Kṣatriyas, and the domestic priests of kings, as well as those whose primary concern is the science of war, constitute the intermediate Rājasa state. (12.46)
The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are attendants of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases— this is the highest destination among those belonging to the Rajas quality.
Ascetics, renunciants, brahmins, and the hosts of celestial chariot-dwellers,
as well as the lunar mansions and the Daityas— this is the first, the Sāttvika state.
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries, the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second, the sāttvika goal.
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—these, the wise declare, are the supreme state characterized by sattva. || 12.50 ||
The threefold course of each individual quality is proclaimed by nine verses [12.42–50].
Thus has been fully described this entire transmigratory existence, consisting of all elemental beings, which is threefold and of three kinds according to the three types of action.

Those which have not been mentioned here should also be understood as being included within the threefold classification by virtue of their similarity to what has been stated; such is this concluding verse (12.51).
Through attachment to the senses and by not practicing the Dharma, the ignorant and lowest of men go to evil transmigrations. 12.52.

The addiction to the senses, the practice of what is forbidden, the non-practice of dharma, and the failure to perform the duties of the cultured—because of these practices of what is forbidden and the failure to perform the duties of the cultured, those who have not performed expiation become sinful and enter into the cycles of transmigration. For what reason? Because they are ignorant, due to their failure to perform expiation for each transgression. And for this very reason, they are called the lowest of men. In that regard, this section is commenced as a supplement to the performance of expiation, in order to demonstrate the ripening of the karma of those who practice what is forbidden and have not performed expiation. (12.52)
Learn now all that specific womb into which this living soul enters in this world, and by what particular karma, in due order. (12.53)
Having endured terrible hells for many series of years, upon their exhaustion,
those who have committed great sins enter these transmigrations.
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; of a cow, a goat, a sheep, or a wild beast; of a bird; or of a Caṇḍāla or a Pulkasa. (12.55)
A Brahmin who repeatedly drinks liquor [is reborn] among worms, insects, moths, dung-eating creatures, birds, and indeed among predatory beings. 12.56.
A Brahmin who steals [gold] becomes, by the thousands, a spider, a snake, a lizard, aquatic animals, predatory beasts, or Piśācas. (12.57)
The violator of the Guru's bed [is reborn] hundreds of times as grasses, shrubs, and creepers, as well as among carnivorous beasts with fangs, and among those who perform cruel deeds.
Those who eat forbidden food become carnivorous beasts of prey or worms;
those who consort with women of the lowest castes become ghosts; and thieves become beings who kill one another. (12.59)
Having entered into union with outcasts, having approached the wife of another,
and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, men become Brahma-rākṣasas.
Having stolen gems, pearls, corals, and various other jewels out of greed, a man is born among those who work with gold.

By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl; by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing meat, a mongoose; and by stealing ghee, a *svā* (dog).
The vulture [eats] flesh, the cormorant the fat, the oil-drinking bird indeed [eats] oil;
the cricket [eats] salt, and the crane [eats] curd.
By stealing silk, one becomes a partridge; by stealing linen, a frog;
by stealing cotton cloth, a curlew; by stealing a cow, an iguana; and by stealing molasses, a *vāgguda*.
The chuchundarī [eats] auspicious fragrances, while the peacock [eats] leaf-vegetables;
the porcupine [eats] various kinds of prepared food, while the hedgehog [eats] unprepared food.
By stealing fire, one becomes a cricket; by stealing household utensils, a house-builder;
and by stealing dyed garments, one is born as a jīvajīvaka bird.
A wolf [seizes] a deer; a tiger, a horse; a monkey, fruit and roots; a bear, a woman; a cuckoo, water; a camel, vehicles; and a goat, livestock. (12.67)
"Only a small amount of water is to be drunk; the water is for the frog"—in this case, [the word *jala*] is used for the purpose of sprinkling. (12.53–67)
Having forcibly seized any kind of another's property, or having consumed an offering that was not consecrated by sacrifice, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal. (12.68)
Women also who commit theft according to this same method become the wives of these very same creatures. (12.69)
Indeed, when the social classes fall away from their respective duties without reaching the state of an outcaste,
they pass through sinful transmigrations and enter into servitude among bandits.

From this verse beginning with “Through addiction to the senses and by not practicing dharma,” the ripening of the fruit of action characterized by misfortune has been described for those who indulge in what is forbidden and have not performed expiation. Now, the ripening of action characterized by misfortune must be demonstrated for those who have fallen from their own duty through the non-performance of what is prescribed for the disciplined; therefore, this [section] is commenced. (12.68–70)
A Brahmin fallen from his own dharma becomes a *preta* named Ulkāmukha who eats what has been vomited;
a Kṣatriya becomes a *kūṭapūtana* who eats impure matter and corpses. (12.71)
A Vaiśya who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a *preta* named Maitrākṣijyotika, feeding on pus;
and a Śūdra, having fallen from his own dharma, becomes a *preta* clothed in rags.

A *śiṅguruka* is one who wears a fragment of cloth. Since this is so, it has been said: "Therefore, for the sake of purification, one must constantly perform penance (*prāyaścitta*)," lest there be such a long-lasting and undesirable ripening of the fruit of karma for one who has not performed penance—as in the words: "Having reached terrible hells for many groups of years, upon the exhaustion of that [karma]... This [consequence] follows. Now he again touches upon the fruit of the repeated performance of censurable actions. (12.71–72)
In whatever manner those whose nature is directed toward sense-objects indulge in them, in that same manner skillfulness in those very things arises for them. 12.73
Through the repetition of those evil deeds, those of small intelligence encounter sufferings in various births here in this world. (12.74)
Due to the habitual performance of censurable acts, those who have not performed expiation attain such undesirable states as these. (12.73–74)
There is the tossing about in the fierce hells such as Tāmisra,
as well as the forests of sword-leaves and the like, and the binding and cutting.
And various torments indeed, such as being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of burning sand mixed with grit, and the unbearable Kumbhīpāka hells.
And he [experienced] births in various wombs that are mostly full of suffering,
as well as constant afflictions from cold and heat, and manifold fears.
Repeatedly dwelling in the womb, and dreadful birth; painful bondages, and even the state of being a servant to others. (12.78)
The separation from kinsmen and loved ones, as well as dwelling with wicked people; the acquisition and loss of wealth, and the gaining of friends and enemies. || 12.79 ||
And [he saw] old age which is indeed incurable, the affliction by various diseases, those manifold sufferings, and death itself, which is difficult to overcome.
With whatever disposition one performs any particular action, with a body of that same nature one experiences its corresponding fruit. (12.81)

With seven verses, he shows the undesirable fruit [of action]. Whatever action one performs with a disposition that is *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa*—meaning, by means of a body corresponding to that *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa* state—one experiences that respective fruit; that is, one experiences a *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa* result, depending on whether it is a state abounding in *sattva*, *rajas*, or *tamas*. Since this is so—the attainment of undesirable fruits resulting from action abounding in *rajas* and *tamas* due to the cause of unwholesome intentions (*akuśalasaṃkalpa*)—therefore, by avoiding those, one must act with a wholesome intention (*kuśalasaṃkalpa*). (12.75–81)
Thus has been fully described to you the arising of the fruits of actions—
those rooted in wholesome or unwholesome intentions, characterized by the teachings of the scriptures, as well as their opposites, which are characterized by lack of purpose. Now,
learn this action of a Brahmin that brings about the highest good.

By the force of the context concerning penance (*prāyaścitta*), it should be understood that the rule to be described—beginning with the study of the Veda—though intended for the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), also serves to purify the self; for in this way, the context is maintained. Alternatively, in this treatise, the rules pertaining to worldly prosperity (*ābhyudayika*) were stated previously; now, however, learn this ritual action of the Brahmin which brings about the highest good, for the sake of attaining the world of Brahmā or for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*). This being so, just as the Upaniṣads—the secret portions (*rahasya*) spoken in the Brāhmaṇas—are at the end of the Veda for the sake of the highest good, so too these Upaniṣads are prescribed at the end of this Dharmaśāstra for the sake of the highest good. (12.82)
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses,
non-violence, and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good.

Some, however, recite "giving" (*dāna*) in this first quarter [of the verse], while others recite "meditation" (*dhyāna*). In that context, "study of the Vedas" (*vedābhyāsa*) refers to the constant practice of the Veda—including its limbs (*aṅga*), sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), and secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*)—without conflict with obligatory duties (*nityakarman*). By the word "austerity" (*tapas*), the obligatory duties are denoted, as well as the lunar fast (*cāndrāyaṇa*) and other such observances. "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) consists of the contemplation of the deities who are parts of the ritual acts, along with the restraint of the senses, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), and service to the teacher, as previously described. (12.83)
And among all these auspicious actions here, a certain action has been declared to be more conducive to the highest good for a person. (12.84)
This presentation is for the purpose of praising knowledge. || 12.84 ||
And for all of these, knowledge of the Self is remembered as supreme; for that is the foremost of all sciences, since immortality is attained through it. 12.85

This verse is for the purpose of praising self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*). Therefore, it is understood that in the preceding passage there was indeed a mention of knowledge (*jñāna*), not a mention of meditation (*dhyāna*), nor a mention of giving (*dāna*). And self-knowledge is the primordial knowledge of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) as distinct from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and so forth. For when that [knowledge] exists, the qualified person—having realized the true nature of the field and the knower of the field, remaining impartial, having conquered the senses, and having removed all defects—does not identify with sense objects and carries out his duty as prescribed by scripture in its entirety. Because of this, what was stated is appropriate: "For by that, immortality is attained. This includes the realization of the Supreme Self, whether in its collective or individual aspects, according to the Vedānta and Upaniṣads, or the knowledge of the deities who are auxiliary to ritual action; all of this is subsumed under the term "self-knowledge," both by implication and because there is no contradiction. (12.85)
Of these six aforementioned types of action, it should be known that Vedic action is always more conducive to welfare, both in this world and after death.
This is a praise of the previously taught Vedic obligatory rites (*nityakarman*); here, he states the reason for this eulogy. 12.86.
But in the Vedic path of action, all these [stages] without exception are included in their respective ritual injunctions, one after another. (12.87)

The study of the Vedas serves as an auxiliary to the injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*), such as the recitation of hymns (*śastra*), praises (*stotra*), the offering of oblations (*graha*), and officiating at sacrifices. Austerity (*tapas*) consists of the *upasat* vows and other such observances that are limbs of ritual action. Knowledge (*jñāna*) refers to what has been described as the discernment of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña-vijñāna*) and so forth. Restraint of the senses (*indriya-saṃyama*) includes such rules as "one should not eat meat" and "one should not engage in sexual intercourse. Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is exemplified by the rule: "Therefore, on this night, one should not sever the life-breath of any living being. Service to the guru (*gurusevā*) is the attendance upon the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). All of this constitutes Vedic ritual action (*vaidika-karma*). (12.87)
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, consisting of the active and the renunciate.
And this twofold nature of action arises from a distinction in its causes; for that reason, it is said here:

"Action performed with desire, whether in this world or the next, is called *pravṛtta* (active). Even that which is preceded by knowledge is corrupted by [worldly] intention, how much more so that which is preceded by ignorance?"
But that which is free from desire and preceded by knowledge is taught as the path of cessation (nivṛtti). || 12.89 ||

And here, since knowledge is taught in relation to the cessation of action, it follows by implication that the intention born of ignorance is the cause for engagement in action. Now, [the text] teaches the difference in results arising from these two distinct causes, further demonstrating their twofold nature. 12.89.
By practicing active karma, one attains equality of power with the gods;
but by practicing the path of cessation, one indeed transcends the five elements.

He becomes subtle, having either the body of air or the body of space. Thus it has been said: "Having become like air and possessing his own form, he attains that supreme Brahman. Alternatively, he teaches this liberation by means of another method through the expression "transcending the five elements. Now, this is commenced for the purpose of praising meditation or knowledge:
"Seeing the Self equally in all beings and all beings in the Self..."
The meaning is that he perceives the Supreme Self through equanimity, seeing all beings as his own self.

An "ātmayājī" (sacrificer to the Self) is one who has desisted from ritual action and possesses supreme self-restraint. By means of this higher discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), the result is stated: "Thus disciplined."
He attains self-sovereignty. || 12.91 ||

By means of the state of being a "self-sacrificer" (ātmayājin) as described and taught in the Śruti, one becomes fit for liberation; one becomes independent in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) and is no longer subject to the bondage of karma and afflictions (kleśa). Furthermore, this discernment (prasaṃkhyāna), when free from the grasp of passion and aversion, leads to liberation. Alternatively, this verse may be intended as a praise of self-restraint (saṃyama). As for the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna), it has already been refined in the preceding section. Or rather, because both purposes are possible, it applies to both places. (12.91)
Having abandoned even those duties as they have been described, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, in tranquility, and in the study of the Vedas.

The statement that one should "abandon even the aforementioned duties" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to extol the knowledge of the Self, tranquility, and the practice of the Vedas. For there can be no abandonment of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) by one's own will; however, their abandonment according to the scriptures is occasional, as in the case of the *Puruṣamedha* sacrifice and others, where they are not performed. This triad [of knowledge, tranquility, and Vedic study] refers to those persons who are ineligible for such rites in the absence of those [obligatory duties]. 12.92.
For this is the complete equipment for the birth of a Brāhmaṇa, especially so;
by the use of the word "especially," it is not so for the Kṣatriya or the Vaiśya.
Having attained this, the twice-born indeed becomes one who has accomplished his duty, and not otherwise. (12.93)
This is a concluding verse of praise for the six Vedic duties, beginning with the study of the Vedas, which pertain to those who are qualified. 12.93.
The Veda is the eternal eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
it is inconceivable and immeasurable—such is the established nature of the Vedic scripture.

The Veda is the eye for the person entitled to perform rites, in order to establish the existence of the ancestors, the gods, and human beings, and so that they may become constituent parts of ritual action. It is called an "eye" because, like an eye, its purpose is vision. Since the ancestors partake only of what is offered by Vedic injunctions, the Veda is said to be their eye. Furthermore, it is inconceivable because it is not of human origin, and the Vedic scripture is immeasurable in terms of its results. Therefore... 12.94.
Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—all those are fruitless after death, for they are said to result in darkness. (12.95)

Those *smṛtis* which are outside the Veda—meaning those *āgamas*—originate from human perspectives. Whatever erroneous views (*kudṛṣṭis*) exist within their respective scriptures, all of them are fruitless after death because they prescribe actions that contradict the qualification for the higher realms. Since dharma is rooted in qualification, and because that qualification is absent, those *smṛtis* are declared to be grounded in darkness (*tamas*). And because... (12.95)
Whatever other things there may be besides these, which arise and pass away, they are fruitless and false because they belong to the past. (12.96)

Therefore, the Veda alone is independent in its instruction, being free from reliance on anything else, and because it further conforms to the authoritative scriptures (*pramāṇa-śāstra*). The Dharmaśāstra has that [Veda] as its source, but other works of that kind do not; they are human compositions designated by the names of their authors. And since this is so, therefore... (12.96)
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life in their distinctness—the past, the present, and the future—all these are established from the Veda. (12.97)

The fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*) has existed in the past; from where? From this present cycle of four ages (*caturyuga*). The present fourfold caste system is the subject under discussion, and that which will be in the future is likewise the same—namely, that which exists in the coming cycle of four ages. Alternatively, this reference to the three periods of time regarding the fourfold caste system is made with respect to a divine cycle of four ages, or with respect to a *kalpa* of Brahmā. It is established through the Veda alone, and not from any other source, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), because its nature is that of a scripture (*śāstra*). He demonstrates this: just as when the state of being an animal is common to cows, buffaloes, horses, and so forth, the distinction between their species is inferred solely from the observation of specific individual forms and structures; in the same way, there is no inference for a distinction between the species of Brāhmaṇas and the others despite their common humanity, by which a distinction of species among them could be perceived through inference. This being the case, the fourfold caste system is defined solely by scripture, such as: "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires," and so forth. And thus it has been said: "Among all castes who are equal... and so forth. This example is cited based on the fact that the *Smṛti* restates the meaning of the Veda. This being so, what the author of the scripture stated—that everything is established from the Veda—is logical. Alternatively, this statement—"the fourfold caste system... is established from the Veda"—is made with reference to the qualification (*adhikāra*) for those [castes]. In this way, the three worlds—which are the destinations (*gati*) of the fruits of actions—and the four stages of life (*āśrama*) are to be explained as before. The neuter gender in the words "past," "present," and "future" is used in view of the neuter gender of the word *cāturvarṇya*; elsewhere, however, it is to be understood as an illustration, since [the word] is masculine. (12.97)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are established through the Veda alone, by virtue of their origin, qualities, and functions. (12.98)

For those things such as sound (*śabda*) and the rest—which, in realms such as heaven, consist of bodies and objects of sense, and serve as causes for excellent and desired enjoyments—are established through the Veda alone, not from other systems of philosophy (*darśana*) such as the words of the Buddha and others. Is this direct? No; rather, it is through the production of qualities and actions (*guṇakarma*). "Production" means for the sake of [the manifestation of] qualities and actions. Through the production of qualities and actions—that is, for the sake of producing the aforementioned sounds and so forth—there is also the action of quality (*guṇakarma*) which assists the person (*puruṣa*). Thus there is worldly renown: "What quality (*guṇa*) has assisted me? meaning what service (*upakāra*)? It is for the sake of quality, that is, for the sake of the desired human goal (*puruṣārtha*). "Action" refers to that called *dharma*. By which *dharma* alone assists the person, and not *adharma*; for the sake of specifying that, this mention of "qualities and actions" is made. This being so, the Veda is not the direct cause of sound and the rest; rather, by way of the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra*, it exists for the sake of producing sound and the rest through the action of quality known as *dharma*. And thus, the Veda is not the direct cause of the production of sound and the rest, but rather through the mediation of *dharma*. This praise of the Veda is to be understood by implication (*sāmarthya*) in this other manner. Alternatively, sound and the rest are established through the Veda alone, because the production—that is, the arising—of qualities and actions, namely *dharma*, [proceeds] from the Veda. From the Veda comes *dharma*; and from *dharma* come sound and the rest in realms such as heaven. Therefore, this is said: "They are established through *dharma* alone. Or else, this is the third reading of the fourth quarter of this verse: "They are established through the Veda alone, from the production of qualities and actions. Why? From the Veda. But the meaning is exactly as taught immediately above. (12.98)
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of a living being's purpose.

And thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "The oblation is offered into the fire; that fire causes it to go to the sun; the sun rains it down by means of its rays; through that, food comes into being; from food arises the birth and sustenance of living beings"—so it is known. And here too it has been stated: "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun," and so forth. Therefore, I consider this [treatise] to be supreme for accomplishing the goals of man, because it is the instruction in dharma for this living being; for this reason [it is composed]. 12.99

One who is learned in the Vedic scriptures is worthy of the command of an army, the sovereignty of a kingdom, the leadership of the administration of justice, and even the lordship over all the worlds.
In some way or another, he praises the Veda by virtue of the context; here he states the reason for this. 12.100.
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees, so does one who knows the Vedas burn away the faults of his own actions. 12.101
For this reason,
one who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the scriptures, regardless of which stage of life he dwells in, becomes fit for union with Brahman even while remaining in this very world. 12.102

Those who possess the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them are better than those who merely possess the texts; those who possess knowledge are superior to those who merely retain them; and those who act with resolve are superior to those who merely possess knowledge. (12.103)

Those who uphold the texts are "the upholders" (*dhāriṇaḥ*). Here, the elision of the first member of the compound should be understood, as in *satyabhāmā* for *bhāmā*, or *devadatta* for *datta*. Those who possess knowledge are superior to those who merely uphold [the texts], because they partake of a greater fruit due to a particular excellence of effort. Those who are resolute—those who perform ritual actions—are superior to those who possess knowledge. This is because: || 12.102–103 ||
"Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good.
This states the purpose of their combined application:
"By austerity one destroys impurity; by knowledge one attains immortality. (12.104)

Through austerity (*tapas*) one destroys impurity (*kalmaṣa*). It was stated previously that by the word "austerity" the obligatory rites (*nitya-karmāṇi*), both those based on the Vedas (*śrauta*) and those based on tradition (*smārta*), are meant; by the performance of those obligatory rites, one destroys impurity. And so it has been said in the section on expiation (*prāyaścitta*): "The daily study of the Veda according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), and forbearance—these quickly purify even sins born of the greatest transgressions (*mahāpātaka*). Through knowledge (*vidyā*)—that is, through the realization of the Supreme Self and so forth, as stated previously in the context—it one attains immortality (*amṛta*). This summarizes the previously taught combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action, because they are not mutually contradictory. "One attains immortality" means that one reaches liberation (*mokṣa*) or the state of Brahman (*brahmatva*). (12.104)
Perception, inference, and the scripture consisting of various traditions—these three must be thoroughly understood by one who desires purity in dharma. (12.105)

The purification of *dharma* is not achieved through perception (*pratyakṣa*), but through inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*), because the instruction of that [perception] is for the sake of purifying inference. Since inference is preceded by that [perception], it is supplementary to scripture. Furthermore, perception is indeed accepted in some cases; for, according to this view, since it is supplementary to both, the mention of perception is appropriate. Inference also has scripture as its object. This being so, reasoning (*tarka*) is the reality of perception and inference, while the treatise (*śāstra*) consists of various scriptures. The Veda has many branches: "The Ṛgveda has twenty-one branches, the Yajurveda has one hundred, and the Sāmaveda has a thousand paths. Alternatively, the treatise consists of various scriptures, namely the *Dharmaśāstra* with its many branches; or else, because they are not in conflict, both are included under the names of *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. Now, he explains the purpose of the cognition of the reality of inference. (12.105)
He who examines the instruction on dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures—he, and no other, knows dharma. (12.106)

The *ārṣa* (the words of the seers) is so called because it is uncreated (*akṛtaka*). The teaching of Dharma is *smṛti*. Thus, this is called the *Dharmaśāstra*. These two [the Veda and the Smṛti] must not contradict the Vedic scriptures; and by the mention of the "Veda," the inclusion of the *Smṛti* is also understood here by implication, even though it is not explicitly stated, because the Śruti depends upon it. Its non-mention, however, is due to the fear of breaking the meter. This being the case, the expression "not contradicting the Vedic and Smṛti scriptures" is justified. Alternatively, the mention of the "Veda" is for the sake of illustration, as the Smṛti is also primary. Furthermore, that reasoning (*tarka*) is of two kinds, which is why he qualifies it as "not contradicting the Vedic and scriptural teachings. He who investigates with reasoning when there is doubt, contradiction, or suspicion of redundancy—he knows the Dharma, not the mere logician. Thus says the *Itihāsa*: "My dear, do you not serve those Brāhmaṇas who are Lokāyatikas? For these fools, who consider themselves wise, are skilled only in what is harmful. Or [it may mean] "mere scripture. And thus is the verse of Vyāsa, repeating the words of Bhīmasena:
"O King, like that of a dull-witted and small-minded Vedic scholar, your intellect is destroyed by mere rote recitation; it does not perceive subtle meanings. Thus [he spoke].

And thus, this very [verse] defines, by way of implication, that what is called *nyāyānumāna* (logical inference) is, in the ultimate sense, *tarka* (reasoning) that is not in contradiction with the Vedic scriptures. Therefore, anything else that contradicts them is *nyāyānumāna* that is merely a semblance of reasoning (*tarkābhāsa*). Accordingly, an example of a semblance of reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*) was stated in the passage: "of the inconceivable and the immeasurable. Nor is there here an exclusion of other means of valid cognition such as comparison (*upamāna*), because they are included within *tarka* and *āgama* (scriptural tradition) as appropriate. By the word *ārṣa*, the *mantras* are understood. Thus, in the work of Śaunaka, he shows the *mantras* of the seers (*ārṣa*): "This is the *ārṣa* of Vasiṣṭha; this is the *ārṣa* of Viśvāmitra. The *Brāhmaṇa* portion, however, consists of the instruction on *dharma*. The rest is the same. Alternatively, the meaning is stated according to another reading: "But he who investigates the *ārṣa* instruction on *dharma* by means of reasoning that does not contradict the *Smṛti* scriptures, he knows *dharma*, and no other. This meaning is more appropriate because it occurs in the context of the *Smṛti*. In this view, the mention of "not contradicting the Veda" includes the *Veda* because it depends on the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of both *mantra* and *Brāhmaṇa*. Consequently, it is also logical in the view that the *Smṛti* possesses independence. Furthermore, it is especially so in the view that [the *Smṛti*] originates from the indicative marks of *mantra* and *Brāhmaṇa*, and in the case of recollecting the meaning of lost branches of the Veda. Thus, in all three interpretations of the verse, this is a praise of *nyāya*, because its purpose is the thorough adoption (*saṃparigraha*) of that [reasoning]. And the thorough adoption of *nyāya*, together with the exposition of the scriptural teachings (*āgama-śāstra*), should serve for the purification of *dharma*. And thus the *Śruti* is known: "The gods went from this world to that world. Having seen them, they said, 'How shall we become non-*ārṣa*? [They gave] *karma* to the seer (*ṛṣi*) for these [gods]. Therefore, whatever a learned Brāhmaṇa reasons upon becomes *ārṣa*. Hence, the thorough adoption of *tarka* that does not contradict the *Veda* and the *Smṛti* scriptures is justified. Now, in order to clarify that purpose, and wishing to show the purpose of the instruction on *nyāya* from the subsequent section, he says this: [Verse 12.106]
This action leading to the supreme good has been explained in its entirety; now the secret of this treatise on the Laws of Manu is being taught. 12.107.
He respectfully inclines the listeners toward hearing the meaning of the subsequent section. 12.107.
If it should be asked how one should act regarding those dharmas that have not been specifically prescribed, whatever learned Brahmins may declare, that shall be the dharma, free from doubt. (12.108)

Regarding those duties whose characteristics for expiation have not been recorded or taught, as well as others, there is by implication a twofold tradition that has not been recorded: both with texts and without texts. Alternatively, the fact that it has not been recorded consists in the non-observation of such a twofold tradition. When a doubt arises as to what should be done regarding duties that have not been recorded—that is, are unknown—he says this: "That which the learned (śiṣṭas) declare shall be the law, free from doubt. This means that they harbor no hostility toward anything, whether it be recorded or unrecorded. And having established this, it was said: "And the conduct of the virtuous. He now states the definition of a learned Brāhmaṇa. 12.108.
Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been mastered in accordance with the Dharma,
are to be known as cultured Brahmins, whose authority is based on both revelation and direct perception.

"With its supplements" (*saparibṛṃhaṇaḥ*) means together with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*). Alternatively, the Veda is said to be "with its supplements" when accompanied by its ancillaries, namely the *Mīmāṃsā*, the *Nyāyavistara*, the *Dharmaśāstra*, and the *Purāṇas*. And when explained in this way, the inclusion of the [six] treatises (*prakaraṇa*) is accomplished, as well as the inclusion of the various branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) through the mention of the *Mīmāṃsā* and so forth. In the absence of that... (12.109)
Whatever dharma another assembly of ten, or even three, who are established in virtuous conduct, might determine, one should not call that into question. 12.110
He shows this:

"One who possesses the threefold knowledge, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma, and the first three stages of life—this assembly shall consist of at least ten members. (12.111)

By the term *traividyas* (those learned in the three Vedas), those who have studied the three Vedas are meant. A *hetuka* is one who, though learned in the three Vedas, is also a student of the science of logic (*tarka-śāstra*) that does not contradict scripture and reason. A *tarkī* is one who, though not a *hetuka*, possesses such intuitive power (*pratibhāna*) that he can infer and exclude [faults], and who, even without having studied the science of logic, naturally adheres to what is right according to principle. A *nairukta* is one who specializes in etymology alone. A *dharmapāṭhaka* is one who recites the Dharma, even if he is not of the aforementioned types. The "three stages of life" (*traya āśramiṇaḥ*) refers to the first three—householders and so forth—excluding the wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*). Others, however, following the reading of Gautama—"the student, the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller"—include the ascetic (*tāpasa*) as the third, because of the prohibition against an ascetic entering a village. When there is doubt regarding the Dharma, ten persons who are neither hostile nor partial, being knowers of the scriptures, become authoritative; thus it has been stated as a general characteristic of all Smṛtis: "practiced by the wise and the virtuous," and so forth. Alternatively, he states these very same categories collectively as a triad. (12.111)

One who knows the Rigveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Samaveda—this assembly of at least three members is to be recognized for the resolution of doubts concerning dharma. (12.112)

These aforementioned individuals, who have reached the further shore of the fourteen branches of knowledge and have attained the characteristics of the learned, are spoken of as being threefold; or else, it refers to one endowed with those very characteristics. 12.112

Even if he is alone, whatever dharma a most excellent twice-born man who knows the Vedas determines should be known as the supreme dharma; it is not [dharma] proclaimed by tens of thousands of the ignorant.
The deprecatory explanatory passage regarding the ignorant is intended for their desistance. 12.113.
Among those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist on their birth alone—even if they have gathered by the thousands—the status of an assembly does not exist. (12.114)
Now, in order to refute their instruction on the Dharma, he states the fault: || 12.114 ||
