Whatever those who are shrouded in darkness, the fools who do not know the Dharma, proclaim as such, that sin becomes tenfold and follows after those speakers. (12.115)
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
the Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.

This concluding verse pertains to those actions, such as the study of the Vedas and so forth, which lead to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Accordingly, some maintain that it was stated for the purpose of prohibiting their impairment: "Learn this rule of action leading to the supreme good for a Brahmin" (MDh 12.82). We, however, declare that this is intended as a summary of the entirety of Dharma, because from this point onward no purely secular duties (*kevaladharma*) will be taught. This is confirmed by the immediately following verse (12.115–116).
Thus that Blessed Lord, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
has told me all this, the supreme secret of the Dharma.

The venerable Bhṛgu spoke thus to his disciples who were listening: "And so, this very matter is recorded in the first chapter of the exposition of the Dharmaśāstra, concerning which it is said: 'This Bhṛgu will proclaim to you this treatise in its entirety; for this sage has learned all of this from me in its fullness. (MDh 1.59)

If this is the summary of all dharmas, then for what purpose are the subsequent verses? They are for the purpose of the meditation (*upāsanā*) upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Accordingly, what follows will deal exclusively with the inner self (*adhyātma*), and no further dharmas will be taught, as they have already been stated. This being the case, the preceding verse serves as a summary of all the dharmas mentioned therein, but not of the entire treatise (*śāstra*). The treatise, however, will subsequently summarize its subject matter—the Supreme Self—along with the means of meditation and the inner self:
"The twice-born who recites this treatise of Manu, proclaimed by Bhrigu..."

"He becomes possessed of right conduct always and shall attain his desired goal" (MDh 12.126). This secret of Dharma is not only what has been stated in the summary of Dharma beginning with "Thus that Blessed Lord, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds," and so forth; rather, this other secret of Dharma concerning the Supreme Self, consisting of its enumeration and taking the form of meditation on the inner self (adhyātma-upāsana), is now being declared. (12.117)
One who is composed should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within the self;
for by perceiving everything within the self, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness.

Some say that this "discernment" (*prasaṃkhyāna*) concerning the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field), which takes the form of internal meditation (*adhyātmopāsanā*), is a secret doctrine of Dharma. This is not so, because it would be contradictory; for [the author] will later state: "The ruler of all," and so forth. Therefore, this mention of the "Self" (*ātman*) must be understood as referring exclusively to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). We shall demonstrate this accordingly. Now, let us explain the verse. Whatever he will say—both "being" (*sat*) and "non-being" (*asat*)—that is called the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) together with its modifications, comprising both the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*). "In the Self" (*ātmani*) means in the Supreme Self, the reality of all the Upanishads of every Vedic branch. Some hold that it is "superimposed" (*adhyasta*) and established upon Him, depending on whether one adopts the view of distinct functions subordinate to Him or the view of non-difference through identity with His essence. "One should perceive" (*saṃpaśyet*) means "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*). How so? Just as we have stated. Thus, the root *paś* should be understood in the sense of meditation. Its qualification is "composed" (*samāhita*): one should perceive with a composed mind through faith, conviction, or the restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*). This is either a commendatory statement regarding the result (*phalārthavāda*) or an injunction regarding the result (*phalavidhi*): "For perceiving everything in the Self, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness," meaning one perceives all this as being the Supreme Self. And because... (12.118)
The self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the self.
For the self indeed produces the connection to action for these embodied beings. (12.119)

The meaning is that for this reason the Supreme Self alone is the deity, and all [deities] such as the Vasus are established within the self (adhyātma), the elements (adhibhūta), the deities (adhidaivata), and the sacrifice (adhiyajña). And therefore, it follows that one should see everything as abiding in the Self. By this term "abiding in the Self," only the position of difference (bheda-pakṣa) is understood, not the position of non-difference (abheda-pakṣa). Such being the case, any statement regarding non-difference here is treated as a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda), because it contradicts both scripture and logical reasoning. This being so, the Supreme Self alone, abiding in each respective deity who is a constituent part of the ritual, produces the connection with action (karmayoga) through the functions of receiving (saṃpradāna-kāraka) and being the object (karman) of actions such as giving. For whom? For these embodied beings who are authorized in the duties prescribed by the scriptures, whether they pertain to the primary goal or other matters. Thus, this is understood as an explanatory praise (arthavāda) for the rule concerning those authorized. Now, he shows the yoga of meditation concerning the Supreme Self—which pertains to the internal self—by means of an external summary. 12.119.
One should place space within the cavities, wind within movement and touch,
the supreme fire within digestion and sight, water within moisture, and earth within solid forms.

One should establish the space within the spaces; one should establish the external space—known as that which pertains to the deities and the elements—within the internal spaces by means of meditation through the demonstration of identity with the deity. In this same way, it should be understood that one should establish the external air within the internal functions of movement and touch. Likewise, in the case of the bodily functions of digestion and vision, the phrase "one should establish the supreme light"—of what is it the supreme? Of the air, according to the instruction—should be supplied everywhere. Regarding the internal moisture, one should establish the waters; since the waters being established are the object of the action, they are indicated here in the accusative case as "the waters" (*apaḥ*). And [one should establish] the earth among the material forms; thus it is in every instance. (12.120)
One should meditate on the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the stride, Hara in strength, Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation.
Thus, while all internal [elements] and so forth are established as distinct deities, [the reality] remains undivided. 12.121
One should know the Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, radiant like gold, and attainable through the mind in deep sleep. 12.122
One does not [identify] the transmigrating self as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). And so it is in all the Vedas, the Upaniṣads, and the Yoga treatises. Vyāsa also said thus:
"But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them."

The Ruler of all those who hold authority in every state, even including Brahmā and the others. To this effect, a Brāhmaṇa passage should be cited, beginning with: "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable One... Furthermore, the phrase "smaller than the small" demonstrates the supreme subtlety of the Supreme Self compared to other transmigrating souls. By the description "having the luster of gold," its purity is expressed. Thus, in the Rahasyabrāhmaṇa of the Vājasaneyins' Upaniṣad, it says: "He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death; having known that very Self... The phrase "accessible to the dream-consciousness" is intended to establish its true nature. For just as in the state of deep sleep, the reality of the transmigrating soul exists in a peaceful form where specific karma, afflictions, pleasure, and pain have subsided, so too can this reality of the Supreme Self be understood by the mind through the "dream-consciousness" as being eternally of such a nature. Therefore it is said: "One should know the Supreme Person as accessible to the dream-consciousness. Its "supremacy" is stated here in relation to other persons. Likewise, it has been repeatedly illustrated as the object of superimposition, and as the Supreme Self existing within the established distinctions of the deities who are parts of ritual action. (12.122)
Some call him Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati; some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman. (12.123)

Thus, this Brahman, established as the presiding principle over all deities, is attained even by one who worships deities such as Agni and the rest. Accordingly, the *Agnirahasya* Brāhmaṇa of the Vājasaneyins states: "The Adhvaryus worship Him as Agni," and so forth. Furthermore, at the end of that section, it clearly demonstrates this point: "In whatever way they worship Him, that very thing He becomes; having become that, He protects them. Therefore, one should worship Him in this manner through all these [forms]," and so on. And because: 12.123.
Pervading all beings with his five forms known as the great elements, he is eternally subject to birth, growth, and decay through the exhaustion of his own karma and afflictions.
It causes living beings to revolve like a wheel.

Or for the enjoyment of that [state]. It is understood that he is the controller of all horses. Now, demonstrating the conclusion of the aforementioned yoga of meditation, he declares this fruit of it: 12.124.
Thus, he who perceives the Self as established in all beings,
But having seen for themselves by their own selves that which was taught by the Self, they practice it throughout their lives according to the instruction.
Having attained complete equanimity, he reaches the supreme state of Brahmā.

This rule regarding the fruit is to be understood through both scripture and reasoning; it is not a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of the fruit. Having thus concluded this fruit of the yoga of the supreme self, of *prasaṃkhyāna*, and of meditation (*upāsana*), the scripture now concludes [the work]. 12.125.
Thus, by reciting this Mānava Śāstra proclaimed by Bhṛgu, a twice-born man becomes eternally possessed of right conduct and shall attain his desired goal.

For one who is awakened by the scripture necessarily becomes possessed of right conduct even if they were not previously disciplined, let alone one who is already disciplined; for it is observed in the world that when a cause exists, its fruit necessarily follows, and through the performance of that [cause], the attainment of desired objects occurs. (12.126)
[Thus ends the Commentary on the Treatise of Manu composed by Bhāruci.]
